data.title: Phase IIb dose-ranging study of the oral JAK inhibitor tofacitinib (CP-690,550) or adalimumab monotherapy versus placebo in patients with active rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To compare the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of 5 doses of oral tofacitinib (CP-690,550) or adalimumab monotherapy with placebo for the treatment of active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in patients with an inadequate response to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.
METHODS
In this 24-week, double-blind, phase IIb study, patients with RA (n = 384) were randomized to receive placebo, tofacitinib at 1, 3, 5, 10, or 15 mg administered orally twice a day, or adalimumab at 40 mg injected subcutaneously every 2 weeks (total of 6 injections) followed by oral tofacitinib at 5 mg twice a day for 12 weeks. The primary end point was the responder rate according to the American College of Rheumatology 20% improvement criteria (ACR20) at week 12.
RESULTS
Treatment with tofacitinib at a dose of ≥3 mg twice a day resulted in a rapid response with significant efficacy when compared to placebo, as indicated by the primary end point (ACR20 response at week 12), achieved in 39.2% (3 mg; P ≤ 0.05), 59.2% (5 mg; P < 0.0001), 70.5% (10 mg; P < 0.0001), and 71.9% (15 mg; P < 0.0001) in the tofacitinib group and 35.9% of patients in the adalimumab group (P = 0.105), compared with 22.0% of patients receiving placebo. Improvements were sustained at week 24, according to the ACR20, ACR50, and ACR70 response rates as well as classifications of remission according to the 3-variable Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) using C-reactive protein and the 4-variable DAS28 using the erythrocyte sedimentation rate. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) in patients across all tofacitinib treatment arms (n = 272) were urinary tract infection (7.7%), diarrhea (4.8%), headache (4.8%), and bronchitis (4.8%).
CONCLUSION
Tofacitinib monotherapy at ≥3 mg twice a day was efficacious in the treatment of patients with active RA over 24 weeks and demonstrated a manageable safety profile.

data.title: Benefit-risk analysis of upadacitinib versus adalimumab in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and higher or lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Evaluate the risks and benefits of upadacitinib 15 mg vs adalimumab in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate based on cardiovascular (CV) risk.
METHODS
In SELECT-COMPARE, patients received upadacitinib 15 mg, placebo or adalimumab 40 mg every other week, with background methotrexate. This post hoc analysis assessed patients with lower (age <65 years; no CV risk factors) and higher CV risk (age ≥65 years and/or ≥1 CV risk factor). Safety and efficacy outcomes were compared between upadacitinib and adalimumab over the short term (~6 months) and long term (5 years) based on CV risk.
RESULTS
The study included 211 lower-risk patients (upadacitinib, n=129; adalimumab, n=82) and 767 higher-risk patients (upadacitinib, n=522; adalimumab, n=245). Rates of malignancy excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC), major adverse cardiovascular event and venous thromboembolism were comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab in both risk groups but numerically higher in the higher-risk group. Upadacitinib showed higher rates of herpes zoster versus adalimumab in both risk groups and numerically higher rates of serious infection and NMSC in the higher-risk group. Upadacitinib demonstrated consistently better efficacy outcomes, including 28-joint Disease Activity Score (C reactive protein) <2.6, Clinical Disease Activity Index remission and Boolean remission at 6 months, which were generally maintained through 5 years.
CONCLUSIONS
Regardless of baseline CV risk, upadacitinib demonstrated comparable safety to adalimumab, except for higher rates of herpes zoster in both CV risk groups and NMSC and serious infections in the higher-risk group. Upadacitinib consistently showed better clinical and functional outcomes than adalimumab. The benefit-risk profile of upadacitinib in RA patients was favourable, independent of CV risk category, in both short and long term.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) who have an inadequate response to methotrexate (MTX), JAK inhibitors (notably upadacitinib and tofacitinib) demonstrate comparable or lower rates of serious infections and consistently better or equal rates of sustained clinical remission or low disease activity compared with TNF inhibitors (particularly adalimumab), based on head-to-head and comparative randomized trials and long-term follow-up.

# Evidence on Sustained Clinical Remission and Low Disease Activity

- In SELECT-COMPARE, a phase 3 RCT, upadacitinib 15 mg daily provided superior clinical responses versus placebo and was noninferior to, and in several domains superior to, adalimumab at week 12 (ACR20 71% vs 36% placebo; DAS28-CRP <2.6 29% vs 6% placebo), with continued advantages at week 26 in achieving low disease activity or remission compared with both placebo and adalimumab (P ≤ 0.001) while inhibiting radiographic progression. Serious infections up to week 26 were comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab, and overall safety was generally similar, with higher herpes zoster and CPK elevations reported with upadacitinib and higher discontinuations and serious AEs with adalimumab. <cite id="31287230">In SELECT-COMPARE, upadacitinib 15 mg daily improved signs, symptoms, and function versus placebo and was superior to adalimumab on several endpoints at week 12, with more patients achieving low disease activity or remission at week 26 than with placebo or adalimumab; radiographic progression was inhibited; serious infections up to week 26 were comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab, while discontinuations and serious AEs were higher with adalimumab and herpes zoster and CPK elevations were more frequent with upadacitinib.</cite>

- Over 3 years in the SELECT-COMPARE long-term extension, upadacitinib maintained numerically better clinical responses than adalimumab across endpoints, including low disease activity and remission, with generally comparable rates of serious infections and other safety outcomes; upadacitinib showed higher rates of herpes zoster and certain laboratory/adverse effects but similar rates of serious infections, malignancies (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer), major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, and deaths. <cite id="35121639">At 3 years, upadacitinib continued to show numerically better clinical responses than adalimumab across endpoints including low disease activity and remission, with generally comparable rates of adverse events, serious infections, malignancies (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer), major adverse cardiac events, venous thromboembolism, and deaths; herpes zoster, lymphopenia, hepatic disorder, and CPK elevations occurred more often with upadacitinib.</cite>

- In a post hoc analysis stratified by cardiovascular risk, upadacitinib demonstrated consistently better efficacy outcomes than adalimumab at 6 months (DAS28-CRP <2.6, CDAI remission, Boolean remission), which were maintained through 5 years, with similar overall safety and comparable rates of serious infections between upadacitinib and adalimumab in both low- and high-risk groups. <cite id="40461266">Regardless of baseline cardiovascular risk, upadacitinib showed comparable safety to adalimumab, with higher herpes zoster rates and numerically higher serious infections and nonmelanoma skin cancer in the higher-risk group; efficacy outcomes at 6 months (DAS28-CRP <2.6, CDAI remission, Boolean remission) were better with upadacitinib and were generally maintained through 5 years.</cite>

- Tofacitinib in a phase IIb study outperformed adalimumab on ACR20 at week 12 (tofacitinib ≥3 mg twice daily: 59–72% achieving ACR20 vs 35.9% with adalimumab; 39.2% with 3 mg, P ≤ 0.05), with sustained improvements at week 24 including ACR50/70 and DAS28-defined remission, indicating that JAK inhibition can achieve deeper and more durable responses than TNF monotherapy in MTX-inadequate responders. <cite id="21952978">Tofacitinib at ≥3 mg twice daily achieved significantly higher ACR20 (59–72% vs 35.9% with adalimumab; 39.2% with 3 mg, P ≤ 0.05) and sustained improvements at week 24, including ACR50/70 and DAS28-defined remission, outperforming adalimumab.</cite>

# Safety: Rates of Serious Infections

- In SELECT-COMPARE, serious infections up to week 26 were comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab, whereas discontinuations due to adverse events and overall serious AEs were more frequent with adalimumab; upadacitinib had higher rates of herpes zoster but similar rates of other serious infections. <cite id="31287230">In SELECT-COMPARE, serious infections up to week 26 were comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab, while serious adverse events and discontinuations were higher with adalimumab; upadacitinib had higher herpes zoster rates.</cite>

- In the 3-year SELECT-COMPARE LTE, serious infections remained broadly comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab, with no significant differences in malignancy (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer), major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, or deaths; higher-risk patients had numerically higher rates of these events, but not necessarily higher absolute infection rates versus TNF inhibitors. <cite id="35121639">Over 3 years, rates of serious infections and other safety outcomes (malignancies excluding NMSC, major adverse cardiac events, venous thromboembolism, deaths) were generally comparable between upadacitinib and adalimumab; efficacy advantages persisted with upadacitinib.</cite>

- In the benefit–risk post hoc analysis, upadacitinib had similar overall safety to adalimumab, with higher herpes zoster rates and numerically higher serious infections and nonmelanoma skin cancer specifically in higher-risk patients, suggesting no clear infection signal versus TNF inhibitors overall, but a trade-off of more herpes zoster with potential excess in higher-risk subgroups. <cite id="40461266">Upadacitinib showed comparable overall safety to adalimumab, with higher herpes zoster rates in both risk groups and numerically higher serious infections and nonmelanoma skin cancer in higher-risk patients, while efficacy remained superior.</cite>

# Interpretation and Practical Takeaways

- Remission/low disease activity: Across randomized trials, JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) achieve higher rates of ACR and DAS28-defined remission/low disease activity than TNF monotherapy (adalimumab) in MTX-inadequate RA, with these advantages maintained over multiyear follow-up. <cite id="31287230,21952978,35121639,40461266">JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) achieved superior or equal clinical responses to adalimumab in RA with MTX inadequate response, including higher rates of remission/low disease activity, with benefits maintained through multiyear follow-up.</cite>

- Serious infections: JAK inhibitors did not show higher overall rates of serious infections than TNF inhibitors in head-to-head RCTs or long-term extensions; in some analyses, TNF inhibitors had higher rates of serious AEs and discontinuations, while JAK inhibitors had more herpes zoster, which may reflect vaccine-related or reactivation patterns rather than a broad infection increase. <cite id="31287230,35121639,40461266">Serious infections were generally comparable between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors, with higher discontinuations/serious AEs noted for TNF therapy and higher herpes zoster rates for JAK inhibitors.</cite>

- Overall: For RA patients inadequately controlled on methotrexate, JAK inhibitors provide superior or comparable efficacy toward sustained remission/low disease activity relative to TNF inhibitors, with similar rates of serious infections and a distinct adverse effect profile (more herpes zoster but fewer discontinuations), making them a reasonable alternative when TNF inhibitors are ineffective or poorly tolerated. <cite id="31287230,35121639,40461266,21952978">JAK inhibitors offer superior efficacy toward remission/low disease activity versus TNF inhibitors in MTX-inadequate RA, with similar serious infection rates and a different adverse effect profile (more herpes zoster but fewer discontinuations), supporting their use as an alternative to TNF inhibitors when response is inadequate.</cite>

<snippet id="35946801">Title: The challenge of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis descriptive epidemiology: to estimate low incidence rates across complex phenotypes in different geographic areas.
Authors: Logroscino, Giancarlo, Urso, Daniele, Tortelli, Rosanna | Year: 2022 | Journal: Current opinion in neurology
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare progressive neurodegenerative disease of motor neurons with a fatal outcome. The rareness of the disease and the rapidly fatal course are the main challenges for the ALS epidemiological research. The understanding of ALS has clearly advanced in the recent years both in the genetics and in the leading pathways of disease determinants. Epidemiological research has played a primary role in these discoveries.
RECENT FINDINGS
Epidemiological studies have shown a variation of incidence, mortality and prevalence of ALS between geographical areas and different populations, supporting the notion that genetic factors, linked to populations' ancestries, along with environmental and lifestyle factors, play a significant role in the occurrence of the disease. The burden of motor neuron diseases is increasing and currently more relevant in high-income countries but increasing at the highest rate in low and middle-income countries. The ALS phenotype is not restricted to motor functions. C9orf72 repeat expansion seems to present a recognizable phenotype characterized by earlier disease onset, the presence of cognitive and behavioural impairment.
SUMMARY
Population-based disease registries have played a major role in developing new knowledge on ALS, in characterizing genotype-phenotype correlations, in discovering new genetic modifiers and finally in planning research and health services, considering the high cost of motor neuron disease care. Epidemiological research based on multicentre international collaboration is essential to provide new data on ALS, especially in some regions of the world with poor data.</snippet>
<snippet id="29659621">Title: Referral bias in ALS epidemiological studies.
Authors: Logroscino, Giancarlo, Marin, Benoit, Piccininni, Marco et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: PloS one
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Despite concerns about the representativeness of patients from ALS tertiary centers as compared to the ALS general population, the extent of referral bias in clinical studies remains largely unknown. Using data from EURALS consortium we aimed to assess nature, extent and impact of referral bias.
METHODS
Four European ALS population-based registries located in Ireland, Piedmont, Puglia, Italy, and Limousin, France, covering 50 million person-years, participated. Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder affecting upper and lower motor neurons. Due to its rarity and rapidly progressive nature, studying the epidemiology of ALS is challenging, and a comprehensive picture of the global burden of this disease is lacking. The objective of this systematic review was to describe the global incidence and prevalence of ALS.
METHODS
We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Global Health, PsycInfo, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL to identify articles published between January 1, 2010, and May 6, 2021. data.title: The challenge of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis descriptive epidemiology: to estimate low incidence rates across complex phenotypes in different geographic areas.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare progressive neurodegenerative disease of motor neurons with a fatal outcome. The rareness of the disease and the rapidly fatal course are the main challenges for the ALS epidemiological research. The understanding of ALS has clearly advanced in the recent years both in the genetics and in the leading pathways of disease determinants. Epidemiological research has played a primary role in these discoveries.
RECENT FINDINGS
Epidemiological studies have shown a variation of incidence, mortality and prevalence of ALS between geographical areas and different populations, supporting the notion that genetic factors, linked to populations' ancestries, along with environmental and lifestyle factors, play a significant role in the occurrence of the disease. The burden of motor neuron diseases is increasing and currently more relevant in high-income countries but increasing at the highest rate in low and middle-income countries. The ALS phenotype is not restricted to motor functions. C9orf72 repeat expansion seems to present a recognizable phenotype characterized by earlier disease onset, the presence of cognitive and behavioural impairment.
SUMMARY
Population-based disease registries have played a major role in developing new knowledge on ALS, in characterizing genotype-phenotype correlations, in discovering new genetic modifiers and finally in planning research and health services, considering the high cost of motor neuron disease care. Epidemiological research based on multicentre international collaboration is essential to provide new data on ALS, especially in some regions of the world with poor data.

data.title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Descriptive Epidemiology: The Origin of Geographic Difference.
data.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) epidemiology has rapidly developed in the last 30 years alongside the evolving changes in concepts in the field of clinical ALS and also due to the recent proposals of new classification system for motor neuron diseases. Many of these changes in the clinical scenario have been determined through the results of ALS population-based studies conducted in the last 20 years primarily in Europe. All the evidences converge to show that ALS risk is different across continents and ethnicities. In a European registry consortium named EURALS, ALS incident cases were drawn from a source population comprising almost 24 million people across Europe (ALS cases: 1028) and the estimated incidence was 2.2 per 100,000 person-years (py) for the general population. In contrast, other population-based studies have measured the lowest incidence in East Asia to be 0.89 per 100,000 py and in South Asia to be 0.79 per 100,000 py. A large part of Africa, Latin America and Asia does not have any population-based studies. The origin of geographic difference in ALS incidence is a matter of debate. Probably, this is partly due to genes (C9ORF72) and partly due to environmental risk factors. The rapid disappearance of ALS Foci in Guam, Kii, and West Guinea underline the importance of changes in lifestyle and environmental factors. The Global Burden of Disease, a project aiming to describe the burden of all diseases and injuries across all the countries of the world with a standardized protocol, has collected heterogeneous sources of data to estimate the burden of motor neuron diseases. The demographic changes related to increased expectation of life and the growth of the world population indicate that the load of motor neuron disease is rapidly moving toward 400 thousand prevalent cases. The burden is expected to shift toward Asia and Africa in the next decades for the rapid increase of expectation of life of countries with high demographic impact.

# Key Epidemiologic Patterns of ALS: Incidence/Prevalence by Region and Effects of Age, Sex, and Ancestry

## Global and Regional Incidence and Prevalence
- A recent systematic review of population-based studies reported that ALS incidence varies widely worldwide, ranging from 0.26 per 100,000 person‑years in Ecuador to 23.46 per 100,000 person‑years in Japan, while point prevalence ranges from 1.57 per 100,000 in Iran to 11.80 per 100,000 in the United States. These differences reflect heterogeneous case ascertainment and the absence of registries in many regions, leading to gaps and variability in estimates. <cite id="37308302">Incidence ranged from 0.26 per 100,000 person-years in Ecuador to 23.46 per 100,000 person-years in Japan, and point prevalence ranged from 1.57 per 100,000 in Iran to 11.80 per 100,000 in the United States; variability reflects gaps in registry coverage</cite>
- European population‑based registries (EURALS consortium) estimate an incidence of about 2.2 per 100,000 person‑years across much of Europe, with evidence that risk differs by continent and ethnicity. <cite id="30602169">A European registry consortium (EURALS) estimated incidence at 2.2 per 100,000 person‑years and showed that ALS risk differs across continents and ethnicities</cite>
- Regional examples illustrate substantial heterogeneity:
  - Lombardy, Italy: standardized incidence rate of 2.09 per 100,000 person‑years (2.43 in men; 1.76 in women), rising up to ages 65–74, stable over time, and moderate geographic variation across provinces. <cite id="17210896">In Lombardy, the standardized incidence rate was 2.09 per 100,000/year (2.43 in men; 1.76 in women), peaked in 65–74 years, was stable over time, and varied moderately across provinces</cite>
  - Southern Germany (Swabia): age‑standardized incidence around 2.5 per 100,000 person‑years, with capture‑recapture suggesting about 18.9% of cases were missing in the registry (estimated true ASR ≈ 3.1 per 100,000). <cite id="24722455">In Southern Germany, the age-standardized incidence was 2.5 per 100,000 person-years, and capture-recapture estimated 18.9% missing cases (ASR ≈ 3.1 per 100,000)</cite>
  - United States (Chicago–Detroit cohort): combined crude incidence 1.44–1.73 per 100,000 person‑years (2009–2011), with notable survival differences by race/ethnicity. <cite id="36200180">In the Chicago and Detroit cohort, crude incidence was 1.44, 1.53, and 1.73 per 100,000 person-years (2009–2011)</cite>

- A broader synthesis emphasizes that incidence and prevalence are higher and rising most rapidly in high‑income regions, while many parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia lack population‑based data, creating uncertainty about true burden in these regions. <cite id="35946801">The burden of motor neuron disease is increasing and more relevant in high-income countries but rising fastest in low and middle-income countries; many regions lack population-based data</cite> <cite id="30602169">Large parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia lack population-based studies, and risk differs by continent and ethnicity</cite>

## Age, Sex, and Ancestry Effects
- Age: Incidence rises with age, with many registries showing a peak in middle to late adulthood (e.g., Lombardy peak at 65–74 years; Swabia mean age at onset ~64–66 years). <cite id="17210896">Incidence rose up to ages 65–74 years in Lombardy</cite> <cite id="24722455">Mean age at onset was 63.8 years in men and 66.0 in women, with age distribution peaking at 70–74 years</cite>
- Sex: Multiple population‑based cohorts show a male predominance in incidence (e.g., Lombardy: 2.43 in men vs 1.76 in women; Swabia overall gender ratio 1.1:1, with male‑predominant spinal‑onset ALS). <cite id="17210896">Incidence was higher in men than women overall (2.43 vs 1.76) and for definite ALS subtypes</cite> <cite id="24722455">The gender ratio was 1.1:1 overall, and incidence was higher in men for spinal-onset and definite ALS</cite>
- Ancestry and geography: Population‑based evidence indicates lower incidence in East and South Asia (≈0.89–0.79 per 100,000 person‑years) and higher incidence in parts of Europe and Japan, with genetic risk (notably C9ORF72) and ancestry linked to differences. <cite id="37308302">Incidence was lowest in East Asia (0.89 per 100,000 person-years) and South Asia (0.79 per 100,000 person-years)</cite> <cite id="35946801">Variation in incidence and prevalence across regions supports roles for ancestry-linked genetic factors and environmental/lifestyle factors</cite> <cite id="30602169">Risk differs across continents and ethnicities, with C9ORF72 and environmental factors implicated</cite>

## Phenotype, Onset Site, and Referral Bias
- Onset site and phenotype influence incidence patterns; for example, bulbar vs spinal onset differ by sex and survival, and C9ORF72 expansion is associated with earlier onset and cognitive/behavioral features. <cite id="17210896">Bulbar vs spinal onset showed different incidence patterns by sex and survival; bulbar-onset ALS had lower incidence than spinal-onset</cite> <cite id="35946801">C9orf72 repeat expansion is associated with earlier onset and cognitive/behavioral impairment</cite>
- Referral bias can distort epidemiologic inferences: patients referred to tertiary centers are younger, less likely to have bulbar onset, more likely to have familial antecedents, and have longer survival than registry‑ascertained populations in the same regions. <cite id="29659621">Tertiary-center cohorts showed younger age, lower bulbar onset, higher familial antecedents, and longer survival compared with regional registry populations; comparison with local registries helps quantify referral bias</cite>

## Temporal Trends and Survival
- Short‑term temporal clustering was not evident in some large registries (e.g., Lombardy 1998–2002 showed no clusters over 5 years), though long‑term secular trends require longer follow‑up. <cite id="17210896">No temporal and geographic clusters were detected over a 5-year period in Lombardy</cite>
- Survival varies by demographics and diagnosis timing; in the Chicago–Detroit cohort, median survival was 2.2 years, with 30% surviving ≥5 years, and longer survival among women and non‑Whites (with exceptions in younger age groups). <cite id="36200180">Median survival was 2.2 years, 30% survived ≥5 years; female PALS and those with longer time from onset to diagnosis had longer survival, and nonwhites had longer survival than whites except in younger categories</cite>

## Data Gaps and Implications
- Many regions (especially parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia) lack population‑based registries, leading to uncertain prevalence/incidence and potential misestimation of global burden as life expectancy rises and populations age. <cite id="35946801">The burden is increasing and shifting toward low- and middle-income countries; the ALS phenotype burden is rising most rapidly there</cite> <cite id="30602169">Large parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia lack population-based studies, limiting accurate burden estimates</cite>
- Methodological care is needed to reduce referral bias and improve ascertainment (e.g., linking tertiary-center data with population registries), and to standardize definitions across studies. <cite id="29659621">Referral bias affects cohorts from tertiary centers; comparison with local registries improves ascertainment and interpretation</cite> <cite id="37308302">Variability in estimates underscores the need for robust, standardized population-based data</cite>

## Summary
- Incidence typically ranges from roughly 0.7–3 per 100,000 person‑years across well‑ascertained registries, with higher rates in Europe and Japan and lower rates in parts of East and South Asia; prevalence reflects case duration and survival, with point prevalence estimates up to roughly 12 per 100,000 in high‑income regions. <cite id="37308302">Incidence ranges from 0.26 to 23.46 per 100,000 person-years globally, with point prevalence from 1.57 to 11.80 per 100,000</cite> <cite id="30602169">European incidence around 2.2 per 100,000 person-years contrasts with lower incidence in East and South Asia</cite> <cite id="24722455">Southern Germany shows ~2.5 per 100,000 incidence with substantial ascertainment completeness</cite> <cite id="17210896">Lombardy shows ~2.09 per 100,000 incidence with male predominance and age peak 65–74</cite>
- Risk is influenced by age (rising incidence with age), sex (male predominance in many cohorts), and ancestry (with lower incidence in East/South Asia and higher risk signals in Europe/Japan; C9ORF72 and environmental exposures likely contribute). <cite id="17210896">Age-specific and sex-specific incidence increases, with higher rates in men</cite> <cite id="24722455">Overall male-to-female ratio ~1.1:1 and higher spinal-onset incidence in men</cite> <cite id="37308302">Incidence differences by region suggest roles for genetic and environmental factors</cite> <cite id="30602169">Risk differs across continents and ethnicities, implicating C9ORF72 and environmental risk</cite>
- Regional examples and cohort data highlight the need for improved ascertainment and standardized surveillance to accurately map ALS incidence, prevalence, and risk factors across geographies. <cite id="29659621">Referral bias can bias epidemiologic inferences; local registries improve representativeness</cite> <cite id="37308302">Global variability and gaps in registry coverage limit precise burden estimates</cite>

<snippet id="32945632">Title: Avelumab Maintenance Therapy for Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
Authors: Powles, Thomas, Park, Se Hoon, Voog, Eric et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Platinum-based chemotherapy is standard-of-care first-line treatment for advanced urothelial carcinoma. However, progression-free survival and overall survival are limited by chemotherapy resistance.
METHODS
In a phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer who did not have disease progression with first-line chemotherapy (four to six cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin) to receive best supportive care with or without maintenance avelumab. The primary end point was overall survival, assessed among all patients who underwent randomization (overall population) and among those with tumors positive for programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Secondary end points included progression-free survival and safety.
RESULTS
Among all 700 patients who underwent randomization, the addition of maintenance avelumab to best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival as compared with best supportive care alone (control). Overall survival at 1 year was 71.3% in the avelumab group and 58.4% in the control group (median overall survival, 21.4 months vs. 14.3 months; hazard ratio for death, 0.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.56 to 0.86; P = 0.001). Avelumab also significantly prolonged overall survival in the PD-L1-positive population; overall survival at 1 year was 79.1% in the avelumab group and 60.4% in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.79; P<0.001). The median progression-free survival was 3.7 months in the avelumab group and 2.0 months in the control group in the overall population (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.75) and 5.7 months and 2.1 months, respectively, in the PD-L1-positive population (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.43 to 0.73). The incidence of adverse events from any cause was 98.0% in the avelumab group and 77.7% in the control group; the incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 47.4% and 25.2%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
Maintenance avelumab plus best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival, as compared with best supportive care alone, among patients with urothelial cancer who had disease that had not progressed with first-line chemotherapy. (Funded by Pfizer and Merck [Darmstadt, Germany]; JAVELIN Bladder 100 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02603432.).</snippet>
<snippet id="37071838">Title: Avelumab First-Line Maintenance for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Results From the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Trial After ≥2 Years of Follow-Up.
Authors: Powles, Thomas, Park, Se Hoon, Caserta, Claudia et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: Clinical trials frequently include multiple end points that mature at different times. The initial report, typically based on the primary end point, may be published when key planned coprimary or secondary analyses are not yet available. Clinical Trial Updates provide an opportunity to disseminate additional results from studies, published in JCO or elsewhere, for which the primary end point has already been reported. Initial results from the phase III JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02603432) showed that avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance plus best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) versus BSC alone in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma (aUC) who were progression-free after 1L platinum-containing chemotherapy. Avelumab 1L maintenance treatment is now a standard of care for aUC. Here, we report updated data with ≥ 2 years of follow-up in all patients, including OS (primary end point), PFS, safety, and additional novel analyses. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive avelumab plus BSC (n = 350) or BSC alone (n = 350). At data cutoff (June 4, 2021), median follow-up was 38.0 months and 39.6 months, respectively; 67 patients (19.5%) had received ≥2 years of avelumab treatment. OS remained longer with avelumab plus BSC versus BSC alone in all patients (hazard ratio, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.63 to 0.91]; 2-sided P = .0036). Investigator-assessed PFS analyses also favored avelumab. Longer-term safety was consistent with previous analyses; no new safety signals were identified with longer treatment duration. In conclusion, longer-term follow-up continues to show clinically meaningful efficacy benefits with avelumab 1L maintenance plus BSC versus BSC alone in patients with aUC. An interactive visualization of data reported in this article is available.</snippet>
<snippet id="38702396">Title: The evolving treatment landscape of metastatic urothelial cancer.
Authors: Roviello, Giandomenico, Santoni, Matteo, Sonpavde, Guru P et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Nature reviews. Urology
Abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is currently the first-line standard of care for patients with metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC); however, up to 50% of patients are ineligible for cisplatin, necessitating alternative treatment options. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been shown to be effective in cisplatin-ineligible patients. However, despite advances in the first-line setting, the prognosis remains poor, and challenges persist in selecting optimal therapies, treatment sequences and combination regimens. Maintenance therapy with avelumab revealed improved overall (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) compared with best supportive care alone in patients with platinum-responsive mUC. Antibody-drug conjugates and targeted therapy with fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitors have shown promise in selected patients, particularly in patients with metastatic disease that has progressed despite platinum-based chemotherapy. At the European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in 2023, groundbreaking results were presented from two phase III trials, EV-302/KEYNOTE-A39 and CheckMate 901, focusing on previously untreated mUC. In the former, the combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab showed significant improvements in OS, PFS and overall response rate compared with chemotherapy alone; the combination of nivolumab with gemcitabine-cisplatin chemotherapy demonstrated a significant extension in median OS, PFS and overall response rate compared with chemotherapy alone. In addition, erdafitinib therapy resulted in significantly longer OS than chemotherapy among patients with mUC and FGFR alterations after previous treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors. This comprehensive summary of the current treatment landscape for mUC incorporates clinical trial evidence and discussion of agents that are currently under investigation to provide support for clinical decision making and understanding of future therapeutic approaches.</snippet>
<snippet id="38994180">Title: Switch Maintenance Therapy for Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
Authors: Ahmed, Ramsha, Gupta, Shilpa | Year: 2022 | Journal: Bladder cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
While switch maintenance therapy is being increasingly investigated in solid tumors, it is a standard in only a few. We conducted a systematic review on switch maintenance therapy for metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION
In this systematic review, we conducted a literature search in PubMed and Cochrane databases up to 2021, based on PRISMA statement guidelines. One hundred and fifty eight articles were identified and after a three-step selection process and six articles, using different agents were included in evidence synthesis. The primary end points were effect on overall survival, progression free survival, safety and tolerability.
EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS
In the pre-immunotherapy era, targeted therapies like sunitinib, lapatinib and vinflunine were studied as switch maintenance therapy in metastatic urothelial carcinoma but did not show any overall survival benefit. Use of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents have shown promise as switch maintenance therapy; pembrolizumab showed improvement in progression free survival in a phase 2 trial and avelumab showed improvement in overall survival and progression free survival in the phase 3 JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial.
CONCLUSION
Immunotherapy with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents has emerged as an effective switch maintenance strategy in patients with metastatic urothelial carcinoma. Intensification of the immunotherapy backbone in this setting can potentially further enhance outcomes. Emerging evidence shows a potential role of Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors in this setting as well. Results from ongoing and planned studies will help us understand which switch maintenance approaches would be most effective for improving outcomes in metastatic urothelial carcinoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="37677821">Title: Avelumab First-Line Maintenance Therapy: Managing Patients With Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma.
Authors: Lapuente, Maria, Conway, Dawn, Wood, Laura S et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Clinical journal of oncology nursing
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The phase 3 of JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial demonstrated that avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance in addition to best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival compared to best supportive care alone. It is now the standard of care for platinum-eligible patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma that has not progressed with 1L platinum-containing chemotherapy.

This article provides considerations for oncology nurses to effectively implement avelumab 1L maintenance treatment in the clinical setting.
METHODS
This article reviews clinical evidence and implications for oncology nurses caring for patients receiving avelumab 1L maintenance treatment.
FINDINGS
Oncology nurses can provide comprehensive care for patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma and ensure the safe and appropriate use of avelumab 1L maintenance treatment by educating patients and caregivers, ensuring correct administration, and promptly recognizing and managing immune-related adverse events.</snippet>

<snippet id="40318950">Title: Avelumab First-line Maintenance for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Long-term Analyses of Patient-reported Outcomes and Quality-adjusted Time Without Symptoms or Toxicity from the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Trial.
Authors: Grivas, Petros, Aragon-Ching, Jeanny B, Bellmunt, Joaquim et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: European urology oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
In JAVELIN Bladder 100, avelumab first-line maintenance plus best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival versus BSC alone, with no detrimental impact on quality of life (QOL), in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma without progression following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. We report long-term analyses of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in patients treated with avelumab (any duration or ≥12 mo) and a post hoc analysis comparing quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity (Q-TWiST) between arms.
METHODS
PROs were assessed using National Comprehensive Cancer Network/Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy Bladder Symptom Index-18 (FBlSI-18) and EuroQol 5-level EQ-5D (EQ-5D-5L). Q-TWiST was calculated as the utility-weighted sum of mean time in three health states: time with all-cause grade 3/4 toxicity prior to progression, time without grade 3/4 toxicity or symptoms of progression, and time after progression.
KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS
In the overall avelumab plus BSC arm (n = 350) and the subgroup treated for ≥12 mo (n = 118), completion rates for PRO assessments during treatment were >80%. FBlSI-18 total and EQ-5D-5L index scores remained stable throughout 24 mo of treatment, with no clinically important changes from baseline. The mean Q-TWiST was 18.46 mo with avelumab plus BSC versus 15.13 mo with BSC alone (22% relative improvement). Limitations include open-label trial design and small patient numbers at later cycles.
CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
Patients receiving avelumab had preserved health-related QOL and control of cancer-related symptoms with manageable toxicity, further supporting avelumab first-line maintenance as the recommended treatment for advanced urothelial carcinoma not progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="37794707">Title: Case-control matching-guided exposure-efficacy relationship for avelumab in patients with urothelial carcinoma.
Authors: Soltantabar, Pooneh, Alhadab, Ali, Hibma, Jennifer et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: CPT: pharmacometrics & systems pharmacology
Abstract: Exposure-response (E-R) analyses are an integral component of understanding the benefit/risk profile of novel oncology therapeutics. These analyses are typically conducted using data from the treatment arm to characterize the relationship between drug exposure (low vs. high) and efficacy or safety outcomes. For example, outcomes of patients with lower exposure in the treatment arm (e.g., Q1) might be compared to outcomes of those with higher drug exposure (Q2, Q3, and Q4). Outcomes from the lowest exposure quartile may be also compared to the control arm to evaluate whether the Q1 subgroup derived clinical benefit. However, the sample size and the distribution of patient baseline characteristics and disease risk factors are not balanced in such a comparison (Q1 vs. control), which may bias the analysis and causal interpretation of clinical benefit in the Q1 subgroup. Herein, we report the use of case-control matching to account for this bias and better understand the E-R relationship for avelumab in urothelial carcinoma, a PD-L1 inhibitor approved for the treatment of several cancers. Data from JAVELIN-100 was utilized which is a phase III study of avelumab in first-line maintenance treatment in patients with urothelial carcinoma; this clinical study demonstrated superiority of avelumab versus best-supportive care leading to approval in the United States, Europe, and other countries. A post hoc case-control matching method was implemented to compare the efficacy outcome between Q1 avelumab subgroup and matched patients extracted from the control arm with similar baseline characteristics, which showed a clinically relevant difference in overall survival in favor of the Q1 avelumab subgroup. This analysis demonstrates the importance of accounting for imbalance in important baseline covariates when comparing efficacy outcomes between subgroups within the treatment arm versus the control arm.</snippet>

<snippet id="40451703">Title: Avelumab and taxol chemotherapy in platinum-refractory or ineligible metastatic urothelial carcinoma (AVETAX trial).
Authors: Garje, Rohan, Ravindra, Aditya, Rahim, Bilal et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Urologic oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
This study investigates the role of taxanes and immunotherapy for inoperable advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma in patients unable to tolerate or refractory to platinum-based regimens. We aimed to determine the safety and estimate the efficacy of a combination of avelumab and docetaxel in treating advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
METHODS
This phase 1b, single-arm, open-label clinical trial involved adults with advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, progressing during or after platinum-containing chemotherapy, within 12 months of neoadjuvant or adjuvant platinum-containing chemotherapy, or ineligible for platinum regimens. Primary objectives were determining the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of docetaxel with avelumab and estimating efficacy via the objective response rate (ORR). In Phase I, docetaxel (45, 60, 75 mg/m²) was combined with 10 mg/kg avelumab every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by avelumab biweekly as maintenance. The expansion cohort received treatment at the MTD of 75 mg/m² docetaxel with 10 mg/kg of avelumab.

Twenty-one patients with advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma were studied: 8 cisplatin-refractory and 13 cisplatin-ineligible. The 75 mg/m² dose of docetaxel with 10 mg/kg avelumab was safe, with 1 dose-limiting toxicity (neutropenic fever). The ORR was 52.4% (95% CI: 29.8%-74.3%). Median progression-free survival and overall survival were 14.6 months (95% CI: 2.8-15.8) and 16.6 months (95% CI: 13.2-not reached), respectively.

The combination of avelumab and docetaxel shows favorable safety and efficacy in treating advanced or metastatic bladder cancer.

<snippet id="37121850">Title: Avelumab First-line Maintenance Therapy for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Comprehensive Clinical Subgroup Analyses from the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Phase 3 Trial.
Authors: Grivas, Petros, Park, Se Hoon, Voog, Eric et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: European urology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In the phase 3 JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial, avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance + best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) versus BSC alone in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma (aUC) who were progression-free following 1L platinum-based chemotherapy, leading to regulatory approval in various countries.
OBJECTIVE
To analyze clinically relevant subgroups from JAVELIN Bladder 100.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
Patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic UC without progression on 1L gemcitabine + cisplatin or carboplatin were randomized to receive avelumab + BSC (n = 350) or BSC alone (n = 350). Median follow-up was >19 mo in both arms (data cutoff October 21, 2019). This trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT02603432.
OUTCOME MEASUREMENTS AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
OS (primary endpoint) and PFS were analyzed in protocol-specified and post hoc subgroups using the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS AND LIMITATIONS
Hazard ratios (HRs) for OS with avelumab + BSC versus BSC alone were <1.0 across all subgroups examined, including patients treated with 1L cisplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50-0.93) or carboplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46-0.90), patients with PD-L1 + tumors treated with carboplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.39-1.14), and patients whose best response to chemotherapy was a complete response (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.46-1.37), partial response (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84), or stable disease (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46-1.06). Observations were similar for PFS. Limitations include the smaller size and post hoc evaluation without multiplicity adjustment for some subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
Analyses of OS and PFS in clinically relevant subgroups were consistent with results for the overall population, further supporting avelumab 1L maintenance as standard-of-care treatment for patients with aUC who are progression-free following 1L platinum-based chemotherapy.
PATIENT SUMMARY
In the JAVELIN Bladder 100 study, maintenance treatment with avelumab helped many different groups of people with advanced cancer of the urinary tract to live longer.</snippet>
<snippet id="37608243">Title: Avelumab as First-Line Maintenance Treatment in Locally Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
Authors: Mansinho, André, Cruz, Andreia, Marconi, Lorenzo et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Advances in therapy
Abstract: This work provides a summary of guideline recommendations and an expert position on the use of maintenance avelumab therapy based on a review of current international clinical practice guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (UC). A PubMed literature search was conducted in March 2022 (updated in July 2023) to identify guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic UC. An expert panel (four oncologists and one urologist) reviewed the guidelines and clinical evidence, and discussed practical questions regarding the use of avelumab maintenance therapy in this clinical setting. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network, European Association of Urology and European Society for Medical Oncology guidelines recommend first-line cisplatin-containing chemotherapy for cisplatin-eligible patients, carboplatin-gemcitabine for cisplatin-ineligible patients who are fit for carboplatin, or immunotherapy with programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) inhibitors (e.g. atezolizumab) in platinum-ineligible patients. Maintenance avelumab is recommended in patients with response/stable disease following chemotherapy (regardless of PD-L1 status). In patients who relapse after/during chemotherapy, options include immunotherapy, erdafitinib [in those with fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) mutations], enfortumab vedotin or further chemotherapy. The expert panel provided the following practical guidance: (1) consider maintenance avelumab in all eligible patients; (2) continue avelumab until disease progression/unacceptable toxicity; (3) ideally, administer six cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy prior to maintenance avelumab; (4) perform radiological evaluation after four chemotherapy cycles and prior to maintenance avelumab; (5) carboplatin-gemcitabine followed by maintenance avelumab is preferred in cisplatin-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 expression), but consider first-line immunotherapy in PD-L1-positive patients and platinum-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 status); and (6) for patients who relapse on avelumab, second-line options include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors (in those with FGFR mutations) or clinical trial inclusion. In conclusion, avelumab maintenance therapy is recommended following platinum-based chemotherapy in all eligible patients with locally advanced or metastatic UC, continued until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.</snippet>

# Bottom line

Yes. In patients with metastatic or unresectable locally advanced urothelial carcinoma who did not progress after first-line platinum chemotherapy, adding maintenance avelumab to best supportive care improved overall survival compared with best supportive care alone, regardless of whether the response to chemotherapy was complete response, partial response, or stable disease. The benefit was clinically meaningful and was observed in both the overall population and in prespecified subgroups, including those stratified by chemotherapy regimen and by best response to chemotherapy. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab plus best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival compared with best supportive care alone in patients with urothelial cancer who had not progressed after first-line platinum chemotherapy</cite> <cite id="37121850">Across subgroups, hazard ratios for overall survival favored avelumab plus best supportive care, including patients with complete response, partial response, or stable disease on chemotherapy</cite> <cite id="37794707">Post hoc matching analyses also showed a clinically relevant overall survival advantage for the lowest avelumab-exposure subgroup compared with matched best supportive care controls</cite>.

# Key evidence

- **JAVELIN Bladder 100 (NEJM, 2020)**: In a phase 3 trial of 700 patients, maintenance avelumab improved overall survival versus best supportive care in the overall population (median 21.4 vs 14.3 months; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56–0.86) and in the PD-L1–positive subgroup (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.40–0.79). Progression-free survival also improved (median 3.7 vs 2.0 months overall; 5.7 vs 2.1 months PD-L1 positive). <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab significantly prolonged overall survival and improved progression-free survival compared with best supportive care</cite>.

- **Updated JAVELIN Bladder 100 (JCO, 2023)**: With longer follow-up, the overall survival advantage persisted (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.91), reinforcing the durability of benefit. <cite id="37071838">Longer-term follow-up continues to show clinically meaningful overall survival benefits with avelumab first-line maintenance plus best supportive care</cite>.

- **Subgroup analyses (European Urology, 2023)**: The survival benefit was consistent across clinically relevant subgroups. For overall survival, hazard ratios were 0.69 with cisplatin–gemcitabine and 0.64 with carboplatin–gemcitabine; in PD-L1–positive tumors treated with carboplatin–gemcitabine, HR was 0.67. By best chemotherapy response: complete response HR 0.80, partial response HR 0.62, stable disease HR 0.70; all HRs favored avelumab. Similar results were seen for progression-free survival. <cite id="37121850">Hazard ratios for overall survival were <1.0 across subgroups, including complete response, partial response, and stable disease</cite>.

- **Guideline synthesis and expert consensus**: Major guidelines and expert reviews recommend maintenance avelumab for patients with response or stable disease on platinum chemotherapy, irrespective of PD-L1 status, as a standard-of-care option in platinum-eligible patients. <cite id="37608243">Maintenance avelumab is recommended after response or stable disease following chemotherapy, continued until progression or unacceptable toxicity</cite> <cite id="38702396">Maintenance avelumab improved overall survival and progression-free survival compared with best supportive care in platinum-responsive metastatic urothelial cancer</cite>.

- **Quality-of-life and exposure-response considerations**: Long-term patient-reported outcomes showed no detrimental impact on quality of life with avelumab maintenance, and exposure–response analyses indicated that even lower-exposure avelumab subgroups had clinically relevant survival advantages over matched best supportive care controls. <cite id="40318950">Avelumab plus best supportive care prolonged overall survival with preserved quality of life and improved quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity versus best supportive care alone</cite> <cite id="37794707">Case–control matching showed a clinically relevant overall survival benefit for the lowest avelumab-exposure subgroup compared with best supportive care controls</cite>.

# Interpretation for your question

Maintenance avelumab after a response or stable disease on platinum chemotherapy improves overall survival compared with observation or best supportive care in metastatic urothelial carcinoma, and this benefit is observed across different chemotherapy regimens and response categories, including stable disease. The magnitude of benefit is clinically meaningful, with hazard ratios consistently below 1.0 and median overall survival gains of several months to over a year in real-world follow-up. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab improved overall survival versus best supportive care in the overall population and PD-L1–positive subgroup</cite> <cite id="37121850">Subgroup analyses, including stable disease, showed consistent overall survival benefits</cite> <cite id="37071838">Updated analyses confirmed sustained overall survival advantage</cite>.

# Practical considerations

- Continue avelumab maintenance until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, ideally after completing 4–6 cycles of platinum chemotherapy, with radiologic reassessment before starting maintenance. <cite id="37608243">Continue avelumab until progression or unacceptable toxicity; consider six cycles of platinum chemotherapy before maintenance, with imaging after four cycles</cite>.

- In cisplatin-ineligible patients, carboplatin–gemcitabine followed by avelumab maintenance is a preferred approach; in PD-L1–positive cisplatin-ineligible patients, first-line immunotherapy may be considered regardless of PD-L1 status per guidelines. <cite id="37608243">Carboplatin–gemcitabine followed by avelumab is preferred in cisplatin-ineligible patients; consider first-line immunotherapy in PD-L1–positive or platinum-ineligible patients</cite>.

- For patients who relapse on or after avelumab, options include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors (with FGFR alterations), or clinical trials. <cite id="37608243">Second-line options after avelumab relapse include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors in FGFR-mutated disease, or clinical trials</cite>.

# Limitations

- Subgroup analyses (e.g., by best chemotherapy response) are post hoc and not adjusted for multiplicity; however, directionally consistent benefits across diverse subgroups strengthen confidence. <cite id="37121850">Subgroup analyses were post hoc and without multiplicity adjustment, but hazard ratios remained favorable for avelumab</cite>.

- The control arm received best supportive care rather than active observation; thus, direct comparisons to observation alone are not available from this trial. <cite id="32945632">The control arm was best supportive care with no active experimental therapy</cite>.

# Conclusion

For metastatic urothelial carcinoma that has not progressed after platinum chemotherapy, maintenance avelumab improves overall survival compared with best supportive care or observation, including in patients with stable disease, and offers a durable, clinically meaningful benefit supported by guideline recommendations and real-world follow-up. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab significantly prolonged overall survival versus best supportive care</cite> <cite id="37121850">Benefits were observed across complete response, partial response, and stable disease subgroups</cite> <cite id="37071838">Long-term follow-up confirms sustained overall survival advantage</cite> <cite id="37608243">Guidelines recommend maintenance avelumab for response or stable disease regardless of PD-L1 status</cite>.

data.title: Avelumab Maintenance Therapy for Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Platinum-based chemotherapy is standard-of-care first-line treatment for advanced urothelial carcinoma. However, progression-free survival and overall survival are limited by chemotherapy resistance.
METHODS
In a phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer who did not have disease progression with first-line chemotherapy (four to six cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin) to receive best supportive care with or without maintenance avelumab. The primary end point was overall survival, assessed among all patients who underwent randomization (overall population) and among those with tumors positive for programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Secondary end points included progression-free survival and safety.
RESULTS
Among all 700 patients who underwent randomization, the addition of maintenance avelumab to best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival as compared with best supportive care alone (control). Overall survival at 1 year was 71.3% in the avelumab group and 58.4% in the control group (median overall survival, 21.4 months vs. 14.3 months; hazard ratio for death, 0.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.56 to 0.86; P = 0.001). Avelumab also significantly prolonged overall survival in the PD-L1-positive population; overall survival at 1 year was 79.1% in the avelumab group and 60.4% in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.79; P<0.001). The median progression-free survival was 3.7 months in the avelumab group and 2.0 months in the control group in the overall population (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.75) and 5.7 months and 2.1 months, respectively, in the PD-L1-positive population (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.43 to 0.73). The incidence of adverse events from any cause was 98.0% in the avelumab group and 77.7% in the control group; the incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 47.4% and 25.2%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS

data.title: Avelumab First-Line Maintenance for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Results From the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Trial After ≥2 Years of Follow-Up.
data.abstract: Clinical trials frequently include multiple end points that mature at different times. The initial report, typically based on the primary end point, may be published when key planned coprimary or secondary analyses are not yet available. Clinical Trial Updates provide an opportunity to disseminate additional results from studies, published in JCO or elsewhere, for which the primary end point has already been reported. Initial results from the phase III JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02603432) showed that avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance plus best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) versus BSC alone in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma (aUC) who were progression-free after 1L platinum-containing chemotherapy. Avelumab 1L maintenance treatment is now a standard of care for aUC. Here, we report updated data with ≥ 2 years of follow-up in all patients, including OS (primary end point), PFS, safety, and additional novel analyses. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive avelumab plus BSC (n = 350) or BSC alone (n = 350). At data cutoff (June 4, 2021), median follow-up was 38.0 months and 39.6 months, respectively; 67 patients (19.5%) had received ≥2 years of avelumab treatment. OS remained longer with avelumab plus BSC versus BSC alone in all patients (hazard ratio, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.63 to 0.91]; 2-sided P = .0036). Investigator-assessed PFS analyses also favored avelumab. Longer-term safety was consistent with previous analyses; no new safety signals were identified with longer treatment duration. In conclusion, longer-term follow-up continues to show clinically meaningful efficacy benefits with avelumab 1L maintenance plus BSC versus BSC alone in patients with aUC. An interactive visualization of data reported in this article is available.

data.title: The evolving treatment landscape of metastatic urothelial cancer.
data.abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is currently the first-line standard of care for patients with metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC); however, up to 50% of patients are ineligible for cisplatin, necessitating alternative treatment options. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been shown to be effective in cisplatin-ineligible patients. However, despite advances in the first-line setting, the prognosis remains poor, and challenges persist in selecting optimal therapies, treatment sequences and combination regimens. Maintenance therapy with avelumab revealed improved overall (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) compared with best supportive care alone in patients with platinum-responsive mUC. Antibody-drug conjugates and targeted therapy with fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitors have shown promise in selected patients, particularly in patients with metastatic disease that has progressed despite platinum-based chemotherapy. At the European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in 2023, groundbreaking results were presented from two phase III trials, EV-302/KEYNOTE-A39 and CheckMate 901, focusing on previously untreated mUC. In the former, the combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab showed significant improvements in OS, PFS and overall response rate compared with chemotherapy alone; the combination of nivolumab with gemcitabine-cisplatin chemotherapy demonstrated a significant extension in median OS, PFS and overall response rate compared with chemotherapy alone. In addition, erdafitinib therapy resulted in significantly longer OS than chemotherapy among patients with mUC and FGFR alterations after previous treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors. This comprehensive summary of the current treatment landscape for mUC incorporates clinical trial evidence and discussion of agents that are currently under investigation to provide support for clinical decision making and understanding of future therapeutic approaches.

data.title: Switch Maintenance Therapy for Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
While switch maintenance therapy is being increasingly investigated in solid tumors, it is a standard in only a few. We conducted a systematic review on switch maintenance therapy for metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION
In this systematic review, we conducted a literature search in PubMed and Cochrane databases up to 2021, based on PRISMA statement guidelines. One hundred and fifty eight articles were identified and after a three-step selection process and six articles, using different agents were included in evidence synthesis. The primary end points were effect on overall survival, progression free survival, safety and tolerability.
EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS
In the pre-immunotherapy era, targeted therapies like sunitinib, lapatinib and vinflunine were studied as switch maintenance therapy in metastatic urothelial carcinoma but did not show any overall survival benefit. Use of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents have shown promise as switch maintenance therapy; pembrolizumab showed improvement in progression free survival in a phase 2 trial and avelumab showed improvement in overall survival and progression free survival in the phase 3 JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial.
CONCLUSION
Immunotherapy with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents has emerged as an effective switch maintenance strategy in patients with metastatic urothelial carcinoma. Intensification of the immunotherapy backbone in this setting can potentially further enhance outcomes. Emerging evidence shows a potential role of Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors in this setting as well. Results from ongoing and planned studies will help us understand which switch maintenance approaches would be most effective for improving outcomes in metastatic urothelial carcinoma.

data.title: Avelumab First-Line Maintenance Therapy: Managing Patients With Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The phase 3 of JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial demonstrated that avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance in addition to best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival compared to best supportive care alone. It is now the standard of care for platinum-eligible patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma that has not progressed with 1L platinum-containing chemotherapy.
OBJECTIVES
This article provides considerations for oncology nurses to effectively implement avelumab 1L maintenance treatment in the clinical setting.
METHODS
This article reviews clinical evidence and implications for oncology nurses caring for patients receiving avelumab 1L maintenance treatment.
FINDINGS
Oncology nurses can provide comprehensive care for patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma and ensure the safe and appropriate use of avelumab 1L maintenance treatment by educating patients and caregivers, ensuring correct administration, and promptly recognizing and managing immune-related adverse events.

data.title: Avelumab First-line Maintenance for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Long-term Analyses of Patient-reported Outcomes and Quality-adjusted Time Without Symptoms or Toxicity from the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
In JAVELIN Bladder 100, avelumab first-line maintenance plus best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival versus BSC alone, with no detrimental impact on quality of life (QOL), in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma without progression following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. We report long-term analyses of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in patients treated with avelumab (any duration or ≥12 mo) and a post hoc analysis comparing quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity (Q-TWiST) between arms.
METHODS
PROs were assessed using National Comprehensive Cancer Network/Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy Bladder Symptom Index-18 (FBlSI-18) and EuroQol 5-level EQ-5D (EQ-5D-5L). Q-TWiST was calculated as the utility-weighted sum of mean time in three health states: time with all-cause grade 3/4 toxicity prior to progression, time without grade 3/4 toxicity or symptoms of progression, and time after progression.
KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS
In the overall avelumab plus BSC arm (n = 350) and the subgroup treated for ≥12 mo (n = 118), completion rates for PRO assessments during treatment were >80%. FBlSI-18 total and EQ-5D-5L index scores remained stable throughout 24 mo of treatment, with no clinically important changes from baseline. The mean Q-TWiST was 18.46 mo with avelumab plus BSC versus 15.13 mo with BSC alone (22% relative improvement). Limitations include open-label trial design and small patient numbers at later cycles.
CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
Patients receiving avelumab had preserved health-related QOL and control of cancer-related symptoms with manageable toxicity, further supporting avelumab first-line maintenance as the recommended treatment for advanced urothelial carcinoma not progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy.

data.title: Case-control matching-guided exposure-efficacy relationship for avelumab in patients with urothelial carcinoma.
data.abstract: Exposure-response (E-R) analyses are an integral component of understanding the benefit/risk profile of novel oncology therapeutics. These analyses are typically conducted using data from the treatment arm to characterize the relationship between drug exposure (low vs. high) and efficacy or safety outcomes. For example, outcomes of patients with lower exposure in the treatment arm (e.g., Q1) might be compared to outcomes of those with higher drug exposure (Q2, Q3, and Q4). Outcomes from the lowest exposure quartile may be also compared to the control arm to evaluate whether the Q1 subgroup derived clinical benefit. However, the sample size and the distribution of patient baseline characteristics and disease risk factors are not balanced in such a comparison (Q1 vs. control), which may bias the analysis and causal interpretation of clinical benefit in the Q1 subgroup. Herein, we report the use of case-control matching to account for this bias and better understand the E-R relationship for avelumab in urothelial carcinoma, a PD-L1 inhibitor approved for the treatment of several cancers. Data from JAVELIN-100 was utilized which is a phase III study of avelumab in first-line maintenance treatment in patients with urothelial carcinoma; this clinical study demonstrated superiority of avelumab versus best-supportive care leading to approval in the United States, Europe, and other countries. A post hoc case-control matching method was implemented to compare the efficacy outcome between Q1 avelumab subgroup and matched patients extracted from the control arm with similar baseline characteristics, which showed a clinically relevant difference in overall survival in favor of the Q1 avelumab subgroup. This analysis demonstrates the importance of accounting for imbalance in important baseline covariates when comparing efficacy outcomes between subgroups within the treatment arm versus the control arm.

data.title: Complete Response after Avelumab Maintenance Therapy: Successful Management of Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract:
UNLABELLED
Urothelial carcinoma is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancer types in the world and despite progress in treatment, it remains a lethal disease in the metastatic stage. Because of its high programmed cell death ligand 1 protein expression, it is associated with an increased response to immune checkpoints inhibitors. In the past few years, the gold standard for first-line treatment of metastatic urothelial carcinoma has been platinum-based chemotherapy, and avelumab (PD-1 inhibitor) maintenance therapy for non-progressing tumours. After the remarkable benefit demonstrated in the EV-302 study, the guidelines were recently revised to include enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab as the new standard of care in this setting. Despite the new recommendations, in some countries, this combination is still pending approval. Furthermore, for patients who are ineligible for enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab, platinum-based chemotherapy followed by avelumab maintenance therapy continues to be a preferred treatment option. This report presents a woman diagnosed with metastatic urothelial carcinoma with histologically confirmed complete response after cisplatin and gemcitabine chemotherapy and avelumab as maintenance therapy, which has been reported in only a few cases in the literature.
LEARNING POINTS
Urothelial carcinoma is associated with high mortality despite significant progresses in treatment.In metastatic urothelial carcinoma the first-line treatment was recently changed, with enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab being approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency. Until now, platinum-based chemotherapy and avelumab maintenance therapy for non-progressing tumours was the only standard of care for these patients.In the literature, few cases have been reported with complete response to avelumab maintenance therapy.

data.title: Avelumab and taxol chemotherapy in platinum-refractory or ineligible metastatic urothelial carcinoma (AVETAX trial).
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
This study investigates the role of taxanes and immunotherapy for inoperable advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma in patients unable to tolerate or refractory to platinum-based regimens. We aimed to determine the safety and estimate the efficacy of a combination of avelumab and docetaxel in treating advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
METHODS
This phase 1b, single-arm, open-label clinical trial involved adults with advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, progressing during or after platinum-containing chemotherapy, within 12 months of neoadjuvant or adjuvant platinum-containing chemotherapy, or ineligible for platinum regimens. Primary objectives were determining the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of docetaxel with avelumab and estimating efficacy via the objective response rate (ORR). In Phase I, docetaxel (45, 60, 75 mg/m²) was combined with 10 mg/kg avelumab every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by avelumab biweekly as maintenance. The expansion cohort received treatment at the MTD of 75 mg/m² docetaxel with 10 mg/kg of avelumab.
RESULTS
Twenty-one patients with advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma were studied: 8 cisplatin-refractory and 13 cisplatin-ineligible. The 75 mg/m² dose of docetaxel with 10 mg/kg avelumab was safe, with 1 dose-limiting toxicity (neutropenic fever). The ORR was 52.4% (95% CI: 29.8%-74.3%). Median progression-free survival and overall survival were 14.6 months (95% CI: 2.8-15.8) and 16.6 months (95% CI: 13.2-not reached), respectively.
CONCLUSION
The combination of avelumab and docetaxel shows favorable safety and efficacy in treating advanced or metastatic bladder cancer.
