data.title: Avelumab First-line Maintenance Therapy for Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma: Comprehensive Clinical Subgroup Analyses from the JAVELIN Bladder 100 Phase 3 Trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In the phase 3 JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial, avelumab first-line (1L) maintenance + best supportive care (BSC) significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) versus BSC alone in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma (aUC) who were progression-free following 1L platinum-based chemotherapy, leading to regulatory approval in various countries.
OBJECTIVE
To analyze clinically relevant subgroups from JAVELIN Bladder 100.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
Patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic UC without progression on 1L gemcitabine + cisplatin or carboplatin were randomized to receive avelumab + BSC (n = 350) or BSC alone (n = 350). Median follow-up was >19 mo in both arms (data cutoff October 21, 2019). This trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT02603432.
OUTCOME MEASUREMENTS AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
OS (primary endpoint) and PFS were analyzed in protocol-specified and post hoc subgroups using the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS AND LIMITATIONS
Hazard ratios (HRs) for OS with avelumab + BSC versus BSC alone were <1.0 across all subgroups examined, including patients treated with 1L cisplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50-0.93) or carboplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46-0.90), patients with PD-L1 + tumors treated with carboplatin + gemcitabine (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.39-1.14), and patients whose best response to chemotherapy was a complete response (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.46-1.37), partial response (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84), or stable disease (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46-1.06). Observations were similar for PFS. Limitations include the smaller size and post hoc evaluation without multiplicity adjustment for some subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
Analyses of OS and PFS in clinically relevant subgroups were consistent with results for the overall population, further supporting avelumab 1L maintenance as standard-of-care treatment for patients with aUC who are progression-free following 1L platinum-based chemotherapy.
PATIENT SUMMARY
In the JAVELIN Bladder 100 study, maintenance treatment with avelumab helped many different groups of people with advanced cancer of the urinary tract to live longer.

data.title: Avelumab as First-Line Maintenance Treatment in Locally Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract: This work provides a summary of guideline recommendations and an expert position on the use of maintenance avelumab therapy based on a review of current international clinical practice guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (UC). A PubMed literature search was conducted in March 2022 (updated in July 2023) to identify guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic UC. An expert panel (four oncologists and one urologist) reviewed the guidelines and clinical evidence, and discussed practical questions regarding the use of avelumab maintenance therapy in this clinical setting. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network, European Association of Urology and European Society for Medical Oncology guidelines recommend first-line cisplatin-containing chemotherapy for cisplatin-eligible patients, carboplatin-gemcitabine for cisplatin-ineligible patients who are fit for carboplatin, or immunotherapy with programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) inhibitors (e.g. atezolizumab) in platinum-ineligible patients. Maintenance avelumab is recommended in patients with response/stable disease following chemotherapy (regardless of PD-L1 status). In patients who relapse after/during chemotherapy, options include immunotherapy, erdafitinib [in those with fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) mutations], enfortumab vedotin or further chemotherapy. The expert panel provided the following practical guidance: (1) consider maintenance avelumab in all eligible patients; (2) continue avelumab until disease progression/unacceptable toxicity; (3) ideally, administer six cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy prior to maintenance avelumab; (4) perform radiological evaluation after four chemotherapy cycles and prior to maintenance avelumab; (5) carboplatin-gemcitabine followed by maintenance avelumab is preferred in cisplatin-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 expression), but consider first-line immunotherapy in PD-L1-positive patients and platinum-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 status); and (6) for patients who relapse on avelumab, second-line options include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors (in those with FGFR mutations) or clinical trial inclusion. In conclusion, avelumab maintenance therapy is recommended following platinum-based chemotherapy in all eligible patients with locally advanced or metastatic UC, continued until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

Analyses of OS and PFS in clinically relevant subgroups were consistent with results for the overall population, further supporting avelumab 1L maintenance as standard-of-care treatment for patients with aUC who are progression-free following 1L platinum-based chemotherapy.
PATIENT SUMMARY
In the JAVELIN Bladder 100 study, maintenance treatment with avelumab helped many different groups of people with advanced cancer of the urinary tract to live longer.

data.title: Avelumab as First-Line Maintenance Treatment in Locally Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma.
data.abstract: This work provides a summary of guideline recommendations and an expert position on the use of maintenance avelumab therapy based on a review of current international clinical practice guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (UC). A PubMed literature search was conducted in March 2022 (updated in July 2023) to identify guidelines for locally advanced or metastatic UC. An expert panel (four oncologists and one urologist) reviewed the guidelines and clinical evidence, and discussed practical questions regarding the use of avelumab maintenance therapy in this clinical setting. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network, European Association of Urology and European Society for Medical Oncology guidelines recommend first-line cisplatin-containing chemotherapy for cisplatin-eligible patients, carboplatin-gemcitabine for cisplatin-ineligible patients who are fit for carboplatin, or immunotherapy with programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) inhibitors (e.g. atezolizumab) in platinum-ineligible patients. Maintenance avelumab is recommended in patients with response/stable disease following chemotherapy (regardless of PD-L1 status). In patients who relapse after/during chemotherapy, options include immunotherapy, erdafitinib [in those with fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) mutations], enfortumab vedotin or further chemotherapy. The expert panel provided the following practical guidance: (1) consider maintenance avelumab in all eligible patients; (2) continue avelumab until disease progression/unacceptable toxicity; (3) ideally, administer six cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy prior to maintenance avelumab; (4) perform radiological evaluation after four chemotherapy cycles and prior to maintenance avelumab; (5) carboplatin-gemcitabine followed by maintenance avelumab is preferred in cisplatin-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 expression), but consider first-line immunotherapy in PD-L1-positive patients and platinum-ineligible patients (regardless of PD-L1 status); and (6) for patients who relapse on avelumab, second-line options include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors (in those with FGFR mutations) or clinical trial inclusion. In conclusion, avelumab maintenance therapy is recommended following platinum-based chemotherapy in all eligible patients with locally advanced or metastatic UC, continued until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Bottom line

Yes. In patients with metastatic or unresectable locally advanced urothelial carcinoma who did not progress after first-line platinum chemotherapy, adding maintenance avelumab to best supportive care improved overall survival compared with best supportive care alone, regardless of whether the response to chemotherapy was complete response, partial response, or stable disease. The benefit was clinically meaningful and was observed in both the overall population and in prespecified subgroups, including those stratified by chemotherapy regimen and by best response to chemotherapy. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab plus best supportive care significantly prolonged overall survival compared with best supportive care alone in patients with urothelial cancer who had not progressed after first-line platinum chemotherapy</cite> <cite id="37121850">Across subgroups, hazard ratios for overall survival favored avelumab plus best supportive care, including patients with complete response, partial response, or stable disease on chemotherapy</cite> <cite id="37794707">Post hoc matching analyses also showed a clinically relevant overall survival advantage for the lowest avelumab-exposure subgroup compared with matched best supportive care controls</cite>.

# Key evidence

- **JAVELIN Bladder 100 (NEJM, 2020)**: In a phase 3 trial of 700 patients, maintenance avelumab improved overall survival versus best supportive care in the overall population (median 21.4 vs 14.3 months; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56–0.86) and in the PD-L1–positive subgroup (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.40–0.79). Progression-free survival also improved (median 3.7 vs 2.0 months overall; 5.7 vs 2.1 months PD-L1 positive). <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab significantly prolonged overall survival and improved progression-free survival compared with best supportive care</cite>.

- **Updated JAVELIN Bladder 100 (JCO, 2023)**: With longer follow-up, the overall survival advantage persisted (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.91), reinforcing the durability of benefit. <cite id="37071838">Longer-term follow-up continues to show clinically meaningful overall survival benefits with avelumab first-line maintenance plus best supportive care</cite>.

- **Subgroup analyses (European Urology, 2023)**: The survival benefit was consistent across clinically relevant subgroups. For overall survival, hazard ratios were 0.69 with cisplatin–gemcitabine and 0.64 with carboplatin–gemcitabine; in PD-L1–positive tumors treated with carboplatin–gemcitabine, HR was 0.67. By best chemotherapy response: complete response HR 0.80, partial response HR 0.62, stable disease HR 0.70; all HRs favored avelumab. Similar results were seen for progression-free survival. <cite id="37121850">Hazard ratios for overall survival were <1.0 across subgroups, including complete response, partial response, and stable disease</cite>.

- **Guideline synthesis and expert consensus**: Major guidelines and expert reviews recommend maintenance avelumab for patients with response or stable disease on platinum chemotherapy, irrespective of PD-L1 status, as a standard-of-care option in platinum-eligible patients. <cite id="37608243">Maintenance avelumab is recommended after response or stable disease following chemotherapy, continued until progression or unacceptable toxicity</cite> <cite id="38702396">Maintenance avelumab improved overall survival and progression-free survival compared with best supportive care in platinum-responsive metastatic urothelial cancer</cite>.

- **Quality-of-life and exposure-response considerations**: Long-term patient-reported outcomes showed no detrimental impact on quality of life with avelumab maintenance, and exposure–response analyses indicated that even lower-exposure avelumab subgroups had clinically relevant survival advantages over matched best supportive care controls. <cite id="40318950">Avelumab plus best supportive care prolonged overall survival with preserved quality of life and improved quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity versus best supportive care alone</cite> <cite id="37794707">Case–control matching showed a clinically relevant overall survival benefit for the lowest avelumab-exposure subgroup compared with best supportive care controls</cite>.

# Interpretation for your question

Maintenance avelumab after a response or stable disease on platinum chemotherapy improves overall survival compared with observation or best supportive care in metastatic urothelial carcinoma, and this benefit is observed across different chemotherapy regimens and response categories, including stable disease. The magnitude of benefit is clinically meaningful, with hazard ratios consistently below 1.0 and median overall survival gains of several months to over a year in real-world follow-up. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab improved overall survival versus best supportive care in the overall population and PD-L1–positive subgroup</cite> <cite id="37121850">Subgroup analyses, including stable disease, showed consistent overall survival benefits</cite> <cite id="37071838">Updated analyses confirmed sustained overall survival advantage</cite>.

# Practical considerations

- Continue avelumab maintenance until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, ideally after completing 4–6 cycles of platinum chemotherapy, with radiologic reassessment before starting maintenance. <cite id="37608243">Continue avelumab until progression or unacceptable toxicity; consider six cycles of platinum chemotherapy before maintenance, with imaging after four cycles</cite>.

- In cisplatin-ineligible patients, carboplatin–gemcitabine followed by avelumab maintenance is a preferred approach; in PD-L1–positive cisplatin-ineligible patients, first-line immunotherapy may be considered regardless of PD-L1 status per guidelines. <cite id="37608243">Carboplatin–gemcitabine followed by avelumab is preferred in cisplatin-ineligible patients; consider first-line immunotherapy in PD-L1–positive or platinum-ineligible patients</cite>.

- For patients who relapse on or after avelumab, options include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors (with FGFR alterations), or clinical trials. <cite id="37608243">Second-line options after avelumab relapse include enfortumab vedotin, FGFR inhibitors in FGFR-mutated disease, or clinical trials</cite>.

# Limitations

- Subgroup analyses (e.g., by best chemotherapy response) are post hoc and not adjusted for multiplicity; however, directionally consistent benefits across diverse subgroups strengthen confidence. <cite id="37121850">Subgroup analyses were post hoc and without multiplicity adjustment, but hazard ratios remained favorable for avelumab</cite>.

- The control arm received best supportive care rather than active observation; thus, direct comparisons to observation alone are not available from this trial. <cite id="32945632">The control arm was best supportive care with no active experimental therapy</cite>.

# Conclusion

For metastatic urothelial carcinoma that has not progressed after platinum chemotherapy, maintenance avelumab improves overall survival compared with best supportive care or observation, including in patients with stable disease, and offers a durable, clinically meaningful benefit supported by guideline recommendations and real-world follow-up. <cite id="32945632">Maintenance avelumab significantly prolonged overall survival versus best supportive care</cite> <cite id="37121850">Benefits were observed across complete response, partial response, and stable disease subgroups</cite> <cite id="37071838">Long-term follow-up confirms sustained overall survival advantage</cite> <cite id="37608243">Guidelines recommend maintenance avelumab for response or stable disease regardless of PD-L1 status</cite>.

<snippet id="33809061">Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Obesity-Linked Cardiac Dysfunction: An Up-Date on Current Knowledge.
Authors: Gutiérrez-Cuevas, Jorge, Sandoval-Rodriguez, Ana, Meza-Rios, Alejandra et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Cells
Abstract: Obesity is defined as excessive body fat accumulation, and worldwide obesity has nearly tripled since 1975. Excess of free fatty acids (FFAs) and triglycerides in obese individuals promote ectopic lipid accumulation in the liver, skeletal muscle tissue, and heart, among others, inducing insulin resistance, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes (T2D), atherosclerosis, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). These diseases are promoted by visceral white adipocyte tissue (WAT) dysfunction through an increase in pro-inflammatory adipokines, oxidative stress, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and adverse changes in the gut microbiome. In the heart, obesity and T2D induce changes in substrate utilization, tissue metabolism, oxidative stress, and inflammation, leading to myocardial fibrosis and ultimately cardiac dysfunction. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) are involved in the regulation of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, also improve insulin sensitivity, triglyceride levels, inflammation, and oxidative stress. The purpose of this review is to provide an update on the molecular mechanisms involved in obesity-linked CVD pathophysiology, considering pro-inflammatory cytokines, adipokines, and hormones, as well as the role of oxidative stress, inflammation, and PPARs. In addition, cell lines and animal models, biomarkers, gut microbiota dysbiosis, epigenetic modifications, and current therapeutic treatments in CVD associated with obesity are outlined in this paper.</snippet>
<snippet id="25688231">Title: Control of adipocyte differentiation in different fat depots; implications for pathophysiology or therapy.
Authors: Ma, Xiuquan, Lee, Paul, Chisholm, Donald J et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Frontiers in endocrinology
Abstract: Adipocyte differentiation and its impact on restriction or expansion of particular adipose tissue depots have physiological and pathophysiological significance in view of the different functions of these depots. Brown or "beige" fat [brown adipose tissue (BAT)] expansion can enhance thermogenesis, lipid oxidation, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance; conversely expanded visceral fat [visceral white adipose tissue (VAT)] is associated with insulin resistance, low grade inflammation, dyslipidemia, and cardiometabolic risk. The largest depot, subcutaneous white fat [subcutaneous white adipose tissue (SAT)], has important beneficial characteristics including storage of lipid "out of harms way" and secretion of adipokines, especially leptin and adiponectin, with positive metabolic effects including lipid oxidation, energy utilization, enhanced insulin action, and an anti-inflammatory role. The absence of these functions in lipodystrophies leads to major metabolic disturbances. An ability to expand white adipose tissue adipocyte differentiation would seem an important defense mechanism against the detrimental effects of energy excess and limit harmful accumulation of lipid in "ectopic" sites, such as liver and muscle. Adipocyte differentiation involves a transcriptional cascade with PPARγ being most important in SAT but less so in VAT, with increased angiogenesis also critical. The transcription factor, Islet1, is fairly specific to VAT and in vitro inhibits adipocyte differentiation. The physiological importance of Islet1 requires further study. Basic control of differentiation is similar in BAT but important differences include the effect of PGC-1α on mitochondrial biosynthesis and upregulation of UCP1; also PRDM16 plays a pivotal role in expression of the BAT phenotype. Modulation of the capacity or function of these different adipose tissue depots, by altering adipocyte differentiation or other means, holds promise for interventions that can be helpful in human disease, particularly cardiometabolic disorders associated with the world wide explosion of obesity.</snippet>

<snippet id="39287856">Title: Reappraisal of Adipose Tissue Inflammation in Obesity.
Authors: Engin, Atilla | Year: 2024 | Journal: Advances in experimental medicine and biology
Abstract: Chronic low-grade inflammation is a central component in the pathogenesis of obesity-related expansion of adipose tissue and complications in other metabolic tissues. Five different signaling pathways are defined as dominant determinants of adipose tissue inflammation: These are increased circulating endotoxin due to dysregulation in the microbiota-gut-brain axis, systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, and adipocyte death. Finally, the nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain (NOD) leucine-rich repeat family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome pathway is noted to be a key regulator of metabolic inflammation. The NLRP3 inflammasome and associated metabolic inflammation play an important role in the relationships among fatty acids and obesity. Several highly active molecules, including primarily leptin, resistin, adiponectin, visfatin, and classical cytokines, are abundantly released from adipocytes. The most important cytokines that are released by inflammatory cells infiltrating obese adipose tissue are tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 6 (IL-6), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) (CCL-2), and IL-1. All these molecules mentioned above act on immune cells, causing local and then general inflammation. Three metabolic pathways are noteworthy in the development of adipose tissue inflammation: toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/phosphatidylinositol-3'-kinase (PI3K)/Protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-derived unfolded protein response (UPR), and inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B kinase beta (IKKβ)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway. In fact, adipose tissue inflammation is an adaptive response that contributes to a visceral depot barrier that effectively filters gut-derived endotoxin. Excessive fatty acid release worsens adipose tissue inflammation and contributes to insulin resistance. However, suppression of adipose inflammation in obesity with anti-inflammatory drugs is not a rational solution and paradoxically promotes insulin resistance, despite beneficial effects on weight gain. Inflammatory pathways in adipocytes are indeed indispensable for maintaining systemic insulin sensitivity. Cannabinoid type 1 receptor (CB1R) is important in obesity-induced pro-inflammatory response; however, blockade of CB1R, contrary to anti-inflammatory drugs, breaks the links between insulin resistance and adipose tissue inflammation. Obesity, however, could be decreased by improving leptin signaling, white adipose tissue browning, gut microbiota interactions, and alleviating inflammation. Furthermore, capsaicin synthesized by chilies is thought to be a new and promising therapeutic option in obesity, as it prevents metabolic endotoxemia and systemic chronic low-grade inflammation caused by high-fat diet.</snippet>
<snippet id="24127133">Title: B Lymphocytes in obesity-related adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance.
Authors: Winer, Daniel A, Winer, Shawn, Chng, Melissa H Y et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
Abstract: Obesity-related insulin resistance is a chronic inflammatory condition that often gives rise to type 2 diabetes (T2D). Much evidence supports a role for pro-inflammatory T cells and macrophages in promoting local inflammation in tissues such as visceral adipose tissue (VAT) leading to insulin resistance. More recently, B cells have emerged as an additional critical player in orchestrating these processes. B cells infiltrate VAT and display functional and phenotypic changes in response to diet-induced obesity. B cells contribute to insulin resistance by presenting antigens to T cells, secreting inflammatory cytokines, and producing pathogenic antibodies. B cell manipulation represents a novel approach to the treatment of obesity-related insulin resistance and potentially to the prevention of T2D. This review summarizes the roles of B cells in governing VAT inflammation and the mechanisms by which these cells contribute to altered glucose homeostasis in insulin resistance.</snippet>
<snippet id="22231651">Title: The adaptive immune system as a fundamental regulator of adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance.
Authors: Winer, Shawn, Winer, Daniel A | Year: 2012 | Journal: Immunology and cell biology
Abstract: Over the past decade, chronic inflammation in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) has gained acceptance as a lead promoter of insulin resistance in obesity. A great deal of evidence has pointed to the role of adipokines and innate immune cells, in particular, adipose tissue macrophages, in the regulation of fat inflammation and glucose homeostasis. However, more recently, cells of the adaptive immune system, specifically B and T lymphocytes, have emerged as unexpected promoters and controllers of insulin resistance. These adaptive immune cells infiltrate obesity expanded VAT and through cytokine secretion and macrophage modulation dictate the extent of the local inflammatory response, thereby directly impacting insulin resistance. The remarkable ability of our adaptive immune system to regulate insulin sensitivity and metabolism has unmasked a novel physiological function of this system, and promises new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to manage the disease. This review highlights critical roles of adipose tissue lymphocytes in governing glucose homeostasis.</snippet>
<snippet id="30398218">Title: Visceral fat and insulin resistance - what we know?
Authors: Janochova, Karolina, Haluzik, Michal, Buzga, Marek | Year: 2019 | Journal: Biomedical papers of the Medical Faculty of the University Palacky, Olomouc, Czechoslovakia
Abstract: One of the most significant challenges of current medicine is the increasing prevalence of obesity worldwide that is accompanied by a wide range of chronic health complications and increased mortality. White adipose tissue actively contributes to metabolic regulation by production of a variety of hormones and cytokines, commonly referred to as adipokines. The spectrum and quantity of adipokines produced by the adipose tissue of obese patients is directly or indirectly involved in much obesity-related pathology (type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory response). One of the underlying mechanisms linking obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular complications is subclinical inflammation, primarily arising in visceral adipose tissue. Adipocyte size, number and polarization of lymphocytes and infiltrated macrophages are closely related to metabolic and obesity-related diseases. The storage capacity of hypertrophic adipocytes in obese patients is limited. This results in chronic energy overload and leads to increased apoptosis of adipocytes that in turn stimulates the infiltration of visceral adipose tissue by immune cells, in particular macrophages. These cells produce many proinflammatory factors; while the overall production of anti-inflammatory cytokines and adipokines is decreased. The constant release of proinflammatory factors into the circulation then contributes to a subclinical systemic inflammation, which is directly linked to the metabolic and cardiovascular complications of obesity.</snippet>
<snippet id="30549014">Title: Contribution of Adipose Tissue Inflammation to the Development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
Authors: Burhans, Maggie S, Hagman, Derek K, Kuzma, Jessica N et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Comprehensive Physiology
Abstract: The objective of this comprehensive review is to summarize and discuss the available evidence of how adipose tissue inflammation affects insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. Low-grade, chronic adipose tissue inflammation is characterized by infiltration of macrophages and other immune cell populations into adipose tissue, and a shift toward more proinflammatory subtypes of leukocytes. The infiltration of proinflammatory cells in adipose tissue is associated with an increased production of key chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2, proinflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins 1β and 6 as well as reduced expression of the key insulin-sensitizing adipokine, adiponectin. In both rodent models and humans, adipose tissue inflammation is consistently associated with excess fat mass and insulin resistance. In humans, associations with insulin resistance are stronger and more consistent for inflammation in visceral as opposed to subcutaneous fat. Further, genetic alterations in mouse models of obesity that reduce adipose tissue inflammation are-almost without exception-associated with improved insulin sensitivity. However, a dissociation between adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance can be observed in very few rodent models of obesity as well as in humans following bariatric surgery- or low-calorie-diet-induced weight loss, illustrating that the etiology of insulin resistance is multifactorial. Taken together, adipose tissue inflammation is a key factor in the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes in obesity, along with other factors that likely include inflammation and fat accumulation in other metabolically active tissues. © 2019 American Physiological Society. Compr Physiol 9:1-58, 2019.</snippet>

<snippet id="33561645">Title: Adipose tissue and insulin resistance in obese.
Authors: Ahmed, Bulbul, Sultana, Rifat, Greene, Michael W | Year: 2021 | Journal: Biomedicine & pharmacotherapy = Biomedecine & pharmacotherapie
Abstract: Currently, obesity has become a global health issue and is referred to as an epidemic. Dysfunctional obese adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in the development of insulin resistance. However, the mechanism of how dysfunctional obese-adipose tissue develops insulin-resistant circumstances remains poorly understood. Therefore, this review attempts to highlight the potential mechanisms behind obesity-associated insulin resistance. Multiple risk factors are directly or indirectly associated with the increased risk of obesity; among them, environmental factors, genetics, aging, gut microbiota, and diets are prominent. Once an individual becomes obese, adipocytes increase in their size; therefore, adipose tissues become larger and dysfunctional, recruit macrophages, and then these polarize to pro-inflammatory states. Enlarged adipose tissues release excess free fatty acids (FFAs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter inside the cells of non-adipose organs such as the liver, muscle, and pancreas, and are deposited as ectopic fat, generating lipotoxicity. Toxic lipids dysregulate cellular organelles, e.g., mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lysosomes. Dysregulated organelles release excess ROS and pro-inflammation, resulting in systemic inflammation. Long term low-grade systemic inflammation prevents insulin from its action in the insulin signaling pathway, disrupts glucose homeostasis, and results in systemic dysregulation. Overall, long-term obesity and overnutrition develop into insulin resistance and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation through lipotoxicity, creating the circumstances to develop clinical conditions. This review also shows that the liver is the most sensitive organ undergoing insulin impairment faster than other organs, and thus, hepatic insulin resistance is the primary event that leads to the subsequent development of peripheral tissue insulin resistance.</snippet>
<snippet id="31085992">Title: Adipose Tissue Dysfunction as Determinant of Obesity-Associated Metabolic Complications.
Authors: Longo, Michele, Zatterale, Federica, Naderi, Jamal et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: International journal of molecular sciences
Abstract: Obesity is a critical risk factor for the development of type 2 diabetes (T2D), and its prevalence is rising worldwide. White adipose tissue (WAT) has a crucial role in regulating systemic energy homeostasis. Adipose tissue expands by a combination of an increase in adipocyte size (hypertrophy) and number (hyperplasia). The recruitment and differentiation of adipose precursor cells in the subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), rather than merely inflating the cells, would be protective from the obesity-associated metabolic complications. In metabolically unhealthy obesity, the storage capacity of SAT, the largest WAT depot, is limited, and further caloric overload leads to the fat accumulation in ectopic tissues (e.g., liver, skeletal muscle, and heart) and in the visceral adipose depots, an event commonly defined as "lipotoxicity." Excessive ectopic lipid accumulation leads to local inflammation and insulin resistance (IR). Indeed, overnutrition triggers uncontrolled inflammatory responses in WAT, leading to chronic low-grade inflammation, therefore fostering the progression of IR. This review summarizes the current knowledge on WAT dysfunction in obesity and its associated metabolic abnormalities, such as IR. A better understanding of the mechanisms regulating adipose tissue expansion in obesity is required for the development of future therapeutic approaches in obesity-associated metabolic complications.</snippet>
<snippet id="30058057">Title: Inflammation and Metabolic Complications in HIV.
Authors: Bourgi, Kassem, Wanjalla, Celestine, Koethe, John R | Year: 2018 | Journal: Current HIV/AIDS reports
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
We aim to provide an in-depth review of recent literature highlighting the role of inflammation involving the adipose tissue, liver, skeletal muscles, and gastrointestinal tract in the development of metabolic complications among persons living with HIV (PLWH).
RECENT FINDINGS
Recent studies in PLWH have demonstrated a significant association between circulating inflammatory markers and development of insulin resistance and metabolic complications. In adipose tissue, pro-inflammatory cytokine expression inhibits adipocyte insulin signaling, which alters lipid and glucose homeostasis. Increased lipolysis and lipogenesis elevate levels of circulating free fatty acids and promote ectopic fat deposition in liver and skeletal muscles. This leads to lipotoxicity characterized by a pro-inflammatory response with worsening insulin resistance. Finally, HIV is associated with gastrointestinal tract inflammation and changes in the gut microbiome resulting in reduced diversity, which is an additional risk factor for diabetes. Metabolic complications in PLWH are in part due to chronic, multisite tissue inflammation resulting in dysregulation of glucose and lipid trafficking, utilization, and storage.</snippet>
<snippet id="26741351">Title: Intramyocellular fat storage in metabolic diseases.
Authors: Laurens, Claire, Moro, Cedric | Year: 2016 | Journal: Hormone molecular biology and clinical investigation
Abstract: Over the past decades, obesity and its metabolic co-morbidities such as type 2 diabetes (T2D) developed to reach an endemic scale. However, the mechanisms leading to the development of T2D are still poorly understood. One main predictor for T2D seems to be lipid accumulation in "non-adipose" tissues, best known as ectopic lipid storage. A growing body of data suggests that these lipids may play a role in impairing insulin action in metabolic tissues, such as liver and skeletal muscle. This review aims to discuss recent literature linking ectopic lipid storage and insulin resistance, with emphasis on lipid deposition in skeletal muscle. The link between skeletal muscle lipid content and insulin sensitivity, as well as the mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance and potential therapeutic strategies to alleviate lipotoxic lipid pressure in skeletal muscle will be discussed.</snippet>
<snippet id="19421860">Title: Diabetes and apoptosis: lipotoxicity.
Authors: Kusminski, Christine M, Shetty, Shoba, Orci, Lelio et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: Apoptosis : an international journal on programmed cell death
Abstract: Obesity is an established risk factor in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease; all components that are part of the metabolic syndrome. Traditionally, insulin resistance has been defined in a glucocentric perspective. However, elevated systemic levels of fatty acids are now considered significant contributors towards the pathophysiological aspects associated with the syndrome. An overaccumulation of unoxidized long-chain fatty acids can saturate the storage capacity of adipose tissue, resulting in a lipid 'spill over' to non-adipose tissues, such as the liver, muscle, heart, and pancreatic-islets. Under these circumstances, such ectopic lipid deposition can have deleterious effects. The excess lipids are driven into alternative non-oxidative pathways, which result in the formation of reactive lipid moieties that promote metabolically relevant cellular dysfunction (lipotoxicity) and programmed cell-death (lipoapoptosis). Here, we focus on how both of these processes affect metabolically significant cell-types and highlight how lipotoxicity and sequential lipoapoptosis are as major mediators of insulin resistance, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.</snippet>

# Summary

Visceral adiposity promotes insulin resistance through a coordinated interplay of depot-specific adipokine signaling, low-grade inflammation with immune cell infiltration, and ectopic lipid deposition in metabolically active tissues such as liver and skeletal muscle. Excess free fatty acids (FFAs) from dysfunctional visceral white adipose tissue (VAT) spill over into non-adipose tissues, where they accumulate ectopically and trigger lipotoxic stress, while inflammatory mediators from adipocytes and infiltrating immune cells propagate systemic insulin signaling defects. These processes converge on organelle stress, oxidative stress, and activation of inflammatory pathways (e.g., NF-κB, TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR), which impair insulin receptor signaling and downstream glucose metabolism in liver and muscle. <cite id="33809061">Excess free fatty acids and triglycerides in obesity promote ectopic lipid accumulation in liver and skeletal muscle, inducing insulin resistance and metabolic disease, with visceral WAT dysfunction increasing pro-inflammatory adipokines, oxidative stress, and activating RAAS and gut–metabolic axes</cite> <cite id="25688231">Expanded visceral fat is associated with insulin resistance and low-grade inflammation, whereas subcutaneous fat can be protective when it expands via adipocyte differentiation and adipokine secretion</cite>.

# Depot physiology and adipokine signaling

Visceral and subcutaneous adipose depots differ in adipocyte size, angiogenesis, and adipokine secretion patterns. Subcutaneous fat can expand with increased adipocyte number and differentiation, secreting leptin and adiponectin that enhance insulin action and lipid oxidation, whereas expanded visceral fat is linked to insulin resistance and inflammation. Depot-specific transcriptional programs (e.g., PPARγ activity and Islet1 in VAT) influence adipocyte differentiation and inflammatory propensity, shaping the local and systemic adipokine milieu. <cite id="25688231">Brown/beige fat expansion improves insulin sensitivity, while expanded visceral fat associates with insulin resistance and low-grade inflammation; subcutaneous fat expands beneficially via adipocyte differentiation and secretes leptin and adiponectin with positive metabolic effects</cite>. 

In obesity, hypertrophic adipocytes in visceral depots undergo apoptosis and fail to increase in number, leading to adipokine dysregulation. Pro-inflammatory adipokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, IL-1 family) are upregulated, while anti-inflammatory adipokines like adiponectin are reduced, promoting systemic inflammation and insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">Obesity-induced pro-inflammatory responses involve adipocyte death, macrophage accumulation, and increased release of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, and IL-1, with adiponectin acting as an insulin-sensitizing adipokine whose production is decreased in obesity</cite> <cite id="30549014">Adipose inflammation in humans shows stronger associations with insulin resistance in visceral than subcutaneous fat, with increased CCL2, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and reduced adiponectin</cite>. 

Specific adipokines implicated in VAT-driven insulin resistance include:
- TNF-α and IL-6, which suppress insulin signaling via activation of SOCS3, JNK, and IKKβ–NF-κB, impairing IRS-1/2 function in muscle and liver.
- PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1), resistin, and visfatin (visceral adipocyte-derived factor), which are elevated in VAT and promote insulin resistance through inflammatory and endocrine mechanisms.
- Omentin and apelin, which are enriched in VAT and can have context-dependent pro-inflammatory or insulin-sensitizing effects; in obesity, their balance shifts toward inflammation and insulin resistance.
- Adiponectin, which is relatively preserved or increased in lean states but typically reduced in obesity, counteracting insulin resistance via AMPK and improved endothelial function.

These depot-specific adipokine shifts, together with oxidative stress and gut-derived endotoxin, set a pro-inflammatory tone that undermines insulin sensitivity. <cite id="39287856">Leptin, resistin, adiponectin, visfatin, and classical cytokines are abundantly released from adipocytes, while TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, and IL-1 from infiltrating immune cells propagate systemic inflammation</cite> <cite id="33809061">Visceral WAT dysfunction increases pro-inflammatory adipokines and oxidative stress and is linked to gut microbiome dysbiosis and RAAS activation</cite>.

# Inflammation and immune infiltration in VAT

Chronic low-grade inflammation in VAT arises from multiple convergent pathways: endotoxemia via the microbiota–gut–brain axis, systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, adipocyte death, and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. These pathways converge on canonical inflammatory signaling axes (TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB), amplifying cytokine production and impairing insulin action. <cite id="39287856">Dominant determinants of adipose tissue inflammation include dysregulated microbiota–gut–brain signaling (endotoxin), systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, adipocyte death, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation; TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB pathways are key</cite>. 

Adaptive immune cells (B and T lymphocytes) infiltrate obesity-expanded VAT and actively promote insulin resistance by antigen presentation, cytokine secretion (e.g., IL-1 family), and modulation of macrophage polarization, while innate immune cells (macrophages) are central in early inflammatory responses. These immune programs increase local and systemic cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), which directly impair insulin signaling in target tissues. <cite id="24127133">B cells infiltrate VAT, present antigens to T cells, secrete inflammatory cytokines, and produce pathogenic antibodies contributing to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="22231651">Adaptive immune cells (B and T lymphocytes) in obesity-expanded VAT regulate inflammation and insulin resistance via cytokine secretion and macrophage modulation</cite> <cite id="30549014">Macrophage infiltration and shift to proinflammatory subtypes in adipose tissue increase TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and reduce adiponectin, with stronger links to insulin resistance in visceral fat</cite> <cite id="30398218">Adipocyte hypertrophy and apoptosis in visceral fat drive macrophage infiltration and proinflammatory cytokine production, promoting systemic inflammation linked to metabolic and cardiovascular complications</cite>. 

These inflammatory mediators also alter lipid metabolism in adipose tissue, increasing lipolysis and lipogenesis, thereby elevating circulating FFAs and promoting ectopic deposition in liver and muscle. <cite id="30058057">Pro-inflammatory cytokines in adipose tissue inhibit adipocyte insulin signaling, increasing lipolysis and lipogenesis, raising FFAs, and promoting ectopic fat deposition in liver and skeletal muscle, which worsens insulin resistance</cite>.

# Ectopic lipid deposition, lipotoxicity, and tissue-specific mechanisms

When adipose storage capacity is exceeded, FFAs (NEFAs) spill over into liver and skeletal muscle, where they are re-esterified and stored as triglyceride or accumulate as intramyocellular lipid (IMCL) and hepatic fat. In metabolically active tissues, this "ectopic" lipid triggers lipotoxicity via multiple mechanisms:

- Lipid species and organelle stress: Excess NEFAs generate toxic intermediates (e.g., diacylglycerols, ceramides, DAGs) that disrupt insulin receptor signaling and impair glucose uptake in muscle and hepatocytes; they also provoke mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, leading to ROS production and inflammatory signaling. <cite id="33561645">Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter non-adipose cells (liver, muscle, pancreas), are deposited as ectopic fat, and generate lipotoxicity that dysregulates mitochondria, ER, and lysosomes, increasing ROS and inflammation and blocking insulin action</cite> <cite id="19421860">Unoxidized long-chain fatty acids saturate adipose storage capacity, causing lipid spill over to liver, muscle, heart, and pancreatic islets; non-oxidative metabolism produces reactive lipid moieties that promote lipotoxic dysfunction and lipoapoptosis</cite>. 

- Skeletal muscle: Intramyocellular lipid accumulation correlates with insulin resistance; lipotoxic lipids impair mitochondrial β-oxidation, activate JNK and IKK pathways, perturb Ca2+ handling, and reduce GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane, diminishing glucose uptake. ER stress and UPR activation in muscle further dampen insulin signaling. <cite id="26741351">A growing body of data links ectopic lipid storage to impaired insulin action in skeletal muscle, with IMCL content and mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance and therapeutic strategies discussed</cite> <cite id="33561645">Ectopic lipid in muscle induces organelle stress and ROS, contributing to systemic inflammation and insulin resistance</cite>. 

- Liver: Hepatic steatosis from FFA overflux impairs insulin signaling via lipotoxic species and ER stress, while Kupffer cell activation and cytokine production propagate inflammation. Defective very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) secretion and lipid handling exacerbate hepatocellular stress and insulin resistance. <cite id="33561645">The liver is the most sensitive organ to insulin impairment in obesity, with hepatic insulin resistance preceding peripheral insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="30058057">Elevated FFAs promote hepatic and muscle ectopic fat deposition, lipotoxicity, and worsening insulin resistance via pro-inflammatory responses</cite>. 

- Systemic inflammation from adipose tissue: Inflammatory cytokines from VAT (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1) and immune infiltration further sensitize hepatocytes and myocytes to lipotoxic effects by amplifying NF-κB and ER stress pathways, creating a feed-forward cycle of inflammation and insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, and MCP-1 from adipocytes and infiltrating immune cells drive local and systemic inflammation that contributes to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="30549014">Adipose tissue inflammation is consistently associated with excess fat mass and insulin resistance, with stronger associations in visceral fat</cite>. 

# Integrated mechanism linking visceral adiposity to insulin resistance

1) Depot-specific biology: Visceral adipocytes enlarge and die, fail to differentiate, and secrete pro-inflammatory adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, resistin, visfatin, PAI-1), while anti-inflammatory adipokines (adiponectin) decline. <cite id="39287856">Adipocyte death and macrophage accumulation in VAT increase pro-inflammatory cytokines and reduce adiponectin</cite> <cite id="30549014">Visceral fat shows stronger adipokine shifts linked to insulin resistance</cite>. 

2) Inflammatory signaling hubs: VAT inflammation engages TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB pathways, increasing TNF-α/IL-6/IL-1 and recruiting/activating immune cells (macrophages, T and B cells), which propagate systemic cytokines that blunt insulin signaling in muscle and liver. <cite id="39287856">TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB are dominant pathways in adipose inflammation</cite> <cite id="24127133">B and T cells in VAT contribute to insulin resistance via inflammatory cytokines and immune modulation</cite>. 

3) Lipid flux and ectopic deposition: Adipokine- and cytokine-driven alterations in adipose lipid handling increase circulating FFAs; NEFAs are deposited ectopically in liver and muscle. Lipid accumulation triggers organelle stress, ROS, and inflammatory cascades that impair insulin receptor tyrosine kinase activity, IRS-1/2 serine phosphorylation, and downstream glucose transport and glycogen synthesis in hepatocytes and myocytes. <cite id="33561645">Excess FFAs drive ectopic lipid deposition and lipotoxicity across non-adipose tissues, disrupting organelles and insulin signaling</cite> <cite id="26741351">Skeletal muscle lipid content and mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance are linked to IMCL accumulation</cite> <cite id="30058057">Increased lipolysis and lipogenesis elevate FFAs and promote ectopic fat deposition with lipotoxic inflammation</cite>. 

4) Feed-forward amplification: Inflammatory cytokines and lipotoxic species mutually reinforce each other, reducing adipose storage capacity and insulin sensitivity, and promoting systemic insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">Adipose inflammation is an adaptive response that contributes to a visceral depot barrier for endotoxin; excessive fatty acid release worsens adipose inflammation and contributes to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="33809061">Visceral WAT dysfunction increases oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory adipokines, promoting systemic insulin resistance</cite>.

- Visceral adiposity is a stronger driver of systemic insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat, consistent with depot-specific inflammatory and adipokine profiles and greater ectopic lipid deposition in metabolically active organs. <cite id="30549014">Associations with insulin resistance are stronger for inflammation in visceral than subcutaneous fat</cite> <cite id="33561645">Hepatic insulin resistance develops earlier and is primary in obesity</cite>.

- Visceral adiposity drives insulin resistance through a coordinated adipokine-inflammatory program and ectopic lipid deposition. data.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Obesity-Linked Cardiac Dysfunction: An Up-Date on Current Knowledge.
data.abstract: Obesity is defined as excessive body fat accumulation, and worldwide obesity has nearly tripled since 1975. Excess of free fatty acids (FFAs) and triglycerides in obese individuals promote ectopic lipid accumulation in the liver, skeletal muscle tissue, and heart, among others, inducing insulin resistance, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes (T2D), atherosclerosis, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). These diseases are promoted by visceral white adipocyte tissue (WAT) dysfunction through an increase in pro-inflammatory adipokines, oxidative stress, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and adverse changes in the gut microbiome. In the heart, obesity and T2D induce changes in substrate utilization, tissue metabolism, oxidative stress, and inflammation, leading to myocardial fibrosis and ultimately cardiac dysfunction. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) are involved in the regulation of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, also improve insulin sensitivity, triglyceride levels, inflammation, and oxidative stress. The purpose of this review is to provide an update on the molecular mechanisms involved in obesity-linked CVD pathophysiology, considering pro-inflammatory cytokines, adipokines, and hormones, as well as the role of oxidative stress, inflammation, and PPARs. In addition, cell lines and animal models, biomarkers, gut microbiota dysbiosis, epigenetic modifications, and current therapeutic treatments in CVD associated with obesity are outlined in this paper.

data.title: Control of adipocyte differentiation in different fat depots; implications for pathophysiology or therapy.
data.abstract: Adipocyte differentiation and its impact on restriction or expansion of particular adipose tissue depots have physiological and pathophysiological significance in view of the different functions of these depots. Brown or "beige" fat [brown adipose tissue (BAT)] expansion can enhance thermogenesis, lipid oxidation, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance; conversely expanded visceral fat [visceral white adipose tissue (VAT)] is associated with insulin resistance, low grade inflammation, dyslipidemia, and cardiometabolic risk. The largest depot, subcutaneous white fat [subcutaneous white adipose tissue (SAT)], has important beneficial characteristics including storage of lipid "out of harms way" and secretion of adipokines, especially leptin and adiponectin, with positive metabolic effects including lipid oxidation, energy utilization, enhanced insulin action, and an anti-inflammatory role. The absence of these functions in lipodystrophies leads to major metabolic disturbances. An ability to expand white adipose tissue adipocyte differentiation would seem an important defense mechanism against the detrimental effects of energy excess and limit harmful accumulation of lipid in "ectopic" sites, such as liver and muscle. Adipocyte differentiation involves a transcriptional cascade with PPARγ being most important in SAT but less so in VAT, with increased angiogenesis also critical. The transcription factor, Islet1, is fairly specific to VAT and in vitro inhibits adipocyte differentiation. The physiological importance of Islet1 requires further study. Basic control of differentiation is similar in BAT but important differences include the effect of PGC-1α on mitochondrial biosynthesis and upregulation of UCP1; also PRDM16 plays a pivotal role in expression of the BAT phenotype. Modulation of the capacity or function of these different adipose tissue depots, by altering adipocyte differentiation or other means, holds promise for interventions that can be helpful in human disease, particularly cardiometabolic disorders associated with the world wide explosion of obesity.

data.title: Reappraisal of Adipose Tissue Inflammation in Obesity.
data.abstract: Chronic low-grade inflammation is a central component in the pathogenesis of obesity-related expansion of adipose tissue and complications in other metabolic tissues. Five different signaling pathways are defined as dominant determinants of adipose tissue inflammation: These are increased circulating endotoxin due to dysregulation in the microbiota-gut-brain axis, systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, and adipocyte death. Finally, the nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain (NOD) leucine-rich repeat family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome pathway is noted to be a key regulator of metabolic inflammation. The NLRP3 inflammasome and associated metabolic inflammation play an important role in the relationships among fatty acids and obesity. Several highly active molecules, including primarily leptin, resistin, adiponectin, visfatin, and classical cytokines, are abundantly released from adipocytes. The most important cytokines that are released by inflammatory cells infiltrating obese adipose tissue are tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 6 (IL-6), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) (CCL-2), and IL-1. All these molecules mentioned above act on immune cells, causing local and then general inflammation. Three metabolic pathways are noteworthy in the development of adipose tissue inflammation: toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/phosphatidylinositol-3'-kinase (PI3K)/Protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-derived unfolded protein response (UPR), and inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B kinase beta (IKKβ)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway. In fact, adipose tissue inflammation is an adaptive response that contributes to a visceral depot barrier that effectively filters gut-derived endotoxin. Excessive fatty acid release worsens adipose tissue inflammation and contributes to insulin resistance. However, suppression of adipose inflammation in obesity with anti-inflammatory drugs is not a rational solution and paradoxically promotes insulin resistance, despite beneficial effects on weight gain. Inflammatory pathways in adipocytes are indeed indispensable for maintaining systemic insulin sensitivity. Cannabinoid type 1 receptor (CB1R) is important in obesity-induced pro-inflammatory response; however, blockade of CB1R, contrary to anti-inflammatory drugs, breaks the links between insulin resistance and adipose tissue inflammation. Obesity, however, could be decreased by improving leptin signaling, white adipose tissue browning, gut microbiota interactions, and alleviating inflammation. Furthermore, capsaicin synthesized by chilies is thought to be a new and promising therapeutic option in obesity, as it prevents metabolic endotoxemia and systemic chronic low-grade inflammation caused by high-fat diet.
data.venue: Advances in experimental medicine and biology

data.title: B Lymphocytes in obesity-related adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance.
data.abstract: Obesity-related insulin resistance is a chronic inflammatory condition that often gives rise to type 2 diabetes (T2D). Much evidence supports a role for pro-inflammatory T cells and macrophages in promoting local inflammation in tissues such as visceral adipose tissue (VAT) leading to insulin resistance. More recently, B cells have emerged as an additional critical player in orchestrating these processes. B cells infiltrate VAT and display functional and phenotypic changes in response to diet-induced obesity. B cells contribute to insulin resistance by presenting antigens to T cells, secreting inflammatory cytokines, and producing pathogenic antibodies. B cell manipulation represents a novel approach to the treatment of obesity-related insulin resistance and potentially to the prevention of T2D. This review summarizes the roles of B cells in governing VAT inflammation and the mechanisms by which these cells contribute to altered glucose homeostasis in insulin resistance.
data.venue: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS

data.title: The adaptive immune system as a fundamental regulator of adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance.
data.abstract: Over the past decade, chronic inflammation in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) has gained acceptance as a lead promoter of insulin resistance in obesity. A great deal of evidence has pointed to the role of adipokines and innate immune cells, in particular, adipose tissue macrophages, in the regulation of fat inflammation and glucose homeostasis. However, more recently, cells of the adaptive immune system, specifically B and T lymphocytes, have emerged as unexpected promoters and controllers of insulin resistance. These adaptive immune cells infiltrate obesity expanded VAT and through cytokine secretion and macrophage modulation dictate the extent of the local inflammatory response, thereby directly impacting insulin resistance. The remarkable ability of our adaptive immune system to regulate insulin sensitivity and metabolism has unmasked a novel physiological function of this system, and promises new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to manage the disease. This review highlights critical roles of adipose tissue lymphocytes in governing glucose homeostasis.

data.title: Visceral fat and insulin resistance - what we know?
data.abstract: One of the most significant challenges of current medicine is the increasing prevalence of obesity worldwide that is accompanied by a wide range of chronic health complications and increased mortality. White adipose tissue actively contributes to metabolic regulation by production of a variety of hormones and cytokines, commonly referred to as adipokines. The spectrum and quantity of adipokines produced by the adipose tissue of obese patients is directly or indirectly involved in much obesity-related pathology (type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory response). One of the underlying mechanisms linking obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular complications is subclinical inflammation, primarily arising in visceral adipose tissue. Adipocyte size, number and polarization of lymphocytes and infiltrated macrophages are closely related to metabolic and obesity-related diseases. The storage capacity of hypertrophic adipocytes in obese patients is limited. This results in chronic energy overload and leads to increased apoptosis of adipocytes that in turn stimulates the infiltration of visceral adipose tissue by immune cells, in particular macrophages. These cells produce many proinflammatory factors; while the overall production of anti-inflammatory cytokines and adipokines is decreased. The constant release of proinflammatory factors into the circulation then contributes to a subclinical systemic inflammation, which is directly linked to the metabolic and cardiovascular complications of obesity.
data.venue: Biomedical papers of the Medical Faculty of the University Palacky, Olomouc, Czechoslovakia

data.title: Contribution of Adipose Tissue Inflammation to the Development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
data.abstract: The objective of this comprehensive review is to summarize and discuss the available evidence of how adipose tissue inflammation affects insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. Low-grade, chronic adipose tissue inflammation is characterized by infiltration of macrophages and other immune cell populations into adipose tissue, and a shift toward more proinflammatory subtypes of leukocytes. The infiltration of proinflammatory cells in adipose tissue is associated with an increased production of key chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2, proinflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins 1β and 6 as well as reduced expression of the key insulin-sensitizing adipokine, adiponectin. In both rodent models and humans, adipose tissue inflammation is consistently associated with excess fat mass and insulin resistance. In humans, associations with insulin resistance are stronger and more consistent for inflammation in visceral as opposed to subcutaneous fat. Further, genetic alterations in mouse models of obesity that reduce adipose tissue inflammation are-almost without exception-associated with improved insulin sensitivity. However, a dissociation between adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance can be observed in very few rodent models of obesity as well as in humans following bariatric surgery- or low-calorie-diet-induced weight loss, illustrating that the etiology of insulin resistance is multifactorial. Taken together, adipose tissue inflammation is a key factor in the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes in obesity, along with other factors that likely include inflammation and fat accumulation in other metabolically active tissues. © 2019 American Physiological Society. Compr Physiol 9:1-58, 2019.

data.title: Adipose tissue and insulin resistance in obese.
data.abstract: Currently, obesity has become a global health issue and is referred to as an epidemic. Dysfunctional obese adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in the development of insulin resistance. However, the mechanism of how dysfunctional obese-adipose tissue develops insulin-resistant circumstances remains poorly understood. Therefore, this review attempts to highlight the potential mechanisms behind obesity-associated insulin resistance. Multiple risk factors are directly or indirectly associated with the increased risk of obesity; among them, environmental factors, genetics, aging, gut microbiota, and diets are prominent. Once an individual becomes obese, adipocytes increase in their size; therefore, adipose tissues become larger and dysfunctional, recruit macrophages, and then these polarize to pro-inflammatory states. Enlarged adipose tissues release excess free fatty acids (FFAs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter inside the cells of non-adipose organs such as the liver, muscle, and pancreas, and are deposited as ectopic fat, generating lipotoxicity. Toxic lipids dysregulate cellular organelles, e.g., mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lysosomes. Dysregulated organelles release excess ROS and pro-inflammation, resulting in systemic inflammation. Long term low-grade systemic inflammation prevents insulin from its action in the insulin signaling pathway, disrupts glucose homeostasis, and results in systemic dysregulation. Overall, long-term obesity and overnutrition develop into insulin resistance and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation through lipotoxicity, creating the circumstances to develop clinical conditions. This review also shows that the liver is the most sensitive organ undergoing insulin impairment faster than other organs, and thus, hepatic insulin resistance is the primary event that leads to the subsequent development of peripheral tissue insulin resistance.

data.title: Adipose Tissue Dysfunction as Determinant of Obesity-Associated Metabolic Complications.
data.abstract: Obesity is a critical risk factor for the development of type 2 diabetes (T2D), and its prevalence is rising worldwide. White adipose tissue (WAT) has a crucial role in regulating systemic energy homeostasis. Adipose tissue expands by a combination of an increase in adipocyte size (hypertrophy) and number (hyperplasia). The recruitment and differentiation of adipose precursor cells in the subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), rather than merely inflating the cells, would be protective from the obesity-associated metabolic complications. In metabolically unhealthy obesity, the storage capacity of SAT, the largest WAT depot, is limited, and further caloric overload leads to the fat accumulation in ectopic tissues (e.g., liver, skeletal muscle, and heart) and in the visceral adipose depots, an event commonly defined as "lipotoxicity." Excessive ectopic lipid accumulation leads to local inflammation and insulin resistance (IR). Indeed, overnutrition triggers uncontrolled inflammatory responses in WAT, leading to chronic low-grade inflammation, therefore fostering the progression of IR. This review summarizes the current knowledge on WAT dysfunction in obesity and its associated metabolic abnormalities, such as IR. A better understanding of the mechanisms regulating adipose tissue expansion in obesity is required for the development of future therapeutic approaches in obesity-associated metabolic complications.

data.title: Inflammation and Metabolic Complications in HIV.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
We aim to provide an in-depth review of recent literature highlighting the role of inflammation involving the adipose tissue, liver, skeletal muscles, and gastrointestinal tract in the development of metabolic complications among persons living with HIV (PLWH).
RECENT FINDINGS
Recent studies in PLWH have demonstrated a significant association between circulating inflammatory markers and development of insulin resistance and metabolic complications. In adipose tissue, pro-inflammatory cytokine expression inhibits adipocyte insulin signaling, which alters lipid and glucose homeostasis. Increased lipolysis and lipogenesis elevate levels of circulating free fatty acids and promote ectopic fat deposition in liver and skeletal muscles. This leads to lipotoxicity characterized by a pro-inflammatory response with worsening insulin resistance. Finally, HIV is associated with gastrointestinal tract inflammation and changes in the gut microbiome resulting in reduced diversity, which is an additional risk factor for diabetes. Metabolic complications in PLWH are in part due to chronic, multisite tissue inflammation resulting in dysregulation of glucose and lipid trafficking, utilization, and storage.

data.title: Intramyocellular fat storage in metabolic diseases.
data.abstract: Over the past decades, obesity and its metabolic co-morbidities such as type 2 diabetes (T2D) developed to reach an endemic scale. However, the mechanisms leading to the development of T2D are still poorly understood. One main predictor for T2D seems to be lipid accumulation in "non-adipose" tissues, best known as ectopic lipid storage. A growing body of data suggests that these lipids may play a role in impairing insulin action in metabolic tissues, such as liver and skeletal muscle. This review aims to discuss recent literature linking ectopic lipid storage and insulin resistance, with emphasis on lipid deposition in skeletal muscle. The link between skeletal muscle lipid content and insulin sensitivity, as well as the mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance and potential therapeutic strategies to alleviate lipotoxic lipid pressure in skeletal muscle will be discussed.
data.venue: Hormone molecular biology and clinical investigation

data.title: Diabetes and apoptosis: lipotoxicity.
data.abstract: Obesity is an established risk factor in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease; all components that are part of the metabolic syndrome. Traditionally, insulin resistance has been defined in a glucocentric perspective. However, elevated systemic levels of fatty acids are now considered significant contributors towards the pathophysiological aspects associated with the syndrome. An overaccumulation of unoxidized long-chain fatty acids can saturate the storage capacity of adipose tissue, resulting in a lipid 'spill over' to non-adipose tissues, such as the liver, muscle, heart, and pancreatic-islets. Under these circumstances, such ectopic lipid deposition can have deleterious effects. The excess lipids are driven into alternative non-oxidative pathways, which result in the formation of reactive lipid moieties that promote metabolically relevant cellular dysfunction (lipotoxicity) and programmed cell-death (lipoapoptosis). Here, we focus on how both of these processes affect metabolically significant cell-types and highlight how lipotoxicity and sequential lipoapoptosis are as major mediators of insulin resistance, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
data.venue: Apoptosis : an international journal on programmed cell death
