# Summary

Visceral adiposity promotes insulin resistance through a coordinated interplay of depot-specific adipokine signaling, low-grade inflammation with immune cell infiltration, and ectopic lipid deposition in metabolically active tissues such as liver and skeletal muscle. Excess free fatty acids (FFAs) from dysfunctional visceral white adipose tissue (VAT) spill over into non-adipose tissues, where they accumulate ectopically and trigger lipotoxic stress, while inflammatory mediators from adipocytes and infiltrating immune cells propagate systemic insulin signaling defects. These processes converge on organelle stress, oxidative stress, and activation of inflammatory pathways (e.g., NF-κB, TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR), which impair insulin receptor signaling and downstream glucose metabolism in liver and muscle. <cite id="33809061">Excess free fatty acids and triglycerides in obesity promote ectopic lipid accumulation in liver and skeletal muscle, inducing insulin resistance and metabolic disease, with visceral WAT dysfunction increasing pro-inflammatory adipokines, oxidative stress, and activating RAAS and gut–metabolic axes</cite> <cite id="25688231">Expanded visceral fat is associated with insulin resistance and low-grade inflammation, whereas subcutaneous fat can be protective when it expands via adipocyte differentiation and adipokine secretion</cite>.

# Depot physiology and adipokine signaling

Visceral and subcutaneous adipose depots differ in adipocyte size, angiogenesis, and adipokine secretion patterns. Subcutaneous fat can expand with increased adipocyte number and differentiation, secreting leptin and adiponectin that enhance insulin action and lipid oxidation, whereas expanded visceral fat is linked to insulin resistance and inflammation. Depot-specific transcriptional programs (e.g., PPARγ activity and Islet1 in VAT) influence adipocyte differentiation and inflammatory propensity, shaping the local and systemic adipokine milieu. <cite id="25688231">Brown/beige fat expansion improves insulin sensitivity, while expanded visceral fat associates with insulin resistance and low-grade inflammation; subcutaneous fat expands beneficially via adipocyte differentiation and secretes leptin and adiponectin with positive metabolic effects</cite>. 

In obesity, hypertrophic adipocytes in visceral depots undergo apoptosis and fail to increase in number, leading to adipokine dysregulation. Pro-inflammatory adipokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, IL-1 family) are upregulated, while anti-inflammatory adipokines like adiponectin are reduced, promoting systemic inflammation and insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">Obesity-induced pro-inflammatory responses involve adipocyte death, macrophage accumulation, and increased release of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, and IL-1, with adiponectin acting as an insulin-sensitizing adipokine whose production is decreased in obesity</cite> <cite id="30549014">Adipose inflammation in humans shows stronger associations with insulin resistance in visceral than subcutaneous fat, with increased CCL2, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and reduced adiponectin</cite>. 

Specific adipokines implicated in VAT-driven insulin resistance include:
- TNF-α and IL-6, which suppress insulin signaling via activation of SOCS3, JNK, and IKKβ–NF-κB, impairing IRS-1/2 function in muscle and liver.
- PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1), resistin, and visfatin (visceral adipocyte-derived factor), which are elevated in VAT and promote insulin resistance through inflammatory and endocrine mechanisms.
- Omentin and apelin, which are enriched in VAT and can have context-dependent pro-inflammatory or insulin-sensitizing effects; in obesity, their balance shifts toward inflammation and insulin resistance.
- Adiponectin, which is relatively preserved or increased in lean states but typically reduced in obesity, counteracting insulin resistance via AMPK and improved endothelial function.

These depot-specific adipokine shifts, together with oxidative stress and gut-derived endotoxin, set a pro-inflammatory tone that undermines insulin sensitivity. <cite id="39287856">Leptin, resistin, adiponectin, visfatin, and classical cytokines are abundantly released from adipocytes, while TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, and IL-1 from infiltrating immune cells propagate systemic inflammation</cite> <cite id="33809061">Visceral WAT dysfunction increases pro-inflammatory adipokines and oxidative stress and is linked to gut microbiome dysbiosis and RAAS activation</cite>.

# Inflammation and immune infiltration in VAT

Chronic low-grade inflammation in VAT arises from multiple convergent pathways: endotoxemia via the microbiota–gut–brain axis, systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, adipocyte death, and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. These pathways converge on canonical inflammatory signaling axes (TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB), amplifying cytokine production and impairing insulin action. <cite id="39287856">Dominant determinants of adipose tissue inflammation include dysregulated microbiota–gut–brain signaling (endotoxin), systemic oxidative stress, macrophage accumulation, adipocyte death, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation; TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB pathways are key</cite>. 

Adaptive immune cells (B and T lymphocytes) infiltrate obesity-expanded VAT and actively promote insulin resistance by antigen presentation, cytokine secretion (e.g., IL-1 family), and modulation of macrophage polarization, while innate immune cells (macrophages) are central in early inflammatory responses. These immune programs increase local and systemic cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), which directly impair insulin signaling in target tissues. <cite id="24127133">B cells infiltrate VAT, present antigens to T cells, secrete inflammatory cytokines, and produce pathogenic antibodies contributing to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="22231651">Adaptive immune cells (B and T lymphocytes) in obesity-expanded VAT regulate inflammation and insulin resistance via cytokine secretion and macrophage modulation</cite> <cite id="30549014">Macrophage infiltration and shift to proinflammatory subtypes in adipose tissue increase TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and reduce adiponectin, with stronger links to insulin resistance in visceral fat</cite> <cite id="30398218">Adipocyte hypertrophy and apoptosis in visceral fat drive macrophage infiltration and proinflammatory cytokine production, promoting systemic inflammation linked to metabolic and cardiovascular complications</cite>. 

These inflammatory mediators also alter lipid metabolism in adipose tissue, increasing lipolysis and lipogenesis, thereby elevating circulating FFAs and promoting ectopic deposition in liver and muscle. <cite id="30058057">Pro-inflammatory cytokines in adipose tissue inhibit adipocyte insulin signaling, increasing lipolysis and lipogenesis, raising FFAs, and promoting ectopic fat deposition in liver and skeletal muscle, which worsens insulin resistance</cite>.

# Ectopic lipid deposition, lipotoxicity, and tissue-specific mechanisms

When adipose storage capacity is exceeded, FFAs (NEFAs) spill over into liver and skeletal muscle, where they are re-esterified and stored as triglyceride or accumulate as intramyocellular lipid (IMCL) and hepatic fat. In metabolically active tissues, this "ectopic" lipid triggers lipotoxicity via multiple mechanisms:

- Lipid species and organelle stress: Excess NEFAs generate toxic intermediates (e.g., diacylglycerols, ceramides, DAGs) that disrupt insulin receptor signaling and impair glucose uptake in muscle and hepatocytes; they also provoke mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, leading to ROS production and inflammatory signaling. <cite id="33561645">Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter non-adipose cells (liver, muscle, pancreas), are deposited as ectopic fat, and generate lipotoxicity that dysregulates mitochondria, ER, and lysosomes, increasing ROS and inflammation and blocking insulin action</cite> <cite id="19421860">Unoxidized long-chain fatty acids saturate adipose storage capacity, causing lipid spill over to liver, muscle, heart, and pancreatic islets; non-oxidative metabolism produces reactive lipid moieties that promote lipotoxic dysfunction and lipoapoptosis</cite>. 

- Skeletal muscle: Intramyocellular lipid accumulation correlates with insulin resistance; lipotoxic lipids impair mitochondrial β-oxidation, activate JNK and IKK pathways, perturb Ca2+ handling, and reduce GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane, diminishing glucose uptake. ER stress and UPR activation in muscle further dampen insulin signaling. <cite id="26741351">A growing body of data links ectopic lipid storage to impaired insulin action in skeletal muscle, with IMCL content and mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance and therapeutic strategies discussed</cite> <cite id="33561645">Ectopic lipid in muscle induces organelle stress and ROS, contributing to systemic inflammation and insulin resistance</cite>. 

- Liver: Hepatic steatosis from FFA overflux impairs insulin signaling via lipotoxic species and ER stress, while Kupffer cell activation and cytokine production propagate inflammation. Defective very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) secretion and lipid handling exacerbate hepatocellular stress and insulin resistance. <cite id="33561645">The liver is the most sensitive organ to insulin impairment in obesity, with hepatic insulin resistance preceding peripheral insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="30058057">Elevated FFAs promote hepatic and muscle ectopic fat deposition, lipotoxicity, and worsening insulin resistance via pro-inflammatory responses</cite>. 

- Systemic inflammation from adipose tissue: Inflammatory cytokines from VAT (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1) and immune infiltration further sensitize hepatocytes and myocytes to lipotoxic effects by amplifying NF-κB and ER stress pathways, creating a feed-forward cycle of inflammation and insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, and MCP-1 from adipocytes and infiltrating immune cells drive local and systemic inflammation that contributes to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="30549014">Adipose tissue inflammation is consistently associated with excess fat mass and insulin resistance, with stronger associations in visceral fat</cite>. 

# Integrated mechanism linking visceral adiposity to insulin resistance

1) Depot-specific biology: Visceral adipocytes enlarge and die, fail to differentiate, and secrete pro-inflammatory adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, resistin, visfatin, PAI-1), while anti-inflammatory adipokines (adiponectin) decline. <cite id="39287856">Adipocyte death and macrophage accumulation in VAT increase pro-inflammatory cytokines and reduce adiponectin</cite> <cite id="30549014">Visceral fat shows stronger adipokine shifts linked to insulin resistance</cite>. 

2) Inflammatory signaling hubs: VAT inflammation engages TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB pathways, increasing TNF-α/IL-6/IL-1 and recruiting/activating immune cells (macrophages, T and B cells), which propagate systemic cytokines that blunt insulin signaling in muscle and liver. <cite id="39287856">TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and IKKβ–NF-κB are dominant pathways in adipose inflammation</cite> <cite id="24127133">B and T cells in VAT contribute to insulin resistance via inflammatory cytokines and immune modulation</cite>. 

3) Lipid flux and ectopic deposition: Adipokine- and cytokine-driven alterations in adipose lipid handling increase circulating FFAs; NEFAs are deposited ectopically in liver and muscle. Lipid accumulation triggers organelle stress, ROS, and inflammatory cascades that impair insulin receptor tyrosine kinase activity, IRS-1/2 serine phosphorylation, and downstream glucose transport and glycogen synthesis in hepatocytes and myocytes. <cite id="33561645">Excess FFAs drive ectopic lipid deposition and lipotoxicity across non-adipose tissues, disrupting organelles and insulin signaling</cite> <cite id="26741351">Skeletal muscle lipid content and mechanisms of lipid-induced insulin resistance are linked to IMCL accumulation</cite> <cite id="30058057">Increased lipolysis and lipogenesis elevate FFAs and promote ectopic fat deposition with lipotoxic inflammation</cite>. 

4) Feed-forward amplification: Inflammatory cytokines and lipotoxic species mutually reinforce each other, reducing adipose storage capacity and insulin sensitivity, and promoting systemic insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">Adipose inflammation is an adaptive response that contributes to a visceral depot barrier for endotoxin; excessive fatty acid release worsens adipose inflammation and contributes to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="33809061">Visceral WAT dysfunction increases oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory adipokines, promoting systemic insulin resistance</cite>. 

# Clinical and mechanistic implications

- Visceral adiposity is a stronger driver of systemic insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat, consistent with depot-specific inflammatory and adipokine profiles and greater ectopic lipid deposition in metabolically active organs. <cite id="30549014">Associations with insulin resistance are stronger for inflammation in visceral than subcutaneous fat</cite> <cite id="33561645">Hepatic insulin resistance develops earlier and is primary in obesity</cite>. 

- Therapeutic modulation of depot biology (e.g., preserving subcutaneous fat expansion via adipocyte differentiation, reducing VAT inflammation, or limiting FFA flux) may improve insulin sensitivity. Strategies targeting inflammasome activation, ER stress/UPR, macrophage polarization, and specific adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, PAI-1, resistin, visfatin) are under investigation. <cite id="39287856">NLRP3 inflammasome is a key regulator of metabolic inflammation; improving leptin signaling, white adipose tissue browning, and alleviating inflammation are promising approaches</cite> <cite id="25688231">Modulating adipocyte differentiation and depot-specific programs holds promise for interventions in cardiometabolic disorders</cite>. 

- Caution is warranted when suppressing adipose inflammation: anti-inflammatory drugs can reduce local adipose inflammation but may paradoxically worsen insulin resistance, whereas targeting CB1 receptors or upstream drivers may be more favorable. <cite id="39287856">Suppression of adipose inflammation with anti-inflammatory drugs is not a rational solution and can promote insulin resistance, whereas CB1R blockade breaks links between insulin resistance and adipose inflammation</cite>. 

# Key takeaways

- Visceral adiposity drives insulin resistance through a coordinated adipokine-inflammatory program and ectopic lipid deposition. Pro-inflammatory adipokines and immune infiltration from VAT propagate systemic cytokines that impair insulin signaling, while FFAs accumulate ectopically in liver and muscle, inducing lipotoxic stress, organelle dysfunction, and inflammation. These processes interact in a feed-forward loop that establishes systemic insulin resistance. <cite id="39287856">Visceral WAT inflammation integrates endotoxin, oxidative stress, immune infiltration, and inflammasome activation via TLR4/PI3K/Akt, ER stress/UPR, and NF-κB pathways</cite> <cite id="33561645">Ectopic lipid deposition and lipotoxicity in liver and muscle disrupt organelles, increase ROS and inflammation, and prevent insulin action</cite> <cite id="30549014">Visceral adipose inflammation shows stronger associations with insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat</cite>.

<snippet id="27433843">Title: Mutations Associated with Acquired Resistance to PD-1 Blockade in Melanoma.
Authors: Zaretsky, Jesse M, Garcia-Diaz, Angel, Shin, Daniel S et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Approximately 75% of objective responses to anti-programmed death 1 (PD-1) therapy in patients with melanoma are durable, lasting for years, but delayed relapses have been noted long after initial objective tumor regression despite continuous therapy. Mechanisms of immune escape in this context are unknown.
METHODS
We analyzed biopsy samples from paired baseline and relapsing lesions in four patients with metastatic melanoma who had had an initial objective tumor regression in response to anti-PD-1 therapy (pembrolizumab) followed by disease progression months to years later.
RESULTS
Whole-exome sequencing detected clonal selection and outgrowth of the acquired resistant tumors and, in two of the four patients, revealed resistance-associated loss-of-function mutations in the genes encoding interferon-receptor-associated Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) or Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), concurrent with deletion of the wild-type allele. A truncating mutation in the gene encoding the antigen-presenting protein beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) was identified in a third patient. JAK1 and JAK2 truncating mutations resulted in a lack of response to interferon gamma, including insensitivity to its antiproliferative effects on cancer cells. The B2M truncating mutation led to loss of surface expression of major histocompatibility complex class I.
CONCLUSIONS
In this study, acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy in patients with melanoma was associated with defects in the pathways involved in interferon-receptor signaling and in antigen presentation. (Funded by the National Institutes of Health and others.).</snippet>
<snippet id="31792460">Title: Integrative molecular and clinical modeling of clinical outcomes to PD1 blockade in patients with metastatic melanoma.
Authors: Liu, David, Schilling, Bastian, Liu, Derek et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has demonstrated efficacy in many tumor types, but predictors of responsiveness to anti-PD1 ICB are incompletely characterized. In this study, we analyzed a clinically annotated cohort of patients with melanoma (n = 144) treated with anti-PD1 ICB, with whole-exome and whole-transcriptome sequencing of pre-treatment tumors. We found that tumor mutational burden as a predictor of response was confounded by melanoma subtype, whereas multiple novel genomic and transcriptomic features predicted selective response, including features associated with MHC-I and MHC-II antigen presentation. Furthermore, previous anti-CTLA4 ICB exposure was associated with different predictors of response compared to tumors that were naive to ICB, suggesting selective immune effects of previous exposure to anti-CTLA4 ICB. Finally, we developed parsimonious models integrating clinical, genomic and transcriptomic features to predict intrinsic resistance to anti-PD1 ICB in individual tumors, with validation in smaller independent cohorts limited by the availability of comprehensive data. Broadly, we present a framework to discover predictive features and build models of ICB therapeutic response.</snippet>
<snippet id="30021886">Title: MHC proteins confer differential sensitivity to CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade in untreated metastatic melanoma.
Authors: Rodig, Scott J, Gusenleitner, Daniel, Jackson, Donald G et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Science translational medicine
Abstract: Combination anti-cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) and anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy promotes antitumor immunity and provides superior benefit to patients with advanced-stage melanoma compared with either therapy alone. T cell immunity requires recognition of antigens in the context of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and class II proteins by CD8 + and CD4 + T cells, respectively. We examined MHC class I and class II protein expression on tumor cells from previously untreated melanoma patients and correlated the results with transcriptional and genomic analyses and with clinical response to anti-CTLA-4, anti-PD-1, or combination therapy. Most (>50% of cells) or complete loss of melanoma MHC class I membrane expression was observed in 78 of 181 cases (43%), was associated with transcriptional repression of HLA-A , HLA-B , HLA-C , and B2M , and predicted primary resistance to anti-CTLA-4, but not anti-PD-1, therapy. Melanoma MHC class II membrane expression on >1% cells was observed in 55 of 181 cases (30%), was associated with interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and IFN-γ-mediated gene signatures, and predicted response to anti-PD-1, but not anti-CTLA-4, therapy. We conclude that primary response to anti-CTLA-4 requires robust melanoma MHC class I expression. In contrast, primary response to anti-PD-1 is associated with preexisting IFN-γ-mediated immune activation that includes tumor-specific MHC class II expression and components of innate immunity when MHC class I is compromised. The benefits of combined checkpoint blockade may be attributable, in part, to distinct requirements for melanoma-specific antigen presentation to initiate antitumor immunity.</snippet>
<snippet id="27821490">Title: Suppression of Type I IFN Signaling in Tumors Mediates Resistance to Anti-PD-1 Treatment That Can Be Overcome by Radiotherapy.
Authors: Wang, Xiaohong, Schoenhals, Jonathan E, Li, Ailin et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Cancer research
Abstract: Immune checkpoint therapies exhibit impressive efficacy in some patients with melanoma or lung cancer, but the lack of response in most cases presses the question of how general efficacy can be improved. In addressing this question, we generated a preclinical tumor model to study anti-PD-1 resistance by in vivo passaging of Kras-mutated, p53-deficient murine lung cancer cells ( p53 R172HΔg/+ K-ras LA1/+ ) in a syngeneic host exposed to repetitive dosing with anti-mouse PD-1 antibodies. PD-L1 (CD274) expression did not differ between the resistant and parental tumor cells. However, the expression of important molecules in the antigen presentation pathway, including MHC class I and II, as well as β2-microglobulin, were significantly downregulated in the anti-PD-1-resistant tumors compared with parental tumors. Resistant tumors also contained fewer CD8 + (CD8α) and CD4 + tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and reduced production of IFNγ. Localized radiotherapy induced IFNβ production, thereby elevating MHC class I expression on both parental and resistant tumor cells and restoring the responsiveness of resistant tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy. Conversely, blockade of type I IFN signaling abolished the effect of radiosensitization in this setting. Collectively, these results identify a mechanism of PD-1 resistance and demonstrate that adjuvant radiotherapy can overcome resistance. These findings have immediate clinical implications for extending the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint therapy in patients. Cancer Res; 77(4); 839-50. ©2016 AACR .</snippet>
<snippet id="31703604">Title: Domatinostat favors the immunotherapy response by modulating the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME).
Authors: Bretz, Anne Catherine, Parnitzke, Ulrike, Kronthaler, Kerstin et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The efficacy of PD-(L)1 blockade depends on the composition of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and is generally higher in tumors with pre-existing cytotoxic T cells (CTL) than in those with low CTL numbers. Nonetheless, a significant proportion of patients with pre-existing immunity fail to respond, indicating a therapeutic potential for combining PD-(L)1 blockade with additional immunomodulatory agents in both CTL-high and -low immune phenotypes. Here, we evaluated domatinostat (4SC-202), a class I-selective histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, for its effect on the TIME and its antitumoral efficacy using syngeneic mouse models with CTL-high or CTL-low tumors.
METHODS
Domatinostat was evaluated in PD-1 blockade-insensitive CTL-low (CT26) and CTL-high (C38) syngeneic models alone and in combination with different immune-inhibitory and -stimulatory approaches. Effects on the immunophenotype were assessed via flow cytometry and RNA-seq analyses. The changes in RNA-seq-based immune signatures determined in a murine setting were investigated in patient samples from the first-dose cohort of the SENSITIZE trial (NCT03278665) evaluating domatinostat combined with pembrolizumab in advanced-stage melanoma patients refractory/nonresponding to PD-1 blockade.
RESULTS
Domatinostat increased the expression of antigen-presenting machinery (APM) genes and MHC class I and II molecules, along with CTL infiltration, in tumors of both immune phenotypes. In combination with PD-(L)1 blockade, domatinostat augmented antitumor effects substantially above the effects of single-agent therapies, displaying greater benefit in tumors with pre-existing CTLs. In this setting, the combination of domatinostat with agonistic anti-4-1BB or both PD-1 and LAG3 blockade further increased the antitumor efficacy. In CTL-low tumors, domatinostat enhanced the expression of genes known to reinforce immune responses against tumors. Specifically, domatinostat increased the expression of Ifng and genes associated with responses to pembrolizumab and nivolumab. Clinically, these findings were confirmed in patients with advanced melanoma treated with domatinostat for 14 days, who demonstrated elevated expression of APM and MHC genes, the IFNG gene, and the IFN-γ and pembrolizumab response signatures in individual tumor samples.
CONCLUSION
In summary, these data suggest a promising potential of domatinostat in combination with immunotherapy to improve the outcome of refractory cancer patients.</snippet>

<snippet id="34215690">Title: STING agonist loaded lipid nanoparticles overcome anti-PD-1 resistance in melanoma lung metastasis via NK cell activation.
Authors: Nakamura, Takashi, Sato, Takanori, Endo, Rikito et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Resistance to an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) is a major obstacle in cancer immunotherapy. The causes of ICI resistance include major histocompatibility complex (MHC)/histocompatibility locus antigen (HLA) class I loss, neoantigen loss, and incomplete antigen presentation. Elimination by natural killer (NK) cells would be expected to be an effective strategy for the treatment of these ICI-resistant tumors. We previously demonstrated that a lipid nanoparticle containing a stimulator of an interferon gene (STING) agonist (STING-LNP) efficiently induced antitumor activity via the activation of NK cells. Thus, we evaluated the potential of reducing ICI resistance by STING-LNPs.
METHODS
Lung metastasis of a B16-F10 mouse melanoma was used as an anti-programmed cell death 1 (anti-PD-1)-resistant mouse model. The mice were intravenously injected with the STING-LNP and the mechanism responsible for the improvement of anti-PD-1 resistance by the STING-LNPs was analyzed by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry. The dynamics of STING-LNP were also investigated.
RESULTS
Although anti-PD-1 monotherapy failed to induce an antitumor effect, the combination of the STING-LNP and anti-PD-1 exerted a synergistic antitumor effect. Our results indicate that the STING-LNP treatment significantly increased the expression of CD3, CD4, NK1.1, PD-1 and interferon (IFN)-γ in lung metastases. This change appears to be initiated by the type I IFN produced by liver macrophages that contain the internalized STING-LNPs, leading to the systemic activation of NK cells that express PD-1. The activated NK cells appeared to produce IFN-γ, resulting in an increase in the expression of the PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) in cancer cells, thus leading to a synergistic antitumor effect when anti-PD-1 is administered.
CONCLUSIONS
We provide a demonstration to show that a STING-LNP treatment can overcome PD-1 resistance in a B16-F10 lung metastasis model. The mechanism responsible for this indicates that NK cells are activated by stimulating the STING pathway which, in turn, induced the expression of PD-L1 on cancer cells. Based on the findings reported herein, the STING-LNP represents a promising candidate for use in combination therapy with anti-PD-1-resistant tumors.</snippet>
<snippet id="29025772">Title: Impaired HLA Class I Antigen Processing and Presentation as a Mechanism of Acquired Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Lung Cancer.
Authors: Gettinger, Scott, Choi, Jungmin, Hastings, Katherine et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Cancer discovery
Abstract: Mechanisms of acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are poorly understood. We leveraged a collection of 14 ICI-resistant lung cancer samples to investigate whether alterations in genes encoding HLA Class I antigen processing and presentation machinery (APM) components or interferon signaling play a role in acquired resistance to PD-1 or PD-L1 antagonistic antibodies. Recurrent mutations or copy-number changes were not detected in our cohort. In one case, we found acquired homozygous loss of B2M that caused lack of cell-surface HLA Class I expression in the tumor and a matched patient-derived xenograft (PDX). Downregulation of B2M was also found in two additional PDXs established from ICI-resistant tumors. CRISPR-mediated knockout of B2m in an immunocompetent lung cancer mouse model conferred resistance to PD-1 blockade in vivo , proving its role in resistance to ICIs. These results indicate that HLA Class I APM disruption can mediate escape from ICIs in lung cancer. Significance: As programmed death 1 axis inhibitors are becoming more established in standard treatment algorithms for diverse malignancies, acquired resistance to these therapies is increasingly being encountered. Here, we found that defective antigen processing and presentation can serve as a mechanism of such resistance in lung cancer. Cancer Discov; 7(12); 1420-35. ©2017 AACR. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 1355 .</snippet>

<snippet id="35471840">Title: Resistance Mechanisms to Anti-PD Cancer Immunotherapy.
Authors: Vesely, Matthew D, Zhang, Tianxiang, Chen, Lieping | Year: 2022 | Journal: Annual review of immunology
Abstract: The transformative success of antibodies targeting the PD-1 (programmed death 1)/B7-H1 (B7 homolog 1) pathway (anti-PD therapy) has revolutionized cancer treatment. However, only a fraction of patients with solid tumors and some hematopoietic malignancies respond to anti-PD therapy, and the reason for failure in other patients is less known. By dissecting the mechanisms underlying this resistance, current studies reveal that the tumor microenvironment is a major location for resistance to occur. Furthermore, the resistance mechanisms appear to be highly heterogeneous. Here, we discuss recent human cancer data identifying mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy. We review evidence for immune-based resistance mechanisms such as loss of neoantigens, defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling, immune inhibitory molecules, and exclusion of T cells. We also review the clinical evidence for emerging mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy, such as alterations in metabolism, microbiota, and epigenetics. Finally, we discuss strategies to overcome anti-PD therapy resistance and emphasize the need to develop additional immunotherapies based on the concept of normalization cancer immunotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="27903500">Title: Primary Resistance to PD-1 Blockade Mediated by JAK1/2 Mutations.
Authors: Shin, Daniel Sanghoon, Zaretsky, Jesse M, Escuin-Ordinas, Helena et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Cancer discovery
Abstract: UNLABELLED
Loss-of-function mutations in JAK1/2 can lead to acquired resistance to anti-programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy. We reasoned that they may also be involved in primary resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. JAK1/2-inactivating mutations were noted in tumor biopsies of 1 of 23 patients with melanoma and in 1 of 16 patients with mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer treated with PD-1 blockade. Both cases had a high mutational load but did not respond to anti-PD-1 therapy. Two out of 48 human melanoma cell lines had JAK1/2 mutations, which led to a lack of PD-L1 expression upon interferon gamma exposure mediated by an inability to signal through the interferon gamma receptor pathway. JAK1/2 loss-of-function alterations in The Cancer Genome Atlas confer adverse outcomes in patients. We propose that JAK1/2 loss-of-function mutations are a genetic mechanism of lack of reactive PD-L1 expression and response to interferon gamma, leading to primary resistance to PD-1 blockade therapy.
SIGNIFICANCE
A key functional result from somatic JAK1/2 mutations in a cancer cell is the inability to respond to interferon gamma by expressing PD-L1 and many other interferon-stimulated genes. <snippet id="27433843">Title: Mutations Associated with Acquired Resistance to PD-1 Blockade in Melanoma.
Authors: Zaretsky, Jesse M, Garcia-Diaz, Angel, Shin, Daniel S et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Approximately 75% of objective responses to anti-programmed death 1 (PD-1) therapy in patients with melanoma are durable, lasting for years, but delayed relapses have been noted long after initial objective tumor regression despite continuous therapy. Mechanisms of immune escape in this context are unknown.
METHODS
We analyzed biopsy samples from paired baseline and relapsing lesions in four patients with metastatic melanoma who had had an initial objective tumor regression in response to anti-PD-1 therapy (pembrolizumab) followed by disease progression months to years later.
RESULTS
Whole-exome sequencing detected clonal selection and outgrowth of the acquired resistant tumors and, in two of the four patients, revealed resistance-associated loss-of-function mutations in the genes encoding interferon-receptor-associated Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) or Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), concurrent with deletion of the wild-type allele. A truncating mutation in the gene encoding the antigen-presenting protein beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) was identified in a third patient. JAK1 and JAK2 truncating mutations resulted in a lack of response to interferon gamma, including insensitivity to its antiproliferative effects on cancer cells. The B2M truncating mutation led to loss of surface expression of major histocompatibility complex class I.

<snippet id="28303311">Title: [Immunotherapy of cancer with checkpoint inhibitors : Not only in malignant melanoma].
Authors: Neubauer, A | Year: 2017 | Journal: Der Internist
Abstract: The newest weapon in cancer therapy is checkpoint inhibition, which is the result of basic immunology research. The success of this therapy is based on the fact that upon light microscopy, many solid tumors harbor lymphocytic cells infiltrating the tumor (TILs), and in many solid tumors, the presence of these TILs are prognostic. Ipilimumab was the first monoclonal antibody developed against a target present on T cells after becoming activated, CTLA-4. In malignant melanoma, ipilimumab showed its beneficial effect as compared to a placebo peptide. However, the therapy with this antibody harbors significant toxicity. Meanwhile, other targets such as PD-1, also expressed on (late) activated T cells, were identified, and therapies with antibodies inhibiting PD-1/PD-L1 are less toxic. Although these antibodies show response only in a minority of patients, the benefit seems durable in some of these patients. In solid tumors such as melanoma or non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), treatment with PD-1 inhibitors has resulted in a significant prolongation of survival, even in first-line treatment. As these drugs have been approved in many indications, it is important to know the drugs and side effects. Resistance towards these drugs are caused by low expression of the natural ligand, PD-L1, in the tumor tissue, as well as acquired loss of signal transduction of interferon-related genes such as JAK1 or JAK2, respectively. Also new in cancer therapy are bispecific T cell engager monoclonal antibodies (BiTEs) such as blinatumomab, and autologous chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells (CAR-Ts). The later have proven their efficacy mainly in hematological neoplasias such as precursor-B-ALL. The dramatic costs of all these new drugs will have an enormous impact on the health care systems in the near future.</snippet>
<snippet id="31310587">Title: Tumor suppressor TET2 promotes cancer immunity and immunotherapy efficacy.
Authors: Xu, Yan-Ping, Lv, Lei, Liu, Ying et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: The Journal of clinical investigation
Abstract: Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding TET DNA dioxygenase occur frequently in hematopoietic malignancy, but rarely in solid tumors which instead commonly have reduced activity. The impact of decreased TET activity in solid tumors is not known. Here we show that TET2 mediates interferon γ (IFNγ)-JAK-STAT signaling pathway to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression, lymphocyte infiltration and cancer immunity. IFNγ stimulated STAT1 to bind TET2 and recruit TET2 to hydroxymethylate chemokine and PD-L1 genes. Reduced TET activity was associated with decreased TH1-type chemokines and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and the progression of human colon cancer. Deletion of Tet2 in murine melanoma and colon tumor cells reduced chemokine expression and TILs, enabling tumors to evade anti-tumor immunity and to resist anti-PD-L1 therapy. Conversely, stimulating TET activity by systematic injection of its co-factor, ascorbate/vitamin C, increased chemokine and TILs, leading to enhanced anti-tumor immunity and anti-PD-L1 efficacy and extended lifespan of tumor-bearing mice. These results suggest an IFNγ-JAK-STAT-TET signaling pathway that mediates tumor response to anti-PD-L1/PD-1 therapy and is frequently disrupted in solid tumors. <snippet id="35471840">Title: Resistance Mechanisms to Anti-PD Cancer Immunotherapy.
Authors: Vesely, Matthew D, Zhang, Tianxiang, Chen, Lieping | Year: 2022 | Journal: Annual review of immunology
Abstract: The transformative success of antibodies targeting the PD-1 (programmed death 1)/B7-H1 (B7 homolog 1) pathway (anti-PD therapy) has revolutionized cancer treatment. However, only a fraction of patients with solid tumors and some hematopoietic malignancies respond to anti-PD therapy, and the reason for failure in other patients is less known. By dissecting the mechanisms underlying this resistance, current studies reveal that the tumor microenvironment is a major location for resistance to occur. Furthermore, the resistance mechanisms appear to be highly heterogeneous. Here, we discuss recent human cancer data identifying mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy. We review evidence for immune-based resistance mechanisms such as loss of neoantigens, defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling, immune inhibitory molecules, and exclusion of T cells. We also review the clinical evidence for emerging mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy, such as alterations in metabolism, microbiota, and epigenetics. Finally, we discuss strategies to overcome anti-PD therapy resistance and emphasize the need to develop additional immunotherapies based on the concept of normalization cancer immunotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="37076040">Title: Immune-checkpoint inhibitor resistance in cancer treatment: Current progress and future directions.
Authors: Zhang, Chenyue, Zhang, Chenxing, Wang, Haiyong | Year: 2023 | Journal: Cancer letters
Abstract: Cancer treatment has been advanced with the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) exemplified by anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) drugs. Patients have reaped substantial benefit from ICIs in many cancer types. However, few patients benefit from ICIs whereas the vast majority undergoing these treatments do not obtain survival benefit. Even for patients with initial responses, they may encounter drug resistance in their subsequent treatments, which limits the efficacy of ICIs. Therefore, a deepening understanding of drug resistance is critically important for the explorations of approaches to reverse drug resistance and to boost ICI efficacy. In the present review, different mechanisms of ICI resistance have been summarized according to the tumor intrinsic, tumor microenvironment (TME) and host classifications. We further elaborated corresponding strategies to battle against such resistance accordingly, which include targeting defects in antigen presentation, dysregulated interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, neoantigen depletion, upregulation of other T cell checkpoints as well as immunosuppression and exclusion mediated by TME. Moreover, regarding the host, several additional approaches that interfere with diet and gut microbiome have also been described in reversing ICI resistance. Additionally, we provide an overall glimpse into the ongoing clinical trials that utilize these mechanisms to overcome ICI resistance. Finally, we summarize the challenges and opportunities that needs to be addressed in the investigation of ICI resistance mechanisms, with the aim to benefit more patients with cancer.</snippet>

<snippet id="34215690">Title: STING agonist loaded lipid nanoparticles overcome anti-PD-1 resistance in melanoma lung metastasis via NK cell activation.
Authors: Nakamura, Takashi, Sato, Takanori, Endo, Rikito et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Resistance to an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) is a major obstacle in cancer immunotherapy. The causes of ICI resistance include major histocompatibility complex (MHC)/histocompatibility locus antigen (HLA) class I loss, neoantigen loss, and incomplete antigen presentation. Elimination by natural killer (NK) cells would be expected to be an effective strategy for the treatment of these ICI-resistant tumors. We previously demonstrated that a lipid nanoparticle containing a stimulator of an interferon gene (STING) agonist (STING-LNP) efficiently induced antitumor activity via the activation of NK cells. Thus, we evaluated the potential of reducing ICI resistance by STING-LNPs.
METHODS
Lung metastasis of a B16-F10 mouse melanoma was used as an anti-programmed cell death 1 (anti-PD-1)-resistant mouse model. The mice were intravenously injected with the STING-LNP and the mechanism responsible for the improvement of anti-PD-1 resistance by the STING-LNPs was analyzed by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry. The dynamics of STING-LNP were also investigated.
RESULTS
Although anti-PD-1 monotherapy failed to induce an antitumor effect, the combination of the STING-LNP and anti-PD-1 exerted a synergistic antitumor effect. Our results indicate that the STING-LNP treatment significantly increased the expression of CD3, CD4, NK1.1, PD-1 and interferon (IFN)-γ in lung metastases. This change appears to be initiated by the type I IFN produced by liver macrophages that contain the internalized STING-LNPs, leading to the systemic activation of NK cells that express PD-1. The activated NK cells appeared to produce IFN-γ, resulting in an increase in the expression of the PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) in cancer cells, thus leading to a synergistic antitumor effect when anti-PD-1 is administered.
CONCLUSIONS
We provide a demonstration to show that a STING-LNP treatment can overcome PD-1 resistance in a B16-F10 lung metastasis model. The mechanism responsible for this indicates that NK cells are activated by stimulating the STING pathway which, in turn, induced the expression of PD-L1 on cancer cells. Based on the findings reported herein, the STING-LNP represents a promising candidate for use in combination therapy with anti-PD-1-resistant tumors.</snippet>

Authors: Liu, David, Schilling, Bastian, Liu, Derek et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has demonstrated efficacy in many tumor types, but predictors of responsiveness to anti-PD1 ICB are incompletely characterized. # Summary of Mechanisms of Primary Resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 Blockade in Human Tumors, with Emphasis on Antigen Presentation and Interferon Signaling

## Overview
Across multiple human tumor cohorts and translational studies, primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade is consistently linked to defects in antigen presentation and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling that undermine T-cell recognition and immune synapse function within the tumor microenvironment. These defects include loss of MHC class I expression, mutations in antigen-processing/presentation genes (e.g., B2M, TAP1/2, ERAP1), and inactivating alterations in IFN-γ pathway components (e.g., JAK1/2), which collectively reduce tumor immunogenicity and responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Reviews of clinical data converge on these mechanisms as among the most reproducible, alongside additional contributors such as T-cell exclusion and immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. <cite id="35471840">Reviews of human cancer data identify defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling as core immune-based mechanisms of resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy</cite> <cite id="37076040">Mechanistic summaries emphasize defects in antigen presentation and dysregulated IFN-γ signaling as prominent causes of immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance</cite>.

## Antigen Presentation Defects

- Loss of MHC class I and B2M alterations: In melanoma, acquired resistance has been associated with loss-of-function mutations in B2M and deletions affecting IFN-γ pathway genes (JAK1/JAK2), leading to loss of MHC class I surface expression and impaired responsiveness to interferon; these alterations directly abrogate CD8+ T-cell recognition and PD-1 inhibitor sensitivity. <cite id="27433843">Paired biopsies from melanoma patients who relapsed on pembrolizumab showed JAK1/2 mutations and a B2M truncation; JAK mutations caused lack of response to IFN-γ, and B2M loss caused loss of MHC class I expression</cite>. In lung cancer, acquired homozygous B2M loss and downregulation of B2M in multiple patient-derived xenografts established from ICI-resistant tumors led to loss of HLA class I expression; CRISPR-mediated B2m knockout in an immunocompetent mouse model conferred in vivo resistance to PD-1 blockade, establishing causality. <cite id="29025772">In lung cancer, acquired B2M loss and reduced B2M expression in ICI-resistant PDXs caused lack of HLA class I, and B2m knockout in a mouse model conferred resistance to PD-1 blockade</cite>.

- MHC class I/II expression and clinical response: Large melanoma cohorts treated with anti-PD-1 show that loss of MHC class I expression predicts primary resistance to PD-1 therapy, whereas tumor-specific MHC class II expression and IFN-γ signatures predict response even when MHC class I is compromised, indicating distinct antigen-presenting requirements for PD-1 sensitivity. <cite id="30021886">In 181 melanoma patients, 43% had complete or >50% loss of MHC class I expression, associated with repression of HLA-A/B/C and B2M and predicting primary resistance to anti-CTLA-4 but not anti-PD-1; conversely, MHC class II expression with IFN-γ signatures predicted response to anti-PD-1, including when MHC class I was compromised</cite>. Transcriptomic profiling further identifies features associated with MHC-I and MHC-II antigen presentation as predictors of selective response and intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1 in melanoma. <cite id="31792460">In 144 melanoma patients treated with anti-PD-1, features linked to MHC-I and MHC-II antigen presentation predicted selective response and intrinsic resistance</cite>.

- Coexisting alterations in antigen processing and IFN-γ signaling: Post-PD-1 settings can reveal convergent genetic hits (e.g., B2M loss plus impaired JAK1 signaling) that jointly mediate pan-T-cell immune escape, with B2M loss conferring CD8+ T-cell resistance and impaired JAK1 affecting CD4+ T-cell function. <cite id="35969233">A melanoma patient who progressed after anti-PD-1 and anti-LAG3 acquired B2M loss and impaired JAK1 signaling that coexisted in progressing tumor cells, mediating resistance via distinct T-cell escape pathways</cite>.

## Interferon Signaling Alterations

- Inactivating JAK1/2 mutations: Primary resistance mediated by JAK1/2 loss-of-function has been documented in human tumors, leading to failure of IFN-γ signaling, lack of PD-L1 induction, and intrinsic resistance to PD-1 blockade. <cite id="27903500">JAK1/2 inactivating mutations were identified in human tumors and in melanoma cell lines, causing inability to signal through the IFN-γ receptor pathway, failure of PD-L1 expression upon IFN-γ exposure, and primary resistance to PD-1 therapy</cite>. Reviews synthesize that such mutations abrogate reactive PD-L1 expression and multiple IFN-stimulated genes, explaining nonresponse to PD-1/PD-L1 agents. <cite id="27903500">Somatic JAK1/2 loss-of-function results in lack of reactive PD-L1 expression and resistance to PD-1 blockade</cite> <cite id="35471840">Human data show that interferon signaling defects are common resistance mechanisms to anti-PD therapy</cite>.

- Downstream interferon pathway disruptions: Epigenetic and enzymatic regulators of IFN-γ–STAT1 signaling (e.g., TET2) influence PD-L1 and chemokine gene expression, lymphocyte infiltration, and immunotherapy responsiveness; reduced TET activity associates with decreased TH1-type chemokines, fewer tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and tumor progression, and genetic deletion in tumor cells impairs anti-PD-L1 efficacy. <cite id="31310587">TET2 mediates IFN-γ–JAK–STAT signaling to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression and lymphocyte infiltration; reduced TET activity is linked to decreased TH1 chemokines, lower TILs, and progression, and Tet2 deletion in tumor cells reduces chemokines/TILs and resistance to anti-PD-L1</cite>.

- Type I IFN axis and radiosensitization: Preclinical humanized models demonstrate that suppression of type I IFN signaling confers resistance to anti-PD-1, while restoring IFN signaling (e.g., via radiotherapy) can re-sensitize tumors by upregulating antigen presentation machinery and PD-L1, highlighting the therapeutic leverage of IFN pathways. <cite id="27821490">In a murine lung cancer model, anti-PD-1–resistant tumors showed downregulation of MHC I/II and β2-microglobulin, fewer TILs, and reduced IFN-γ; radiotherapy induced IFNβ, increased MHC expression, restored anti-PD-1 sensitivity, whereas blocking type I IFN signaling abrogated these effects</cite>.

## Contextualizing Antigen Presentation and IFN Defects

- Heterogeneity by tumor type and prior therapy: Melanoma and lung cancer exemplify antigen presentation defects (B2M loss, MHC I/II dysregulation) and IFN pathway alterations as primary resistance mechanisms, with distinct MHC dependencies for CTLA-4 versus PD-1. <cite id="30021886">Loss of MHC class I predicts primary resistance to anti-CTLA-4 but not anti-PD-1, whereas MHC class II expression and IFN-γ signatures predict PD-1 response</cite>. In melanoma cohorts, MHC presentation features remain strong predictors of intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1 independent of tumor mutational burden. <cite id="31792460">MHC-I and MHC-II features predicted selective response and intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1, and TMB was confounded by melanoma subtype</cite>.

- Clinical validation and emerging biomarkers: Human studies validate HLA class I antigen processing/presentation disruptions as mechanisms of acquired resistance in lung cancer and show that domatinostat (a class I HDAC inhibitor) upregulates antigen-presenting machinery and IFN-γ signatures in tumors and patient samples, enhancing responses in PD-1–resistant settings. <cite id="29025772">HLA class I APM disruption mediated escape from ICIs in lung cancer</cite> <cite id="31703604">Domatinostat increased APM/MHC I/II gene expression and IFN-γ signatures in tumors and melanoma patients, augmenting PD-1 blockade efficacy in preclinical and clinical samples</cite>.

## Conclusions

- Most consistently supported mechanisms of primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in human tumors involve antigen presentation defects (e.g., B2M loss, MHC I/II downregulation) and interferon signaling alterations (e.g., JAK1/2 loss, TET2 dysfunction, type I IFN suppression), which jointly impair T-cell recognition, co-stimulation, and immune infiltration. <cite id="35471840">Defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling are repeatedly observed in human tumors as resistance mechanisms to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy</cite> <cite id="37076040">Dysregulated IFN-γ signaling and defects in antigen presentation are central axes of ICI resistance</cite>.

- These defects show tumor-type–specific prevalence and functional dependencies, with melanoma and lung cancer providing strong clinical and mechanistic evidence. Therapeutic strategies that restore antigen presentation (e.g., via HDAC inhibition) or augment interferon signaling (e.g., radiotherapy) can overcome resistance and re-sensitize tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. <cite id="31703604">HDAC inhibition upregulated antigen presentation and IFN signatures and enhanced PD-1 efficacy in resistant models and patient samples</cite> <cite id="27821490">Restoring type I IFN signaling with radiotherapy increased MHC expression and reversed anti-PD-1 resistance in vivo</cite>.

</answer>

data.abstract: Immune checkpoint therapies exhibit impressive efficacy in some patients with melanoma or lung cancer, but the lack of response in most cases presses the question of how general efficacy can be improved. In addressing this question, we generated a preclinical tumor model to study anti-PD-1 resistance by in vivo passaging of Kras-mutated, p53-deficient murine lung cancer cells ( p53 R172HΔg/+ K-ras LA1/+ ) in a syngeneic host exposed to repetitive dosing with anti-mouse PD-1 antibodies. PD-L1 (CD274) expression did not differ between the resistant and parental tumor cells. However, the expression of important molecules in the antigen presentation pathway, including MHC class I and II, as well as β2-microglobulin, were significantly downregulated in the anti-PD-1-resistant tumors compared with parental tumors. Resistant tumors also contained fewer CD8 + (CD8α) and CD4 + tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and reduced production of IFNγ. Localized radiotherapy induced IFNβ production, thereby elevating MHC class I expression on both parental and resistant tumor cells and restoring the responsiveness of resistant tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy. Conversely, blockade of type I IFN signaling abolished the effect of radiosensitization in this setting. Collectively, these results identify a mechanism of PD-1 resistance and demonstrate that adjuvant radiotherapy can overcome resistance. These findings have immediate clinical implications for extending the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint therapy in patients. Cancer Res; 77(4); 839-50. ©2016 AACR .

data.title: Domatinostat favors the immunotherapy response by modulating the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME).
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The efficacy of PD-(L)1 blockade depends on the composition of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and is generally higher in tumors with pre-existing cytotoxic T cells (CTL) than in those with low CTL numbers. Nonetheless, a significant proportion of patients with pre-existing immunity fail to respond, indicating a therapeutic potential for combining PD-(L)1 blockade with additional immunomodulatory agents in both CTL-high and -low immune phenotypes. Here, we evaluated domatinostat (4SC-202), a class I-selective histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, for its effect on the TIME and its antitumoral efficacy using syngeneic mouse models with CTL-high or CTL-low tumors.
METHODS
Domatinostat was evaluated in PD-1 blockade-insensitive CTL-low (CT26) and CTL-high (C38) syngeneic models alone and in combination with different immune-inhibitory and -stimulatory approaches. Effects on the immunophenotype were assessed via flow cytometry and RNA-seq analyses. The changes in RNA-seq-based immune signatures determined in a murine setting were investigated in patient samples from the first-dose cohort of the SENSITIZE trial (NCT03278665) evaluating domatinostat combined with pembrolizumab in advanced-stage melanoma patients refractory/nonresponding to PD-1 blockade.
RESULTS
Domatinostat increased the expression of antigen-presenting machinery (APM) genes and MHC class I and II molecules, along with CTL infiltration, in tumors of both immune phenotypes. In combination with PD-(L)1 blockade, domatinostat augmented antitumor effects substantially above the effects of single-agent therapies, displaying greater benefit in tumors with pre-existing CTLs. In this setting, the combination of domatinostat with agonistic anti-4-1BB or both PD-1 and LAG3 blockade further increased the antitumor efficacy. In CTL-low tumors, domatinostat enhanced the expression of genes known to reinforce immune responses against tumors. Specifically, domatinostat increased the expression of Ifng and genes associated with responses to pembrolizumab and nivolumab. Clinically, these findings were confirmed in patients with advanced melanoma treated with domatinostat for 14 days, who demonstrated elevated expression of APM and MHC genes, the IFNG gene, and the IFN-γ and pembrolizumab response signatures in individual tumor samples.
CONCLUSION
In summary, these data suggest a promising potential of domatinostat in combination with immunotherapy to improve the outcome of refractory cancer patients.

data.title: STING agonist loaded lipid nanoparticles overcome anti-PD-1 resistance in melanoma lung metastasis via NK cell activation.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Resistance to an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) is a major obstacle in cancer immunotherapy. The causes of ICI resistance include major histocompatibility complex (MHC)/histocompatibility locus antigen (HLA) class I loss, neoantigen loss, and incomplete antigen presentation. Elimination by natural killer (NK) cells would be expected to be an effective strategy for the treatment of these ICI-resistant tumors. We previously demonstrated that a lipid nanoparticle containing a stimulator of an interferon gene (STING) agonist (STING-LNP) efficiently induced antitumor activity via the activation of NK cells. Thus, we evaluated the potential of reducing ICI resistance by STING-LNPs.
METHODS
Lung metastasis of a B16-F10 mouse melanoma was used as an anti-programmed cell death 1 (anti-PD-1)-resistant mouse model. The mice were intravenously injected with the STING-LNP and the mechanism responsible for the improvement of anti-PD-1 resistance by the STING-LNPs was analyzed by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry. The dynamics of STING-LNP were also investigated.
RESULTS
Although anti-PD-1 monotherapy failed to induce an antitumor effect, the combination of the STING-LNP and anti-PD-1 exerted a synergistic antitumor effect. Our results indicate that the STING-LNP treatment significantly increased the expression of CD3, CD4, NK1.1, PD-1 and interferon (IFN)-γ in lung metastases. This change appears to be initiated by the type I IFN produced by liver macrophages that contain the internalized STING-LNPs, leading to the systemic activation of NK cells that express PD-1. The activated NK cells appeared to produce IFN-γ, resulting in an increase in the expression of the PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) in cancer cells, thus leading to a synergistic antitumor effect when anti-PD-1 is administered.
CONCLUSIONS
We provide a demonstration to show that a STING-LNP treatment can overcome PD-1 resistance in a B16-F10 lung metastasis model. The mechanism responsible for this indicates that NK cells are activated by stimulating the STING pathway which, in turn, induced the expression of PD-L1 on cancer cells. Based on the findings reported herein, the STING-LNP represents a promising candidate for use in combination therapy with anti-PD-1-resistant tumors.

data.title: Impaired HLA Class I Antigen Processing and Presentation as a Mechanism of Acquired Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Lung Cancer.
data.abstract: Mechanisms of acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are poorly understood. We leveraged a collection of 14 ICI-resistant lung cancer samples to investigate whether alterations in genes encoding HLA Class I antigen processing and presentation machinery (APM) components or interferon signaling play a role in acquired resistance to PD-1 or PD-L1 antagonistic antibodies. Recurrent mutations or copy-number changes were not detected in our cohort. In one case, we found acquired homozygous loss of B2M that caused lack of cell-surface HLA Class I expression in the tumor and a matched patient-derived xenograft (PDX). Downregulation of B2M was also found in two additional PDXs established from ICI-resistant tumors. CRISPR-mediated knockout of B2m in an immunocompetent lung cancer mouse model conferred resistance to PD-1 blockade in vivo , proving its role in resistance to ICIs. These results indicate that HLA Class I APM disruption can mediate escape from ICIs in lung cancer. Significance: As programmed death 1 axis inhibitors are becoming more established in standard treatment algorithms for diverse malignancies, acquired resistance to these therapies is increasingly being encountered. Here, we found that defective antigen processing and presentation can serve as a mechanism of such resistance in lung cancer. Cancer Discov; 7(12); 1420-35. ©2017 AACR. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 1355 .

data.title: Resistance Mechanisms to Anti-PD Cancer Immunotherapy.
data.abstract: The transformative success of antibodies targeting the PD-1 (programmed death 1)/B7-H1 (B7 homolog 1) pathway (anti-PD therapy) has revolutionized cancer treatment. However, only a fraction of patients with solid tumors and some hematopoietic malignancies respond to anti-PD therapy, and the reason for failure in other patients is less known. By dissecting the mechanisms underlying this resistance, current studies reveal that the tumor microenvironment is a major location for resistance to occur. Furthermore, the resistance mechanisms appear to be highly heterogeneous. Here, we discuss recent human cancer data identifying mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy. We review evidence for immune-based resistance mechanisms such as loss of neoantigens, defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling, immune inhibitory molecules, and exclusion of T cells. We also review the clinical evidence for emerging mechanisms of resistance to anti-PD therapy, such as alterations in metabolism, microbiota, and epigenetics. Finally, we discuss strategies to overcome anti-PD therapy resistance and emphasize the need to develop additional immunotherapies based on the concept of normalization cancer immunotherapy.

data.title: Primary Resistance to PD-1 Blockade Mediated by JAK1/2 Mutations.
data.abstract:
UNLABELLED
Loss-of-function mutations in JAK1/2 can lead to acquired resistance to anti-programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy. We reasoned that they may also be involved in primary resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. JAK1/2-inactivating mutations were noted in tumor biopsies of 1 of 23 patients with melanoma and in 1 of 16 patients with mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer treated with PD-1 blockade. Both cases had a high mutational load but did not respond to anti-PD-1 therapy. Two out of 48 human melanoma cell lines had JAK1/2 mutations, which led to a lack of PD-L1 expression upon interferon gamma exposure mediated by an inability to signal through the interferon gamma receptor pathway. JAK1/2 loss-of-function alterations in The Cancer Genome Atlas confer adverse outcomes in patients. We propose that JAK1/2 loss-of-function mutations are a genetic mechanism of lack of reactive PD-L1 expression and response to interferon gamma, leading to primary resistance to PD-1 blockade therapy.
SIGNIFICANCE
A key functional result from somatic JAK1/2 mutations in a cancer cell is the inability to respond to interferon gamma by expressing PD-L1 and many other interferon-stimulated genes. These mutations result in a genetic mechanism for the absence of reactive PD-L1 expression, and patients harboring such tumors would be unlikely to respond to PD-1 blockade therapy. Cancer Discov; 7(2); 188-201. ©2016 AACR.See related commentary by Marabelle et al., p. 128This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 115.

data.title: Mutations Associated with Acquired Resistance to PD-1 Blockade in Melanoma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Approximately 75% of objective responses to anti-programmed death 1 (PD-1) therapy in patients with melanoma are durable, lasting for years, but delayed relapses have been noted long after initial objective tumor regression despite continuous therapy. Mechanisms of immune escape in this context are unknown.
METHODS
We analyzed biopsy samples from paired baseline and relapsing lesions in four patients with metastatic melanoma who had had an initial objective tumor regression in response to anti-PD-1 therapy (pembrolizumab) followed by disease progression months to years later.
RESULTS
Whole-exome sequencing detected clonal selection and outgrowth of the acquired resistant tumors and, in two of the four patients, revealed resistance-associated loss-of-function mutations in the genes encoding interferon-receptor-associated Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) or Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), concurrent with deletion of the wild-type allele. A truncating mutation in the gene encoding the antigen-presenting protein beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) was identified in a third patient. JAK1 and JAK2 truncating mutations resulted in a lack of response to interferon gamma, including insensitivity to its antiproliferative effects on cancer cells. The B2M truncating mutation led to loss of surface expression of major histocompatibility complex class I.
CONCLUSIONS
In this study, acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy in patients with melanoma was associated with defects in the pathways involved in interferon-receptor signaling and in antigen presentation. (Funded by the National Institutes of Health and others.).

data.title: [Immunotherapy of cancer with checkpoint inhibitors : Not only in malignant melanoma].
data.abstract: The newest weapon in cancer therapy is checkpoint inhibition, which is the result of basic immunology research. The success of this therapy is based on the fact that upon light microscopy, many solid tumors harbor lymphocytic cells infiltrating the tumor (TILs), and in many solid tumors, the presence of these TILs are prognostic. Ipilimumab was the first monoclonal antibody developed against a target present on T cells after becoming activated, CTLA-4. In malignant melanoma, ipilimumab showed its beneficial effect as compared to a placebo peptide. However, the therapy with this antibody harbors significant toxicity. Meanwhile, other targets such as PD-1, also expressed on (late) activated T cells, were identified, and therapies with antibodies inhibiting PD-1/PD-L1 are less toxic. Although these antibodies show response only in a minority of patients, the benefit seems durable in some of these patients. In solid tumors such as melanoma or non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), treatment with PD-1 inhibitors has resulted in a significant prolongation of survival, even in first-line treatment. As these drugs have been approved in many indications, it is important to know the drugs and side effects. Resistance towards these drugs are caused by low expression of the natural ligand, PD-L1, in the tumor tissue, as well as acquired loss of signal transduction of interferon-related genes such as JAK1 or JAK2, respectively. Also new in cancer therapy are bispecific T cell engager monoclonal antibodies (BiTEs) such as blinatumomab, and autologous chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells (CAR-Ts). The later have proven their efficacy mainly in hematological neoplasias such as precursor-B-ALL. The dramatic costs of all these new drugs will have an enormous impact on the health care systems in the near future.

data.title: Tumor suppressor TET2 promotes cancer immunity and immunotherapy efficacy.
data.abstract: Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding TET DNA dioxygenase occur frequently in hematopoietic malignancy, but rarely in solid tumors which instead commonly have reduced activity. The impact of decreased TET activity in solid tumors is not known. Here we show that TET2 mediates interferon γ (IFNγ)-JAK-STAT signaling pathway to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression, lymphocyte infiltration and cancer immunity. IFNγ stimulated STAT1 to bind TET2 and recruit TET2 to hydroxymethylate chemokine and PD-L1 genes. Reduced TET activity was associated with decreased TH1-type chemokines and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and the progression of human colon cancer. Deletion of Tet2 in murine melanoma and colon tumor cells reduced chemokine expression and TILs, enabling tumors to evade anti-tumor immunity and to resist anti-PD-L1 therapy. Conversely, stimulating TET activity by systematic injection of its co-factor, ascorbate/vitamin C, increased chemokine and TILs, leading to enhanced anti-tumor immunity and anti-PD-L1 efficacy and extended lifespan of tumor-bearing mice. These results suggest an IFNγ-JAK-STAT-TET signaling pathway that mediates tumor response to anti-PD-L1/PD-1 therapy and is frequently disrupted in solid tumors. Our findings also suggest TET activity as a biomarker for predicting the efficacy and patient response to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy, and stimulating TET activity as an adjuvant immunotherapy of solid tumors.

data.title: Immune-checkpoint inhibitor resistance in cancer treatment: Current progress and future directions.
data.abstract: Cancer treatment has been advanced with the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) exemplified by anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) drugs. Patients have reaped substantial benefit from ICIs in many cancer types. However, few patients benefit from ICIs whereas the vast majority undergoing these treatments do not obtain survival benefit. Even for patients with initial responses, they may encounter drug resistance in their subsequent treatments, which limits the efficacy of ICIs. Therefore, a deepening understanding of drug resistance is critically important for the explorations of approaches to reverse drug resistance and to boost ICI efficacy. In the present review, different mechanisms of ICI resistance have been summarized according to the tumor intrinsic, tumor microenvironment (TME) and host classifications. We further elaborated corresponding strategies to battle against such resistance accordingly, which include targeting defects in antigen presentation, dysregulated interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, neoantigen depletion, upregulation of other T cell checkpoints as well as immunosuppression and exclusion mediated by TME. Moreover, regarding the host, several additional approaches that interfere with diet and gut microbiome have also been described in reversing ICI resistance. Additionally, we provide an overall glimpse into the ongoing clinical trials that utilize these mechanisms to overcome ICI resistance. Finally, we summarize the challenges and opportunities that needs to be addressed in the investigation of ICI resistance mechanisms, with the aim to benefit more patients with cancer.
