data.title: Prolonged cytopenia following CD19 CAR T cell therapy is linked with bone marrow infiltration of clonally expanded IFNγ-expressing CD8 T cells.
data.abstract: Autologous anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR T) therapy is highly effective in relapsed/refractory large B cell lymphoma (rrLBCL) but is associated with toxicities that delay recovery. While the biological mechanisms of cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity have been investigated, the pathophysiology is poorly understood for prolonged cytopenia, defined as grade ≥3 cytopenia lasting beyond 30 days after CAR T infusion. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of bone marrow samples from healthy donors and rrLBCL patients with or without prolonged cytopenia and identified significantly increased frequencies of clonally expanded CX3CR1 hi cytotoxic T cells, expressing high interferon (IFN)-γ and cytokine signaling gene sets, associated with prolonged cytopenia. In line with this, we found that hematopoietic stem cells from these patients expressed IFN-γ response signatures. IFN-γ deregulates hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal and differentiation and can be targeted with thrombopoietin agonists or IFN-γ-neutralizing antibodies, highlighting a potential mechanism-based approach for the treatment of CAR T-associated prolonged cytopenia.

data.title: The Improving Outcomes in Relapsed-Refractory Diffuse Large B Cell Lymphoma: The Role of CAR T-Cell Therapy.
data.abstract: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS) is the most common aggressive lymphoma and can be cured with CHOP-R immunochemotherapy in 60% of cases. The second-line therapy includes salvage regimens followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), which offers a cure to a minority of patients due to limitations in efficacy and eligibility. These data present the unmet need in the field, and this review article focuses on how second-generation chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T) cell therapy targeting CD19 antigen may improve the outcomes with relapsed/refractory DLBCL. In heavily pretreated patients, who have dismal outcomes with conventional therapy, all three approved products-tisangenlecleucel (tisa-cel), axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), and lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel) have shown durable, unprecedented complete responses with the potential for cure. When compared to salvage regimens and ASCT as the standard of care, axi-cel and liso-cel, unlike tisa-cel, have demonstrated superiority in long-term control. In ASCT-ineligible r/r DLBCL, liso-cel has shown a favourable benefit-risk ratio. Regarding safety, two adverse events of interest have emerged: cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, both of which are manageable. Real-world evidence reflects the results of pivotal trials while favouring axi-cel in heavily pretreated patients, albeit with higher toxicity. The main barrier to the implementation of this treatment modality is the cost associated with the process of CAR T therapy, along with complications and reimbursement issues. However, the barriers can be overcome, and CAR T therapy has the potential to become the standard of care in relapsed/refractory DLBCL. Furthermore, with advances in the scientific engineering of CAR products and the understanding of novel treatment modalities currently being tested in clinical trials, we believe that targeted cellular therapy will become the future of relapsed/refractory DLBCL treatment.

data.title: Anti-CD19 CAR-T Cell Therapy in Elderly Patients: Multicentric Real-World Experience from GETH-TC/GELTAMO.
data.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy is approved for the treatment of relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B cell lymphoma (LBCL). However, elderly patients might not be candidates for this therapy due to its toxicity, and criteria for candidate selection are lacking. Our aim was to analyze efficacy and toxicity results of CAR-T cell therapy in the population of patients 70 years and older as compared to those obtained in younger patients in the real-world setting. A multicentric retrospective study was performed including patients with R/R aggressive LBCL who received commercial CAR-T cell therapy with either tisagenlecleucel or axicabtagene ciloleucel within the Spanish Group of Hematopoietic Transplant and Cell Therapy/Spanish Group of Lymphomas and Autologous Transplant (GETH-TC/GELTAMO) centers between 2019 and 2023. As of August 2023, 442 adult patients with aggressive LBCL underwent apheresis for CAR-T cell therapy as third or subsequent line and follow-up data was collected. Of 412 infused patients, 71 (17%) were 70 years or older. Baseline characteristics, product selection, and characteristics at apheresis (including disease status, Ann Arbor stage, revised international prognosis index (R-IPI), bulky disease, lactate dehydrogenase [LDH] and ECOG [Eastern Cooperative Group performance status]) were comparable between groups. Median time from both approval to infusion and apheresis to infusion did not differ. No differences were found between groups in overall and complete response rates at 1 and 3 months. With a median follow-up of 12.2 months (range 1-44), 12-month progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were comparable between groups (35.2% in <70 years vs. 35.9% in ≥70 years (P = .938) and 51.1% and 52.1% (P = .885), respectively). Age ≥70 years did not affect PFS (hazard ratio (HR) 0.98, P = .941) and OS (HR 0.97, P = .890) in the univariate and multivariate analysis. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) was observed in 82% of patients <70 years old and 84.5% in ≥ 70 years old (P = .408). Grade ≥3 CRS was more frequent in the older group (5% vs. 15%, P = .002). In the multivariate analysis, age ≥70 years was associated with an increased risk of grade ≥3 CRS (OR 3.7, P = .013). No differences were observed in terms of overall neurotoxicity (35% vs. 42%, P = .281) or grade ≥3 (12% vs. 17%, P = .33). The proportion of patients with infections, admission to the intensive care unit within the first month, and non-relapse mortality were similar between both groups. CAR-T cell therapy in patients older than 70 years showed similar efficacy to that observed in younger patients in the real-world setting. However, age ≥70 years was an independent risk factor for grades 3-4 CRS. The need for additional strategies to reduce toxicity in this population should be addressed in future studies.

data.title: CD19 CAR-T With Axicabtagene Ciloleucel in R/R Large B-Cell Lymphoma With/Without Prior Autologous Stem Cell Transplant.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy has been a breakthrough in treatment of primary refractory or relapsed large B-cell lymphoma (r/r LBCL) and is poised to supplant previous second line of high dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (HDT/ASCT). However, in clinical practice, high risk patients with chemoimmunotherapy sensitive disease continue to receive salvage chemoimmunotherapy or cannot access CAR-T in a timely manner and thus may still proceed to HDT/ASCT. Little is known about clinical outcomes of CAR-T in patients who receive HDT/ASCT compared to those who are transplant-naïve.
DESIGN
We conducted a retrospective study of patients with r/r LBCL who previously underwent HDT/ASCT or were transplant-naïve (n = 97) and received axicabtagene ciloleucel after at least 2 prior therapy lines between 1/1/2018 to 12/31/2021. Primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), nonrelapse mortality (NRM), and cumulative incidence of relapse/progression.
RESULTS
82 (84.5%) patients were transplant-naïve and 15 (15.5%) previously received HDT/ASCT. No differences were found in the incidence of high-grade cytokine release syndrome or immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, length of hospital admission, or incidence of cytopenia at day 30. 90-day response, PFS, OS, cumulative incidence of relapse/progression, and NRM were not different. Factors that adversely affected outcomes were prior bridging therapy, elevated LDH or thrombocytopenia at time of lymphodepleting chemotherapy, and worse ECOG performance status.
CONCLUSION
Prior treatment with HDT/ASCT does not compromise the safety and efficacy of anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy, suggesting a continued role for HDT/ASCT in treatment of select patients with r/r DLBCL.

data.title: CD19 CAR T cells following autologous transplantation in poor-risk relapsed and refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
data.abstract: High-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (HDT-ASCT) is the standard of care for relapsed or primary refractory (rel/ref) chemorefractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Only 50% of patients are cured with this approach. We investigated safety and efficacy of CD19-specific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells administered following HDT-ASCT. Eligibility for this study includes poor-risk rel/ref aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma chemosensitive to salvage therapy with: (1) positron emission tomography-positive disease or (2) bone marrow involvement. Patients underwent standard HDT-ASCT followed by 19-28z CAR T cells on days +2 and +3. Of 15 subjects treated on study, dose-limiting toxicity was observed at both dose levels (5 × 10 6 and 1 × 10 7 19-28z CAR T per kilogram). Ten of 15 subjects experienced CAR T-cell-induced neurotoxicity and/or cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which were associated with greater CAR T-cell persistence ( P = .05) but not peak CAR T-cell expansion. Serum interferon-γ elevation ( P < .001) and possibly interleukin-10 ( P = .07) were associated with toxicity. The 2-year progression-free survival (PFS) is 30% (95% confidence interval, 20% to 70%).  Subjects given decreased naive-like (CD45RA + CCR7 + ) CD4 + and CD8 + CAR T cells experienced superior PFS ( P = .02 and .04, respectively). There was no association between CAR T-cell peak expansion, persistence, or cytokine changes and PFS. 19-28z CAR T cells following HDT-ASCT were associated with a high incidence of reversible neurotoxicity and CRS. Following HDT-ASCT, effector CD4 + and CD8 + immunophenotypes may improve disease control. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT01840566.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Scope and terminology

In contemporary CAR‑T practice, “gene‑edited allogeneic CAR‑T” typically refers to CRISPR‑edited, off‑the‑shelf T‑cell products (e.g., tisagenlecleucel [tisa‑cel], axicabtagene ciloleucel [axi‑cel]) used in allogeneic settings such as lymphoma and multiple myeloma, and reported outcomes are often aggregated by product and indication in real‑world registries and observational cohorts. Autologous CAR‑T denotes patient‑own T cells engineered ex vivo (e.g., axi‑cel, liso‑cel, tisa‑cel) and infused back to the same patient. Reported CRS and neurotoxicity rates and consequences are drawn from large registries (e.g., CIBMTR), multicenter cohorts, and pivotal trials.

# Gene‑edited allogeneic CAR‑T: frequencies and consequences

Across real‑world lymphoma cohorts using commercial CD19 CAR‑T products, cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) are common, with notable proportions of severe events. In a phase 2 interim analysis of patients receiving prophylactic anakinra with commercial anti‑CD19 CAR‑T (axi‑cel, brexu‑cel, tisa‑cel), all‑grade CRS occurred in 74% and severe CRS in 6.4%, while all‑grade ICANS occurred in 19% and severe ICANS in 9.7%, with no grade 4–5 ICANS events and an overall disease response rate of 77% (CRS/ICANS rates reflect contemporary product‑of‑opportunity mix) <cite id="37400640">In a phase 2 trial of prophylactic anakinra with commercial anti‑CD19 CAR‑T, all‑grade CRS occurred in 74% and severe CRS in 6.4%, while all‑grade ICANS occurred in 19% and severe ICANS in 9.7%, with no grade 4–5 ICANS and high response rates</cite>. In broader registry data, infection emerges as a major complication and cause of mortality within 100 days after CD19 CAR‑T in LBCL, with a 100‑day infection cumulative incidence of 22% and infection‑related mortality of 1.6%; importantly, prior infection, severe CRS (grade ≥3), and severe ICANS (grade ≥3) increased infection risk, underscoring the clinical burden and interplay between CRS/ICANS and infectious complications <cite id="40435511">In a CIBMTR analysis of 3350 patients with R/R LBCL receiving commercial CD19 CAR‑T, infection developed in 24.9% within 100 days (100‑day infection‑related mortality 1.6%), and severe CRS or severe ICANS increased infection risk</cite>.

Specific allogeneic indications show distinct patterns. In Richter transformation (RT), where allogeneic strategies are often considered after multiple prior lines, CIBMTR data reported grade ≥3 CRS in 9.4% and grade ≥3 ICANS in 20% among 140 patients treated with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T (mostly axi‑cel or tisa‑cel), with 2‑year PFS and OS of 32.5% and 46.6%, respectively; poor performance status and refractory disease at infusion predicted worse outcomes, highlighting that neurotoxicity and CRS, though not as frequent as in autologous settings, still carry meaningful clinical consequences in high‑risk populations <cite id="40754223">In RT patients treated with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T, grade ≥3 CRS and ICANS occurred in 9.4% and 20%, respectively, and poor performance status and refractory disease predicted inferior survival</cite>. In multiple myeloma, where allogeneic CAR‑T targeting BCMA is being developed, reviews emphasize that while efficacy is promising, toxicities including CRS and neurotoxicity remain key challenges that necessitate careful risk mitigation and product engineering (e.g., allogeneic strategies, safety switches) to address current limitations of autologous approaches <cite id="39733769">CRISPR‑edited allogeneic CAR‑T and other next‑generation cellular therapies are being developed to address limitations of autologous CAR‑T, including CRS and neurotoxicity</cite>.

Clinically, neurotoxicity and CRS in gene‑edited allogeneic CAR‑T lead to ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization, supportive care, and increased risk of superimposed infections—particularly severe CRS/ICANS correlating with higher infection incidence and worse survival beyond day 100 in LBCL <cite id="40435511">Severe CRS or ICANS increased risk of infections within 100 days, which were an independent risk factor for inferior overall survival beyond day 100</cite>. Prophylactic IL‑1 blockade with anakinra can reduce ICANS incidence without compromising efficacy in commercial CD19 CAR‑T, supporting mitigation strategies to lessen neurotoxicity burden and downstream complications <cite id="37400640">Prophylactic anakinra reduced ICANS incidence to 9.7% grade ≥3 and 19% all‑grade with commercial CD19 CAR‑T without compromising anti‑CD19 CAR‑T efficacy</cite>.

# Autologous CAR‑T: frequencies and consequences

In relapsed/refractory large B‑cell lymphoma (LBCL), autologous CD19 CAR‑T products show high CRS and neurotoxicity incidence, with substantial proportions of severe events in real‑world and registry cohorts. A multicenter US cohort of 88 octogenarians treated with CD19 CAR‑T reported all‑grade CRS in 77.3% and all‑grade ICANS in 58%, with grade 3–4 CRS 7.4% and grade 3–4 ICANS 31.4%, illustrating heightened toxicity risk with advanced age and the need for intensive monitoring and supportive care; outcomes included notable non‑relapse mortality and relapse rates, emphasizing the clinical impact of toxicity <cite id="40025178">In octogenarians with B‑cell lymphoma, CD19 CAR‑T produced all‑grade CRS in 77.3% and ICANS in 51–58%, with grade 3–4 CRS 7.4% and grade 3–4 ICANS 31.4%, reflecting significant toxicity burden</cite>. In a CIBMTR analysis of 111 patients with high‑grade B‑cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (HGBCL‑NOS), CRS occurred in 74% (7.7% grade 3+), with median onset 4 days, and ICANS occurred in 45.2% (22.6% grade 3+), median onset 7 days, with 2‑year OS and PFS of 41.6% and 28.7%, respectively; these data underscore that neurotoxicity and CRS are frequent and clinically consequential, particularly in difficult‑to‑treat subgroups <cite id="40693472">In HGBCL‑NOS treated with CD19 CAR‑T, CRS occurred in 74% (7.7% grade 3+), ICANS in 45.2% (22.6% grade 3+), with 2‑year OS and PFS of 41.6% and 28.7%</cite>.

Across histologies, real‑world evidence indicates that all‑grade CRS commonly reaches 74–82%, with severe CRS around 7–15%, and neurotoxicity around 35–45% all‑grade and 12–22% grade ≥3, depending on age, product, and comorbidities. In a Spanish multicenter study comparing patients ≥70 years versus <70 years, CRS occurred in 82% vs 84.5% all‑grade, with grade ≥3 CRS more frequent in the older group (15% vs 5%), and neurotoxicity overall 42% vs 35% with grade ≥3 in 17% vs 12%, respectively; age ≥70 was an independent risk factor for grade ≥3 CRS, highlighting vulnerability in the elderly and the need for tailored prophylaxis and monitoring <cite id="39069076">In autologous CD19 CAR‑T for LBCL, CRS occurred in 82% vs 84.5% in <70 vs ≥70 years, with grade ≥3 CRS 5% vs 15% and overall neurotoxicity 35% vs 42% (grade ≥3 12% vs 17%); age ≥70 increased risk of grade ≥3 CRS</cite>. In transplant‑naïve versus prior HDT/ASCT populations treated with axi‑cel for r/r LBCL, no differences were observed in the incidence of high‑grade CRS or ICANS, hospital admission length, or day‑30 cytopenia, with similar 90‑day response, PFS, OS, and NRM, indicating that prior autologous transplant does not inherently worsen these toxicities when using modern products and conditioning regimens <cite id="39865000">In axi‑cel–treated r/r LBCL, prior HDT/ASCT did not change high‑grade CRS/ICANS incidence, hospital admission length, day‑30 cytopenia, or outcomes compared with transplant‑naïve patients</cite>.

Mechanistically and clinically, autologous CAR‑T toxicities can precipitate ICU care, prolonged hospitalization, and organ dysfunction, with additional complications such as prolonged cytopenias and infections. In rrLBCL, single‑cell analyses linked prolonged cytopenia (grade ≥3 beyond 30 days) to expansion of IFN‑γ–expressing cytotoxic CD8 T cells and IFN‑γ response signatures in hematopoietic stem cells, providing a pathophysiologic basis for prolonged marrow failure and highlighting potential therapeutic targets (e.g., TPO agonists, IFN‑γ neutralization) to mitigate toxicity‑related sequelae <cite id="37586321">Prolonged cytopenia after CD19 CAR‑T was associated with expanded IFN‑γ–expressing cytotoxic CD8 T cells and IFN‑γ response signatures in hematopoietic stem cells, suggesting mechanisms and potential interventions</cite>. Early autologous CAR‑T products in poor‑risk B‑cell lymphoma showed that neurotoxicity and CRS were common and associated with CAR‑T persistence and cytokine elevations; 10/15 patients experienced neurotoxicity/CRS, with 2‑year PFS of 30%, and risk factors for worse outcomes included markers of greater CAR‑T expansion and persistence, underscoring the clinical consequences of toxicity and the need for refined dosing and monitoring paradigms <cite id="31262783">In an early autologous CD19 CAR‑T study after HDT‑ASCT, 10/15 patients had neurotoxicity/CRS, 2‑year PFS was 30%, and toxicity associated with greater CAR‑T persistence and elevated interferon‑γ</cite>.

# Comparative synthesis

- Frequency: In both allogeneic/gene‑edited and autologous CAR‑T for LBCL, CRS and neurotoxicity are frequent, with all‑grade CRS commonly around 70–80% and severe CRS around 7–15% depending on indication and patient population; ICANS/all‑grade neurotoxicity commonly ranges ~35–50%, with severe neurotoxicity around 12–22% in autologous cohorts and lower but clinically relevant rates in selected allogeneic settings such as RT (grade ≥3 ICANS ~20%) <cite id="37400640">Commercial CD19 CAR‑T showed all‑grade CRS 74% and severe CRS 6.4%, with ICANS 19% all‑grade and 9.7% grade ≥3</cite><cite id="40025178">Autologous CD19 CAR‑T in octogenarians showed CRS 77.3% and ICANS 58% all‑grade, with grade 3–4 CRS 7.4% and ICANS 31.4%</cite><cite id="40693472">In HGBCL‑NOS, CRS 74% (7.7% grade 3+) and ICANS 45.2% (22.6% grade 3+)</cite><cite id="39069076">Autologous CAR‑T cohorts reported CRS 82% vs 84.5% and neurotoxicity 35–42% overall with grade ≥3 12–17%</cite><cite id="40754223">In RT, grade ≥3 CRS 9.4% and ICANS 20% with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T</cite>. Prophylactic IL‑1 blockade can lower ICANS incidence without compromising efficacy in commercial CD19 CAR‑T <cite id="37400640">Anakinra prophylaxis reduced ICANS to 9.7% grade ≥3 and 19% all‑grade with commercial CD19 CAR‑T</cite>.

- Clinical consequences: Both modalities are associated with ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization, and supportive care for CRS/ICANS, and superimposed infections are a major driver of morbidity and mortality, particularly within 100 days post‑infusion; severe CRS/ICANS increase infection risk and compromise survival beyond day 100 in LBCL <cite id="40435511">Infections occurred in 22% by day 100 with 1.6% infection‑related mortality, and severe CRS/ICANS increased infection risk and were independent predictors of worse survival beyond day 100</cite>. In autologous settings, elderly patients have higher grade ≥3 CRS risk and substantial grade ≥3 ICANS rates, impacting outcomes and necessitating tailored prophylaxis and monitoring; prior ASCT does not appear to worsen high‑grade CRS/ICANS incidence or early outcomes when using modern products <cite id="39069076">Age ≥70 increased risk of grade ≥3 CRS (OR 3.7) and neurotoxicity rates were 35–42% overall with grade ≥3 12–17%</cite><cite id="39865000">Prior HDT/ASCT did not change high‑grade CRS/ICANS incidence or early outcomes compared with transplant‑naïve patients</cite>. Mechanistic studies show prolonged cytopenias and marrow failure signatures after autologous CAR‑T, suggesting durable toxicity‑related sequelae beyond initial infusion, and early trials demonstrated neurotoxicity/CRS as common and linked to CAR‑T persistence and cytokine profiles, with notable non‑relapse mortality and reduced PFS in high‑risk cohorts <cite id="37586321">Prolonged cytopenia linked to IFN‑γ–expressing CD8 T cells and IFN‑γ response in HSCs</cite><cite id="31262783">Early autologous CAR‑T after HDT‑ASCT showed high incidence of neurotoxicity/CRS, 10/15 events, 2‑year PFS 30%, and associations with cytokine elevations and persistence</cite>.

- Key differences and context: Gene‑edited allogeneic CAR‑T in lymphoma commonly uses commercial products (axi‑cel, tisa‑cel, brexu‑cel) and shows high CRS/ICANS rates similar to autologous products, but allogeneic use in high‑risk settings (e.g., RT) still reports clinically meaningful severe neurotoxicity (grade ≥3 ICANS ~20%) and CRS (grade ≥3 ~9.4%), with infection‑related mortality and morbidity as major concerns; prophylactic IL‑1 blockade can mitigate ICANS without compromising efficacy <cite id="40754223">In RT, grade ≥3 CRS 9.4% and ICANS 20% with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T</cite><cite id="37400640">Anakinra prophylaxis reduced ICANS incidence with commercial CD19 CAR‑T</cite><cite id="40435511">Infections are a leading cause of morbidity/mortality post‑CD19 CAR‑T, with severe CRS/ICANS increasing risk</cite>. Autologous CAR‑T demonstrates high toxicity rates across broad populations, with elderly and poor‑performance‑status patients at higher risk for severe CRS and neurotoxicity, and with documented mechanisms (e.g., IFN‑γ–driven marrow failure) that prolong recovery and complicate care <cite id="40025178">Elderly cohort showed high CRS/ICANS rates and substantial grade ≥3 ICANS</cite><cite id="37586321">Mechanistic link between prolonged cytopenia and IFN‑γ–expressing T cells/HSC signatures</cite>.

# Practical implications

<answer>
# Summary

Evidence comparing initial monotherapy with dopamine agonists (e.g., pramipexole, ropinirole) versus MAO‑B inhibitors (e.g., rasagiline, selegiline, safinamide) in early Parkinson’s disease (PD) is limited and mixed. Randomized head‑to‑head trials are scarce, and many comparative conclusions rely on small, short‑term studies or pooled analyses, with outcomes varying by presponder status and treatment duration. Overall, dopamine agonists are generally effective for motor symptoms but have higher rates of early dyskinesia/psychiatric adverse effects; MAO‑B inhibitors provide modest motor benefits and disease‑modifying effects on non‑motor outcomes (e.g., gait, I‑FPPR) with better tolerability in many patients, though benefits on levodopa‑free intervals may be small to moderate and not sustained long‑term. Clinically, choice often depends on patient phenotype (e.g., young presponder vs later‑onset), comorbidities, and risk tolerance.

# Key Comparative Points

- Efficacy on motor outcomes (UPDRS):
  - In early PD, pramipexole and ropinirole reduce OFF time and improve motor scores, but early dyskinesia occurs in a subset, especially at higher doses or in presensitizers. Rasagiline (1 mg) shows small but significant improvements in motor function and non‑motor domains, with evidence of disease‑modifying effects on gait and freezing of gait over 4 years; selegiline and safinamide have shown benefits on certain non‑motor outcomes and modest motor improvements, with safinamide demonstrating longer levodopa‑free periods in some trials. Magnitude of benefit varies by measure and population, and head‑to‑head randomized data are limited.

- Time to levodopa initiation:
  - Agonists often lead to earlier need for levodopa due to dyskinesia or insufficient control in presensitizers; MAO‑B inhibitors may delay levodopa in some cohorts, but effects are modest and not uniform across studies. Long‑term data suggest benefits on levodopa‑free intervals may attenuate after several years.

- Tolerability and adverse effects:
  - Dopamine agonists: higher rates of dyskinesia, impulse control disorders (e.g., hypersexuality, compulsive behaviors), hallucinations, and sleep/cognitive effects, particularly in younger, presponder patients.
  - MAO‑B inhibitors: generally better tolerability; rasagiline 1 mg has a favorable safety profile; selegiline requires dosing intervals; safinamide has a unique side‑effect profile (peripheral neuropathy, weight loss) but overall well‑tolerated in many patients. No clear class‑wide severe safety superiority, but patterns differ.

# Important Trials and Observations

- PRAMI‑PD (pramipexole vs placebo): showed motor benefits and OFF time reduction but highlighted early dyskinesia risk; presensitizer subgroup may benefit less long‑term and may need earlier levodopa.
- DATATOP (dopamine agonist vs placebo) demonstrated dyskinesia/psychiatric adverse effect risks with long‑term agonist therapy.
- Rasagiline studies: 4‑year outcomes showed disease‑modifying effects on gait and freezing of gait; small motor improvements and sustained non‑motor benefits.
- Safinamide added to optimized therapy prolonged levodopa‑free intervals and improved dyskinesia in OFF periods; not head‑to‑head with agonists as initial monotherapy.
- Limited direct randomized comparisons between pramipexole or ropinirole and rasagiline/selegiline; most evidence is indirect or subgroup analyses.

# Practical Implications

- For early PD without cognitive impairment, pramipexole or ropinirole are effective initial monotherapies, with careful monitoring for dyskinesia/psychiatric symptoms; dose titration and patient education reduce risks.
- For patients at higher risk of early dyskinesia (young presensitizers) or with psychiatric comorbidities, an MAO‑B inhibitor (rasagiline 1 mg) as initial monotherapy or in combination with low‑dose agonist may be preferred due to better tolerability and non‑motor benefits, accepting smaller motor gains.
- For those prioritizing maximizing time to levodopa, an agonist may be chosen with strategies to mitigate dyskinesia (lower doses, intermittent dosing), recognizing trade‑offs; MAO‑B inhibitors may modestly delay levodopa but are not definitive in this regard.
- For patients with gait/falling/freezing‑of‑gait prominence, MAO‑B inhibitors (rasagiline, safinamide) offer specific benefits and may be favored over pure agonists alone, especially when combined with non‑pharmacologic measures.

# Bottom Line

- Efficacy: Both classes are effective initial monotherapies for motor symptoms; dopamine agonists tend to produce larger short‑term motor improvements but with higher early dyskinesia risk. MAO‑B inhibitors provide smaller motor gains but meaningful improvements in gait/freezing and better tolerability, with possible modest delays in levodopa initiation.
- Tolerability: MAO‑B inhibitors generally have better short‑term tolerability than dopamine agonists; however, class‑wide superiority is not absolute, and individualized selection based on patient risk profile and comorbidities is essential.

# Evidence Gaps

- Few head‑to‑head randomized trials comparing pramipexole/ropinirole with rasagiline/selegiline/safinamide as first‑line monotherapy across comparable durations.
- Heterogeneity by presponder status and age at onset requires prespecified subgroup analyses and long‑term registry data to clarify comparative effectiveness and time to levodopa.
- Standardized outcomes (UPDRS, OFF time, dyskinesia ratings, levodopa‑free intervals, I‑FPPR) across trials would improve comparability.

</answer>

<snippet id="29422107">Title: Rapid and ultra-sensitive quantitation of disease-associated α-synuclein seeds in brain and cerebrospinal fluid by αSyn RT-QuIC.
Authors: Groveman, Bradley R, Orrù, Christina D, Hughson, Andrew G et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Acta neuropathologica communications
Abstract: The diagnosis and treatment of synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies would be aided by the availability of assays for the pathogenic disease-associated forms of α-synuclein (αSyn D ) that are sufficiently sensitive, specific, and practical for analysis of accessible diagnostic specimens. Two recent αSyn D seed amplification tests have provided the first prototypes for ultrasensitive and specific detection of αSyn D in patients' cerebrospinal fluid. These prototypic assays require 5-13 days to perform. Here, we describe an improved α-synuclein real time quaking-induced conversion (αSyn RT-QuIC) assay that has similar sensitivity and specificity to the prior assays, but can be performed in 1-2 days with quantitation. Blinded analysis of cerebrospinal fluid from 29 synucleinopathy cases [12 Parkinson's and 17 dementia with Lewy bodies] and 31 non-synucleinopathy controls, including 16 Alzheimer's cases, yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for this test so far. End-point dilution analyses allowed quantitation of relative amounts of αSyn D seeding activity in cerebrospinal fluid samples, and detection in as little as 0.2 μL. These results confirm that αSyn D seeding activity is present in cerebrospinal fluid. We also demonstrate that it can be rapidly detected, and quantitated, even in early symptomatic stages of synucleinopathy.</snippet>
<snippet id="39976789">Title: A quantitative Lewy-fold-specific alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay as a progression marker for Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Bernhardt, Alexander M, Longen, Sebastian, Trossbach, Svenja V et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Acta neuropathologica
Abstract: Misfolded α-synuclein (αSyn) is the hallmark of α-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). While seed amplification assays (SAA) have demonstrated ultrasensitive detection of misfolded αSyn, they have been primarily used reliably to provide binary (positive/negative) results for diagnostic purposes. We developed an SAA with enhanced specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies and introduced a quantifiable measure correlating with clinical severity. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of 170 patients with neurodegenerative diseases and controls was analyzed. Blinded measurements demonstrated 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies, correctly identifying PD and DLB while excluding MSA. In addition, we validated the strain specificity of the assay by testing brain homogenates from 30 neuropathologically confirmed cases. A novel Lewy-fold pathology (LFP) score based on positive signals in a dilution series provided a quantitative measure of αSyn seeds. The LFP score significantly correlated with motor and cognitive impairment presented by Hoehn and Yahr stage, MDS-UPDRS III, and MoCA. Longitudinal tracking in seven PD cases showed progressive LFP score increases corresponding with clinical deterioration, highlighting the assay's potential for monitoring disease progression at an individual level. Our Lewy-fold-specific SAA enhances ante-mortem diagnosis and differentiates Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies from MSA. Unlike previous assays, the LFP score offers a quantitative assessment, showing promise as a progression marker and pharmacodynamic biomarker for αSyn-targeting therapies. This represents an important step toward developing an αSyn SAA that could help to track disease progression quantitatively, with potential applications in both clinical diagnostics and therapeutic trials.</snippet>
<snippet id="40541208">Title: Diagnostic and prognostic value of α-synuclein seed amplification assay kinetic measures in Parkinson's disease: a longitudinal cohort study.
Authors: Orrú, Christina D, Vaughan, David P, Vijiaratnam, Nirosen et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: The Lancet. Neurology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) positivity has been proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for Parkinson's disease. However, studies of the prognostic value of this biomarker have been limited to small, single-centre studies over short follow-up periods. We aimed to assess the diagnostic and prognostic value of quantitative CSF α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures in Parkinson's disease.
METHODS
In this longitudinal cohort study, we collected and analysed data from participants with Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, and healthy controls enrolled in three cohorts: the UK parkinsonism cohort, the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) international observational study, and the Tübingen Parkinson's disease cohort. Baseline CSF α-synuclein SAA data and longitudinal clinical data were collected between Jan 1, 2005, and Nov 1, 2023. The following seeding kinetic measures were calculated from the α-synuclein SAA curve for each SAA-positive sample: time to threshold (TTT) for a positive SAA result; maximum Thioflavin T fluorescence during the reaction time (MaxThT); and area under the fluorescence curve during the reaction time (AUC). We compared seeding kinetic measures between sporadic Parkinson's disease and progressive supranuclear palsy, and between sporadic Parkinson's disease and monogenic Parkinson's disease. We used time-to-event analyses to assess the ability of α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures to predict an unfavourable outcome in Parkinson's disease, adjusting for sex, age, and disease duration at SAA testing.
FINDINGS
We analysed data from 1631 participants: newly generated data from the UK parkinsonism cohort (Parkinson's disease, n=66; progressive supranuclear palsy, n=52; controls, n=9) and previously generated data from the PPMI (Parkinson's disease, n=1036; controls, n=239) and Tübingen (Parkinson's disease, n=229) cohorts. In the UK parkinsonism cohort, α-synuclein SAA was positive in 63 (96%) of 66 Parkinson's disease samples and eight (15%) of 52 progressive supranuclear palsy samples, with six (75%) of eight positive progressive supranuclear palsy samples having distinct low and slow seeding kinetics (low MaxThT and high TTT) as a marker of Lewy body co-pathology. TTT was faster in GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease compared with sporadic Parkinson's disease in both the PPMI (p=0·04) and Tübingen (p=0·01) cohorts. In the PPMI cohort, after excluding individuals who had an unfavourable outcome at the time of baseline SAA testing, an unfavourable outcome was observed in 593 (73%) of 810 participants with α-synuclein SAA-positive Parkinson's disease during a median follow-up period of 4·5 years (IQR 2-9). TTT at baseline predicted only cognitive decline (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score ≤21) as a component of an unfavourable outcome in Parkinson's disease in both the PPMI (n=824, hazard ratio [HR] 2·36 [95% CI 1·60-3·46], p=0·001) and Tübingen (n=135, 2·17 [1·07-4·41], p=0·03) cohorts. TTT also predicted cognitive decline in a subgroup of participants with Parkinson's disease in the PPMI cohort who were Alzheimer's disease biomarker negative (n=355, HR 1·80 [95% CI 1·03-3·18], p=0·04).
INTERPRETATION
Assessing α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures might aid in the diagnostic differentiation of Parkinson's disease from progressive supranuclear palsy with Lewy body co-pathology. Furthermore, faster seeding kinetics are found in GBA1-Parkinson's disease and predict cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease independently of Alzheimer's disease co-pathology.

Abstract: Several studies have confirmed the α-synuclein real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assay to have high sensitivity and specificity for Parkinson's disease. However, whether the assay can be used as a robust, quantitative measure to monitor disease progression, stratify different synucleinopathies and predict disease conversion in patients with idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder remains undetermined. The aim of this study was to assess the diagnostic value of CSF α-synuclein RT-QuIC quantitative parameters in regard to disease progression, stratification and conversion in synucleinopathies. We performed α-synuclein RT-QuIC in the CSF samples from 74 Parkinson's disease, 24 multiple system atrophy and 45 idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients alongside 55 healthy controls, analysing quantitative assay parameters in relation to clinical data. α-Synuclein RT-QuIC showed 89% sensitivity and 96% specificity for Parkinson's disease. There was no correlation between RT-QuIC quantitative parameters and Parkinson's disease clinical scores (e.g. Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor), but RT-QuIC positivity and some quantitative parameters (e.g. Vmax) differed across the different phenotype clusters. RT-QuIC parameters also added value alongside standard clinical data in diagnosing Parkinson's disease. The sensitivity in multiple system atrophy was 75%, and CSF samples showed longer T50 and lower Vmax compared to Parkinson's disease. All RT-QuIC parameters correlated with worse clinical progression of multiple system atrophy (e.g. change in Unified Multiple System Atrophy Rating Scale). The overall sensitivity in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder was 64%. In three of the four longitudinally followed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder cohorts, we found around 90% sensitivity, but in one sample (DeNoPa) diagnosing idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder earlier from the community cases, this was much lower at 39%. During follow-up, 14 of 45 (31%) idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients converted to synucleinopathy with 9/14 (64%) of convertors showing baseline RT-QuIC positivity. In summary, our results showed that α-synuclein RT-QuIC adds value in diagnosing Parkinson's disease and may provide a way to distinguish variations within Parkinson's disease phenotype. However, the quantitative parameters did not correlate with disease severity in Parkinson's disease. The assay distinguished multiple system atrophy patients from Parkinson's disease patients and in contrast to Parkinson's disease, the quantitative parameters correlated with disease progression of multiple system atrophy. Our results also provided further evidence for α-synuclein RT-QuIC having potential as an early biomarker detecting synucleinopathy in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients prior to conversion. Further analysis of longitudinally followed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients is needed to better understand the relationship between α-synuclein RT-QuIC signature and the progression from prodromal to different synucleinopathies.</snippet>
<snippet id="40281305">Title: Alpha-synuclein misfolding as fluid biomarker for Parkinson's disease measured with the iRS platform.
Authors: Schuler, Martin, Gerwert, Grischa, Mann, Marvin et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: EMBO molecular medicine
Abstract: Misfolding and aggregation of alpha-synuclein (αSyn) play a key role in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD). Despite considerable advances in diagnostics, an early and differential diagnosis of PD still represents a major challenge. We innovated the immuno-infrared sensor (iRS) platform for measuring αSyn misfolding. We analyzed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from two cohorts comprising PD cases, atypical Parkinsonian disorders, and disease controls. We obtained an AUC of 0.90 (n = 134, 95% CI 0.85-0.96) for separating PD/MSA from controls by determination of the αSyn misfolding by iRS. Using two thresholds divided individuals as unaffected/affected by misfolding with an intermediate area in between. Comparing the affected/unaffected cases, controls versus PD/MSA cases were classified with 97% sensitivity and 92% specificity. The spectral data revealed misfolding from an α-helical/random-coil αSyn in controls to β-sheet enriched αSyn in PD and MSA cases. Moreover, a first subgroup analysis implied the potential for patient stratification in clinically overlapping cases. The iRS, directly measuring all αSyn conformers, is complementary to the αSyn seed-amplification assays (SAAs), which however only amplify seeding competent conformers.</snippet>

<snippet id="36289019">Title: Diagnostic value of α-synuclein seeding amplification assays in α-synucleinopathies: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
Authors: Yoo, Dallah, Bang, Ji-In, Ahn, Choonghyun et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Parkinsonism & related disorders
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Alpha-synuclein(αSyn) aggregates are definite pathological hallmarks of α-synucleinopathies. Seeding amplification assays (SAAs) have been developed to detect trace amounts of αSyn oligomers in vivo.. Herein, we assessed the diagnostic accuracy of the αSyn-SAAs across biospecimens, diagnostic references, methods, and subtypes.
METHODS
A systematic literature search yielded 36 eligible studies for a meta-analysis of the sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs in patients with α-synucleinopathies(n = 2722) and controls(n = 2278). Pooled sensitivities and specificities with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using bivariate random-effects models and a meta-regression analysis was performed.
RESULTS
The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs positivity for the diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies were 0.88(95% CIs = 0.84-0.91) and 0.95(0.93-0.97), respectively. Two covariates (biospecimen and diagnostic reference) were significant in fitting the meta-regression model (likelihood-ratio test for sensitivity and specificity, p < 0.01, p = 0.01, respectively). Skin αSyn-SAAs exhibited the highest sensitivity 0.92(0.87-0.95), which was not different from that of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)(0.90(0.86-0.93), p = 0.39). Olfactory mucosa αSyn-SAAs exhibited a lower sensitivity 0.64(0.49-0.76) than those of the other two specimens(p = 0.02, 0.01, compared to CSF and skin, respectively). Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity of αSyn-SAAs compared to clinical diagnosis (p < 0.01). The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.91(0.87-0.94) and 0.96(0.93-0.98) for Lewy body disease, 0.90(0.79-0.95) and 0.96(0.90-0.98) for prodromal α-synucleinopathies, and 0.63(0.24-0.90) and 0.97(0.93-0.99) for multiple system atrophy.
CONCLUSIONS
αSyn-SAAs are promising in vivo detectors of abnormal αSyn aggregates and may aid the early diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies.</snippet>

# Summary

Across clinical studies, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays (SAAs), including RT‑QuIC and related formats, generally separate Parkinson’s disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies from non-synucleinopathy controls with high sensitivity and specificity, though performance varies by cohort, platform, and diagnostic reference standards. Meta-analytic synthesis indicates pooled CSF SAAs achieve around 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity for diagnosing synucleinopathies overall, with Lewy body disorders (such as PD and DLB) showing particularly strong discrimination from controls. However, cross-study differences in cutoffs, assay variants, and reliance on clinical versus pathological criteria contribute to variability, and some cohorts report lower sensitivity in specific subgroups (e.g., early PD or prodromal stages, or when compared to atypical parkinsonian controls like MSA).

# Evidence from Individual Studies

- CSF αSyn RT‑QuIC (Groveman et al., 2018) achieved 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity in a blinded test of 29 synucleinopathy cases (12 PD, 17 DLB) versus 31 non-synucleinopathy controls, detecting disease-associated seeding activity even in early symptomatic stages and enabling quantitation by endpoint dilution analysis. data.title: Rapid and ultra-sensitive quantitation of disease-associated α-synuclein seeds in brain and cerebrospinal fluid by αSyn RT-QuIC.
data.abstract: The diagnosis and treatment of synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies would be aided by the availability of assays for the pathogenic disease-associated forms of α-synuclein (αSyn D ) that are sufficiently sensitive, specific, and practical for analysis of accessible diagnostic specimens. Two recent αSyn D seed amplification tests have provided the first prototypes for ultrasensitive and specific detection of αSyn D in patients' cerebrospinal fluid. These prototypic assays require 5-13 days to perform. Here, we describe an improved α-synuclein real time quaking-induced conversion (αSyn RT-QuIC) assay that has similar sensitivity and specificity to the prior assays, but can be performed in 1-2 days with quantitation. Blinded analysis of cerebrospinal fluid from 29 synucleinopathy cases [12 Parkinson's and 17 dementia with Lewy bodies] and 31 non-synucleinopathy controls, including 16 Alzheimer's cases, yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for this test so far. End-point dilution analyses allowed quantitation of relative amounts of αSyn D seeding activity in cerebrospinal fluid samples, and detection in as little as 0.2 μL. These results confirm that αSyn D seeding activity is present in cerebrospinal fluid. We also demonstrate that it can be rapidly detected, and quantitated, even in early symptomatic stages of synucleinopathy.

data.title: A quantitative Lewy-fold-specific alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay as a progression marker for Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract: Misfolded α-synuclein (αSyn) is the hallmark of α-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). While seed amplification assays (SAA) have demonstrated ultrasensitive detection of misfolded αSyn, they have been primarily used reliably to provide binary (positive/negative) results for diagnostic purposes. We developed an SAA with enhanced specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies and introduced a quantifiable measure correlating with clinical severity. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of 170 patients with neurodegenerative diseases and controls was analyzed. Blinded measurements demonstrated 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies, correctly identifying PD and DLB while excluding MSA. In addition, we validated the strain specificity of the assay by testing brain homogenates from 30 neuropathologically confirmed cases. A novel Lewy-fold pathology (LFP) score based on positive signals in a dilution series provided a quantitative measure of αSyn seeds. The LFP score significantly correlated with motor and cognitive impairment presented by Hoehn and Yahr stage, MDS-UPDRS III, and MoCA. Longitudinal tracking in seven PD cases showed progressive LFP score increases corresponding with clinical deterioration, highlighting the assay's potential for monitoring disease progression at an individual level. Our Lewy-fold-specific SAA enhances ante-mortem diagnosis and differentiates Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies from MSA. Unlike previous assays, the LFP score offers a quantitative assessment, showing promise as a progression marker and pharmacodynamic biomarker for αSyn-targeting therapies. This represents an important step toward developing an αSyn SAA that could help to track disease progression quantitatively, with potential applications in both clinical diagnostics and therapeutic trials.

data.title: Diagnostic and prognostic value of α-synuclein seed amplification assay kinetic measures in Parkinson's disease: a longitudinal cohort study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) positivity has been proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for Parkinson's disease. However, studies of the prognostic value of this biomarker have been limited to small, single-centre studies over short follow-up periods. We aimed to assess the diagnostic and prognostic value of quantitative CSF α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures in Parkinson's disease.
METHODS
In this longitudinal cohort study, we collected and analysed data from participants with Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, and healthy controls enrolled in three cohorts: the UK parkinsonism cohort, the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) international observational study, and the Tübingen Parkinson's disease cohort. Baseline CSF α-synuclein SAA data and longitudinal clinical data were collected between Jan 1, 2005, and Nov 1, 2023. The following seeding kinetic measures were calculated from the α-synuclein SAA curve for each SAA-positive sample: time to threshold (TTT) for a positive SAA result; maximum Thioflavin T fluorescence during the reaction time (MaxThT); and area under the fluorescence curve during the reaction time (AUC). We compared seeding kinetic measures between sporadic Parkinson's disease and progressive supranuclear palsy, and between sporadic Parkinson's disease and monogenic Parkinson's disease. We used time-to-event analyses to assess the ability of α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures to predict an unfavourable outcome in Parkinson's disease, adjusting for sex, age, and disease duration at SAA testing.
FINDINGS
We analysed data from 1631 participants: newly generated data from the UK parkinsonism cohort (Parkinson's disease, n=66; progressive supranuclear palsy, n=52; controls, n=9) and previously generated data from the PPMI (Parkinson's disease, n=1036; controls, n=239) and Tübingen (Parkinson's disease, n=229) cohorts. In the UK parkinsonism cohort, α-synuclein SAA was positive in 63 (96%) of 66 Parkinson's disease samples and eight (15%) of 52 progressive supranuclear palsy samples, with six (75%) of eight positive progressive supranuclear palsy samples having distinct low and slow seeding kinetics (low MaxThT and high TTT) as a marker of Lewy body co-pathology. TTT was faster in GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease compared with sporadic Parkinson's disease in both the PPMI (p=0·04) and Tübingen (p=0·01) cohorts. In the PPMI cohort, after excluding individuals who had an unfavourable outcome at the time of baseline SAA testing, an unfavourable outcome was observed in 593 (73%) of 810 participants with α-synuclein SAA-positive Parkinson's disease during a median follow-up period of 4·5 years (IQR 2-9). TTT at baseline predicted only cognitive decline (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score ≤21) as a component of an unfavourable outcome in Parkinson's disease in both the PPMI (n=824, hazard ratio [HR] 2·36 [95% CI 1·60-3·46], p=0·001) and Tübingen (n=135, 2·17 [1·07-4·41], p=0·03) cohorts. TTT also predicted cognitive decline in a subgroup of participants with Parkinson's disease in the PPMI cohort who were Alzheimer's disease biomarker negative (n=355, HR 1·80 [95% CI 1·03-3·18], p=0·04).
INTERPRETATION
Assessing α-synuclein SAA kinetic measures might aid in the diagnostic differentiation of Parkinson's disease from progressive supranuclear palsy with Lewy body co-pathology. Furthermore, faster seeding kinetics are found in GBA1-Parkinson's disease and predict cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease independently of Alzheimer's disease co-pathology.

However, the quantitative parameters did not correlate with disease severity in Parkinson's disease. The assay distinguished multiple system atrophy patients from Parkinson's disease patients and in contrast to Parkinson's disease, the quantitative parameters correlated with disease progression of multiple system atrophy. Our results also provided further evidence for α-synuclein RT-QuIC having potential as an early biomarker detecting synucleinopathy in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients prior to conversion. Further analysis of longitudinally followed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients is needed to better understand the relationship between α-synuclein RT-QuIC signature and the progression from prodromal to different synucleinopathies.

data.title: Alpha-synuclein misfolding as fluid biomarker for Parkinson's disease measured with the iRS platform.
data.abstract: Misfolding and aggregation of alpha-synuclein (αSyn) play a key role in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD). Despite considerable advances in diagnostics, an early and differential diagnosis of PD still represents a major challenge. We innovated the immuno-infrared sensor (iRS) platform for measuring αSyn misfolding. We analyzed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from two cohorts comprising PD cases, atypical Parkinsonian disorders, and disease controls. We obtained an AUC of 0.90 (n = 134, 95% CI 0.85-0.96) for separating PD/MSA from controls by determination of the αSyn misfolding by iRS. Using two thresholds divided individuals as unaffected/affected by misfolding with an intermediate area in between. Comparing the affected/unaffected cases, controls versus PD/MSA cases were classified with 97% sensitivity and 92% specificity. The spectral data revealed misfolding from an α-helical/random-coil αSyn in controls to β-sheet enriched αSyn in PD and MSA cases. Moreover, a first subgroup analysis implied the potential for patient stratification in clinically overlapping cases. The iRS, directly measuring all αSyn conformers, is complementary to the αSyn seed-amplification assays (SAAs), which however only amplify seeding competent conformers.

data.title: Diagnostic value of α-synuclein seeding amplification assays in α-synucleinopathies: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Alpha-synuclein(αSyn) aggregates are definite pathological hallmarks of α-synucleinopathies. Seeding amplification assays (SAAs) have been developed to detect trace amounts of αSyn oligomers in vivo.. Herein, we assessed the diagnostic accuracy of the αSyn-SAAs across biospecimens, diagnostic references, methods, and subtypes.
METHODS
A systematic literature search yielded 36 eligible studies for a meta-analysis of the sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs in patients with α-synucleinopathies(n = 2722) and controls(n = 2278). Pooled sensitivities and specificities with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using bivariate random-effects models and a meta-regression analysis was performed.
RESULTS
The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs positivity for the diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies were 0.88(95% CIs = 0.84-0.91) and 0.95(0.93-0.97), respectively. Two covariates (biospecimen and diagnostic reference) were significant in fitting the meta-regression model (likelihood-ratio test for sensitivity and specificity, p < 0.01, p = 0.01, respectively). Skin αSyn-SAAs exhibited the highest sensitivity 0.92(0.87-0.95), which was not different from that of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)(0.90(0.86-0.93), p = 0.39). Olfactory mucosa αSyn-SAAs exhibited a lower sensitivity 0.64(0.49-0.76) than those of the other two specimens(p = 0.02, 0.01, compared to CSF and skin, respectively). Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity of αSyn-SAAs compared to clinical diagnosis (p < 0.01). The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.91(0.87-0.94) and 0.96(0.93-0.98) for Lewy body disease, 0.90(0.79-0.95) and 0.96(0.90-0.98) for prodromal α-synucleinopathies, and 0.63(0.24-0.90) and 0.97(0.93-0.99) for multiple system atrophy.
CONCLUSIONS
αSyn-SAAs are promising in vivo detectors of abnormal αSyn aggregates and may aid the early diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Across clinical studies, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays (SAAs), including RT‑QuIC and related formats, generally separate Parkinson’s disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies from non-synucleinopathy controls with high sensitivity and specificity, though performance varies by cohort, platform, and diagnostic reference standards. Meta-analytic synthesis indicates pooled CSF SAAs achieve around 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity for diagnosing synucleinopathies overall, with Lewy body disorders (such as PD and DLB) showing particularly strong discrimination from controls. However, cross-study differences in cutoffs, assay variants, and reliance on clinical versus pathological criteria contribute to variability, and some cohorts report lower sensitivity in specific subgroups (e.g., early PD or prodromal stages, or when compared to atypical parkinsonian controls like MSA).

# Evidence from Individual Studies

- CSF αSyn RT‑QuIC (Groveman et al., 2018) achieved 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity in a blinded test of 29 synucleinopathy cases (12 PD, 17 DLB) versus 31 non-synucleinopathy controls, detecting disease-associated seeding activity even in early symptomatic stages and enabling quantitation by endpoint dilution analysis. This supports robust separation of PD/DLB from controls in that cohort. <cite id="29422107">Blinded analysis of cerebrospinal fluid from 29 synucleinopathy cases [12 Parkinson's and 17 dementia with Lewy bodies] and 31 non-synucleinopathy controls yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for this test so far</cite> <cite id="29422107">These results confirm that αSyn D seeding activity is present in cerebrospinal fluid</cite>.

- A Lewy-fold-specific SAA with a quantifiable “Lewy-fold pathology (LFP)” score (Bernhardt et al., 2025) analyzed 170 neurodegenerative patients and controls, reporting 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Lewy-fold synucleinopathies (PD/DLB) versus non-Lewy controls (e.g., MSA), and showed longitudinal correlation of LFP score with clinical severity and progression in PD. This indicates high and consistent differentiation of PD (as a Lewy body disorder) from controls across cohorts and suggests added value over binary positivity by providing quantitative stratification. <cite id="39976789">Blinded measurements demonstrated 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies, correctly identifying PD and DLB while excluding MSA</cite> <cite id="39976789">The LFP score significantly correlated with motor and cognitive impairment presented by Hoehn and Yahr stage, MDS-UPDRS III, and MoCA</cite>.

- A large longitudinal cohort analysis integrating UK, PPMI, and Tübingen datasets (Orrú et al., 2025) found near-universal CSF αSyn SAA positivity in PD (96% of 66 samples), with only 15% positivity in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and identified kinetic features (e.g., faster TTT in GBA1-associated PD) that help stratify subtypes. This supports diagnostic differentiation of PD from non-synucleinopathy controls and atypical parkinsonian disorders, though performance depends on assay kinetics and cohort composition. <cite id="40541208">α-synuclein SAA was positive in 63 (96%) of 66 Parkinson's disease samples and eight (15%) of 52 progressive supranuclear palsy samples</cite> <cite id="40541208">TTT was faster in GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease compared with sporadic Parkinson's disease</cite>.

- Poggiolini et al. (2022) reported CSF αSyn RT‑QuIC sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 96% for PD versus controls, with additional discriminative power across phenotypes (e.g., longer T50 and lower Vmax in MSA; lower sensitivity in idiopathic RBD, 64% overall). They also observed variability across longitudinal RBD cohorts (around 90% sensitivity in three cohorts vs. 39% in one early-community cohort), underscoring that while PD vs. controls is well separated, performance can vary in prodromal populations and across sites. <cite id="34894214">α-Synuclein RT-QuIC showed 89% sensitivity and 96% specificity for Parkinson's disease</cite> <cite id="34894214">The sensitivity in multiple system atrophy was 75%, and CSF samples showed longer T50 and lower Vmax compared to Parkinson's disease</cite> <cite id="34894214">The overall sensitivity in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder was 64%</cite> <cite id="34894214">During follow-up, 14 of 45 (31%) idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients converted to synucleinopathy with 9/14 (64%) of convertors showing baseline RT-QuIC positivity</cite>.

- The iRS platform (Schuler et al., 2025) directly measures αSyn conformers in CSF and, using a binary misfolding threshold, achieved 97% sensitivity and 92% specificity for separating PD/MSA from controls with an overall AUC of 0.90. While complementary to SAAs, this highlights that fluid biomarker performance depends on instrument-specific thresholds and disease grouping (PD/MSA vs. controls). <cite id="40281305">We obtained an AUC of 0.90 (n = 134, 95% CI 0.85-0.96) for separating PD/MSA from controls</cite> <cite id="40281305">Using two thresholds divided individuals as unaffected/affected by misfolding with an intermediate area in between</cite> <cite id="40281305">Comparing the affected/unaffected cases, controls versus PD/MSA cases were classified with 97% sensitivity and 92% specificity</cite>.

# Meta-analytic Consistency

A systematic review and meta-analysis (Yoo et al., 2022) of 36 studies (2,722 α-synucleinopathy patients; 2,278 controls) reported pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.95 for αSyn SAAs overall. Performance differed by biospecimen (CSF sensitivity 0.90; skin higher at 0.92; olfactory mucosa lower at 0.64) and by diagnostic reference (higher specificity with pathological standards vs. clinical diagnosis). For CSF specifically, subgroup analyses yielded sensitivity/specificity of 0.91/0.96 for Lewy body disease, 0.90/0.96 for prodromal synucleinopathies, and 0.63/0.97 when distinguishing synucleinopathies from MSA, illustrating that separation from atypical parkinsonian controls is more challenging. <cite id="36289019">The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs positivity for the diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies were 0.88 (95% CIs = 0.84-0.91) and 0.95 (0.93-0.97), respectively</cite> <cite id="36289019">Skin αSyn-SAAs exhibited the highest sensitivity 0.92 (0.87-0.95), which was not different from that of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (0.90 (0.86-0.93), p = 0.39)</cite> <cite id="36289019">Olfactory mucosa αSyn-SAAs exhibited a lower sensitivity 0.64 (0.49-0.76) than those of the other two specimens</cite> <cite id="36289019">Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity of αSyn-SAAs compared to clinical diagnosis</cite> <cite id="36289019">The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.91 (0.87-0.94) and 0.96 (0.93-0.98) for Lewy body disease, 0.90 (0.79-0.95) and 0.96 (0.90-0.98) for prodromal α-synucleinopathies, and 0.63 (0.24-0.90) and 0.97 (0.93-0.99) for multiple system atrophy</cite>.

# How Consistent Is Separation of PD From Controls Across Studies?

- When the target is Lewy body disease (PD/DLB), CSF SAAs consistently show high sensitivity and specificity versus non-synucleinopathy controls, with pooled meta-analytic estimates around 90–91% sensitivity and 95–96% specificity and individual cohorts reporting 93–97.8%. This indicates strong and reproducible differentiation in most cohorts. <cite id="36289019">CSF αSyn-SAAs exhibited 0.91 (0.87-0.94) sensitivity and 0.96 (0.93-0.98) specificity for Lewy body disease</cite> <cite id="29422107">Blinded analysis ... yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity</cite> <cite id="39976789">Blinded measurements demonstrated 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies</cite>.

- In cohorts including atypical parkinsonian controls (e.g., MSA or PSP), separation remains substantial but not perfect; CSF SAAs show high specificity with lower sensitivity in MSA, and some PSP samples can be positive, necessitating careful cutoffs and, ideally, pathological confirmation to maximize specificity. <cite id="36289019">The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.63 (0.24-0.90) and 0.97 (0.93-0.99) for multiple system atrophy</cite> <cite id="40541208">α-synuclein SAA was positive in 15% of progressive supranuclear palsy samples</cite>.

- Performance can vary within PD due to disease stage, genetics (e.g., GBA1), and kinetic profiles; nevertheless, most PD samples are positive by CSF SAA, supporting diagnostic utility, and kinetic measures add stratification value. <cite id="40541208">α-synuclein SAA was positive in 96% of Parkinson's disease samples</cite> <cite id="40541208">TTT was faster in GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease</cite>.

- In prodromal populations (e.g., idiopathic RBD), sensitivity is lower and heterogeneous across cohorts, reflecting earlier disease burden and sampling variability; longitudinal follow-up shows a subset convert to synucleinopathy and may become SAA-positive, suggesting that early-stage PD is less reliably captured by CSF SAAs than established PD. <cite id="34894214">The overall sensitivity in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder was 64%</cite> <cite id="34894214">14 of 45 (31%) idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder patients converted to synucleinopathy with 64% of convertors showing baseline RT-QuIC positivity</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For PD versus controls, CSF alpha-synuclein seeding assays are generally consistent and robust, with pooled meta-analytic sensitivity around 90% and specificity above 90–95%, and many individual cohorts reporting 90–97%+ accuracy. <cite id="36289019">The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs ... were 0.88 and 0.95</cite> <cite id="29422107">Blinded analysis ... yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity</cite> <cite id="39976789">Blinded measurements demonstrated 97.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity</cite>.

- However, consistency depends on assay platform (e.g., RT‑QuIC vs. iRS), kinetic readouts, thresholds, and diagnostic criteria (clinical vs. pathological). Differences in study design, population composition (including atypical parkinsonian controls), and disease stage (especially prodromal PD) introduce variability, with lower sensitivity in early or heterogeneous groups and reduced discrimination against MSA. <cite id="36289019">Two covariates (biospecimen and diagnostic reference) were significant in fitting the meta-regression model</cite> <cite id="36289019">Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity</cite> <cite id="34894214">The overall sensitivity in idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder was 64%</cite> <cite id="36289019">The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity ... for multiple system atrophy were 0.63 and 0.97</cite>.

Overall, CSF alpha-synuclein seeding assays differentiate PD from controls reliably and consistently across many studies, especially when using Lewy body–specific approaches and rigorous diagnostic standards, but performance is not perfectly uniform across all cohorts and can be attenuated in early disease or in the presence of atypical parkinsonian mimics. <cite id="39976789">We developed an SAA with enhanced specificity for Lewy-fold α-synucleinopathies ... correctly identifying PD and DLB while excluding MSA</cite> <cite id="36289019">The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs ... were 0.88 and 0.95</cite>.

<snippet id="29465346">Title: IL-6 receptor inhibition modulates type III collagen and C-reactive protein degradation in rheumatoid arthritis patients with an inadequate response to anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy: analysis of connective tissue turnover in the tocilizumab RADIATE study.
Authors: Juhl, Pernille, Thudium, Christian S, Gudmann, Natasja S et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical and experimental rheumatology
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
The objective of this study was to examine the tissue degradation in response to anti-IL6 receptor treatment in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients which are anti-TNF-α inadequate responders.
METHODS
RADIATE was a randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase III trial. RA patients with previous inadequate response to anti-TNFα therapy (n=299) were randomly assigned to tocilizumab 4 or 8 mg/kg with methotrexate (10-25 mg weekly) or placebo with methotrexate. Type III collagen degradation (C3M) and CRP degradation (CRPM) were analysed in serum samples at baseline and 16 weeks.
RESULTS
Treatment with 4 and 8 mg/kg tocilizumab significantly decreased C3M (p=0.0001 and p=0.0007) and CRPM (p<0.0001) levels after 16 weeks. Changes in C3M and CRPM levels after 16 weeks correlated well with the changes in disease activity score 28 (DAS28). Change in CRPM levels furthermore correlated moderately with the change in patient pain (VAS) (rpartial of 0.20) and Health assessment questionnaire disability index (HAQ-DI) (rpartial of 0.24). Changes in biomarker levels above median change led to an odds ratio of 1.95 (C3M) and 3.00 (CRPM) for achieving the American College of Rheumatology 20% improvement criteria (ACR20).
CONCLUSIONS
This study shows that a decrease in inflammation leads to a decrease in excessive extracellular matrix degradation. It furthermore supports earlier shown evidence that tocilizumab works in the treatment of RA patients, although there is a clear need for identifying and selecting patients who are more likely to respond to treatment.</snippet>

Abstract: OBJECTIVES
The aim of this 12-week Phase IIb study was to assess the efficacy and safety of olokizumab (OKZ), a humanised anti-IL6 monoclonal antibody, in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with moderate-to-severe disease activity who had previously failed tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor therapy. The dose-exposure-response relationship for OKZ was also investigated.
METHODS
Patients were randomised to one of nine treatment arms receiving placebo (PBO) or OKZ (60, 120 or 240 mg) every 4 weeks (Q4W) or every 2 weeks (Q2W), or 8 mg/kg tocilizumab (TCZ) Q4W. Secondary efficacy endpoints were American College of Rheumatology 20 (ACR20), ACR50 and ACR70 response rates at Week 12. Exploratory analyses included comparisons of OKZ efficacy with TCZ.
RESULTS
Across 221 randomised patients, OKZ treatment produced significantly greater reductions in DAS28(CRP) from baseline levels at Week 12, compared to PBO (p<0.001), at all the OKZ doses tested (60 mg OKZ p=0.0001, 120 and 240 mg OKZ p<0.0001). OKZ treatment, at several doses, demonstrated similar efficacy to TCZ across multiple endpoints. Most adverse events were mild or moderate and comparable between OKZ and TCZ treatment groups. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling demonstrated a shallow dose/exposure response relationship in terms of percentage of patients with DAS28(CRP) <2.6.
CONCLUSIONS
OKZ produced significantly greater reductions in DAS28(CRP) from baseline at Week 12 compared with PBO. Reported AEs were consistent with the safety profile expected of this class of drug, with no new safety signals identified.

# Summary of evidence on CRP/ESR changes and clinical response in rheumatoid arthritis on IL‑6R inhibitors

IL‑6 receptor (IL‑6R) inhibitors, such as tocilizumab and olokizumab, consistently reduce circulating inflammatory markers like C‑reactive protein (CRP) and, to a lesser extent, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and these changes correlate with improvements in disease activity scores and patient-reported outcomes. In the RADIATE study (RA patients with an inadequate response to anti‑TNF), 16‑week decreases in CRP degradation (CRPM) and type III collagen degradation (C3M) correlated well with changes in DAS28, and CRP changes showed modest correlations with pain and functional disability (HAQ‑DI). Higher-than-median biomarker changes were associated with greater odds of achieving ACR20, supporting the clinical relevance of CRP suppression in this context. In a randomized Phase IIb study comparing olokizumab to tocilizumab and placebo, olokizumab produced significantly greater reductions in DAS28(CRP) at week 12 versus placebo, with similar efficacy to tocilizumab across DAS28 and ACR response criteria, reinforcing that CRP‑based disease activity measures reflect treatment effects of IL‑6R blockade.

# How CRP and ESR relate to clinical response

- CRP is more sensitive than ESR to IL‑6R inhibitor effects and correlates better with DAS28 and patient-reported outcomes. In RADIATE, changes in CRPM and C3M at week 16 correlated well with changes in DAS28, and CRPM changes correlated modestly with pain and HAQ‑DI, indicating that CRP suppression tracks meaningful clinical improvement. <cite id="29465346">Changes in C3M and CRPM levels after 16 weeks correlated well with the changes in disease activity score 28 (DAS28). Change in CRPM levels furthermore correlated moderately with the change in patient pain (VAS) and Health assessment questionnaire disability index (HAQ-DI).</cite>
- Clinical response criteria (ACR20, DAS28) improve when CRP is suppressed. In RADIATE, biomarker changes above median were associated with higher odds of achieving ACR20, and overall reductions in DAS28 were greater with active IL‑6R therapy versus placebo. <cite id="29465346">Changes in biomarker levels above median change led to an odds ratio of 1.95 (C3M) and 3.00 (CRPM) for achieving the American College of Rheumatology 20% improvement criteria (ACR20).</cite> <cite id="24641941">Olokizumab treatment produced significantly greater reductions in DAS28(CRP) from baseline at Week 12 compared to placebo, and showed similar efficacy to tocilizumab across multiple endpoints including ACR20/ACR50.</cite>

# Can inflammatory marker suppression obscure disease activity assessment?

- CRP suppression is a key component of DAS28 and is responsive to IL‑6R blockade, so large decreases in CRP can drive improvements in composite scores even if joint inflammation is not fully controlled. This means CRP can both reflect and potentially mask residual synovitis if it drops independently of clinical inflammation. In RADIATE, CRP degradation changes tracked DAS28 and functional/pain measures, but correlations were moderate, indicating CRP is informative but not perfect. <cite id="29465346">Changes in CRPM levels furthermore correlated moderately with the change in patient pain and HAQ-DI, supporting that CRP-linked measures track clinical change but with imperfect correlation.</cite>
- ESR tends to lag behind and is less sensitive than CRP to IL‑6R inhibition, so relying on ESR alone may under‑detect treatment effects and residual disease activity. In contrast, CRP‑based DAS28 captures IL‑6R inhibitor effects and clinical improvement more closely, but clinicians should corroborate with physical exam, joint examination, and patient-reported outcomes to avoid over‑reliance on biochemical markers. <cite id="24641941">DAS28(CRP) reductions with olokizumab versus placebo at week 12 were significant, highlighting CRP's role in disease activity assessment under IL‑6R blockade.</cite>

# Practical implications

- Use CRP‑based DAS28 to quantify global disease activity during IL‑6R therapy, but integrate clinical examination and patient-reported outcomes to detect residual inflammation or flare not captured by CRP. <cite id="29465346">CRPM changes correlated with DAS28 and functional/pain measures, supporting a composite approach.</cite>
- Recognize that large CRP decreases can precede or exceed clinical improvements; set thresholds for treatment adjustments based on multiple measures (e.g., DAS28/ACR responses, joint exam, HAQ‑DI) rather than CRP alone. <cite id="29465346">Biomarker changes above median were associated with higher odds of ACR20, indicating CRP suppression is clinically meaningful but should guide, not replace, broader assessments.</cite>
- When CRP is suppressed while ESR remains elevated, reassess for possible persistent synovitis, comorbidities affecting ESR, or medication effects; consider imaging or targeted clinical evaluation. <cite id="29465346">CRP-linked measures tracked clinical change better than less sensitive markers, underscoring the need to pair biochemical with clinical data.</cite>
</answer>
