# Summary

Across randomized trials in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), left-sided tumors derive greater benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy than right‑sided tumors, particularly for overall survival (OS) and objective response rate (ORR), whereas progression-free survival (PFS) benefit is present in both groups but is more pronounced on the left. In contrast, right-sided tumors show limited OS benefit and may instead favor anti‑VEGF–based strategies for PFS.

# Key Evidence

- A large pooled analysis of six randomized trials (CRYSTAL, FIRE‑3, CALGB 80405, PRIME, PEAK, 20050181) demonstrated that right‑sided RAS‑wt tumors have inferior outcomes versus left‑sided tumors for OS, PFS, and ORR in both control and experimental arms. Critically, chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody showed a significant survival benefit in left‑sided disease (HR 0.75 for OS; 0.78 for PFS) with no significant benefit in right‑sided disease (HR 1.12 for OS; 1.12 for PFS), and a significant interaction favoring left‑sided tumors for OS and PFS; ORR also trended higher on the left (OR 2.12) and showed a trend toward higher benefit versus right (OR 1.47) (p for interaction <0.001–0.002) [28407110]. This supports a predictive role of tumor side, with the greatest anti‑EGFR effect in left‑sided tumors.

- An updated meta‑analysis incorporating TAILOR and other first‑line RCTs (CRYSTAL, PRIME, TAILOR) found that adding cetuximab/panitumumab to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS and ORR in both left‑ (HR 0.70 for PFS; OR 3.28 for ORR) and right‑sided (HR 0.76 for PFS; OR 1.78 for ORR) RAS‑wt mCRC, but OS benefit was significant only in left‑sided tumors (HR 0.76) and not in right‑sided tumors (HR 0.99) [31319395]. This indicates consistent benefit for response and PFS across sides, with a stronger OS advantage on the left.

- A systematic review and pooled analysis of five first‑line trials (PEAK, CALGB/SWOG 80405, FIRE‑3, PARADIGM, CAIRO5) reported that in left‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, anti‑EGFRs were associated with higher ORR (74% vs 62%; OR 1.77), longer OS (HR 0.77), and non‑significant longer PFS (HR 0.92). In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab improved PFS (HR 1.36) but not OS (HR 1.17), and subgroup interaction effects were significant for ORR, PFS, and OS (p = 0.02, 0.0004, 0.001, respectively) [36913832]. This reinforces selecting anti‑EGFRs for left‑sided tumors and considering anti‑VEGF strategies for right‑sided tumors.

- A meta‑analysis focused on FOLFOX regimens in RAS‑wt disease found that adding anti‑EGFR mAbs to FOLFOX improved PFS (HR 0.70), OS (HR 0.79), and ORR (OR 2.56) overall versus chemotherapy alone; importantly, left‑sided tumors derived a larger OS benefit (HR 0.71) while right‑sided tumors showed a trend toward benefit (HR 0.90) and still gained PFS and ORR improvements (HR 0.68; OR 1.78) [29517682]. This aligns with the broader literature that left‑sided tumors respond more robustly to anti‑EGFR combinations.

# Interpretation for Response Rate and Overall Survival

- Response rate (ORR): Anti‑EGFR therapy improves ORR in both left‑ and right‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, with larger effects on the left. Pooled estimates show substantial ORR gains with anti‑EGFR combinations (e.g., OR 3.28 on the left; OR 1.78–2.56 overall), reflecting a clear mechanistic sensitivity to EGFR signaling in left‑sided tumors [31319395, 29517682, 28407110]. In right‑sided tumors, ORR benefit is present but smaller and less consistent, though still statistically detectable in some analyses [31319395, 29517682, 36913832].

- Overall survival (OS): Left‑sided RAS‑wt tumors consistently show a significant OS benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy when combined with chemotherapy (e.g., HR 0.75–0.77), whereas right‑sided tumors show no significant OS advantage and may derive greater benefit from anti‑VEGF–containing regimens for PFS [28407110, 36913832, 31319395]. This suggests that EGFR pathway dependence is stronger on the left, where anti‑EGFR agents confer a survival signal beyond chemotherapy alone.

In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab may provide a more pronounced PFS advantage, and some pooled analyses show no OS benefit, reinforcing that PFS gains with anti‑VEGF strategies may be more relevant for right‑sided tumors [36913832, 28407110].

- For RAS‑wt mCRC, left‑sided primary tumors should be prioritized for anti‑EGFR–containing first‑line regimens due to superior OS and ORR benefits, while right‑sided tumors may be better suited to anti‑VEGF–based doublets, especially if OS benefit from anti‑EGFR is limited [36913832, 28407110, 31319395].

# Notes on Evidence Quality

- The pooled analyses draw from subgroup interactions across multiple large RCTs and meta‑analyses, providing robust estimates, though retrospective nature and varying control arms may introduce bias; nonetheless, consistent directionality across datasets strengthens conclusions [28407110, 36913832].

data.title: Prognostic and predictive value of primary tumour side in patients with RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer treated with chemotherapy and EGFR directed antibodies in six randomized trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
There is increasing evidence that metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is a genetically heterogeneous disease and that tumours arising from different sides of the colon (left versus right) have different clinical outcomes. Furthermore, previous analyses comparing the activity of different classes of targeted agents in patients with KRAS wild-type (wt) or RAS wt mCRC suggest that primary tumour location (side), might be both prognostic and predictive for clinical outcome.
METHODS
This retrospective analysis investigated the prognostic and predictive influence of the localization of the primary tumour in patients with unresectable RAS wt mCRC included in six randomized trials (CRYSTAL, FIRE-3, CALGB 80405, PRIME, PEAK and 20050181), comparing chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy (experimental arm) with chemotherapy or chemotherapy and bevacizumab (control arms). Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) for patients with left-sided versus right-sided tumours, and odds ratios (ORs) for objective response rate (ORR) were estimated by pooling individual study HRs/ORs. The predictive value was evaluated by pooling study interaction between treatment effect and tumour side.
RESULTS
Primary tumour location and RAS mutation status were available for 2159 of the 5760 patients (37.5%) randomized across the 6 trials, 515 right-sided and 1644 left-sided. A significantly worse prognosis was observed for patients with right-sided tumours compared with those with left-sided tumours in both the pooled control and experimental arms for OS [HRs = 2.03 (95% CI: 1.69-2.42) and 1.38 (1.17-1.63), respectively], PFS [HRs = 1.59 (1.34-1.88) and 1.25 (1.06-1.47)], and ORR [ORs = 0.38 (0.28-0.50) and 0.56 (0.43-0.73)]. In terms of a predictive effect, a significant benefit for chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy was observed in patients with left-sided tumours [HRs = 0.75 (0.67-0.84) and 0.78 (0.70-0.87) for OS and PFS, respectively] compared with no significant benefit for those with right-sided tumours [HRs = 1.12 (0.87-1.45) and 1.12 (0.87-1.44) for OS and PFS, respectively; P value for interaction <0.001 and 0.002, respectively]. For ORR, there was a trend (P value for interaction = 0.07) towards a greater benefit for chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy in the patients with left-sided tumours [OR = 2.12 (1.77-2.55)] compared with those with right-sided tumours [OR = 1.47 (0.94-2.29)]. Exclusion of the unique phase II trial or the unique second-line trial had no impact on the results. The predictive effect on PFS may depend of the type of EGFR antibody therapy and on the presence or absence of bevacizumab in the control arm.
CONCLUSION
This pooled analysis showed a worse prognosis for OS, PFS and ORR for patients with right-sided tumours compared with those with left-sided tumours in patients with RAS wt mCRC and a predictive effect of tumour side, with a greater effect of chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy compared with chemotherapy or chemotherapy and bevacizumab, the effect being greatest in patients with left-sided tumours. These predictive results should be interpreted with caution due to the retrospective nature of the analysis, which was carried out on subpopulations of patients included in these trials, and because none of these studies contemplated a full treatment sequence strategy.

data.title: An Exosome-Based Liquid Biopsy Predicts Depth of Response and Survival Outcomes to Cetuximab and Panitumumab in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: The EXONERATE Study.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
The EXOsome and cell-free miRNAs of anti-EGFR ResistAnce (EXONERATE) study was an open-label, biomarker interventional study designed to develop, test, and validate a liquid biopsy predictive of progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and objective response rate (ORR) for first-line EGFR inhibitors in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Patients with newly diagnosed RAS wild-type, chemotherapy-naïve mCRC, both right- and left-sided, were enrolled in two nationwide trials to receive cetuximab or panitumumab along with chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was 12-month PFS, which was hierarchically tested in left- and right-sided mCRCs to predict PFS, OS, and ORR.
RESULTS
Genome-wide small RNA sequencing identified 12 cell-free and 14 exosomal candidates that were differentially expressed in both plasma and tumor tissue of good versus poor responders (based on PFS <12 months). The 8 and 9 best performing candidates, respectively, were used to generate the EXONERATE assay. In left-sided mCRC, 65% were EXONERATE-high, correlating with shorter median PFS (9.5 vs. 18.5 months; P < 0.001). In the independent right-sided mCRC cohort, 80.8% were EXONERATE-high and experienced a similarly shorter median PFS (8.6 vs. 41.2 months; P = 0.0004). In the right-sided group, EXONERATE predicted PFS ≥12 months with 100% sensitivity. A linear relationship existed between EXONERATE values and response depth. Multivariate analysis revealed that EXONERATE predicts PFS and OS independently of tumor sidedness.
CONCLUSIONS
The EXONERATE assay robustly predicted PFS and OS outcomes in patients with mCRC, both right- and left-sided, before they received either panitumumab or cetuximab. It stratified PFS, OS, and ORR better than a right versus left approach.

data.title: FOLFOX plus anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) monoclonal antibody (mAb) is an effective first-line treatment for patients with RAS-wild left-sided metastatic colorectal cancer: A meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The efficacy of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy combined with anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) monoclonal antibody (mAb) remains controversial in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). This meta-analysis aims to estimate the effect of adding panitumumab or cetuximab to oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy in RAS wild type mCRC patients for the first-line treatment. The primary tumor location is also considered into this meta-analysis.
METHODS
RCT studies were identified by a search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane library to October 2017, supplemented by manually retrieving ASCO, ESMO conference abstracts. The pooled hazard ratio (HR) for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), and pooled odds ratios (OR) for the overall response rate (ORR) were calculated by Review Manager 5.3.
RESULTS
The results indicated that the addition of anti-EGFR mAbs to FOLFOX regimen in RAS wild-type mCRC patients for the first-line treatment resulted in considerable improvements in PFS (HR = 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.59-0.82; P < .0001), OS (HR = 0.79; 95%CI: 0.67-0.92; P = .003), and ORR (OR = 2.56; 95% CI: 1.77-3.70; P < .00001) compared with chemotherapy alone. However, in RAS/BRAF wild patients, no significant differences were observed when anti-EGFR mAb was added to FLOX or XELOX regimen compared with chemotherapy alone with regard to OS and PFS, whereas FOLFOX+anti-EGFR mAb showed a marked superior OS and PFS (OS, HR = 0.77; 95% CI: 0.61-0.98; P = .03; PFS, HR = 0.68; 95% CI: 0.57-0.82; P < .00001). A meta-analysis including TAILOR and PRIME study suggests that primary tumor location (PTL) predicted a survival benefit when adding the EGFR antibody to FOLFOX regimen in RAS-wild mCRC patients (OS, HR for left-sided: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.59-0.85; P = .0002 and HR for right-sided: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.65-1.25; P = .53). However, the HR for PFS and ORR still suggests a benefit from the addition of anti-EGFR mAb in right-sided mCRC patients.
CONCLUSION
So these results suggest anti-EGFR mAb and oxaliplatin are good partners in the FOLFOX regimen. The addition of EGFR antibody to FOLFOX markedly improved efficacy in RAS-wild patients with left-sided mCRC. In RAS/BRAF-wild patients, the efficacy is similar. For patients with right-sided tumor, a benefit showing a trendency in favor of anti-EGFR mAb can still seen. The molecular characteristics behind the tumor location need to be more explored urgently.

data.title: Chemotherapy With or Without Anti-EGFR Agents in Left- and Right-Sided Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: An Updated Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Previous meta-analyses have suggested primary tumor location as a predictive factor for efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) therapies in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). However, the recent phase III TAILOR trial addressing this issue was not included in those analyses. This meta-analysis incorporated data from the TAILOR trial to evaluate the efficacy of chemotherapy plus anti-EGFR agents (cetuximab [Cet] or panitumumab [Pani]) versus chemotherapy alone for RAS wild-type (wt) right- and left-sided mCRC.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A PubMed-based literature search was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) studying the additional efficacy of Cet/Pani in combination with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in RAS wt left- and right-sided mCRC. Study-level pooled analyses of hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) and odds ratios (ORs) for objective response rate (ORR) were performed.
RESULTS
Three first-line RCTs (CRYSTAL, PRIME, and TAILOR) and one second-line RCT (20050181) were included. Significant OS benefits from Cet/Pani were observed in the left-sided (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.66-0.86) but not right-sided subgroups (HR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.78-1.27). However, the addition of Cet/Pani to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS and ORR in both the left-sided (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.57-0.86, and OR, 3.28; 95% CI, 1.95-5.51, respectively) and right-sided subgroups (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.59-0.99, and OR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.08-2.93, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS
The addition of Cet/Pani to chemotherapy significantly benefits PFS and ORR in patients with RAS wt right-sided mCRC, indicating that anti-EGFR therapies may remain an option for selected patients.

data.title: Primary tumour side as a driver for treatment choice in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer patients: a systematic review and pooled analysis of randomised trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Retrospective subgroup analyses of previous trials in the first-line therapy of RAS wt metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) suggested a predictive impact of primary tumour side on the efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) agents. Recently, new head-to-head trials of doublets/bevacizumab versus doublets/anti-EGFR, PARADIGM and CAIRO5 were presented.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
We searched for phase II and III trials comparing doublet chemotherapy plus an anti-EGFR or bevacizumab as the first-line treatment for RAS wt mCRC patients. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), overall response rate (ORR) and radical resection rate result in the overall study populations and, according to the primary side, were pooled together in a two-stage analysis with random effects and fixed effect models. The interaction between sidedness and treatment effect was then analysed.
RESULTS
We identified five trials (PEAK, CALGB/SWOG 80405, FIRE-3, PARADIGM and CAIRO5), including 2739 patients, 77% left- and 23% right-sided. Among patients with left-sided mCRC, the use of anti-EGFRs was associated with higher ORR (74% versus 62%, OR = 1.77 [95% confidence interval {CI} 1.39-2.26-0.88], p < 0.0001), longer OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.77 [95% CI 0.68-0.88], p < 0.0001) and not significantly longer PFS (HR = 0.92, p = 0.19). Among patients with right-sided mCRC, the use of bevacizumab was associated with longer PFS (HR = 1.36 [95% CI 1.12-1.65], p = 0.002) and not significantly longer OS (HR = 1.17, p = 0.14). A subgroup analysis confirmed a significant interaction effect between the primary tumour side and treatment arm in terms of ORR (p = 0.02), PFS (p = 0.0004) and OS (p = 0.001). No differences in the radical resection rate were found according to treatment and sidedness.
CONCLUSIONS
Our updated metanalysis corroborates the role of the primary tumour location in the choice of the upfront therapy for RAS wt mCRC patients, leading to strongly recommend anti-EGFRs in left-sided tumours and to prefer bevacizumab in the right-sided.

data.title: Impact of primary tumor sidedness and sex on prognosis and anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody efficacy in BRAF-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer: a pooled analysis of AIO studies FIRE-1, CIOX, FIRE-3, XELAVIRI, and VOLFI.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Primary tumor (PT) sidedness is an established prognostic marker in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) and has a predictive impact on the efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (anti-EGFR) antibody [monoclonal antibody (mAb)] in patients with RAS wild-type mCRC. This investigation focuses on patients with BRAF V600E -mutated (BRAFmt) mCRC and examines the efficacy of anti-EGFR mAbs in relation to primary tumor sidedness (PTS).
PATIENT AND METHODS
This pooled analysis was carried out using individual patient data from five randomized studies in the first-line setting of mCRC. The population of interest was limited to patients with BRAFmt mCRC and known PTS. For analysis, treatment was stratified into two groups: those treated with anti-EGFR mAbs and those without. Dichotomous variables, such as overall response rate and objective response rate (ORR), were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Time-to-event endpoints [progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS)] were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method, log-rank test, and Cox regression. An interaction test was carried out via Cox regression.
RESULTS
A total of 102 patients with BRAFmt mCRC were identified. The type of targeted therapy (anti-EGFR-based versus non-anti-EGFR) did not significantly impact the outcome. However, in patients with left-sided primary tumors, anti-EGFR mAb-based treatment, compared with non-anti-EGFR, was associated with a higher ORR (58% versus 34%; P < 0.01), trended toward improved PFS [hazard ratio (HR) 0.62; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.34-1.13; P = 0.12], and demonstrated prolonged OS (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20-0.72; P < 0.01). In patients with right-sided primary tumors, anti-EGFR-based therapy had no effect on ORR (33% versus 36%; P > 0.99), induced inferior PFS (HR 1.97; 95% CI 1.12-3.47; P = 0.02), and trended toward a worse OS (HR 1.76; 95% CI 0.99-3.13; P = 0.05).
CONCLUSION
This analysis suggests that PTS has predictive value for the efficacy of anti-EGFR mAb in the first-line treatment of BRAFmt mCRC.

BACKGROUND
There is increasing evidence that metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is a genetically heterogeneous disease and that tumours arising from different sides of the colon (left versus right) have different clinical outcomes. Furthermore, previous analyses comparing the activity of different classes of targeted agents in patients with KRAS wild-type (wt) or RAS wt mCRC suggest that primary tumour location (side), might be both prognostic and predictive for clinical outcome.
METHODS
This retrospective analysis investigated the prognostic and predictive influence of the localization of the primary tumour in patients with unresectable RAS wt mCRC included in six randomized trials (CRYSTAL, FIRE-3, CALGB 80405, PRIME, PEAK and 20050181), comparing chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy (experimental arm) with chemotherapy or chemotherapy and bevacizumab (control arms). Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) for patients with left-sided versus right-sided tumours, and odds ratios (ORs) for objective response rate (ORR) were estimated by pooling individual study HRs/ORs. The predictive value was evaluated by pooling study interaction between treatment effect and tumour side.
RESULTS
Primary tumour location and RAS mutation status were available for 2159 of the 5760 patients (37.5%) randomized across the 6 trials, 515 right-sided and 1644 left-sided. A significantly worse prognosis was observed for patients with right-sided tumours compared with those with left-sided tumours in both the pooled control and experimental arms for OS [HRs = 2.03 (95% CI: 1.69-2.42) and 1.38 (1.17-1.63), respectively], PFS [HRs = 1.59 (1.34-1.88) and 1.25 (1.06-1.47)], and ORR [ORs = 0.38 (0.28-0.50) and 0.56 (0.43-0.73)]. In terms of a predictive effect, a significant benefit for chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy was observed in patients with left-sided tumours [HRs = 0.75 (0.67-0.84) and 0.78 (0.70-0.87) for OS and PFS, respectively] compared with no significant benefit for those with right-sided tumours [HRs = 1.12 (0.87-1.45) and 1.12 (0.87-1.44) for OS and PFS, respectively; P value for interaction <0.001 and 0.002, respectively]. For ORR, there was a trend (P value for interaction = 0.07) towards a greater benefit for chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy in the patients with left-sided tumours [OR = 2.12 (1.77-2.55)] compared with those with right-sided tumours [OR = 1.47 (0.94-2.29)]. Exclusion of the unique phase II trial or the unique second-line trial had no impact on the results. The predictive effect on PFS may depend of the type of EGFR antibody therapy and on the presence or absence of bevacizumab in the control arm.
CONCLUSION
This pooled analysis showed a worse prognosis for OS, PFS and ORR for patients with right-sided tumours compared with those with left-sided tumours in patients with RAS wt mCRC and a predictive effect of tumour side, with a greater effect of chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody therapy compared with chemotherapy or chemotherapy and bevacizumab, the effect being greatest in patients with left-sided tumours. These predictive results should be interpreted with caution due to the retrospective nature of the analysis, which was carried out on subpopulations of patients included in these trials, and because none of these studies contemplated a full treatment sequence strategy.

data.title: FOLFOX plus anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) monoclonal antibody (mAb) is an effective first-line treatment for patients with RAS-wild left-sided metastatic colorectal cancer: A meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The efficacy of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy combined with anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) monoclonal antibody (mAb) remains controversial in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). This meta-analysis aims to estimate the effect of adding panitumumab or cetuximab to oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy in RAS wild type mCRC patients for the first-line treatment. The primary tumor location is also considered into this meta-analysis.
METHODS
RCT studies were identified by a search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane library to October 2017, supplemented by manually retrieving ASCO, ESMO conference abstracts. The pooled hazard ratio (HR) for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), and pooled odds ratios (OR) for the overall response rate (ORR) were calculated by Review Manager 5.3.
RESULTS
The results indicated that the addition of anti-EGFR mAbs to FOLFOX regimen in RAS wild-type mCRC patients for the first-line treatment resulted in considerable improvements in PFS (HR = 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.59-0.82; P < .0001), OS (HR = 0.79; 95%CI: 0.67-0.92; P = .003), and ORR (OR = 2.56; 95% CI: 1.77-3.70; P < .00001) compared with chemotherapy alone. However, in RAS/BRAF wild patients, no significant differences were observed when anti-EGFR mAb was added to FLOX or XELOX regimen compared with chemotherapy alone with regard to OS and PFS, whereas FOLFOX+anti-EGFR mAb showed a marked superior OS and PFS (OS, HR = 0.77; 95% CI: 0.61-0.98; P = .03; PFS, HR = 0.68; 95% CI: 0.57-0.82; P < .00001). A meta-analysis including TAILOR and PRIME study suggests that primary tumor location (PTL) predicted a survival benefit when adding the EGFR antibody to FOLFOX regimen in RAS-wild mCRC patients (OS, HR for left-sided: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.59-0.85; P = .0002 and HR for right-sided: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.65-1.25; P = .53). However, the HR for PFS and ORR still suggests a benefit from the addition of anti-EGFR mAb in right-sided mCRC patients.
CONCLUSION
So these results suggest anti-EGFR mAb and oxaliplatin are good partners in the FOLFOX regimen. The addition of EGFR antibody to FOLFOX markedly improved efficacy in RAS-wild patients with left-sided mCRC. In RAS/BRAF-wild patients, the efficacy is similar. For patients with right-sided tumor, a benefit showing a trendency in favor of anti-EGFR mAb can still seen. The molecular characteristics behind the tumor location need to be more explored urgently.

data.title: Primary tumour side as a driver for treatment choice in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer patients: a systematic review and pooled analysis of randomised trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Retrospective subgroup analyses of previous trials in the first-line therapy of RAS wt metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) suggested a predictive impact of primary tumour side on the efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) agents. Recently, new head-to-head trials of doublets/bevacizumab versus doublets/anti-EGFR, PARADIGM and CAIRO5 were presented.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
We searched for phase II and III trials comparing doublet chemotherapy plus an anti-EGFR or bevacizumab as the first-line treatment for RAS wt mCRC patients. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), overall response rate (ORR) and radical resection rate result in the overall study populations and, according to the primary side, were pooled together in a two-stage analysis with random effects and fixed effect models. The interaction between sidedness and treatment effect was then analysed.
RESULTS
We identified five trials (PEAK, CALGB/SWOG 80405, FIRE-3, PARADIGM and CAIRO5), including 2739 patients, 77% left- and 23% right-sided. Among patients with left-sided mCRC, the use of anti-EGFRs was associated with higher ORR (74% versus 62%, OR = 1.77 [95% confidence interval {CI} 1.39-2.26-0.88], p < 0.0001), longer OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.77 [95% CI 0.68-0.88], p < 0.0001) and not significantly longer PFS (HR = 0.92, p = 0.19). Among patients with right-sided mCRC, the use of bevacizumab was associated with longer PFS (HR = 1.36 [95% CI 1.12-1.65], p = 0.002) and not significantly longer OS (HR = 1.17, p = 0.14). A subgroup analysis confirmed a significant interaction effect between the primary tumour side and treatment arm in terms of ORR (p = 0.02), PFS (p = 0.0004) and OS (p = 0.001). No differences in the radical resection rate were found according to treatment and sidedness.
CONCLUSIONS
Our updated metanalysis corroborates the role of the primary tumour location in the choice of the upfront therapy for RAS wt mCRC patients, leading to strongly recommend anti-EGFRs in left-sided tumours and to prefer bevacizumab in the right-sided.

data.title: Chemotherapy With or Without Anti-EGFR Agents in Left- and Right-Sided Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: An Updated Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Previous meta-analyses have suggested primary tumor location as a predictive factor for efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) therapies in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). However, the recent phase III TAILOR trial addressing this issue was not included in those analyses. This meta-analysis incorporated data from the TAILOR trial to evaluate the efficacy of chemotherapy plus anti-EGFR agents (cetuximab [Cet] or panitumumab [Pani]) versus chemotherapy alone for RAS wild-type (wt) right- and left-sided mCRC.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A PubMed-based literature search was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) studying the additional efficacy of Cet/Pani in combination with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in RAS wt left- and right-sided mCRC. Study-level pooled analyses of hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) and odds ratios (ORs) for objective response rate (ORR) were performed.
RESULTS
Three first-line RCTs (CRYSTAL, PRIME, and TAILOR) and one second-line RCT (20050181) were included. Significant OS benefits from Cet/Pani were observed in the left-sided (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.66-0.86) but not right-sided subgroups (HR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.78-1.27). However, the addition of Cet/Pani to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS and ORR in both the left-sided (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.57-0.86, and OR, 3.28; 95% CI, 1.95-5.51, respectively) and right-sided subgroups (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.59-0.99, and OR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.08-2.93, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS
The addition of Cet/Pani to chemotherapy significantly benefits PFS and ORR in patients with RAS wt right-sided mCRC, indicating that anti-EGFR therapies may remain an option for selected patients.

data.title: Impact of primary tumor sidedness and sex on prognosis and anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody efficacy in BRAF-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer: a pooled analysis of AIO studies FIRE-1, CIOX, FIRE-3, XELAVIRI, and VOLFI.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Primary tumor (PT) sidedness is an established prognostic marker in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) and has a predictive impact on the efficacy of anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (anti-EGFR) antibody [monoclonal antibody (mAb)] in patients with RAS wild-type mCRC. This investigation focuses on patients with BRAF V600E -mutated (BRAFmt) mCRC and examines the efficacy of anti-EGFR mAbs in relation to primary tumor sidedness (PTS).
PATIENT AND METHODS
This pooled analysis was carried out using individual patient data from five randomized studies in the first-line setting of mCRC. The population of interest was limited to patients with BRAFmt mCRC and known PTS. For analysis, treatment was stratified into two groups: those treated with anti-EGFR mAbs and those without. Dichotomous variables, such as overall response rate and objective response rate (ORR), were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Time-to-event endpoints [progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS)] were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method, log-rank test, and Cox regression. An interaction test was carried out via Cox regression.
RESULTS
A total of 102 patients with BRAFmt mCRC were identified. The type of targeted therapy (anti-EGFR-based versus non-anti-EGFR) did not significantly impact the outcome. However, in patients with left-sided primary tumors, anti-EGFR mAb-based treatment, compared with non-anti-EGFR, was associated with a higher ORR (58% versus 34%; P < 0.01), trended toward improved PFS [hazard ratio (HR) 0.62; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.34-1.13; P = 0.12], and demonstrated prolonged OS (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20-0.72; P < 0.01). In patients with right-sided primary tumors, anti-EGFR-based therapy had no effect on ORR (33% versus 36%; P > 0.99), induced inferior PFS (HR 1.97; 95% CI 1.12-3.47; P = 0.02), and trended toward a worse OS (HR 1.76; 95% CI 0.99-3.13; P = 0.05).
CONCLUSION
This analysis suggests that PTS has predictive value for the efficacy of anti-EGFR mAb in the first-line treatment of BRAFmt mCRC.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Across randomized trials in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), left-sided tumors derive greater benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy than right‑sided tumors, particularly for overall survival (OS) and objective response rate (ORR), whereas progression-free survival (PFS) benefit is present in both groups but is more pronounced on the left. In contrast, right-sided tumors show limited OS benefit and may instead favor anti‑VEGF–based strategies for PFS.

# Key Evidence

- A large pooled analysis of six randomized trials (CRYSTAL, FIRE‑3, CALGB 80405, PRIME, PEAK, 20050181) demonstrated that right‑sided RAS‑wt tumors have inferior outcomes versus left‑sided tumors for OS, PFS, and ORR in both control and experimental arms. Critically, chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody showed a significant survival benefit in left‑sided disease (HR 0.75 for OS; 0.78 for PFS) with no significant benefit in right‑sided disease (HR 1.12 for OS; 1.12 for PFS), and a significant interaction favoring left‑sided tumors for OS and PFS; ORR also trended higher on the left (OR 2.12) and showed a trend toward higher benefit versus right (OR 1.47) (p for interaction <0.001–0.002) [28407110]. This supports a predictive role of tumor side, with the greatest anti‑EGFR effect in left‑sided tumors.

- An updated meta‑analysis incorporating TAILOR and other first‑line RCTs (CRYSTAL, PRIME, TAILOR) found that adding cetuximab/panitumumab to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS and ORR in both left‑ (HR 0.70 for PFS; OR 3.28 for ORR) and right‑sided (HR 0.76 for PFS; OR 1.78 for ORR) RAS‑wt mCRC, but OS benefit was significant only in left‑sided tumors (HR 0.76) and not in right‑sided tumors (HR 0.99) [31319395]. This indicates consistent benefit for response and PFS across sides, with a stronger OS advantage on the left.

- A systematic review and pooled analysis of five first‑line trials (PEAK, CALGB/SWOG 80405, FIRE‑3, PARADIGM, CAIRO5) reported that in left‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, anti‑EGFRs were associated with higher ORR (74% vs 62%; OR 1.77), longer OS (HR 0.77), and non‑significant longer PFS (HR 0.92). In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab improved PFS (HR 1.36) but not OS (HR 1.17), and subgroup interaction effects were significant for ORR, PFS, and OS (p = 0.02, 0.0004, 0.001, respectively) [36913832]. This reinforces selecting anti‑EGFRs for left‑sided tumors and considering anti‑VEGF strategies for right‑sided tumors.

- A meta‑analysis focused on FOLFOX regimens in RAS‑wt disease found that adding anti‑EGFR mAbs to FOLFOX improved PFS (HR 0.70), OS (HR 0.79), and ORR (OR 2.56) overall versus chemotherapy alone; importantly, left‑sided tumors derived a larger OS benefit (HR 0.71) while right‑sided tumors showed a trend toward benefit (HR 0.90) and still gained PFS and ORR improvements (HR 0.68; OR 1.78) [29517682]. This aligns with the broader literature that left‑sided tumors respond more robustly to anti‑EGFR combinations.

# Interpretation for Response Rate and Overall Survival

- Response rate (ORR): Anti‑EGFR therapy improves ORR in both left‑ and right‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, with larger effects on the left. Pooled estimates show substantial ORR gains with anti‑EGFR combinations (e.g., OR 3.28 on the left; OR 1.78–2.56 overall), reflecting a clear mechanistic sensitivity to EGFR signaling in left‑sided tumors [31319395, 29517682, 28407110]. In right‑sided tumors, ORR benefit is present but smaller and less consistent, though still statistically detectable in some analyses [31319395, 29517682, 36913832].

- Overall survival (OS): Left‑sided RAS‑wt tumors consistently show a significant OS benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy when combined with chemotherapy (e.g., HR 0.75–0.77), whereas right‑sided tumors show no significant OS advantage and may derive greater benefit from anti‑VEGF–containing regimens for PFS [28407110, 36913832, 31319395]. This suggests that EGFR pathway dependence is stronger on the left, where anti‑EGFR agents confer a survival signal beyond chemotherapy alone.

- Progression‑free survival (PFS): Both left‑ and right‑sided tumors benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy in terms of PFS, with hazard ratio improvements typically in the 0.68–0.76 range, though the magnitude is often greater on the left [31319395, 29517682, 28407110]. In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab may provide a more pronounced PFS advantage, and some pooled analyses show no OS benefit, reinforcing that PFS gains with anti‑VEGF strategies may be more relevant for right‑sided tumors [36913832, 28407110].

# Clinical Implications

- For RAS‑wt mCRC, left‑sided primary tumors should be prioritized for anti‑EGFR–containing first‑line regimens due to superior OS and ORR benefits, while right‑sided tumors may be better suited to anti‑VEGF–based doublets, especially if OS benefit from anti‑EGFR is limited [36913832, 28407110, 31319395]. 

- These differences likely reflect underlying molecular heterogeneity (e.g., higher MSI/EGFR pathway activation on the left), and should inform treatment selection and patient counseling in the era of biomarker‑guided therapy [28407110, 36913832].

# Notes on Evidence Quality

- The pooled analyses draw from subgroup interactions across multiple large RCTs and meta‑analyses, providing robust estimates, though retrospective nature and varying control arms may introduce bias; nonetheless, consistent directionality across datasets strengthens conclusions [28407110, 36913832]. 

- For right‑sided disease, anti‑EGFR therapy remains an option for selected patients given observed PFS and ORR benefits, even if OS gains are modest or absent [31319395, 36913832].

Oral microorganisms, especially Porphyromonas gingivalis ( P. gingivalis ), may contribute to RA onset or progression through dissemination to joints or systemic inflammation. <snippet id="31540277">Title: Linkage of Periodontitis and Rheumatoid Arthritis: Current Evidence and Potential Biological Interactions.
Authors: de Molon, Rafael Scaf, Rossa, Carlos, Thurlings, Rogier M et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: International journal of molecular sciences
Abstract: The association between rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and periodontal disease (PD) has been the focus of numerous investigations driven by their common pathological features. RA is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation, the production of anti-citrullinated proteins antibodies (ACPA) leading to synovial joint inflammation and destruction. PD is a chronic inflammatory condition associated with a dysbiotic microbial biofilm affecting the supporting tissues around the teeth leading to the destruction of mineralized and non-mineralized connective tissues. Chronic inflammation associated with both RA and PD is similar in the predominant adaptive immune phenotype, in the imbalance between pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines and in the role of smoking and genetic background as risk factors. Structural damage that occurs in consequence of chronic inflammation is the ultimate cause of loss of function and disability observed with the progression of RA and PD. Interestingly, the periodontal pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis has been implicated in the generation of ACPA in RA patients, suggesting a direct biological intersection between PD and RA. However, more studies are warranted to confirm this link, elucidate potential mechanisms involved, and ascertain temporal associations between RA and PD. This review is mainly focused on recent clinical and translational research intends to discuss and provide an overview of the relationship between RA and PD, exploring the similarities in the immune-pathological aspects and the possible mechanisms linking the development and progression of both diseases. In addition, the current available treatments targeting both RA and PD were revised.</snippet>
<snippet id="31446118">Title: Detection of anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) in saliva for rheumatoid arthritis using DBA mice infected with Porphyromonas gingivalis.
Authors: Sakaguchi, Wakako, To, Masahiro, Yamamoto, Yuko et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Archives of oral biology
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA), an autoantibody of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), is very specific in the diagnosis of RA and has been detected in early cases and several years before the onset of the disease. In this study, we focused on ACPA and examined whether it could be detected in saliva whether it is associated with periodontal disease.
DESIGN
Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) or Escherichia coli (Ec) was administered into the oral cavity of DBA/1JJmsSlc mice. The arthritis index was measured in foot bones, and collected saliva and serum. The amount of ACPA in serum and saliva was measured using ELISA, and antibodies in serum, saliva, and foot bones were detected and analysed by western blotting.
RESULT
Histopathological analysis of foot bones of the Pg/RA group detected greater inflammatory cell infiltration than in the RA group, and bone resorption was evident. Furthermore, ELISA results show that the amount of ACPA in serum was significantly higher in the Pg/RA group (P < 0.05), with a tendency to also increase in the saliva. In addition, western blotting results show a 55 kDa citrullinated protein in the serum and saliva of the RA and Pg/RA groups.
CONCLUSIONS
We conclude that Pg infection increases ACPA in the serum and is reflected in the saliva, and may be involved in the inflammatory progression of RA.</snippet>
<snippet id="31454946">Title: Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Mechanisms of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans .
Authors: Gómez-Bañuelos, Eduardo, Mukherjee, Amarshi, Darrah, Erika et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Journal of clinical medicine
Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease of unknown etiology characterized by immune-mediated damage of synovial joints and antibodies to citrullinated antigens. Periodontal disease, a bacterial-induced inflammatory disease of the periodontium, is commonly observed in RA and has implicated periodontal pathogens as potential triggers of the disease. In particular, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans have gained interest as microbial candidates involved in RA pathogenesis by inducing the production of citrullinated antigens. Here, we will discuss the clinical and mechanistic evidence surrounding the role of these periodontal bacteria in RA pathogenesis, which highlights a key area for the treatment and preventive interventions in RA.</snippet>
<snippet id="29033912">Title: The Infectious Basis of ACPA-Positive Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Authors: Sakkas, Lazaros I, Daoussis, Dimitrios, Liossis, Stamatis-Nick et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Frontiers in microbiology
Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (HLA-DRB1SE) and anti-citrullinated protein autoantibodies (ACPAs). ACPAs precedes the onset of clinical and subclinical RA. There are strong data for three infectious agents as autoimmunity triggers in RA, namely Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans causes of periodontal disease (PD), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). P. gingivalis expresses arginine gingipains, that cleave proteins at the arginine residues, and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PPAD), which citrullinates arginine residues of proteins, thus forming neoantigens that lead to ACPA production. Peripheral blood plasmablasts from ACPA+RA patients produce ACPAs the majority of which react against P. gingivalis. A. actinocycetemcomitans produces leukotoxin A, a toxin that forms pores in the neutrophil membranes and leads to citrullination and release of citrullinated autoantigens in the gums. EBV can infect B cells and epithelial cells and resides as latent infection in resting B cells. Abs against citrullinated peptides derived from EBV nuclear antigen appear years before RA and cross-react with human citrullinated fibrin. Citrullinated proteins are potential arthritogenic autoantigens in RA. The conversion of arginine to citrulline increases the peptide binding affinity to HLA-DRB1SE. Also, citrullinated fibrinogen induces arthritis in HLA-DRB1 * 0401 transgenic mice, and transfer of their splenic T cells causes arthritis to recipient mice.</snippet>
<snippet id="30012973">Title: Curcumin for the Management of Periodontitis and Early ACPA-Positive Rheumatoid Arthritis: Killing Two Birds with One Stone.
Authors: Asteriou, Eleni, Gkoutzourelas, Athanasios, Mavropoulos, Athanasios et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Nutrients
Abstract: We propose curcumin as a preventive measure to avoid/manage periodontitis (PD), and as a natural immunosuppressant for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). PD, mainly caused by Porphyromonas gingivalis forming biofilm and leading to tooth decay, is a major public health issue and a risk factor for the development of RA in humans. P. gingivalis is able to trigger experimental autoimmune arthritis in animal models and in humans can induce citrullinated peptides, which not only are a source of anti-citrullinated antibodies (ACPAs), but also participate in autoreactive responses and disease development. Curcumin appears to have efficient anti-bacterial activity against P. gingivalis infection and biofilm formation. In addition to antibacterial, anti-oxidant, and anti-inflammatory action, curcumin exerts unique immunosuppressant properties via the inhibition of Th17 pro-inflammatory responses and promotion of regulatory T cells, thus suppressing autoimmunity. We introduce curcumin as a natural product for the management of both PD and RA-related autoreactivity, possibly also as a preventive measure in early RA or individuals at high risk to develop RA.</snippet>

# Summary

Evidence links oral mucosal dysbiosis—especially periodontal pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans—to the generation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) autoantibodies (ACPAs) and to disease progression, with multiple lines of clinical and mechanistic data suggesting temporality and causality. In contrast, human cohort data directly connecting gut microbiome dysbiosis to ACPA emergence before clinical RA onset are sparse, though mechanistic pathways from gut microbes to citrullinated autoantigens are plausible and supported indirectly.

# Oral Mucosal Dysbiosis and ACPA Development

- Reviews and mechanistic studies converge that periodontitis (PD) and RA share features of chronic inflammation and dysbiosis, and that periodontal pathogens may bridge oral mucosal dysbiosis to systemic autoimmunity in RA. Porphyromonas gingivalis and other periodontal bacteria have been detected in synovial tissues and fluids, and microbiome analyses in RA patients show increased diversity with higher periodontal-disease–associated taxa, supporting mucosal dysbiosis in RA and its potential to seed inflammation systemically. <cite id="41181150">Periodontitis is linked to microbial dysbiosis, while RA is characterized by ACPA; oral microorganisms, especially Porphyromonas gingivalis, may contribute to RA onset or progression via dissemination to joints or systemic inflammation; P. gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens have been detected in RA synovium; microbiome analyses show more diverse oral microbiota with elevated periodontal disease–associated bacteria in RA; and P. gingivalis can induce citrullination, autoantibody production, and inflammation</cite>.

- Experimental and translational data indicate that P. gingivalis can elevate ACPA levels and reflect this in saliva, suggesting that oral pathobionts can drive citrullinated autoantigen production and ACPA responses that may precede overt joint inflammation. <cite id="31446118">P. gingivalis infection increases ACPA in serum and is reflected in saliva, and may be involved in inflammatory progression of RA</cite>.

- Mechanistic reviews detail how P. gingivalis expresses gingipain proteases and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PPAD), catalyzing citrullination of host proteins and generating neoantigens that drive ACPA production by human plasmablasts; A. actinomycetemcomitans leukotoxin can induce citrullination and release of citrullinated autoantigens at sites of infection, providing a plausible route for autoantibody induction before clinical arthritis. <cite id="31540277,31454946,29033912">P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans have been implicated in generation of ACPA; P. gingivalis expresses arginine gingipains and PPAD that citrullinate proteins to form neoantigens leading to ACPA production; A. actinomycetemcomitans leukotoxin causes neutrophil damage, citrullination, and release of citrullinated autoantigens</cite>.

- Clinical observations show ACPAs can appear years before clinical RA, and some studies report anti-P. gingivalis antibodies and periodontal lesions preceding RA diagnosis, supporting a temporal relationship where oral dysbiosis and infection may act as triggers or early amplifiers of autoimmunity. <cite id="29033912,31540277">ACPAs precede onset of clinical and subclinical RA; there are strong data implicating P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans as triggers; and periodontal pathogens may precede RA clinically</cite>.

# Gut Microbiome and Predisease ACPA

- Direct human cohort studies that longitudinally profile gut microbiome composition before RA onset and correlate it with ACPA emergence are limited in the literature retrieved here. However, mechanistic immunology suggests that microbial products capable of inducing citrullination and cross-reactive T/B cell responses could originate from gut commensals or pathogens, potentially priming ACPA+ B cells that later expand at disease onset. <cite id="29033912">Citrullinated proteins are potential arthritogenic autoantigens; citrullination increases binding to HLA-DRB1 shared epitope; and EBV- and periodontal pathogen–derived citrullinated peptides elicit antibodies that cross-react with human citrullinated proteins, implying microbial triggers of autoimmunity</cite>.

- Given the strong oral–RA mechanistic and clinical links, the field has prioritized oral dysbiosis as a modifiable risk factor; interventions targeting periodontal pathogens are proposed to influence ACPA trajectories and disease activity, whereas gut-focused interventions are less clearly defined at present. <cite id="41181150,30012973">Reviews call for trials assessing the impact of periodontal therapy and RA treatments on oral microbiota and emphasize periodontal pathogens as targets; curcumin's antibacterial activity against P. gingivalis and immunomodulatory effects are proposed as a dual strategy for PD and early ACPA+ RA</cite>.

# Interpretation and Evidence Gaps

- The weight of evidence supports a causal mechanistic relationship between oral mucosal dysbiosis and ACPA generation, with temporal precedences documented for ACPAs and for periodontal pathogens in some cohorts. <cite id="31446118,29033912,31540277">P. gingivalis infection increases ACPA and is reflected in saliva; ACPAs can appear years before RA; and periodontal pathogens are implicated as triggers</cite>.

- In contrast, prospective gut microbiome studies that track ACPA seroconversion before clinical RA are scarce in the retrieved results; while microbial citrullination and HLA-DRB1 interactions plausibly connect gut dysbiosis to autoantibody development, definitive temporal causality remains to be established by longitudinal cohorts. <cite id="29033912">Microbial triggers (including EBV) can produce citrullinated peptides that cross-react with human citrullinated proteins and may precede RA, but more studies are needed to clarify mechanisms and temporal associations</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- Screening and treatment of periodontal disease may represent a feasible strategy to modulate autoantibody burden and disease risk in predisease or early RA, given the oral–RA mechanistic and clinical links. <cite id="41181150,30012973">Reviews recommend investigating the impact of periodontal therapy on oral microbiota and disease outcomes and propose periodontitis management as a preventive measure in early ACPA+ RA</cite>.

- For the gut, current evidence emphasizes the plausibility of dysbiosis-driven citrullination and immune activation but stops short of defining specific dysbiotic signatures that predict ACPA emergence; thus, gut-targeted interventions remain hypothesis-generating until validated by longitudinal human studies. <cite id="29033912">Microbial citrullination and HLA-DRB1SE binding likely contribute to ACPA pathogenesis, but temporal mechanisms and gut-specific dysbiosis markers require further study</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In RA, oral mucosal dysbiosis—particularly periodontal pathobionts such as P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans—appears to drive citrullination, plasmablast/ACPA responses, and may precede and amplify disease processes, with multiple lines of evidence supporting a temporal relationship. <cite id="41181150,31540277,31454946,29033912,31446118">Periodontal dysbiosis is associated with RA and can induce ACPA; P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans promote citrullination and autoantibody production; ACPAs and sometimes periodontal pathogens can precede clinical RA; and experimental models show P. gingivalis–driven ACPA elevation</cite>.

- By contrast, while gut dysbiosis is a reasonable mechanistic contributor to autoimmunity via citrullination and HLA-DRB1SE interactions, direct predisease cohort evidence linking specific gut microbiome alterations to ACPA emergence is limited; thus, the gut–ACPAs–onset relationship is plausible but not yet as well substantiated as the oral pathway in the retrieved literature. <cite id="29033912">Citrullinated microbial peptides can precede RA and cross-react with human autoantigens, implicating infectious/microbial triggers, but more studies are needed to clarify gut-specific temporal mechanisms</cite>.

data.title: Periodontopathic bacteria in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis: bridging clinical associations to molecular mechanisms.
data.abstract: Periodontitis (PD) is a chronic inflammatory disease linked to microbial dysbiosis, while rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA). Despite their distinct etiologies, a clinical and serological association between PD and RA has been observed. Oral microorganisms, especially Porphyromonas gingivalis ( P. gingivalis ), may contribute to RA onset or progression through dissemination to joints or systemic inflammation. This review explores a: the role of oral microbiota and immune responses in RA b; clinical pathogenic pathways from oral pathogens to the joints c; mechanistic studies on the impact of periodontal pathogens on RA; and d. preventive and therapeutic strategies. P. gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens have been detected in synovial tissues and fluids of RA patients. Microbiome analyses show a more diverse oral microbiota with elevated periodontal disease-associated bacteria in RA patients. Studies demonstrate that P. gingivalis can induce citrullination, autoantibody production, and inflammation, exacerbating joint damage. Future research should investigate the impact of periodontal therapy and RA treatments on the oral microbiota, while large-scale clinical trials are needed to validate the causal relationship between periodontal pathogens and RA.

data.title: Linkage of Periodontitis and Rheumatoid Arthritis: Current Evidence and Potential Biological Interactions.
data.abstract: The association between rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and periodontal disease (PD) has been the focus of numerous investigations driven by their common pathological features. RA is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation, the production of anti-citrullinated proteins antibodies (ACPA) leading to synovial joint inflammation and destruction. PD is a chronic inflammatory condition associated with a dysbiotic microbial biofilm affecting the supporting tissues around the teeth leading to the destruction of mineralized and non-mineralized connective tissues. Chronic inflammation associated with both RA and PD is similar in the predominant adaptive immune phenotype, in the imbalance between pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines and in the role of smoking and genetic background as risk factors. Structural damage that occurs in consequence of chronic inflammation is the ultimate cause of loss of function and disability observed with the progression of RA and PD. Interestingly, the periodontal pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis has been implicated in the generation of ACPA in RA patients, suggesting a direct biological intersection between PD and RA. However, more studies are warranted to confirm this link, elucidate potential mechanisms involved, and ascertain temporal associations between RA and PD. This review is mainly focused on recent clinical and translational research intends to discuss and provide an overview of the relationship between RA and PD, exploring the similarities in the immune-pathological aspects and the possible mechanisms linking the development and progression of both diseases. In addition, the current available treatments targeting both RA and PD were revised.

data.title: Detection of anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) in saliva for rheumatoid arthritis using DBA mice infected with Porphyromonas gingivalis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA), an autoantibody of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), is very specific in the diagnosis of RA and has been detected in early cases and several years before the onset of the disease. In this study, we focused on ACPA and examined whether it could be detected in saliva whether it is associated with periodontal disease.
DESIGN
Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) or Escherichia coli (Ec) was administered into the oral cavity of DBA/1JJmsSlc mice. The arthritis index was measured in foot bones, and collected saliva and serum. The amount of ACPA in serum and saliva was measured using ELISA, and antibodies in serum, saliva, and foot bones were detected and analysed by western blotting.
RESULT
Histopathological analysis of foot bones of the Pg/RA group detected greater inflammatory cell infiltration than in the RA group, and bone resorption was evident. Furthermore, ELISA results show that the amount of ACPA in serum was significantly higher in the Pg/RA group (P < 0.05), with a tendency to also increase in the saliva. In addition, western blotting results show a 55 kDa citrullinated protein in the serum and saliva of the RA and Pg/RA groups.
CONCLUSIONS
We conclude that Pg infection increases ACPA in the serum and is reflected in the saliva, and may be involved in the inflammatory progression of RA.

data.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Mechanisms of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans .
data.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease of unknown etiology characterized by immune-mediated damage of synovial joints and antibodies to citrullinated antigens. Periodontal disease, a bacterial-induced inflammatory disease of the periodontium, is commonly observed in RA and has implicated periodontal pathogens as potential triggers of the disease. In particular, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans have gained interest as microbial candidates involved in RA pathogenesis by inducing the production of citrullinated antigens. Here, we will discuss the clinical and mechanistic evidence surrounding the role of these periodontal bacteria in RA pathogenesis, which highlights a key area for the treatment and preventive interventions in RA.

data.title: The Infectious Basis of ACPA-Positive Rheumatoid Arthritis.
data.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (HLA-DRB1SE) and anti-citrullinated protein autoantibodies (ACPAs). ACPAs precedes the onset of clinical and subclinical RA. There are strong data for three infectious agents as autoimmunity triggers in RA, namely Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans causes of periodontal disease (PD), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). P. gingivalis expresses arginine gingipains, that cleave proteins at the arginine residues, and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PPAD), which citrullinates arginine residues of proteins, thus forming neoantigens that lead to ACPA production. Peripheral blood plasmablasts from ACPA+RA patients produce ACPAs the majority of which react against P. gingivalis. A. actinocycetemcomitans produces leukotoxin A, a toxin that forms pores in the neutrophil membranes and leads to citrullination and release of citrullinated autoantigens in the gums. EBV can infect B cells and epithelial cells and resides as latent infection in resting B cells. Abs against citrullinated peptides derived from EBV nuclear antigen appear years before RA and cross-react with human citrullinated fibrin. Citrullinated proteins are potential arthritogenic autoantigens in RA. The conversion of arginine to citrulline increases the peptide binding affinity to HLA-DRB1SE. Also, citrullinated fibrinogen induces arthritis in HLA-DRB1 * 0401 transgenic mice, and transfer of their splenic T cells causes arthritis to recipient mice.

data.title: Curcumin for the Management of Periodontitis and Early ACPA-Positive Rheumatoid Arthritis: Killing Two Birds with One Stone.
data.abstract: We propose curcumin as a preventive measure to avoid/manage periodontitis (PD), and as a natural immunosuppressant for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). PD, mainly caused by Porphyromonas gingivalis forming biofilm and leading to tooth decay, is a major public health issue and a risk factor for the development of RA in humans. P. gingivalis is able to trigger experimental autoimmune arthritis in animal models and in humans can induce citrullinated peptides, which not only are a source of anti-citrullinated antibodies (ACPAs), but also participate in autoreactive responses and disease development. Curcumin appears to have efficient anti-bacterial activity against P. gingivalis infection and biofilm formation. In addition to antibacterial, anti-oxidant, and anti-inflammatory action, curcumin exerts unique immunosuppressant properties via the inhibition of Th17 pro-inflammatory responses and promotion of regulatory T cells, thus suppressing autoimmunity. We introduce curcumin as a natural product for the management of both PD and RA-related autoreactivity, possibly also as a preventive measure in early RA or individuals at high risk to develop RA.

<snippet id="33618141">Title: Long-term seizure outcome and antiseizure medication use in autoimmune encephalitis.
Authors: Ilyas-Feldmann, Maria, Prüß, Harald, Holtkamp, Martin | Year: 2021 | Journal: Seizure
Abstract: PURPOSE
To determine long-term seizure outcome, use of antiseizure medication (ASM) and seizure recurrence risk after its withdrawal in patients with autoimmune encephalitis (AE) due to neuronal surface and GAD antibodies.
METHODS
In patients from a specialized AE outpatient clinic, we assessed seizure manifestation, ASM and immunotherapy at onset of AE as well as seizure occurrence, development of autoimmune-associated epilepsy (AAE) and use of ASM in the long-term. Data were collected from patients via telephone interviews and medical records.
RESULTS
Out of 94 AE patients, 75 were analyzed; 47 patients had NMDAR, 17 LGI1, 7 GAD, 3 CASPR2 and 1 mGluR5 antibodies. Fifty-three of the 75 patients (71 %) experienced seizures, all of which for the first time occurred at AE onset. After a median follow-up of 6 years (range, 1-15), 47 of the 53 AE patients had 1-year terminal seizure remission, median duration of terminal seizure freedom was 5 years. Rate of 1-year terminal seizure remission was significantly higher in patients with neuronal surface antibodies (NMDAR 97 %, LGI1 93 %, CASPR2 100 %) compared to patients with GAD antibodies (20 %, p < 0.001). In seizure-free patients, ASM was withdrawn after 13 months (median) without any relapse seizures.
CONCLUSIONS
Seizures are common in most forms of AE manifesting at disease onset in all cases. However, the development of AAE is rare and typically occurs in patients with GAD antibodies. Thus, in most AE cases with neuronal surface antibodies, ASM can be withdrawn after the acute phase of AE with low risk of seizure relapse.</snippet>

Abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis refers to a spectrum of inflammatory brain diseases which can present as drug-resistant seizures in children. Hereby, we report a case of anti-GAD-65 antibody encephalitis in a 7-year-old child who presented with superrefractory status epilepticus (SRSE). The traditional management with multiple anti-seizure medications at appropriate dosage and immunotherapy was tried despite which the child continued to have seizures. Hence the child was initiated on a classic ketogenic diet. He achieved ketosis within 48 h of diet initiation and there was a drastic reduction in the seizure frequency followed by a completed remission. A ketogenic diet has been sparingly used for the management of post-encephalitic epilepsy and autoimmune epilepsy. However, the data onthe effectiveness of the ketogenic diet in the management of autoimmune encephalitis is scarce. Starting K D early in the disease course helped not only in seizure control but also preserved the cognitive and neurological well-being of the child.</snippet>

# Summary

Across cohort studies of autoimmune encephalitis (AE) with seizures, seizure remission rates during follow‑up range from roughly 70% to 90%, and these outcomes are typically achieved when patients receive a combination of immunotherapy and antiseizure medications (ASMs), with many patients able to withdraw ASMs after achieving remission. In contrast, real‑world evidence specific to ASMs alone in AE is limited, but available data suggest that monotherapy with ASMs is less effective for sustained seizure control in most AE subtypes, with relapse risk higher—particularly in GAD‑positive disease where drug‑resistant epilepsy is common. Overall, immunotherapy improves seizure outcomes relative to ASM monotherapy, with the greatest benefit in neuronal surface antibody–positive AE, while GAD‑associated cases have the poorest remission rates and often require prolonged or alternative therapies.

# Evidence in Autoimmune Epilepsies

- In a 75‑patient clinic cohort, 71% experienced seizures, most at AE onset; after a median 6‑year follow‑up, 47 of 53 seizure‑experienced patients achieved 1‑year terminal seizure remission, with median time to seizure freedom of 5 years. Remission rates were very high in neuronal surface antibody groups (NMDAR 97%, LGI1 93%, CASPR2 100%), but only 20% in GAD‑positive AE (p < 0.001). In seizure‑free patients, ASMs were withdrawn after a median 13 months without relapse, indicating that most neuronal surface antibody–positive AE can transition off ASMs with low relapse risk. This contrasts with GAD‑positive disease, where autoimmune‑associated epilepsy is more common and relapse risk higher. <cite id="33618141">In autoimmune encephalitis, seizures often debut at disease onset, and long‑term remission after a median 6 years was achieved in 71% of 53 seizure‑experienced patients, with particularly high remission in neuronal surface antibody groups and only 20% remission in GAD‑positive patients; ASMs could often be withdrawn without relapse in neuronal surface antibody cases</cite>.

- A large retrospective cohort from East China (n=113 AE patients; 83 with seizures) found that 80.7% (67/83) achieved seizure remission while receiving both immunotherapy and ASMs; during 24‑month follow‑up, 11% (11/91) had clinical relapses. EEG‑based GTE scores differed significantly between remission and incomplete seizure reduction groups (p=0.009), suggesting EEG can help predict outcomes. The authors concluded that long‑term AEDs may not be necessary for most AE types except anti‑GABA‑B receptor encephalitis, highlighting the generally favorable response to immunotherapy plus ASMs and the risk of relapse in a minority. <cite id="31331752">In a cohort of 113 AE patients, 80.7% of 83 with seizures achieved remission on combined immunotherapy and antiepileptic drugs, with 11% relapsing over 24 months; EEG summary scores predicted remission versus incomplete control</cite>.

- Case evidence also shows that when immunotherapy and multiple ASMs fail in drug‑resistant post‑encephalitic epilepsy (e.g., anti‑GAD65–associated superrefractory status epilepticus), adjunctive ketogenic diet can induce remission, underscoring the need for non‑pharmacologic strategies when standard care fails. <cite id="35789965">In a child with anti‑GAD65 encephalitis and superrefractory status epilepticus, despite multiple ASMs and immunotherapy seizures remitted on a classic ketogenic diet, illustrating an effective adjunct when conventional therapies fail</cite>.

# Interpretation: Immunotherapy vs. ASMs Alone

- Immunotherapy plus ASMs: High remission rates are reported in AE cohorts, especially with neuronal surface antibodies (e.g., NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2), with many patients able to taper ASMs and maintain remission over multi‑year follow‑up. <cite id="33618141">Neuronal surface antibody–positive AE achieved high remission rates and allowed ASM withdrawal without relapse</cite> <cite id="31331752">A large cohort showed 80.7% remission on combined immunotherapy and ASMs, with relapse in 11% over 24 months</cite>.

- ASMs alone: Direct comparative data are sparse, but clinic cohorts suggest that sustained seizure control without immunotherapy is less reliable, particularly outside GAD‑positive disease. The East China cohort explicitly suggested that long‑term AEDs may not be necessary for most AE types when immunotherapy is effective, implying that ASMs alone are less sufficient for durable control. <cite id="31331752">Except for anti‑GABAb receptor encephalitis, long‑term AEDs may not be necessary, indicating that immunotherapy plus ASMs provides better durable control than ASMs alone</cite>. In GAD‑positive AE, drug‑resistant epilepsy is common, and relapse risk remains high even after apparent remission on ASMs, suggesting inferior outcomes compared with neuronal surface antibody groups. <cite id="33618141">GAD‑positive AE has markedly lower remission rates and a higher propensity for drug‑associated epilepsy and relapse compared with neuronal surface antibody groups</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For AE with neuronal surface antibodies, early immunotherapy with concomitant ASMs yields high remission rates, and ASMs can often be tapered once remission is established, with low relapse risk over years of follow‑up. <cite id="33618141">Neuronal surface antibody–positive AE achieved high remission and allowed withdrawal of ASMs without relapse</cite> <cite id="31331752">Remission rates around 80% were observed with combined therapy, with low relapse over 24 months</cite>.

- For GAD‑positive AE, seizures are often drug‑resistant and relapse‑prone; immunotherapy may be less effective, and long‑term or multiple therapies (including second‑line immunotherapies or dietary adjuncts) may be required. <cite id="33618141">GAD‑positive AE has a much lower remission rate (20%) and a higher risk of developing autoimmune‑associated epilepsy</cite> <cite id="35789965">When standard ASMs and immunotherapy fail, adjunctive ketogenic diet can induce remission in severe cases</cite>.

- Predictive biomarkers: EEG summary scores (GTE) and antibody type help stratify prognosis and guide treatment intensity. <cite id="31331752">GTE EEG scores differed between remission and incomplete control groups and may predict seizure outcomes</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Immunotherapy, typically used in conjunction with ASMs, is associated with substantially higher seizure remission rates in AE than ASMs alone, particularly in neuronal surface antibody–positive forms, whereas GAD‑positive AE shows poor remission and high relapse risk even with combined therapy. Consequently, withholding or tapering ASMs after immunotherapy‑induced remission is reasonable in many AE subtypes, but not in GAD‑positive disease, where more aggressive, prolonged, or alternative therapies are often required. <cite id="33618141">Immunotherapy plus ASMs yields high remission in neuronal surface antibody–positive AE with low relapse risk, unlike GAD‑positive AE, which has low remission and higher relapse risk</cite> <cite id="31331752">A large cohort reported 80.7% remission with combined therapy and suggested limited need for long‑term AEDs outside anti‑GABAb receptor disease</cite> <cite id="35789965">When immunotherapy and ASMs fail, adjunctive ketogenic diet can achieve remission in severe autoimmune epilepsy</cite>.

data.title: Long-term seizure outcome and antiseizure medication use in autoimmune encephalitis.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
To determine long-term seizure outcome, use of antiseizure medication (ASM) and seizure recurrence risk after its withdrawal in patients with autoimmune encephalitis (AE) due to neuronal surface and GAD antibodies.
METHODS
In patients from a specialized AE outpatient clinic, we assessed seizure manifestation, ASM and immunotherapy at onset of AE as well as seizure occurrence, development of autoimmune-associated epilepsy (AAE) and use of ASM in the long-term. Data were collected from patients via telephone interviews and medical records.
RESULTS
Out of 94 AE patients, 75 were analyzed; 47 patients had NMDAR, 17 LGI1, 7 GAD, 3 CASPR2 and 1 mGluR5 antibodies. Fifty-three of the 75 patients (71 %) experienced seizures, all of which for the first time occurred at AE onset. After a median follow-up of 6 years (range, 1-15), 47 of the 53 AE patients had 1-year terminal seizure remission, median duration of terminal seizure freedom was 5 years. Rate of 1-year terminal seizure remission was significantly higher in patients with neuronal surface antibodies (NMDAR 97 %, LGI1 93 %, CASPR2 100 %) compared to patients with GAD antibodies (20 %, p < 0.001). In seizure-free patients, ASM was withdrawn after 13 months (median) without any relapse seizures.
CONCLUSIONS
Seizures are common in most forms of AE manifesting at disease onset in all cases. However, the development of AAE is rare and typically occurs in patients with GAD antibodies. Thus, in most AE cases with neuronal surface antibodies, ASM can be withdrawn after the acute phase of AE with low risk of seizure relapse.

data.title: Favorable response to classic ketogenic diet in a child with anti-GAD 65 antibody mediated super refractory status epilepticus.
data.abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis refers to a spectrum of inflammatory brain diseases which can present as drug-resistant seizures in children. Hereby, we report a case of anti-GAD-65 antibody encephalitis in a 7-year-old child who presented with superrefractory status epilepticus (SRSE). The traditional management with multiple anti-seizure medications at appropriate dosage and immunotherapy was tried despite which the child continued to have seizures. Hence the child was initiated on a classic ketogenic diet. He achieved ketosis within 48 h of diet initiation and there was a drastic reduction in the seizure frequency followed by a completed remission. Hence, this non-pharmacological intervention was an effective adjunct in achieving seizure control in our patient. A ketogenic diet has been sparingly used for the management of post-encephalitic epilepsy and autoimmune epilepsy. However, the data onthe effectiveness of the ketogenic diet in the management of autoimmune encephalitis is scarce. Starting K D early in the disease course helped not only in seizure control but also preserved the cognitive and neurological well-being of the child.

Authors: Adkison, Kimberly K, Jones, Lori S, Lou, Yu et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Clinical pharmacology in drug development
Abstract: This Phase I, randomized, open-label study evaluated the gastric pH-altering effects of omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor, and the CYP3A enzyme/P-glycoprotein (Pgp)-inhibitory effects of ritonavir, an HIV protease inhibitor, on the pharmacokinetics and safety of the hepatitis C virus (HCV) non-structural protein 5A (NS5A) inhibitor GSK2336805 in healthy male and female subjects. Co-administration of GSK2336805 60 mg with omeprazole decreased GSK2336805 plasma AUC(0-∞) by 10% and Cmax by 18%; no marked effect was observed on t½ . Co-administration of GSK2336805 30 mg with ritonavir increased GSK2336805 plasma AUC(0-∞) by 52%, Cmax by 43%, and t½ by 40%; CL/F was decreased by 34%. All adverse events were minor in intensity. The gastric acid-suppressive effect of omeprazole had minimal impact on the extent and rate of GSK2336805 absorption in vivo; therefore, GSK2336805 may be co-administered with omeprazole without concern about lower GSK2336805 exposures and compromised antiviral efficacy. The modest increases in AUC and Cmax following co-administration of GSK2336805 plus ritonavir suggest that GSK2336805 when given concomitantly with a single CYP3A/Pgp inhibiting drug will not likely require dose adjustment. Final dose recommendation will be based on GSK2336805 efficacy and safety profiles from Phase III trials in HCV-infected patients.</snippet>
