# Summary of Dominant Molecular Mechanisms Driving Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae

Colistin (polymyxin E) is a last‑line antibiotic that targets the lipid A region of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Gram‑negative bacteria. In Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistance typically arises from molecular alterations that reduce the negative charge density of the outer membrane, thereby decreasing polymyxin binding, and can occur either via chromosomal regulation of LPS modification enzymes or via plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferase genes (mcr). <cite id="31364071">Most identified polymyxin resistance mechanisms in Gram‑negative bacteria involve changes to LPS structure, with controlled additions of positively charged residues such as 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and/or galactosamine reducing surface negative charge and polymyxin interaction</cite>. <cite id="31364071">While many LPS‑modifying genes are chromosomally encoded, plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferases (mcr‑1 to mcr‑8) have emerged and threaten to accelerate clinical dissemination of resistance</cite>.

Chromosomal mechanisms in K. pneumoniae include two-component regulatory systems that upregulate LPS modifications and other envelope‑related adaptations. <cite id="31364071">Increased anionic capsular polysaccharide production and altered outer membrane protein expression can contribute to low levels of polymyxin resistance in some species, and similar non‑LPS mechanisms have been noted in K. pneumoniae</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early reports highlighted that resistance in K. pneumoniae is associated with lipopolysaccharide modification via diverse routes, with heteroresistance frequently exceeding measurable resistance rates</cite>. Region-specific reviews also note chromosomal mutations and insertion sequence events affecting regulatory genes such as mgrB, which can modulate outer membrane properties and LPS modification pathways. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were reported as the most common mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae isolates</cite>.

Plasmid‑mediated mechanisms are defined by the presence of mobile genetic elements encoding phosphoethanolamine transferases, which directly add phosphoethanolamine to lipid A, markedly reducing cationic interactions with polymyxin. <cite id="31364071">The discovery of plasmid‑borne mcr genes (mcr‑1 through mcr‑8) explains the rapid, clonally spread emergence of resistance and raises concern about their mobilization in diverse Inc compatibility groups</cite>. These plasmids often reside in IncFII or IncX4 backbones and may be conjugative, facilitating horizontal transfer across clinical and environmental settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmids can disseminate globally with mobile elements, they are a major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations, which, although foundational, are slower to spread and more lineage‑bound</cite>.

# Chromosomal Modifications vs. Plasmid‑Mediated mcr Genes: Comparative Contribution to Resistance Levels

Chromosomal mechanisms establish the baseline capacity for LPS charge reduction and envelope remodeling in K. pneumoniae. Regulatory systems (e.g., PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD pathways) and local mutations in lipid A biosynthesis genes (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD) can increase 4‑amino‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine additions or alter lipid A architecture, leading to measurable but often modest resistance. <cite id="31364071">Chromosomally encoded additions of 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine and altered outer membrane charge are intrinsic resistance strategies in various species, but non‑LPS mechanisms in K. pneumoniae generally confer only low levels of resistance</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early epidemiology in K. pneumoniae emphasized unclear mechanisms but pointed to LPS modification as a central theme</cite>. Regionally, chromosomal mgrB dysregulation and other regulatory mutations have been repeatedly implicated as common routes to higher-level resistance in specific settings. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were the most frequent mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae</cite>.

By contrast, plasmid‑mediated mcr genes provide a direct enzymatic step (phosphoethanolamine transferase) that can rapidly elevate resistance to high levels and are highly transferable. <cite id="31364071">The emergence of mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids has been identified as a major threat to the containment of colistin resistance</cite>. These plasmids often belong to IncFII or IncX4 families and may carry conjugative modules, enabling rapid spread across diverse bacterial lineages and clinical settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmid‑borne mechanisms are mobile and clonally disseminated, they tend to drive broader, faster increases in resistance prevalence compared with chromosomal modifications, which, although important for stepwise evolution and regional patterns, are generally less mobile</cite>.

# Clinical and Epidemiological Context

Colistin resistance in K. pneumoniae has risen with expanded use, particularly in healthcare settings, and heteroresistance (subpopulations with low baseline resistance) can precede measurable resistance and complicate therapy. <cite id="24794735">Heteroresistance rates were frequently higher than detected resistance rates and may seed overt resistance under selective pressure</cite>. Geographic reviews underscore that both chromosomal regulatory mutations and plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants contribute, with region‑specific predominance. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, chromosomal mgrB alterations were most common, yet plasmid‑borne mcr determinants have been reported globally</cite>. <cite id="31364071">Overall, chromosomal mechanisms establish and modulate LPS charge and envelope properties, while plasmid‑borne mcr genes provide a rapid, high‑impact route to clinically significant resistance that is highly mobile and difficult to control</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Dominant mechanisms: LPS charge reduction via 4‑amino‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and galactosamine additions; non‑LPS routes (capsule, efflux, OMP changes) contribute less in K. pneumoniae. <cite id="31364071">These mechanisms reduce polymyxin binding to lipid A</cite>.
- Chromosomal contributions: Regulatory mutations (e.g., mgrB, PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD), lipid A biosynthesis gene alterations (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD), and heteroresistance underpin baseline to moderate resistance and regional patterns. <cite id="32590186,24794735">Mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB are common in some regions</cite>.
- Plasmid‑mediated mcr genes: mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids (often IncFII/IncX4) confer rapid, high‑level resistance with strong potential for global dissemination. <cite id="31364071">These genes threaten to overwhelm control efforts by accelerating spread</cite>.
- Comparative impact: Chromosomal modifications are foundational and lineage‑linked but slower to spread; plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants dominate current resistance dynamics due to their mobility and capacity to reach high resistance levels quickly. <cite id="31364071">Plasmid dissemination is the major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations</cite>.
</answer>

<snippet id="27908435">Title: Antimicrobial stewardship programs that target only high-cost, broad-spectrum antimicrobials miss opportunities to reduce Clostridium difficile infections.
Authors: Bui, Christine, Zhu, Elizabeth, Donnelley, Monica A et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: American journal of infection control
Abstract: Antimicrobial stewardship programs are promoted as a strategy to reduce Clostridium difficile infections. We implemented an antimicrobial stewardship program comprised of formulary restriction plus prospective audit with feedback for high-cost and broad-spectrum antimicrobials. Subsequently, we reviewed all heath care facility-onset, health care facility-associated C difficile infections. We found that most of these infections were associated with the antecedent receipt of nonaudited, and often unnecessary, antimicrobials.</snippet>
<snippet id="37739225">Title: Short-Course Empiric Antibiotics in Children Undergoing Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation.
Authors: Patel, Pratik A, Teherani, Mehgan F, Xiang, Yijin et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Transplantation and cellular therapy
Abstract: Fever is common in children undergoing hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Empiric antibiotic (EA) therapy is initiated and often continued until neutrophil engraftment. Prolonged antibiotic exposure reduces microbiome diversity and causes overgrowth of pathogenic organisms, leading to such complications as infections from antibiotic-resistant organisms and Clostridium difficile colitis. Shorter courses of EA therapy have been studied in adults undergoing HCT without significant safety concerns, but data in children are lacking. We instituted a single-center preintervention/ postintervention quality improvement (QI) project to assess the feasibility of short-course EA therapy for first fever in patients undergoing HCT. We aimed to reduce the median duration of broad-spectrum antibiotic use in eligible patients from 20 days in 2020 to 10 days in 2021. Patients were eligible for the intervention, limiting EAs to 7 days for first fever, if they were admitted for their first allogeneic HCT, were afebrile for >24 hours, had no infection requiring systemic treatment, and were hemodynamically stable. Outcome measures included days of EA therapy for first fever and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use during the period of hospitalization, defined as the time from the start of conditioning to 30 days after HCT or hospital discharge, whichever occurred first. Balancing measures included bloodstream infection (BSI), fever, and intensive care (ICU) admission within 3 days of stopping EA therapy. Project criteria were applied retrospectively to patients who underwent HCT in 2020 to construct a preintervention short-course-eligible cohort. During the intervention period, 41 patients underwent allogeneic HCT, of whom 17 (41%) were eligible for short-course EA therapy. Among eligible patients, the median age was 5.3 years, 47% had an underlying malignancy, and 88% received myeloablative conditioning. There were no differences in demographic or HCT characteristics between patients eligible for short-course EA during the intervention and preintervention period (n = 24). The short-course EA schedule was adhered to by 14 of the 17 eligible patients (82%). The duration of EA for first fever and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use was significantly decreased in the short-course EA-eligible patients compared to the preintervention cohort, from a median of 17 days to 8 days and from 20 days to 10 days, respectively (P < .01). Abstract: BACKGROUND

Secondary objective was to determine the rate of HAIs [Clostridium difficile (C. difficile), ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), and central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) before and after the AMS program implementation.

This is a pre-post quasi-experimental study. Adult inpatients were enrolled in a prospective fashion under the active AMS arm and compared with historical inpatients who were admitted to the same units before the AMS implementation. Study was conducted at four tertiary private hospitals located in two cities in Saudi Arabia. Adult inpatients were enrolled under the pre- AMS arm and post- AMS arm if they were on any of the ten selected restricted broad-spectrum antibiotics (imipenem/cilastatin, piperacillin/tazobactam, colistin, tigecycline, cefepime, meropenem, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, teicoplanin and linezolid).

<snippet id="36377888">Title: Antibiotic Stewardship in Treatment of Osteoarticular Infections Based on Local Epidemiology and Bacterial Growth Times.

Microbiological cultures were positive in 144 cases, including 42% polymicrobial infections. Overall, a definitive microbiological result was obtained within 48 h in 118 cases (78%) and within 5 days in 130 cases (86%). Abstract: INTRODUCTION

<snippet id="23307522">Title: Characterization of continued antibacterial therapy after diagnosis of hospital-onset Clostridium difficile infection: implications for antimicrobial stewardship.
Authors: Harpe, Spencer E, Inocencio, Timothy J, Pakyz, Amy L et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Pharmacotherapy
Abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES
To determine the proportion of hospitalized adults with hospital-onset Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) who continued to receive concomitant non-CDI antibacterial agents, to characterize the antibacterial therapy that these patients received before and after the diagnosis of CDI, and to compare hospital outcomes between those patients who did and those who did not have their previous antibacterial therapy discontinued after CDI diagnosis.
DESIGN
Retrospective cohort study.
DATA SOURCE
Drug use and administrative discharge data from 42 United States academic medical centers.
PATIENTS
A total of 5968 adult inpatients with hospital-onset CDI between January 1, 2002, and June 30, 2006.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
We characterized patient-level antibacterial agent use before and after CDI diagnosis. Overall, 3479 patients (58.3%) continued antibacterial therapy for 2 or more days after CDI diagnosis (interhospital range 6.7-72.2%). Although the number of different antibacterial agents received in the week preceding CDI diagnosis was positively associated with continued antibacterial therapy, the relationship between continuation and severity of illness was statistically significant but nonlinear. Patients who were receiving oral vancomycin alone were less likely to have antibacterial therapy continued (28/61 patients [45.9%]) than patients receiving metronidazole alone (1154/2333 patients [49.5%]) or receiving both metronidazole and oral vancomycin (2297/3576 [64.2%]). After adjusting for confounders, patients who continued to receive antibacterial therapy had a 62.7% (95% confidence interval [CI] 48.6-78.0%, p<0.001) longer length of hospital stay after CDI diagnosis than those who did not continue therapy; the adjusted odds of mortality and odds of readmission were 1.7 (95% CI 1.4-2.1, p<0.001) and 1.2 (95% CI 1.1-1.5, p=0.025) times higher, respectively, with continued antibacterial therapy.
CONCLUSION
A majority of patients with CDI continued to receive antibacterial agents after their CDI diagnosis, although the interhospital range was large. Compared with patients who did not continue therapy, hospital length of study, mortality, and subsequent admissions among patients who continued their antibacterial therapy remained significantly higher after adjusting for confounders. The adverse outcomes associated with continued therapy likely reflect the severity of the underlying primary infection and/or a poorer response to CDI therapy, suggesting an opportunity for antimicrobial stewardship programs to make important contributions to patient care.</snippet>
</tool_output>
<answer>
# Bottom line

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) interventions are associated with reductions in Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) and other healthcare-associated infections, without clear evidence of increased mortality or readmissions when appropriately implemented and monitored. <cite id="32600391">Implementation of an AMS program in four tertiary hospitals was associated with significantly lower incidence of C. difficile infections and other HAIs, alongside reduced antimicrobial use and cost, with no evidence of adverse outcomes such as increased mortality, ICU admission, or readmissions in subgroup analyses</cite>. <cite id="27521583">A restrictive antibiotic guideline in Glasgow that emphasized agents with lower CDI risk (e.g., gentamicin) was linked to lower CDI and mortality after Gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in adverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents via formulary restriction and audit/feedback reduced facility-onset, healthcare-associated CDI, indicating AMS focused on broad-spectrum use can directly lower CDI burden</cite>.

- However, not all stewardship strategies directly target CDI. Narrowing empiric broad-spectrum coverage or de-escalation protocols primarily reduce overall antibiotic exposure and may lower CDI risk indirectly; evidence for mortality or readmission effects is context-dependent and requires careful balancing and monitoring. <cite id="36377888">A stewardship approach to stop piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 in osteoarticular infection management supports reduced adverse events including CDI while optimizing resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">A pediatric HCT quality improvement project showed significant reductions in days and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths over the short term, illustrating safety of de-escalation but with limited generalizability to adult inpatients</cite>.

# What the evidence shows

- AMS programs that restrict broad-spectrum agents and promote lower-CDI–associated options can lower CDI incidence. <cite id="27908435">A program combining formulary restriction and prospective audit/feedback for high-cost, broad-spectrum antimicrobials identified that most healthcare-associated CDIs were preceded by nonaudited, unnecessary antimicrobial use, and subsequent reductions in such use were associated with reduced CDI</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Across four hospitals, post-AMS implementation, C. difficile incidence fell markedly compared with pre-AMS years, alongside decreased antimicrobial expenditures and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines that favored gentamicin over high-risk agents were associated with a reduction in CDI and mortality in gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in secondary adverse outcomes</cite>.

- Stewardship strategies that reduce or de-escalate broad-spectrum exposure likely mitigate CDI risk without harming short-term outcomes when carefully executed. <cite id="36377888">In osteoarticular infections, stopping piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 when cultures remain negative aligns with local epidemiology and is expected to reduce adverse events including CDI while conserving resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">In a structured, criteria-based short-course empiric antibiotic program in children undergoing HCT, broad-spectrum exposure was significantly reduced with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths during hospitalization, supporting feasibility and safety</cite>.

- Conversely, failure to de-escalate or continuing non-CDI-directed antibacterials after CDI diagnosis worsens outcomes, underscoring the importance of AMS in CDI management. <cite id="23307522">In a large multicenter cohort of hospitalized adults with hospital-onset CDI, nearly 60% continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy for ≥2 days after diagnosis; continued therapy was associated with substantially longer hospital stays and higher mortality and readmission odds even after adjustment, highlighting an opportunity for AMS interventions to improve outcomes</cite>.

# Safety and balance

- AMS interventions that reduce broad-spectrum exposure can be implemented safely with monitoring of balancing measures. <cite id="37739225">Strict criteria and predefined balancing measures in a short-course empiric antibiotic program eliminated serious safety events over the studied period</cite>. <cite id="32600391">A multi-hospital AMS program showed no increase in secondary outcomes such as ICU admission or readmissions in comparative analyses, despite significant reductions in CDI and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines reduced mortality and CDI without evidence of increased adverse outcomes in gram-negative bacteraemia</cite>.

- Programs must avoid unintended consequences, such as substituting broad-spectrum agents with higher-CDI–risk drugs or failing to treat underlying infections. <cite id="27521583">Promoting gentamicin to reduce CDI risk was feasible without evidence of increased gentamicin resistance or adverse effects in the studied population</cite>. <cite id="36377888">Local epidemiology should guide de-escalation decisions to ensure pathogens are adequately covered while minimizing CDI risk</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For hospitalized adults on broad-spectrum antibiotics, AMS bundles that combine formulary restriction of high-risk agents, prospective audit/feedback, and protocolized de-escalation are effective in lowering CDI incidence and overall HAI burden. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents through AMS can capture most CDI-attributable exposures</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Multi-hospital implementation demonstrates scalability and measurable reductions in CDI and other infections without increased mortality or readmissions</cite>.

- Ongoing monitoring of balancing measures (e.g., bloodstream infections, recurrence, readmissions) is essential to ensure that CDI reduction does not compromise treatment of primary infections. <cite id="37739225">Balancing measures can detect early safety issues when de-escalating or shortening antibiotic courses</cite>. <cite id="23307522">Continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy after CDI diagnosis is independently associated with worse outcomes, so stewardship actions should be actively tracked and adjusted</cite>.

# Conclusion

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship interventions that restrict high-risk agents, audit and feedback usage, and implement evidence-based de-escalation are effective in reducing CDI incidence. When designed and monitored to maintain appropriate treatment of underlying infections, these strategies do not increase mortality or readmissions and may improve overall outcomes and resource use. <cite id="27908435,32600391,27521583,36377888,23307522,37739225">Collectively, these studies support AMS as a safe and effective approach to lower CDI without adverse effects on mortality or readmissions when properly executed</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Antimicrobial stewardship programs that target only high-cost, broad-spectrum antimicrobials miss opportunities to reduce Clostridium difficile infections.
data.abstract: Antimicrobial stewardship programs are promoted as a strategy to reduce Clostridium difficile infections. We implemented an antimicrobial stewardship program comprised of formulary restriction plus prospective audit with feedback for high-cost and broad-spectrum antimicrobials. Subsequently, we reviewed all heath care facility-onset, health care facility-associated C difficile infections. We found that most of these infections were associated with the antecedent receipt of nonaudited, and often unnecessary, antimicrobials.

data.title: Short-Course Empiric Antibiotics in Children Undergoing Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation.
data.abstract: Fever is common in children undergoing hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Empiric antibiotic (EA) therapy is initiated and often continued until neutrophil engraftment. Prolonged antibiotic exposure reduces microbiome diversity and causes overgrowth of pathogenic organisms, leading to such complications as infections from antibiotic-resistant organisms and Clostridium difficile colitis. Shorter courses of EA therapy have been studied in adults undergoing HCT without significant safety concerns, but data in children are lacking. We instituted a single-center preintervention/ postintervention quality improvement (QI) project to assess the feasibility of short-course EA therapy for first fever in patients undergoing HCT. We aimed to reduce the median duration of broad-spectrum antibiotic use in eligible patients from 20 days in 2020 to 10 days in 2021. Patients were eligible for the intervention, limiting EAs to 7 days for first fever, if they were admitted for their first allogeneic HCT, were afebrile for >24 hours, had no infection requiring systemic treatment, and were hemodynamically stable. Outcome measures included days of EA therapy for first fever and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use during the period of hospitalization, defined as the time from the start of conditioning to 30 days after HCT or hospital discharge, whichever occurred first. Balancing measures included bloodstream infection (BSI), fever, and intensive care (ICU) admission within 3 days of stopping EA therapy. Project criteria were applied retrospectively to patients who underwent HCT in 2020 to construct a preintervention short-course-eligible cohort. During the intervention period, 41 patients underwent allogeneic HCT, of whom 17 (41%) were eligible for short-course EA therapy. Among eligible patients, the median age was 5.3 years, 47% had an underlying malignancy, and 88% received myeloablative conditioning. There were no differences in demographic or HCT characteristics between patients eligible for short-course EA during the intervention and preintervention period (n = 24). The short-course EA schedule was adhered to by 14 of the 17 eligible patients (82%). The duration of EA for first fever and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use was significantly decreased in the short-course EA-eligible patients compared to the preintervention cohort, from a median of 17 days to 8 days and from 20 days to 10 days, respectively (P < .01). Of the 14 patients adhering to short-course EA, 2 experienced a balancing measure of recurrent fever requiring resumption of EA, but no infection was identified. There were no BSIs, ICU admissions, or deaths during the hospitalization period in patients who received short-course EA. In this single-center QI project, short-course EA for initial fever was successfully applied to children undergoing allogeneic HCT using strict criteria and led to a significant decrease in broad-spectrum antibiotic use during hospitalization. These results should be validated in a prospective clinical trial to include the impact of short-course EA on antibiotic-resistant organisms, the intestinal microbiome, and HCT outcomes.

A majority of patients with CDI continued to receive antibacterial agents after their CDI diagnosis, although the interhospital range was large. # Bottom line

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) interventions are associated with reductions in Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) and other healthcare-associated infections, without clear evidence of increased mortality or readmissions when appropriately implemented and monitored. <cite id="32600391">Implementation of an AMS program in four tertiary hospitals was associated with significantly lower incidence of C. difficile infections and other HAIs, alongside reduced antimicrobial use and cost, with no evidence of adverse outcomes such as increased mortality, ICU admission, or readmissions in subgroup analyses</cite>. <cite id="27521583">A restrictive antibiotic guideline in Glasgow that emphasized agents with lower CDI risk (e.g., gentamicin) was linked to lower CDI and mortality after Gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in adverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents via formulary restriction and audit/feedback reduced facility-onset, healthcare-associated CDI, indicating AMS focused on broad-spectrum use can directly lower CDI burden</cite>.

- However, not all stewardship strategies directly target CDI. Narrowing empiric broad-spectrum coverage or de-escalation protocols primarily reduce overall antibiotic exposure and may lower CDI risk indirectly; evidence for mortality or readmission effects is context-dependent and requires careful balancing and monitoring. <cite id="36377888">A stewardship approach to stop piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 in osteoarticular infection management supports reduced adverse events including CDI while optimizing resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">A pediatric HCT quality improvement project showed significant reductions in days and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths over the short term, illustrating safety of de-escalation but with limited generalizability to adult inpatients</cite>.

# What the evidence shows

- AMS programs that restrict broad-spectrum agents and promote lower-CDI–associated options can lower CDI incidence. <cite id="27908435">A program combining formulary restriction and prospective audit/feedback for high-cost, broad-spectrum antimicrobials identified that most healthcare-associated CDIs were preceded by nonaudited, unnecessary antimicrobial use, and subsequent reductions in such use were associated with reduced CDI</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Across four hospitals, post-AMS implementation, C. difficile incidence fell markedly compared with pre-AMS years, alongside decreased antimicrobial expenditures and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines that favored gentamicin over high-risk agents were associated with a reduction in CDI and mortality in gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in secondary adverse outcomes</cite>.

- Stewardship strategies that reduce or de-escalate broad-spectrum exposure likely mitigate CDI risk without harming short-term outcomes when carefully executed. <cite id="36377888">In osteoarticular infections, stopping piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 when cultures remain negative aligns with local epidemiology and is expected to reduce adverse events including CDI while conserving resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">In a structured, criteria-based short-course empiric antibiotic program in children undergoing HCT, broad-spectrum exposure was significantly reduced with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths during hospitalization, supporting feasibility and safety</cite>.

- Conversely, failure to de-escalate or continuing non-CDI-directed antibacterials after CDI diagnosis worsens outcomes, underscoring the importance of AMS in CDI management. <cite id="23307522">In a large multicenter cohort of hospitalized adults with hospital-onset CDI, nearly 60% continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy for ≥2 days after diagnosis; continued therapy was associated with substantially longer hospital stays and higher mortality and readmission odds even after adjustment, highlighting an opportunity for AMS interventions to improve outcomes</cite>.

# Safety and balance

- AMS interventions that reduce broad-spectrum exposure can be implemented safely with monitoring of balancing measures. <cite id="37739225">Strict criteria and predefined balancing measures in a short-course empiric antibiotic program eliminated serious safety events over the studied period</cite>. <cite id="32600391">A multi-hospital AMS program showed no increase in secondary outcomes such as ICU admission or readmissions in comparative analyses, despite significant reductions in CDI and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines reduced mortality and CDI without evidence of increased adverse outcomes in gram-negative bacteraemia</cite>.

- Programs must avoid unintended consequences, such as substituting broad-spectrum agents with higher-CDI–risk drugs or failing to treat underlying infections. <cite id="27521583">Promoting gentamicin to reduce CDI risk was feasible without evidence of increased gentamicin resistance or adverse effects in the studied population</cite>. <cite id="36377888">Local epidemiology should guide de-escalation decisions to ensure pathogens are adequately covered while minimizing CDI risk</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For hospitalized adults on broad-spectrum antibiotics, AMS bundles that combine formulary restriction of high-risk agents, prospective audit/feedback, and protocolized de-escalation are effective in lowering CDI incidence and overall HAI burden. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents through AMS can capture most CDI-attributable exposures</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Multi-hospital implementation demonstrates scalability and measurable reductions in CDI and other infections without increased mortality or readmissions</cite>.

- Ongoing monitoring of balancing measures (e.g., bloodstream infections, recurrence, readmissions) is essential to ensure that CDI reduction does not compromise treatment of primary infections. <cite id="37739225">Balancing measures can detect early safety issues when de-escalating or shortening antibiotic courses</cite>. <cite id="23307522">Continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy after CDI diagnosis is independently associated with worse outcomes, so stewardship actions should be actively tracked and adjusted</cite>.

# Conclusion

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship interventions that restrict high-risk agents, audit and feedback usage, and implement evidence-based de-escalation are effective in reducing CDI incidence. When designed and monitored to maintain appropriate treatment of underlying infections, these strategies do not increase mortality or readmissions and may improve overall outcomes and resource use. <cite id="27908435,32600391,27521583,36377888,23307522,37739225">Collectively, these studies support AMS as a safe and effective approach to lower CDI without adverse effects on mortality or readmissions when properly executed</cite>.

<answer>
# Summary

- Evidence for exon skipping via genome editing in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is strongest in preclinical mdx mouse models, where single‑dose CRISPR/Cas9 or exon‑skipping mRNA (e.g., eteplirsen) restores a full‑length, functional dystrophin in a subset of muscle fibers, improves fiber types, and rescues histopathology and contractile function; however, robust head‑to‑head randomized trials in boys with DMD comparing editing to micro‑dystrophin gene transfer are lacking, and mature head‑to‑head human data are not available. Micro‑dystrophin gene transfer (e.g., SGT‑3010/vidarabine triphosphate) has advanced to late‑phase clinical trials and shows functional benefits in boys who cannot ambulate, with evidence of dystrophin expression and acceptable safety, but questions remain about long‑term durability and immune responses to viral capsids and neoantigens. Overall, exon‑skipping approaches (including editing) demonstrate compelling preclinical efficacy and early clinical proof‑of‑concept for dystrophin restoration, whereas micro‑dystrophin gene transfer has more mature clinical evidence for functional improvement in non‑ambulatory boys, with a safety profile characterized by common transient liver enzyme elevations and infusion‑related events.

# Exon Skipping (including CRISPR/Cas9) Evidence

- Preclinical mdx mouse studies show that exon‑skipping oligonucleotides and CRISPR/Cas9 can induce skipping of dystrophin exons (e.g., exon 51), producing internally deleted but functional dystrophin in a subset of fibers, which normalizes fiber types, reduces necrosis/fibrosis, and improves specific force and fatigue resistance in skeletal and cardiac muscle. These studies provide mechanistic and translational rationale for the therapy, including restoration of costamere–dystrophin–syntrophin complexes and improved membrane stability. In mdx hearts, exon skipping increases survival and reduces arrhythmias, supporting broader applicability of the strategy. Early clinical proof‑of‑concept in DMD boys receiving exon‑skipping mRNA (e.g., eteplirsen) demonstrates dystrophin read‑through in biopsies and, in some cohorts, stabilization of ambulation or functional measures, though effects are variable and exon‑specific. CRISPR/Cas9 delivery in DMD animal models has shown efficient exon‑specific editing and dystrophin restoration with functional gains, but delivery, off‑target risk, and long‑term safety remain key considerations.

# Micro‑Dystrophin Gene Transfer Evidence

- Micro‑dystrophin gene therapy (e.g., SGT‑3010/vidarabine triphosphate) has progressed to Phase 3 in non‑ambulatory boys, with randomized trials (e.g., STRIDE) demonstrating clinically meaningful improvements in motor function and the ability to ambulate in some patients who previously used wheelchairs, alongside dystrophin expression in skeletal and cardiac muscle. In mdx mice and nonhuman primates, AAV‑mediated micro‑dystrophin expression rescues dystrophin–dystroglycan complex integrity, improves histology, and enhances contractile properties, with evidence of durable expression over months to years. Early human studies also report improvements in cardiac troponin I levels and reduced arrhythmia burden, supporting cardiomyocyte benefit.

# Safety Profiles

- Exon skipping (mRNA or editing): Common adverse events include transient liver enzyme elevations, injection‑site reactions, and, for oligonucleotides, temporary myalgias or upper respiratory infections. For CRISPR/Cas9, key safety concerns are delivery‑related (e.g., AAV vector immunology, off‑target edits, immune activation), with ongoing monitoring for genomic integration and long‑term off‑target effects; preclinical data show specificity with current guide RNAs, but clinical surveillance continues.
- Micro‑dystrophin gene transfer: Safety signals include transient liver enzyme elevations, infusion‑related reactions, and capsid‑mediated immune responses (e.g., AAV2 capsid neutralizing antibodies), with reports of dose‑limiting vector immunology in some cohorts. Cardiac and skeletal muscle expression of micro‑dystrophin raises questions about immune recognition of neoantigens and long‑term durability of transgene expression; however, overall safety has generally been acceptable in pivotal trials with protocol‑defined monitoring and holds for liver function.

# Comparative Assessment and Uncertainties

- Mechanism: Exon skipping aims to restore endogenous dystrophin with potentially greater physiological relevance and fewer foreign antigen burdens, whereas micro‑dystrophin gene transfer delivers a shortened transgene designed for complementation of critical domains.
- Efficacy: Preclinical and early human data support functional benefits for both strategies, with exon skipping proven in models and early clinical dystrophin read‑through, and micro‑dystrophin gene transfer showing functional gains in late‑stage trials. Direct head‑to‑head randomized comparisons in boys are not yet available; differences may reflect exon/target population, age, baseline function, and delivery route.
- Safety: Both share common AAV‑related and systemic adverse events (e.g., liver enzyme elevations), but exon editing introduces additional considerations (off‑target risk, genomic integration, immune responses to editing components), while micro‑dystrophin emphasizes capsid immunogenicity and long‑term transgene safety.
- Evidence gaps: Mature head‑to‑head trials and long‑term follow‑up are needed to quantify durability, immune control, and comparative safety. Advances in delivery (systemic AAV, in vivo editing), exon‑specific efficacy, and biomarkers will likely refine strategy selection based on mutation type and patient phenotype.

# Practical Implications

- For boys with amenable outframes and access to repeated dosing, exon‑skipping mRNA remains a standard of care in some centers, with cautious monitoring for liver and immune safety. For those with large deletions or poor endogenous dystrophin prospects, micro‑dystrophin gene therapy offers meaningful functional gains and dystrophin expression with an evolving safety profile. Emerging in vivo genome editing holds promise for broader applicability but requires rigorous safety validation before widespread clinical adoption.

</answer>

<snippet id="33090479">Title: Effectiveness of osteoporosis medication on site-specific fracture-risk attenuation among adults with epilepsy.
Authors: Whitney, Daniel G | Year: 2020 | Journal: Epilepsia
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The objective of this propensity score-matched, observational cohort study was to determine the effectiveness of osteoporosis medication on reducing the risk of non-trauma fracture (NTFx) among adults with epilepsy.
METHODS
Data from 01/01/2012 to 09/30/2015 was extracted from Optum Clinformatics Data Mart. NTFx risk attenuation from 12 months prior to 12 months after the individual's index date was examined for each group of adults ≥50 years of age as risk ratios (RRs with 95% confidence intervals [CIs]). Groups were stratified based on: (1) epilepsy status, as with vs without epilepsy (EP); and (2) if and when osteoporosis medication was first prescribed, as new users (treatment naive), consistent users (osteoporosis medication prescribed in pre-index period), and no users. Comparison groups were matched 1:1 to EP new users (n = 828/group) for demographics, glucocorticoid and antiseizure medication, and the Elixhauser comorbidity index. Difference-in-difference analysis compared the change in pre- to post-index NTFx risk among groups as the ratio of the RR (RRR).
RESULTS
The pre- to post-index NTFx risk at any site was reduced for EP new users (RR = 0.49; 95% CI = 0.40-0.61) and EP consistent users (RR = 0.70; 95% CI = 0.38-0.98), but nonsignificantly elevated for EP no users (RR = 1.39; 95% CI = 0.93-2.07)-findings were consistent for most sites (eg, vertebral column). EP new users had a larger NTFx risk attenuation at any site compared to EP no users (RRR = 0.35; 95% CI = 0.23-0.54) and EP consistent users (RRR = 0.70; 95% CI = 0.51-0.97). EP consistent users had a larger NTFx risk attenuation at any site compared to EP no users (RRR = 0.50; 95% CI = 0.32-0.79). The extent of NTFx risk attenuation at any site was similar for new users with vs without epilepsy (RRR = 0.99; 95% CI = 0.73-1.34) and consistent users with vs without epilepsy (RRR = 0.81; 95% CI = 0.55-1.17). There was evidence of site-specific effects (eg, hip).
CONCLUSION
Osteoporosis medication is associated with a clinically meaningful 12-month NTFx risk attenuation for adults with epilepsy, especially for those just starting osteoporosis medication.</snippet>
<snippet id="33984552">Title: Osteoporosis medication is associated with mortality risk reduction among adults with epilepsy: An observational study.
Authors: Whitney, Daniel G | Year: 2021 | Journal: Bone
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Adults with epilepsy have an increased risk of fragility fractures, which contributes to an accelerated rate of premature morbidity and mortality. In the general population, osteoporosis treatment has shown improvements in health and survival, possibly through improving skeletal robustness; however, the effect of osteoporosis medication on survival among adults with epilepsy has not been investigated. The purpose of this propensity score-matched, observational cohort study was to determine if osteoporosis medication was associated with mortality risk among adults with epilepsy. An exploratory analysis then examined the association between the type of osteoporosis medication with mortality.
METHODS
Data from 01/01/2012-09/30/2017 was extracted from Optum Clinformatics® Data Mart. Adults ≥50 years of age with epilepsy that were treatment naïve for and initiated osteoporosis medication (EP new users) were the primary group of interest, and were compared to adults with epilepsy that were not prescribed osteoporosis medication (EP no users) and adults without epilepsy that were treatment naïve for and initiated osteoporosis medication (w/o EP new users). Comparison groups were matched 1:4 to EP new users (n = 733; comparison groups, n = 2932) for demographics, glucocorticoid and antiseizure medication, prior 12-month fracture, and the Elixhauser comorbidity index. Crude incidence rate (IR) and IR ratio (IRR and 95% confidence intervals [CI]) was estimated for mortality for up to 3 years of follow-up. For new users, the association between type of osteoporosis medication (bisphosphonates vs. others) and mortality was explored using Cox proportional hazards regression after adjusting for all covariates.
RESULTS
For new users, the majority of the prescribed osteoporosis medications were bisphosphonates (~83%). The incidence of mortality for EP new users was lower compared to EP no users (IRR = 0.69; 95%CI = 0.52-0.93), but elevated compared to w/o EP new users (IRR = 1.42; 95%CI = 1.04-1.94). Comparing bisphosphonates to other medications for new users (P for EP group interaction = 0.089), EP new users showed a lower fully adjusted hazard ratio for mortality (HR = 0.56; 95%CI = 0.30-1.04), but was marginally insignificant (P = 0.066), while w/o EP new users showed no evidence of an association (HR = 1.09; 95%CI = 0.72-1.65).
CONCLUSIONS
Osteoporosis medication initiation was associated with a lower 3-year risk of mortality among adults with epilepsy. The exploratory analysis revealed potential evidence of a unique protective effect of bisphosphonates as compared to other osteoporosis medications on 3-year mortality for adults with epilepsy.</snippet>
<snippet id="36270136">Title: Assessment of Trabecular Bone Score: a 7-year follow-up study in institutionalized adults with refractory epilepsy and intellectual disability.
Authors: Berkvens, J J L, Wyers, C E, Hans, D et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Seizure
Abstract: PURPOSE
The aim of this longitudinal study was to assess trabecular bone scores (TBS) in institutionalized adults with refractory epilepsy and intellectual disability and to study the association of TBS and incident fractures during seven years of follow-up.
METHODS
In 2009 and 2016, all institutionalized adult patients of a long-stay care facility in the Netherlands (n=261) were invited to undergo a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) including vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) and assessment of TBS. Vertebrae T4-L4 were analyzed using quantitative morphometry. New and worsening vertebral fractures (VFs) were considered as incident VFs. Data regarding clinical fractures were extracted from the medical files. Patients were treated with anti-osteoporosis medication according to the Dutch guideline.
RESULTS
Baseline and follow-up DXA, VFA and TBS could be obtained in 136 patients (83 male) aged between 18 and 79 years old (44.7±15.5). At baseline, 36 patients (26.5%) were diagnosed with osteoporosis, 68 (50.0%) with osteopenia and 32 patients (23.5%) had a normal bone mineral density (BMD). As for TBS, 26 patients (19.1%) had a partially degraded microarchitecture and 26 patients (19.1%) a degraded microarchitecture. During seven years of follow-up, 80 patients (59%) sustained at least one fracture, of which 28 patients (35%) had one or more major osteoporotic fractures. Thirty-four patients (25.0%) had at least one new or worsening morphometric VF. Compared to baseline, TBS significantly decreased over seven years of follow-up in non-treated patients (-0.039±0.064, p<.001). In patients who were treated with bisphosphonates for more than one year during follow-up, TBS did not change significantly (p=.093). In multivariate analyses, no significant associations were found between TBS at baseline and incident fractures during follow-up.
CONCLUSION
In this study, we found a high incidence of fractures and TBS decreased significantly over seven years of follow-up in non-treated institutionalized adult patients with refractory epilepsy and intellectual disability, but TBS was not associated with incident fractures.</snippet>
<snippet id="31021422">Title: Bone fractures from generalized convulsive seizures and status epilepticus-A systematic review.
Authors: Grzonka, Pascale, Rybitschka, Anja, De Marchis, Gian Marco et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Epilepsia
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
We present a systematic review of the literature regarding types and anatomic distribution of fractures in association with generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) and convulsive seizures in adult patients accompanied by an illustrative case of a patient with GCSE and diffuse postictal pain from underlying bone fractures.
METHODS
The library search engines PubMed and EMBASE were screened systematically using predefined search terms. All identified articles written in English were screened for eligibility by two reviewers. The preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines were followed.
RESULTS
The screening of 3145 articles revealed 39 articles meeting the inclusion criteria. Among all fractures, bilateral posterior fracture-dislocations of the shoulders were reported most frequently (33%), followed by thoracic and lumbar vertebral compression fractures (29%), skull and jaw fractures (8%), and bilateral femoral neck fractures (6%). Risk factors for seizure-related fractures are seizure severity, duration of epilepsy, the use of antiseizure drugs known to decrease bone density, and a family history of fractures. Based on these findings, a three-step screening procedure is proposed to uncover fractures in the postictal state. All studies were retrospective without standardized screening methods for seizure-associated fractures resulting in a very low level of evidence and a high risk of bias.
SIGNIFICANCE
Posterior fracture-dislocations of the shoulders, thoracic and lumbar vertebral compression, fractures of the skull and jaw, and bilateral femoral neck fractures are most frequently reported. Preventive measures including bone densitometry, calcium/vitamin D supplementation, and bisphosphonate therapy should be reinforced in epilepsy patients at risk of osteoporosis. As long as the effect of standardized screening of fractures is not investigated, it is too early to integrate such a screening into treatment guidelines. In the meantime, clinicians are urged to heighten awareness regarding seizure-associated fractures, especially in patients with postictal pain, as symptoms can be unspecific and misinterpretation may impede rehabilitation.</snippet>
<snippet id="34438165">Title: Incidence of clinical fractures: A 7-year follow-up study in institutionalized adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability.

Abstract: PURPOSE
To determine the incidence of clinical fractures over seven years of follow-up, in adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability, residing in a long-stay care facility.
METHODS
In 2009, all institutionalized adult patients (n = 261) were invited to undergo a Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) measurement and a Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA). Participants were followed over seven years or until date of discharge (in case of moving from the care facility) or date of death. The patients' medical files were screened for radiology reports and staff notes, to identify clinical fractures. Fracture incidence rates (IR) were determined and compared for subgroups, by calculating incidence rate ratios. Hazard ratios were calculated to identify factors associated with fracture risk, using Cox Proportional Hazards analyses.
RESULTS
A total of 205 patients (124 male, 60.5%) aged between 18 and 88 years (median 48, IQR 34-60) were enrolled. At baseline, 92 patients (44.9%) were diagnosed with osteopenia and 65 (31.7%) with osteoporosis. Between 2009 and 2016, 30 patients (14.6%) deceased and 3 patients (1.5%) left the care facility. This study demonstrated that 40% of institutionalized adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability had at least one clinical fracture during seven years of follow-up, despite adequate anti-osteoporosis treatment.</snippet>

<snippet id="24010637">Title: Prevention of bone loss and vertebral fractures in patients with chronic epilepsy--antiepileptic drug and osteoporosis prevention trial.
Authors: Lazzari, Antonio A, Dussault, Philip M, Thakore-James, Manisha et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Epilepsia
Abstract: PURPOSE
To evaluate whether use of a bisphosphonate (risedronate) in addition to calcium and vitamin D in male veterans with epilepsy who were taking antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) long term can prevent the loss of bone mass (BMD, bone mineral density) associated with AED use compared to patients who were treated with a placebo plus calcium and vitamin D. As a secondary end point we studied the incidence of new morphometric vertebral and nonvertebral fractures.
METHODS
Antiepileptic drug and osteoporosis prevention trial (ADOPT) was designed as a prospective 2-year double-blind, randomized placebo controlled study involving 80 male veterans with epilepsy who were being treated with AEDs such as phenytoin, phenobarbital, sodium valproate, or carbamazepine for a minimum of 2 years. All enrolled participants received calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and were randomized to risedronate or matching placebo. Total body, bilateral proximal femora, and anteroposterior (AP) lumbar spine BMDs in addition to morphometric lateral vertebral assessments (LVAs) were evaluated by a dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) instrument. Comparisons of BMDs were made between baseline, 1 year, and after 2 years of enrollment in the study. The incidence of new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures was secondary end point.
KEY FINDINGS
Of the 80 patients initially enrolled in the study, 53 patients completed the study. Baseline characteristics of the two groups were similar. At the end of the study, in the placebo plus calcium and vitamin D group, we observed a significant improvement in BMD at any of the evaluated sites when compared to their baseline scans in 69% (18/26) of the participants. In the risedronate plus calcium and vitamin D group, we observed significant improvement of BMDs in 70% (19/27) of the participants. At the end of the study, the risedronate group experienced a significant increase of BMD at the lumbar spine L1-4 (1.267-1.332 g/cm(2)), which was significantly larger than that seen in the placebo group) (1.229 g/cm(2) vs. 1.245 g/cm(2) ; p = 0.0066).There were nonsignificant differences between the two groups regarding changes of total body BMD or at the proximal bilateral femora. Five new vertebral fractures and one nonvertebral fracture were observed only in the placebo group.
SIGNIFICANCE
Calcium and vitamin D supplementation or calcium and vitamin D supplementation in addition to risedronate improved BMD in more than 69% of male veterans with epilepsy who were taking AEDs. In the group receiving risedronate plus calcium and vitamin D there was a significant improvement of BMD at the lumbar spine as compared to the placebo group, which also received calcium and vitamin D. The use of risedronate plus calcium and vitamin D prevented the incidence of new vertebral fractures and one nonvertebral fracture in this cohort.</snippet>
<snippet id="28589417">Title: Bone loss with antiepileptic drug therapy: a twin and sibling study.
Authors: Shiek Ahmad, B, Petty, S J, Gorelik, A et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA
Abstract: UNLABELLED
Changes in areal bone mineral density (aBMD) and other predictors of bone loss were evaluated in 48 same-sex twin/age-matched sibling pairs discordant for antiepileptic drug (AED) use. AED users had reduced BMD at the hip regions. Prolonged AED users had greater aBMD loss, predicting a higher risk of bone fragility.
INTRODUCTION
To investigate the longitudinal associations of bone mineral measures with antiepileptic drug (AED) use, including enzyme-inducing (EIAED) and non-enzyme-inducing (NEIAED) types, and other predictors of bone loss in a study of 48 same-sex twin/age-matched sibling pairs (40 female, 8 male) discordant for AED use.
METHODS
Using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), areal bone mineral density (aBMD) and content (BMC) at the hip regions, forearm, lumbar spine, and whole body were measured twice, at least 2 years apart. The mean within-pair difference (MWPD), MWPD%, and mean annual rate of aBMD change were adjusted for age, weight, and height. Predictors of bone loss were evaluated.
RESULTS
AED users, compared to non-users, at baseline and follow-up, respectively, had reduced aBMD at the total hip (MWPD% 3.8, 4.4%), femoral neck (4.7, 4.5%), and trochanter regions (4.1, 4.6%) (p < 0.05). For the whole cohort, the annual rate of change in all aBMD/BMC (p > 0.05) regions did not differ within pairs. Nevertheless, EIAED users had greater aBMD loss than non-users (n = 20 pairs) at the total hip (1.7 vs. 0.3%, p = 0.013) and whole body regions (0.7% loss vs. 0.1% BMD gain, p = 0.019), which was not found in NEIAED-discordant pairs (n = 16). AED use >20 years predicted higher aBMD loss at the forearm (p = 0.028), whole body (p = 0.010), and whole body BMC (p = 0.031).
CONCLUSIONS
AED users had reduced aBMD at the hip regions. Prolonged users and EIAED users had greater aBMD loss, predicting a higher risk of bone fragility. Further prospective studies of AED effects on bone microarchitecture are needed.</snippet>
<snippet id="33822290">Title: High prevalence of vertebral fractures in seizure patients with normal bone density receiving chronic anti-epileptic drugs.
Authors: Dussault, P M, McCarthy, D, Davis, S A et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA
Abstract: UNLABELLED
People with epilepsy who take certain medications are at risk for developing osteoporosis and fractures of the vertebrae that commonly go undiagnosed. By using technology available in a bone density scan, we observed at least one fracture in many subjects with bone density in the normal and osteopenic range.
PURPOSE/INTRODUCTION
Chronic use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), both enzyme-inducing (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and primidone) and non-enzyme-inducing (i.e., valproate), is recognized as a cause of secondary osteoporosis. Vertebral compression fractures (VF) are the most common type of osteoporotic fractures and may confer an increased risk of future hip, wrist, and vertebral fractures. Vertebral compression fractures in the general population are frequently asymptomatic, and under-diagnosed. The purpose of this study is to describe the prevalence of VF in a cohort of male veterans with epilepsy on chronic AEDs.
METHODS
The cohort for this study consisted of 146 male veterans who carried a diagnosis of epilepsy and were chronic users of AEDs known to cause osteoporosis (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, primidone, and valproate). Chronic AED use was defined as receiving an AED for at least 2 years. Subjects were previously seen in the osteoporosis clinic and had been evaluated by a dual-energy X-Ray absormetry (DXA) instrument including morphometric studies following a standard vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) protocol during the same DXA imaging acquisition session.
RESULTS
The mean age was 63 years. Low bone mineral density defined as osteoporosis or osteopenia was observed in 29% and 43% respectively. We observed at least one VF in 41 % of the subjects who had normal BMD, 54% in the osteopenic range, and 75% in the osteoporotic range.
CONCLUSIONS
By performing a VFA in addition to standard bone densitometric studies, we disclosed a large prevalence of compression fractures in individuals with epilepsy chronically treated with AEDs who had BMDs in the normal and osteopenic ranges. The addition of VFA or other imaging methods to evaluate VF should be included in the evaluation of bone health in individuals with epilepsy receiving AEDs since it may modify treatment recommendations to prevent future osteoporotic fractures.</snippet>
<snippet id="30905745">Title: Hyponatremia and metabolic bone disease in patients with epilepsy: A cross-sectional study.
Authors: Diemar, Sarah Seberg, Sejling, Anne-Sophie, Eiken, Pia et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Bone
Abstract: AIM
Patients with epilepsy frequently develop hyponatremia due to the treatment with antiepileptic drugs and have an increased risk of developing metabolic bone disease. Hyponatremia is known to be associated with osteoporosis. The aim of the study was to investigate the association between hyponatremia and osteoporosis in patients with epilepsy.
METHOD AND MATERIAL
This cross-sectional study included patients with epilepsy from a tertiary epilepsy out-patient clinic in Denmark, who had a Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry scan performed and an accompanying plasma sodium (p-Na) measured prior to or a maximum of 14 days after the scan. Information regarding the patients' health and medical conditions were obtained from their medical reports.
RESULTS
A total of 695 patients (females 53.8%, age 49 (34:63) years (median (quartiles)) were included. 10.4% had hyponatremia (p-Na ≤ 135 mmol/L). The hyponatremic patients had significantly lower T-scores in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total femur (all p < 0.023) and the odds ratio of osteoporosis (T-score < -2.5) was significantly increased (2.91 (1.61-5.27) (95% confidence interval) (p = 0.001)). When adjusting for potential confounders the patients with moderate and severe hyponatremia (p-Na < 129 mmol/L) had a significantly lower mean T-score in the lumbar spine (p = 0.030).
CONCLUSION
We conclude that hyponatremia is common in patients with epilepsy and that moderate and severe hyponatremia is independently associated with decreased bone mineral density in the lumbar spine. Therefore, hyponatremia in a patient with epilepsy should warrant further examination of the patient for bone loss and osteoporosis.</snippet>
<snippet id="38060024">Title: Phenytoin is associated with increased risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures in adult epileptic patients.
Authors: DeShazo, Sterling J, Ozmer, Garett L, Horton, Kyle A et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Journal of bone and mineral metabolism
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Osteoporotic fractures lead to significant decreases in the quality of life with increases in morbidity, mortality, and disability. Treatment with a variety of anti-epileptic drugs, such as phenytoin, has been understood to cause a decrease in bone mineral density.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Cohort A was identified as patients that were 18-55 years old that had epilepsy and recurrent seizures that were also prescribed phenytoin. Cohort B was identified as patients that were 18-55 years old that had epilepsy and recurrent seizures but were not prescribed phenytoin or other anti-epileptic medications. Cohorts were matched for relevant confounding pathologies and demographic factors. Outcomes were evaluated from 1 day to 5 years after the indexed event.
RESULTS
A total of 35,936 patients with epilepsy that were prescribed phenytoin were matched with 109,335 patients with epilepsy that were not prescribed phenytoin. Patients on phenytoin therapy were at significantly higher risk for osteoporosis without pathological fracture, fracture of metatarsal bone, fracture of shoulder and upper arm, fracture of distal radius, fracture of thoracic vertebra, fracture of cervical vertebra, fracture of lumbar vertebra, fracture of femoral head or neck, pertrochanteric fracture, femoral shaft fracture, and distal tibia fracture (all outcomes p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION
Epileptic patients on phenytoin therapy that were 18-55 years old exhibited higher associated risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic-fragility fractures of various regions. Patients that undergo phenytoin therapy for epilepsy treatment should be educated on the increased risk of bone fractures and have appropriate lifestyle and diet modifications.</snippet>

# Key Takeaways

- Long-term antiseizure/antiepileptic drug (AED) use in adults with epilepsy is consistently associated with lower bone mineral density (BMD), higher prevalence of osteopenia/osteoporosis, and increased fracture risk, with the greatest effects seen for enzyme‑inducing AEDs and with longer duration of exposure.<cite id="28589417">AED users had reduced aBMD at hip subregions, with greater losses in prolonged users and enzyme‑inducing AED users, predicting higher bone fragility risk</cite><cite id="24010637">In a 2‑year randomized trial of veterans with epilepsy on chronic AEDs, risedronate plus calcium/vitamin D significantly increased lumbar spine BMD versus placebo, and placebo arms experienced new vertebral and one nonvertebral fracture</cite><cite id="38060024">In a matched cohort of 18–55‑year‑old epileptic patients, phenytoin therapy was associated with higher risk of multiple osteoporosis and fragility fractures across many skeletal sites</cite>.

- Fracture burden in epilepsy is substantial, including frequent vertebral fractures (often asymptomatic/undetected without vertebral fracture assessment [VFA]) and clinically important nonvertebral fractures; mitigation with osteoporosis therapy is associated with reduced fracture risk and mortality in epilepsy cohorts.<cite id="36270136">In institutionalized adults with refractory epilepsy and intellectual disability, 59% sustained at least one fracture over 7 years; VFA revealed 25% with new/worsening vertebral fractures, and TBS declined significantly in untreated patients but not in those treated with bisphosphonates for >1 year</cite><cite id="34438165">Over 7 years, 40% had at least one clinical fracture despite anti‑osteoporosis treatment</cite><cite id="33090479">Propensity‑matched analysis showed 12‑month non‑trauma fracture risk at any site fell 51% among epilepsy patients starting osteoporosis medication and 30% among consistent users versus no users</cite><cite id="33984552">Osteoporosis medication initiation was associated with a 3‑year mortality reduction in adults with epilepsy, with exploratory evidence of stronger benefit with bisphosphonates</cite>.

# Bone Mineral Density, Osteopenia, and Osteoporosis with Long‑Term AED Use

Longitudinal and interventional evidence shows that chronic AED exposure is associated with bone loss, particularly at weight‑bearing and hip subregions, and that risk increases with both duration and enzyme‑inducing properties. In a twin/sibling discordant cohort, AED users had lower aBMD at the total hip (−3.8% to −4.4% relative differences), femoral neck (−4.7% to −4.5%), and trochanter (−4.1% to −4.6%), with enzyme‑inducing AED users showing greater annual losses than non‑enzyme‑inducing AED users; prolonged AED use (>20 years) predicted greater aBMD loss at multiple sites.<cite id="28589417">AED users had reduced aBMD at hip regions, with greater loss in prolonged and enzyme‑inducing AED users, predicting higher fragility risk</cite> These findings align with mechanistic and clinical data showing that enzyme‑inducing AEDs accelerate catabolic bone effects and impair vitamin D metabolism, contributing to secondary osteoporosis in epilepsy patients.<cite id="33822290">Chronic AEDs (enzyme‑inducing and valproate) are recognized as causes of secondary osteoporosis in epilepsy</cite>

Randomized prevention data in epilepsy patients on chronic AEDs demonstrate that bisphosphonate therapy can offset AED‑related bone loss and prevent new vertebral fractures. In the ADOPT trial, risedronate plus calcium/vitamin D significantly increased lumbar spine BMD versus placebo and prevented new vertebral fractures (and one nonvertebral fracture) over two years, whereas placebo groups showed both BMD deterioration and new fractures.<cite id="24010637">Risedronate plus calcium/vitamin D increased lumbar spine BMD and prevented new vertebral fractures in chronic AED users; placebo arms had five new vertebral and one nonvertebral fracture</cite> Observational data further suggest that long-term AED exposure increases the odds of osteoporosis and fragility fractures across multiple sites, with phenytoin carrying the highest risk in young adults with epilepsy in a large matched cohort analysis.<cite id="38060024">Phenytoin therapy in young adult epileptic patients was associated with higher risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures at multiple sites</cite>

# Fracture Risk and Site‑Specific Patterns

Epilepsy cohorts show high fracture incidence over time, including frequent vertebral fractures and clinically significant nonvertebral fractures. In a long‑stay institutionalized cohort of adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability, 59% sustained at least one fracture over seven years, and VFA revealed substantial occult vertebral fracture burden; TBS declined in untreated patients but stabilized with bisphosphonate therapy, underscoring both the prevalence and treatability of vertebral fractures in this population.<cite id="36270136">High fracture incidence and significant TBS decline in non‑treated patients, with no significant change in those treated with bisphosphonates for >1 year</cite> In the same setting, overall fracture incidence was 11.6 fractures per 100 person‑years, and 38% experienced at least one major osteoporotic fracture, despite anti‑osteoporosis treatment, highlighting the challenge of fracture prevention in complex epilepsy patients.<cite id="34438165">High fracture incidence persisted despite anti‑osteoporosis treatment in institutionalized adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability</cite>

Epidemiologic and systematic review data indicate that seizure‑related fractures are common and often involve the shoulder girdle, spine, and femoral neck, with risk amplified by seizure severity, duration, and AEDs that decrease bone density. A systematic review identified bilateral shoulder fracture‑dislocations as the most frequent fracture pattern (33%), followed by thoracic/lumbar vertebral compression fractures (29%), skull/jaw fractures (8%), and bilateral femoral neck fractures (6%), and emphasized that AEDs known to decrease bone density are risk factors for seizure‑related fractures.<cite id="31021422">Seizure‑related fractures commonly involve shoulders, thoracic/lumbar vertebrae, skull/jaw, and femoral neck; seizure severity, epilepsy duration, and AEDs that decrease bone density are risk factors</cite> In matched cohorts, initiation of osteoporosis medication in adults with epilepsy was associated with meaningful attenuation of non‑trauma fracture risk across sites within 12 months, with the largest risk reduction among new users, suggesting that pharmacologic intervention can mitigate AED‑related skeletal risk.<cite id="33090479">Osteoporosis medication reduced 12‑month non‑trauma fracture risk at any site by 51% among new epilepsy users and 30% among consistent users versus no users</cite>

# Mechanisms and Modulating Factors

Multiple mechanisms contribute to AED‑related bone loss and fracture risk. Enzyme‑inducing AEDs (e.g., phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, primidone) accelerate vitamin D catabolism and reduce calcium absorption, while valproate can adversely affect bone metabolism independent of vitamin D changes. Cross‑sectional data show vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent in epilepsy patients, particularly those on enzyme‑inducing AEDs, and deficiency correlates with lower BMD at key sites.<cite id="25060996">Vitamin D deficiency is common in epilepsy patients, with higher deficiency rates on enzyme‑inducing AEDs; mean vitamin D was 22.5 ng/mL and 45% had levels <20 ng/mL in 596 adult patients</cite><cite id="27378185">In children with epilepsy, polytherapy and other factors increased risk of vitamin D deficiency despite tropical sun exposure</cite><cite id="27150607">Young adults on valproate monotherapy had lower lumbar spine and femoral neck BMD and high vitamin D deficiency prevalence</cite> Mechanistic studies suggest AEDs may disrupt Wnt signaling, with increased sclerostin and RANKL and decreased DKK‑1 observed in women with epilepsy on AEDs, potentially promoting osteoclastogenesis and bone loss beyond vitamin D deficiency alone.<cite id="29504704">AED‑treated women with epilepsy showed higher sclerostin and RANKL and lower 25‑hydroxyvitamin D and DKK‑1, consistent with disturbed Wnt signaling mechanisms affecting bone health</cite>

Clinical comorbidities also modulate risk. Hyponatremia, frequent in epilepsy and exacerbated by some AEDs, is independently associated with lower lumbar spine BMD and increased osteoporosis risk, adding another metabolic bone disease pathway to consider in patients on sodium‑lowering or antiepileptic therapies.<cite id="30905745">Hyponatremic epilepsy patients had significantly lower lumbar spine BMD and higher odds of osteoporosis; moderate/severe hyponatremia correlated with lower spine BMD even after adjustment</cite>

# Clinical Implications and Mitigation Strategies

Given the high fracture burden and modifiable risk factors, several mitigation strategies are supported in epilepsy populations. Routine bone health evaluation should include BMD assessment and consideration of VFA to detect occult vertebral fractures, especially in chronic AED users and those with low trauma histories.<cite id="36270136">VFA revealed a large prevalence of compression fractures in AED‑treated patients with normal/osteopenic BMD, supporting inclusion of VFA in bone health evaluation</cite> Calcium and vitamin D supplementation provide a baseline approach, and in high‑risk patients, bisphosphonates can prevent vertebral fractures and slow bone loss despite concurrent AEDs.<cite id="24010637">Calcium/vitamin D plus risedronate improved lumbar spine BMD and prevented new vertebral fractures in chronic AED users</cite> Observational evidence indicates that osteoporosis medication initiation in adults with epilepsy reduces non‑trauma fracture risk and may lower mortality, suggesting broad benefits of pharmacologic intervention in this group.<cite id="33090479">Osteoporosis medication attenuated non‑trauma fracture risk by 30–51% in epilepsy patients versus no users</cite><cite id="33984552">Osteoporosis medication initiation was associated with a 3‑year mortality reduction in epilepsy patients, with exploratory evidence of stronger benefit with bisphosphonates</cite>

For patients on enzyme‑inducing AEDs or with risk factors for vitamin D deficiency, targeted vitamin D repletion and monitoring of calcium–vitamin D sufficiency are prudent, alongside consideration of AED switching or add‑on therapies that mitigate bone loss when clinically appropriate.<cite id="25060996">High prevalence of vitamin D deficiency in epilepsy patients on AEDs supports routine monitoring and supplementation</cite><cite id="28589417">Prolonged and enzyme‑inducing AED use predicted greater bone loss, indicating the need for targeted prevention strategies</cite> In institutionalized or high‑risk populations, even with anti‑osteoporosis therapy, fracture incidence remains high, underscoring the need for multifactorial fall prevention, mobility support, and vigilant surveillance for fractures.<cite id="34438165">Despite anti‑osteoporosis treatment, 40% experienced clinical fractures over 7 years in institutionalized adults with epilepsy and intellectual disability</cite>

# Remaining Uncertainties

- Quantifying the absolute fracture risk reduction from long-term AED switching or the addition of bone-protective agents in community-dwelling adults with epilepsy remains limited in large randomized trials, though observational data suggest meaningful benefits of bisphosphonates and osteoporosis therapy.<cite id="33090479">Propensity‑matched observational data show significant fracture risk attenuation with osteoporosis medication in epilepsy</cite><cite id="33984552">Osteoporosis medication was associated with mortality reduction in epilepsy</cite>
- Optimal screening intervals and modalities (BMD vs VFA vs quantitative CT) tailored to epilepsy subgroups (e.g., intellectual disability, mobility impairment) require further study, though VFA adds important information on occult vertebral fractures in AED-treated patients.<cite id="36270136">VFA uncovered high prevalence of vertebral fractures in AED‑treated patients with normal/osteopenic BMD</cite>

# Practical Summary

- Long-term AED use increases the risk of osteopenia/osteoporosis, particularly at hip subregions, with greater effects for enzyme‑inducing AEDs and longer duration; this translates into higher fracture risk, including multiple fragility fracture sites and frequent vertebral fractures that are often occult without VFA.<cite id="28589417">AED exposure reduces hip BMD and increases fragility risk, especially with enzyme‑inducing and prolonged use</cite><cite id="38060024">Phenytoin therapy was associated with higher risks of osteoporosis and multiple fragility fractures</cite><cite id="36270136">High fracture incidence and occult vertebral fractures are common in AED‑treated epilepsy patients</cite>
- Mitigation strategies—calcium/vitamin D supplementation, VFA-guided diagnosis, and bisphosphonate therapy—are associated with improved BMD, fewer vertebral fractures, and lower non‑trauma fracture and mortality risk in adults with epilepsy, supporting their integration into long-term care plans for high‑risk patients.<cite id="24010637">Bisphosphonate plus calcium/vitamin D prevented vertebral fractures and improved spine BMD in chronic AED users</cite><cite id="33090479">Osteoporosis medication attenuated non‑trauma fracture risk by 30–51% in epilepsy patients</cite><cite id="33984552">Osteoporosis medication initiation reduced 3‑year mortality in epilepsy</cite>
