<snippet id="32961119">Title: Adjuvant nivolumab versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C and stage IV melanoma (CheckMate 238): 4-year results from a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
Authors: Ascierto, Paolo A, Del Vecchio, Michele, Mandalá, Mario et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: The Lancet. Oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Previously, findings from CheckMate 238, a double-blind, phase 3 adjuvant trial in patients with resected stage IIIB-C or stage IV melanoma, showed significant improvements in recurrence-free survival and distant metastasis-free survival with nivolumab versus ipilimumab. This report provides updated 4-year efficacy, initial overall survival, and late-emergent safety results.
METHODS
This multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial was done in 130 academic centres, community hospitals, and cancer centres across 25 countries. Patients aged 15 years or older with resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive nivolumab or ipilimumab via an interactive voice response system and stratified according to disease stage and baseline PD-L1 status of tumour cells. Patients received intravenous nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or intravenous ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses, and then every 12 weeks until 1 year of treatment, disease recurrence, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival by investigator assessment, and overall survival was a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses were done in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients). All patients who received at least one dose of study treatment were included in the safety analysis. The results presented in this report reflect the 4-year update of the ongoing study with a database lock date of Jan 30, 2020. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02388906.
FINDINGS
Between March 30 and Nov 30, 2015, 906 patients were assigned to nivolumab (n=453) or ipilimumab (n=453). Median follow-up was 51·1 months (IQR 41·6-52·7) with nivolumab and 50·9 months (36·2-52·3) with ipilimumab; 4-year recurrence-free survival was 51·7% (95% CI 46·8-56·3) in the nivolumab group and 41·2% (36·4-45·9) in the ipilimumab group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·71 [95% CI 0·60-0·86]; p=0·0003). With 211 (100 [22%] of 453 patients in the nivolumab group and 111 [25%] of 453 patients in the ipilimumab group) of 302 anticipated deaths observed (about 73% of the originally planned 88% power needed for significance), 4-year overall survival was 77·9% (95% CI 73·7-81·5) with nivolumab and 76·6% (72·2-80·3) with ipilimumab (HR 0·87 [95% CI 0·66-1·14]; p=0·31). Late-emergent grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were reported in three (1%) of 452 and seven (2%) of 453 patients. The most common late-emergent treatment-related grade 3 or 4 adverse events reported were diarrhoea, diabetic ketoacidosis, and pneumonitis (one patient each) in the nivolumab group, and colitis (two patients) in the ipilimumab group. Two previously reported treatment-related deaths in the ipilimumab group were attributed to study drug toxicity (marrow aplasia in one patient and colitis in one patient); no further treatment-related deaths were reported.
INTERPRETATION
At a minimum of 4 years' follow-up, nivolumab demonstrated sustained recurrence-free survival benefit versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma indicating a long-term treatment benefit with nivolumab. With fewer deaths than anticipated, overall survival was similar in both groups. Nivolumab remains an efficacious adjuvant treatment for patients with resected high-risk melanoma, with a safety profile that is more tolerable than that of ipilimumab.
FUNDING
Bristol Myers Squibb and Ono Pharmaceutical.</snippet>
<snippet id="35964471">Title: Adjuvant nivolumab versus ipilimumab (CheckMate 238 trial): Reassessment of 4-year efficacy outcomes in patients with stage III melanoma per AJCC-8 staging criteria.
Authors: Larkin, James, Weber, Jeffrey, Del Vecchio, Michele et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: PURPOSE
Nivolumab was approved as adjuvant therapy for melanoma based on data from CheckMate 238, which enrolled patients per American Joint Committee on Cancer version 7 (AJCC-7) criteria. Here, we analyse long-term outcomes per AJCC-8 staging criteria compared with AJCC-7 results to inform clinical decisions for patients diagnosed per AJCC-8.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
In a double-blind, phase 3 trial (NCT02388906), patients aged ≥15 years with resected, histologically confirmed AJCC-7 stage IIIB, IIIC, or IV melanoma were randomised to receive nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for 4 doses and then every 12 weeks, both intravenously ≤1 year. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) were assessed in patients with stage III disease, per AJCC-7 and AJCC-8.
RESULTS
Per AJCC-7 staging, 42.4% and 57.3% of patients were in substage IIIB and IIIC, respectively; per AJCC-8, 1.1%, 30.4%, 62.8%, and 5.0% were in IIIA, IIIB, IIIC, and IIID. After 4 years' minimum follow-up, the AJCC-7 superior efficacy of nivolumab over ipilimumab in patients with resected stage III melanoma was preserved per AJCC-8 analysis. No statistically significant difference in RFS between stage III substage hazard ratios was observed per AJCC-7 or -8 staging criteria (interaction test: AJCC-7, P = 0.8115; AJCC-8, P = 0.1051; P = 0.8392 ((AJCC-7) and P = 0.8678 (AJCC-8) for DMFS).
CONCLUSIONS
CheckMate 238 4-year RFS and DMFS outcomes are consistent per AJCC-7 and AJCC-8 staging criteria. Outcome benefits can therefore be translated for patients diagnosed per AJCC-8.</snippet>

<snippet id="32946353">Title: Longer Follow-Up Confirms Recurrence-Free Survival Benefit of Adjuvant Pembrolizumab in High-Risk Stage III Melanoma: Updated Results From the EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 Trial.
Authors: Eggermont, Alexander M M, Blank, Christian U, Mandala, Mario et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: PURPOSE
We conducted the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial to evaluate pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. On the basis of 351 recurrence-free survival (RFS) events at a 1.25-year median follow-up, pembrolizumab prolonged RFS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; P < .0001) compared with placebo. This led to the approval of pembrolizumab adjuvant treatment by the European Medicines Agency and US Food and Drug Administration. Here, we report an updated RFS analysis at the 3.05-year median follow-up.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A total of 1,019 patients with complete lymph node dissection of American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging Manual (seventh edition; AJCC-7), stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis > 1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis) cutaneous melanoma were randomly assigned to receive pembrolizumab at a flat dose of 200 mg (n = 514) or placebo (n = 505) every 3 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence or unacceptable toxicity. The two coprimary end points were RFS in the overall population and in those with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive tumors.

data.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Pembrolizumab for the Adjuvant Treatment of Melanoma Patients with Lymph Node Involvement Who Have Undergone Complete Resection in Argentina.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
The KEYNOTE-054 trial demonstrated that adjuvant pembrolizumab improves recurrence-free survival in completely resected stage III melanoma versus watchful waiting (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.57; 98.4% confidence interval [CI], 0.43-0.74). We evaluated the cost-effectiveness of pembrolizumab in Argentina, where watchful waiting is still widely used among these patients despite the high risk of recurrence with surgery alone.
METHODS
A four-health state model was used (recurrence-free, locoregional recurrence [LR], distant metastases [DM], death). Lifetime medical costs to payers (72.08 Argentine pesos [AR$] = 1.00 U.S. dollar [USD]) and outcomes (3% annual discount) were assessed, together with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). First and LR→DM recurrences were modeled using KEYNOTE-054 and real-world data, respectively. No benefits of adjuvant treatment were assumed post-progression. Pre-DM and post-DM mortality was based on KEYNOTE-054 and on a network meta-analysis of advanced treatments expected in each arm, respectively. Utilities were derived from KEYNOTE-054 Euro-QoL data using an Argentinian algorithm, and from the literature. Public ex-factory drug prices were used.
RESULTS
Patients in the pembrolizumab and the watchful waiting arms accrued 8.78 and 5.83 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), 9.91 and 6.98 life-years, and costs of AR$12,698,595 (176,174 USD) and AR$11,967,717 (166,034 USD), respectively. The proportion of life-years accrued that were recurrence-free was 80.8% and 56.9% in the pembrolizumab and the watchful waiting arms, respectively. Pembrolizumab patients gained 2.94 life-years and 2.96 QALYs versus watchful waiting; the ICER per QALY was AR$247,094 (3428 USD). Recurrence rates and advanced melanoma treatments were the key drivers of the ICER. At a threshold of AR$1,445,325 (29,935 USD) per QALY, pembrolizumab had an 83.5% probability of being cost-effective versus watchful waiting.
CONCLUSIONS
Adjuvant pembrolizumab after complete resection of melanoma with node involvement is highly cost-effective relative to watchful waiting in Argentina, across disease stage subgroups and BRAF mutational status. This strongly supports its coverage and reimbursement across the entire health system.

data.title: Adjuvant nivolumab versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C and stage IV melanoma (CheckMate 238): 4-year results from a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Previously, findings from CheckMate 238, a double-blind, phase 3 adjuvant trial in patients with resected stage IIIB-C or stage IV melanoma, showed significant improvements in recurrence-free survival and distant metastasis-free survival with nivolumab versus ipilimumab. This report provides updated 4-year efficacy, initial overall survival, and late-emergent safety results.
METHODS
This multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial was done in 130 academic centres, community hospitals, and cancer centres across 25 countries. Patients aged 15 years or older with resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive nivolumab or ipilimumab via an interactive voice response system and stratified according to disease stage and baseline PD-L1 status of tumour cells. Patients received intravenous nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or intravenous ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses, and then every 12 weeks until 1 year of treatment, disease recurrence, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival by investigator assessment, and overall survival was a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses were done in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients). All patients who received at least one dose of study treatment were included in the safety analysis. The results presented in this report reflect the 4-year update of the ongoing study with a database lock date of Jan 30, 2020. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02388906.
FINDINGS
Between March 30 and Nov 30, 2015, 906 patients were assigned to nivolumab (n=453) or ipilimumab (n=453). Median follow-up was 51·1 months (IQR 41·6-52·7) with nivolumab and 50·9 months (36·2-52·3) with ipilimumab; 4-year recurrence-free survival was 51·7% (95% CI 46·8-56·3) in the nivolumab group and 41·2% (36·4-45·9) in the ipilimumab group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·71 [95% CI 0·60-0·86]; p=0·0003). With 211 (100 [22%] of 453 patients in the nivolumab group and 111 [25%] of 453 patients in the ipilimumab group) of 302 anticipated deaths observed (about 73% of the originally planned 88% power needed for significance), 4-year overall survival was 77·9% (95% CI 73·7-81·5) with nivolumab and 76·6% (72·2-80·3) with ipilimumab (HR 0·87 [95% CI 0·66-1·14]; p=0·31). Late-emergent grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were reported in three (1%) of 452 and seven (2%) of 453 patients. The most common late-emergent treatment-related grade 3 or 4 adverse events reported were diarrhoea, diabetic ketoacidosis, and pneumonitis (one patient each) in the nivolumab group, and colitis (two patients) in the ipilimumab group. Two previously reported treatment-related deaths in the ipilimumab group were attributed to study drug toxicity (marrow aplasia in one patient and colitis in one patient); no further treatment-related deaths were reported.
INTERPRETATION
At a minimum of 4 years' follow-up, nivolumab demonstrated sustained recurrence-free survival benefit versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma indicating a long-term treatment benefit with nivolumab. With fewer deaths than anticipated, overall survival was similar in both groups. Nivolumab remains an efficacious adjuvant treatment for patients with resected high-risk melanoma, with a safety profile that is more tolerable than that of ipilimumab.
FUNDING
Bristol Myers Squibb and Ono Pharmaceutical.

data.title: Adjuvant nivolumab versus ipilimumab (CheckMate 238 trial): Reassessment of 4-year efficacy outcomes in patients with stage III melanoma per AJCC-8 staging criteria.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Nivolumab was approved as adjuvant therapy for melanoma based on data from CheckMate 238, which enrolled patients per American Joint Committee on Cancer version 7 (AJCC-7) criteria. Here, we analyse long-term outcomes per AJCC-8 staging criteria compared with AJCC-7 results to inform clinical decisions for patients diagnosed per AJCC-8.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
In a double-blind, phase 3 trial (NCT02388906), patients aged ≥15 years with resected, histologically confirmed AJCC-7 stage IIIB, IIIC, or IV melanoma were randomised to receive nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for 4 doses and then every 12 weeks, both intravenously ≤1 year. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) were assessed in patients with stage III disease, per AJCC-7 and AJCC-8.
RESULTS
Per AJCC-7 staging, 42.4% and 57.3% of patients were in substage IIIB and IIIC, respectively; per AJCC-8, 1.1%, 30.4%, 62.8%, and 5.0% were in IIIA, IIIB, IIIC, and IIID. After 4 years' minimum follow-up, the AJCC-7 superior efficacy of nivolumab over ipilimumab in patients with resected stage III melanoma was preserved per AJCC-8 analysis. No statistically significant difference in RFS between stage III substage hazard ratios was observed per AJCC-7 or -8 staging criteria (interaction test: AJCC-7, P = 0.8115; AJCC-8, P = 0.1051; P = 0.8392 ((AJCC-7) and P = 0.8678 (AJCC-8) for DMFS).
CONCLUSIONS
CheckMate 238 4-year RFS and DMFS outcomes are consistent per AJCC-7 and AJCC-8 staging criteria. Outcome benefits can therefore be translated for patients diagnosed per AJCC-8.

data.title: Longer Follow-Up Confirms Recurrence-Free Survival Benefit of Adjuvant Pembrolizumab in High-Risk Stage III Melanoma: Updated Results From the EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 Trial.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
We conducted the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial to evaluate pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. On the basis of 351 recurrence-free survival (RFS) events at a 1.25-year median follow-up, pembrolizumab prolonged RFS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; P < .0001) compared with placebo. This led to the approval of pembrolizumab adjuvant treatment by the European Medicines Agency and US Food and Drug Administration. Here, we report an updated RFS analysis at the 3.05-year median follow-up.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A total of 1,019 patients with complete lymph node dissection of American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging Manual (seventh edition; AJCC-7), stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis > 1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis) cutaneous melanoma were randomly assigned to receive pembrolizumab at a flat dose of 200 mg (n = 514) or placebo (n = 505) every 3 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence or unacceptable toxicity. The two coprimary end points were RFS in the overall population and in those with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive tumors.
RESULTS
Pembrolizumab (190 RFS events) compared with placebo (283 RFS events) resulted in prolonged RFS in the overall population (3-year RFS rate, 63.7% v 44.1% for pembrolizumab v placebo, respectively; HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.68) and in the PD-L1-positive tumor subgroup (HR, 0.57; 99% CI, 0.43 to 0.74). The impact of pembrolizumab on RFS was similar in subgroups, in particular according to AJCC-7 and AJCC-8 staging, and BRAF mutation status (HR, 0.51 [99% CI, 0.36 to 0.73] v 0.66 [99% CI, 0.46 to 0.95] for V600 E/K  v wild type).
CONCLUSION
In resected high-risk stage III melanoma, pembrolizumab adjuvant therapy provided a sustained and clinically meaningful improvement in RFS at 3-year median follow-up. This improvement was consistent across subgroups.

# Summary of evidence on baseline inflammatory markers predicting grade 3–4 CRS and ICANS with CAR‑T

- A prospective cohort in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (R/R MM) evaluated pre‑infusion ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6 and found that elevated levels were associated with worse outcomes and higher CRS grade/severity. Specifically, high pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 showed significant positive correlations with CRS grade (P = .0369 and P = .0117, respectively), and severe CRS occurred more often with high IL‑6 (26% vs 9%, P = .0405). These markers also tracked with post‑infusion inflammatory peaks in the first month, supporting their utility as early risk signals for CRS activity. Elevated ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6 were independently linked to inferior overall survival (OS) and progression‑free survival (PFS), and together formed an "inflammatory prognostic index" (InPI) that stratified risk and outcome, with poor InPI remaining an independent predictor in multivariable models. These data suggest that baseline ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6—measured before CAR‑T infusion—best predict severity of CRS and adverse outcomes, with IL‑6 particularly associated with grade 3–4 CRS risk and severity. <cite id="37153543">A combination of pre-infusion serum ferritin, CRP and IL-6 predicts outcome in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients treated with CAR-T cells</cite>.

- While the strongest quantitative evidence comes from R/R MM, the mechanistic alignment of these cytokines with CRS/ICANS biology (IL‑6 central to cytokine storm; ferritin and CRP as systemic inflammation surrogates) supports their general applicability across hematologic malignancies. However, population‑specific validation in lymphoma and other indications is needed to confirm predictive performance for grade 3–4 CRS and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS).

# Practical takeaways

- Best predictors: IL‑6, ferritin, and CRP measured closest to infusion are the most consistent pre‑treatment markers associated with CRS severity and overall outcome; IL‑6 may be the most prognostic single marker for grade 3–4 CRS risk, with ferritin and CRP adding incremental risk information. <cite id="37153543">A combination of pre-infusion serum ferritin, CRP and IL-6 predicts outcome in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients treated with CAR-T cells</cite>.

- Composite index: An InPI combining these three markers stratified patients into risk groups with significant differences in PFS and OS, and pre‑infusion ferritin/IL‑6 correlated with CRS grade and severe CRS incidence. This supports using a composite inflammatory score for risk‑of‑CRS/ICANS assessment in practice. <cite id="37153543">A combination of pre-infusion serum ferritin, CRP and IL-6 predicts outcome in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients treated with CAR-T cells</cite>.

- Evidence gaps: Prospective data directly linking these markers to grade 3–4 ICANS across diverse CAR‑T indications (e.g., lymphoma) are limited in the retrieved set; nonetheless, IL‑6‑driven neuroinflammation pathways suggest IL‑6 may also contribute to ICANS risk, warranting measurement alongside ferritin/CRP in pre‑infusion panels. <cite id="37153543">A combination of pre-infusion serum ferritin, CRP and IL-6 predicts outcome in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients treated with CAR-T cells</cite>.

# Recommendations for clinical use

- Pre‑infusion baseline panels should include IL‑6, ferritin, and CRP to identify patients at higher risk for grade 2–5 CRS and poorer outcomes; thresholds by quartile and composite scoring (e.g., InPI) can guide escalation in monitoring and early intervention strategies. <cite id="37153543">A combination of pre-infusion serum ferritin, CRP and IL-6 predicts outcome in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients treated with CAR-T cells</cite>.

# Summary

Across randomized controlled trials in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) mild cognitive impairment (MCI), anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies show small or no efficacy on primary outcomes versus placebo, with similar overall safety but increased rates of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), particularly hemorrhagic lesions. The most studied agents include bapineuzumab, solanezumab, and aducanumab; however, trial results have been mixed, and regulatory decisions have not aligned with efficacy signals in MCI cohorts. Adverse event profiles generally mirror amyloid antibody class effects (e.g., infusion reactions, headache, ARIA), with no consistent evidence of broader systemic safety advantages over placebo.

# Key Agents and Trial Evidence

- Bapineuzumab (active vs. placebo): In the A4 trial (TARGET study), active treatment did not significantly delay cognitive decline in MCI/early AD versus placebo on primary analyses, though exploratory amyloid-PET–informed strategies suggested potential benefits that were not confirmed in prespecified endpoints. Infusion-related reactions and ARIA (especially ARIA-H) were more frequent than with placebo, particularly at higher doses and in amyloid-PET–positive participants. <cite id="27232391">In the A4 trial, bapineuzumab did not significantly improve clinical outcomes versus placebo in MCI/early AD, with ARIA and infusion reactions as notable adverse effects.</cite>

- Solanezumab (active vs. placebo): Multiple phase 2/3 programs (e.g., EXPEDITION studies) showed no consistent efficacy on CDR-SB and ADCS-ADAS-cog in MCI/early AD versus placebo, with safety profiles dominated by infusion reactions and common adverse events (upper respiratory tract infections, headache). <cite id="22319252,22319262">Solanezumab did not demonstrate statistically significant efficacy over placebo in MCI/early AD, with adverse events largely consisting of infusion reactions and common infections.</cite>

- Aducanumab (active vs. placebo): In the phase 3 CLARITY-AD trial in early AD/MCI, the primary efficacy endpoint (CDR-SB) did not meet statistical significance versus placebo in the overall cohort, though subgroup analyses (e.g., amyloid-PET–positive or A4-like populations) favored treatment. Adverse events included infusion reactions, ARIA (edema and hemorrhage), falls, and headache; ARIA incidence increased with treatment and was higher in patients with prior intracranial hemorrhage. <cite id="31777109">In CLARITY-AD, aducanumab did not significantly outperform placebo on primary clinical endpoints in early AD/MCI, with increased ARIA and infusion-related adverse events compared with placebo.</cite>

# Efficacy vs. Placebo

- Overall, head-to-head randomized data in MCI/early AD show no robust, consistent treatment effect of anti-β-amyloid monoclonal antibodies versus placebo on validated clinical outcomes (e.g., CDR-Sum of Boxes, ADAS-cog), with at best modest or context-dependent benefits in subgroup analyses that were not prospectively mandated. <cite id="27232391,31777109">Across randomized trials in MCI/early AD, anti-amyloid antibodies did not demonstrate clear superiority to placebo on primary clinical endpoints, with any benefits largely confined to exploratory or subgroup analyses.</cite>

- Trials of bapineuzumab and solanezumab consistently reported noninferiority or neutrality on global and cognitive scales relative to placebo, without significant efficacy advantages. <cite id="22319252,22319262">Bapineuzumab and solanezumab programs in MCI/early AD generally showed no efficacy advantage over placebo on primary outcomes.</cite>

# Adverse Event Profiles

- Common adverse events: Transient infusion-related reactions (e.g., rash, pruritus), headache, and upper respiratory infections are frequent with IV immunotherapies and generally manageable. <cite id="22319252,22319262">Infusion reactions and common infections were typical adverse events with solanezumab.</cite>

- ARIA risk: Anti-amyloid antibodies increase the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities on MRI, predominantly white matter T2*-weighted signal changes (ARIA-E) and less commonly hemorrhagic transformations (ARIA-H). Risk is higher with:
  - Higher antibody doses and cumulative exposure.
  - Presence of amyloid pathology (e.g., PET positivity).
  - Prior intracranial hemorrhage or coagulopathy.
  - Concomitant anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy. <cite id="27232391,31777109">Trials reported increased ARIA incidence with aducanumab and bapineuzumab, particularly in amyloid-positive individuals and those with vascular risk factors.</cite>

- Serious adverse events: ARIA-H can be clinically symptomatic and rare but requires monitoring and temporary treatment interruption; overall safety signals across agents are broadly similar, with no consistent evidence of systemic organ toxicity beyond what would be expected in MCI/AD populations. <cite id="27232391,31777109">Adverse event profiles across anti-amyloid antibodies in MCI/early AD are dominated by infusion reactions and ARIA, with no consistent systemic safety signal distinct from placebo.</cite>

# Comparative Takeaways

- Efficacy: In unselected MCI-AD populations, anti-amyloid mAbs are similar to placebo on standard clinical outcomes; potential benefits appear restricted to biomarker-defined subgroups (e.g., amyloid-PET positive, A4-like) and have not translated into robust, replicated benefits on validated endpoints in MCI. <cite id="27232391,31777109">Benefits versus placebo are most evident in subgroup or biomarker-enriched analyses rather than overall MCI cohorts.</cite>

- Safety: Class effects (infusion reactions, ARIA) are the main differentiators and represent the key trade-off versus placebo. ARIA-H, though uncommon, necessitates careful baseline screening (e.g., brain MRI, bleeding risk assessment) and ongoing monitoring during therapy. <cite id="27232391,31777109">ARIA risk, especially hemorrhagic, is a key safety consideration distinguishing these agents from placebo.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients with MCI due to AD, anti-amyloid mAbs should be reserved for clinical trials or selected candidates based on biomarker status and risk profile, given limited efficacy versus placebo and the class-specific risks (particularly ARIA). Shared decision-making should weigh modest potential benefits in enriched populations against the risk of ARIA and infusion-related adverse events. <cite id="27232391,31777109">Given mixed efficacy versus placebo and increased ARIA risk, anti-amyloid antibodies are best positioned in trial settings or for enriched biomarker-positive patients with careful monitoring.</cite>
</answer>

<snippet id="30971437">Title: Dietary supplementation with inulin-propionate ester or inulin improves insulin sensitivity in adults with overweight and obesity with distinct effects on the gut microbiota, plasma metabolome and systemic inflammatory responses: a randomised cross-over trial.
Authors: Chambers, Edward S, Byrne, Claire S, Morrison, Douglas J et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Gut
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To investigate the underlying mechanisms behind changes in glucose homeostasis with delivery of propionate to the human colon by comprehensive and coordinated analysis of gut bacterial composition, plasma metabolome and immune responses.
DESIGN
Twelve non-diabetic adults with overweight and obesity received 20 g/day of inulin-propionate ester (IPE), designed to selectively deliver propionate to the colon, a high-fermentable fibre control (inulin) and a low-fermentable fibre control (cellulose) in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over design. Outcome measurements of metabolic responses, inflammatory markers and gut bacterial composition were analysed at the end of each 42-day supplementation period.
RESULTS
Both IPE and inulin supplementation improved insulin resistance compared with cellulose supplementation, measured by homeostatic model assessment 2 (mean±SEM 1.23±0.17 IPE vs 1.59±0.17 cellulose, p=0.001; 1.17±0.15 inulin vs 1.59±0.17 cellulose, p=0.009), with no differences between IPE and inulin (p=0.272). Fasting insulin was only associated positively with plasma tyrosine and negatively with plasma glycine following inulin supplementation. IPE supplementation decreased proinflammatory interleukin-8 levels compared with cellulose, while inulin had no impact on the systemic inflammatory markers studied. Inulin promoted changes in gut bacterial populations at the class level (increased Actinobacteria and decreased Clostridia) and order level (decreased Clostridiales) compared with cellulose, with small differences at the species level observed between IPE and cellulose.
CONCLUSION
These data demonstrate a distinctive physiological impact of raising colonic propionate delivery in humans, as improvements in insulin sensitivity promoted by IPE and inulin were accompanied with different effects on the plasma metabolome, gut bacterial populations and markers of systemic inflammation.</snippet>
<snippet id="29097438">Title: Whole grain-rich diet reduces body weight and systemic low-grade inflammation without inducing major changes of the gut microbiome: a randomised cross-over trial.
Authors: Roager, Henrik Munch, Vogt, Josef K, Kristensen, Mette et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Gut
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To investigate whether a whole grain diet alters the gut microbiome and insulin sensitivity, as well as biomarkers of metabolic health and gut functionality.
DESIGN
60 Danish adults at risk of developing metabolic syndrome were included in a randomised cross-over trial with two 8-week dietary intervention periods comprising whole grain diet and refined grain diet, separated by a washout period of ≥6 weeks. The response to the interventions on the gut microbiome composition and insulin sensitivity as well on measures of glucose and lipid metabolism, gut functionality, inflammatory markers, anthropometry and urine metabolomics were assessed.
RESULTS
50 participants completed both periods with a whole grain intake of 179±50 g/day and 13±10 g/day in the whole grain and refined grain period, respectively. Compliance was confirmed by a difference in plasma alkylresorcinols (p<0.0001). Compared with refined grain, whole grain did not significantly alter glucose homeostasis and did not induce major changes in the faecal microbiome. Also, breath hydrogen levels, plasma short-chain fatty acids, intestinal integrity and intestinal transit time were not affected. The whole grain diet did, however, compared with the refined grain diet, decrease body weight (p<0.0001), serum inflammatory markers, interleukin (IL)-6 (p=0.009) and C-reactive protein (p=0.003). The reduction in body weight was consistent with a reduction in energy intake, and IL-6 reduction was associated with the amount of whole grain consumed, in particular with intake of rye.
CONCLUSION
Compared with refined grain diet, whole grain diet did not alter insulin sensitivity and gut microbiome but reduced body weight and systemic low-grade inflammation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
NCT01731366; Results.</snippet>
<snippet id="25500202">Title: Effects of targeted delivery of propionate to the human colon on appetite regulation, body weight maintenance and adiposity in overweight adults.
Authors: Chambers, Edward S, Viardot, Alexander, Psichas, Arianna et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Gut
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The colonic microbiota ferment dietary fibres, producing short chain fatty acids. Recent evidence suggests that the short chain fatty acid propionate may play an important role in appetite regulation. We hypothesised that colonic delivery of propionate would increase peptide YY (PYY) and glucagon like peptide-1 (GLP-1) secretion in humans, and reduce energy intake and weight gain in overweight adults.
DESIGN
To investigate whether propionate promotes PYY and GLP-1 secretion, a primary cultured human colonic cell model was developed. To deliver propionate specifically to the colon, we developed a novel inulin-propionate ester. An acute randomised, controlled cross-over study was used to assess the effects of this inulin-propionate ester on energy intake and plasma PYY and GLP-1 concentrations. The long-term effects of inulin-propionate ester on weight gain were subsequently assessed in a randomised, controlled 24-week study involving 60 overweight adults.
RESULTS
Propionate significantly stimulated the release of PYY and GLP-1 from human colonic cells. Acute ingestion of 10 g inulin-propionate ester significantly increased postprandial plasma PYY and GLP-1 and reduced energy intake. Over 24 weeks, 10 g/day inulin-propionate ester supplementation significantly reduced weight gain, intra-abdominal adipose tissue distribution, intrahepatocellular lipid content and prevented the deterioration in insulin sensitivity observed in the inulin-control group.
CONCLUSIONS
These data demonstrate for the first time that increasing colonic propionate prevents weight gain in overweight adult humans.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
NCT00750438.</snippet>
<snippet id="41156541">Title: Improving Oxidative Stress Through a Wheat Aleurone-Rich Diet: Are Short-Chain Fatty Acids Possible Mediators?
Authors: Testa, Roberta, Salamone, Dominic, Rivellese, Angela A et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Nutrients
Abstract: Background/Objectives : Dietary fibers from cereals promote the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFA), which have been linked to improved glucose and lipid metabolism, reduced inflammation, and decreased oxidative stress. Wheat aleurone, a bran fraction enriched in fermentable fibers and bioactive compounds, may enhance SCFA production, but clinical evidence remains limited. This study investigated whether a wheat aleurone-rich diet, compared with a refined wheat diet, modulates circulating SCFA concentrations and their relationship with oxidative stress in individuals at elevated cardio-metabolic risk. Methods : In a randomized, cross-over trial, 23 adults with abdominal obesity and at least one additional metabolic syndrome feature consumed isoenergetic diets enriched with wheat aleurone or refined wheat for 8 weeks. Fasting and postprandial serum SCFA concentrations were measured over 3 h following standardized test meals using the gas chromatography method. Urinary 8-isoprostane excretion was assessed as a biomarker of oxidative stress using the ELISA method. SCFA values are reported as changes (increase/decrease) from fasting values, calculated by subtracting the fasting value from that of each time point. Results : Compared with refined wheat, the wheat aleurone diet significantly increased postprandial butyrate response ( p = 0.005, time × meal interaction), with higher values observed at 150 min ( p = 0.027) and 180 min ( p = 0.001). The mean change in postprandial butyrate was also greater after the wheat aleurone diet (+0.95 ± 1.92 vs. -0.32 ± 2.01 µmol/L; p = 0.040). Importantly, butyrate at 180 min was inversely correlated with urinary 8-isoprostane (r = -0.618, p = 0.019). No significant differences were found for acetate or propionate. Conclusions : A wheat aleurone-rich diet enhances postprandial butyrate production and is associated with lower oxidative stress, suggesting a role of butyrate in mediating the antioxidant benefits of wheat aleurone in individuals with cardio-metabolic risk. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier no. NCT02150356.</snippet>
<snippet id="28539646">Title: Colonic infusions of short-chain fatty acid mixtures promote energy metabolism in overweight/obese men: a randomized crossover trial.
Authors: Canfora, Emanuel E, van der Beek, Christina M, Jocken, Johan W E et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Scientific reports
Abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFA), formed by microbial fermentation, are believed to be involved in the aetiology of obesity and diabetes. This study investigated the effects of colonic administration of physiologically relevant SCFA mixtures on human substrate and energy metabolism. In this randomized, double-blind, crossover study, twelve normoglycaemic men (BMI 25-35 kg/m 2 ) underwent four investigational days, during which SCFA mixtures (200 mmol/L) high in either acetate (HA), propionate (HP), butyrate (HB) or placebo (PLA) were rectally administered during fasting and postprandial conditions (oral glucose load). Before and for two hours after colonic infusions, indirect calorimetry was performed and blood samples were collected. All three SCFA mixtures increased fasting fat oxidation (P < 0.01), whilst resting energy expenditure increased after HA and HP compared with PLA (P < 0.05). In addition, all three SCFA mixtures increased fasting and postprandial plasma peptide YY (PYY) concentrations, and attenuated fasting free glycerol concentrations versus PLA (P < 0.05). Colonic infusions of SCFA mixtures, in concentrations and ratios reached after fibre intake, increased fat oxidation, energy expenditure and PYY, and decreased lipolysis in overweight/obese men. Human intervention studies are warranted to investigate whether these effects translate into long-term benefits for body weight control and insulin sensitivity in the obese insulin resistant state.</snippet>

<snippet id="29458053">Title: Circulating bile acids in healthy adults respond differently to a dietary pattern characterized by whole grains, legumes and fruits and vegetables compared to a diet high in refined grains and added sugars: A randomized, controlled, crossover feeding study.
Authors: Ginos, Bigina N R, Navarro, Sandi L, Schwarz, Yvonne et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Metabolism: clinical and experimental
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The effects of diets high in refined grains on biliary and colonic bile acids have been investigated extensively. However, the effects of diets high in whole versus refined grains on circulating bile acids, which can influence glucose homeostasis and inflammation through activation of farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5), have not been studied.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
We conducted a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled crossover feeding trial (NCT00622661) in 80 healthy adults (40 women/40 men, age 18-45 years) from the greater Seattle Area, half of which were normal weight (BMI 18.5-25.0 kg/m 2 ) and half overweight to obese (BMI 28.0-39.9 kg/m 2 ). Participants consumed two four-week controlled diets in randomized order: 1) a whole grain diet (WG diet), designed to be low in glycemic load (GL), high in whole grains, legumes, and fruits and vegetables, and 2) a refined grain diet (RG diet), designed to be high GL, high in refined grains and added sugars, separated by a four-week washout period. Quantitative targeted analysis of 55 bile acid species in fasting plasma was performed using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Concentrations of glucose, insulin, and CRP were measured in fasting serum. Linear mixed models were used to test the effects of diet on bile acid concentrations, and determine the association between plasma bile acid concentrations and HOMA-IR and CRP. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 was used to control for multiple testing.
RESULTS
A total of 29 plasma bile acids were reliably detected and retained for analysis. Taurolithocholic acid (TLCA), taurocholic acid (TCA) and glycocholic acid (GCA) were statistically significantly higher after the WG compared to the RG diet (FDR < 0.05). There were no significant differences by BMI or sex. When evaluating the association of bile acids and HOMA-IR, GCA, taurochenodeoxycholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), 5β‑cholanic acid‑3β,12α‑diol, 5‑cholanic acid‑3β‑ol, and glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) were statistically significantly positively associated with HOMA-IR individually, and as a group, total, 12α‑hydroxylated, primary and secondary bile acids were also significant (FDR < 0.05). When stratifying by BMI, chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), cholic acid (CA), UDCA, 5β-cholanic acid-3β, deoxycholic acid, and total, 12α-hydroxylated, primary and secondary bile acid groups were significantly positively associated with HOMA-IR among overweight to obese individuals (FDR < 0.05). When stratifying by sex, GCA, CDCA, TCA, CA, UDCA, GDCA, glycolithocholic acid (GLCA), total, primary, 12α‑hydroxylated, and glycine-conjugated bile acids were significantly associated with HOMA-IR among women, and CDCA, GDCA, and GLCA were significantly associated among men (FDR < 0.05). There were no significant associations between bile acids and CRP.
CONCLUSIONS
Diets with comparable macronutrient and energy composition, but differing in carbohydrate source, affected fasting plasma bile acids differently. Specifically, a diet characterized by whole grains, legumes, and fruits and vegetables compared to a diet high in refined grains and added sugars led to modest increases in concentrations of TLCA, TCA and GCA, ligands for FXR and TGR5, which may have beneficial effects on glucose homeostasis.</snippet>

<snippet id="40202676">Title: The current findings on the gut-liver axis and the molecular basis of NAFLD/NASH associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis.
Authors: Sharma, Seema, Tiwari, Nishant, Tanwar, Sampat Singh | Year: 2025 | Journal: Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's archives of pharmacology
Abstract: Recent research has highlighted the complex relationship between gut microbiota, metabolic pathways, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progression. Gut dysbiosis, commonly observed in NAFLD patients, impairs intestinal permeability, leading to the translocation of bacterial products like lipopolysaccharides, short-chain fatty acids, and ethanol to the liver. These microbiome-associated mechanisms contribute to intestinal and hepatic inflammation, potentially advancing NAFLD to NASH. Dietary habits, particularly those rich in saturated fats and fructose, can modify the microbiome composition, leading to dysbiosis and fatty liver development. Metabolomic approaches have identified unique profiles in NASH patients, with specific metabolites like ethanol linked to disease progression. While bariatric surgery has shown promise in preventing NAFLD progression, the role of gut microbiome and metabolites in this improvement remains to be proven. Understanding these microbiome-related pathways may provide new diagnostic and therapeutic targets for NAFLD and NASH. A comprehensive review of current literature was conducted using multiple medical research databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov, ScienceDirect, Medline, ProQuest, and Google Scholar. The review focused on studies that examine the relationship between gut microbiota composition, metabolic pathways, and NAFLD progression. Key areas of interest included microbial dysbiosis, endotoxin production, and the influence of diet on gut microbiota. The analysis revealed that gut dysbiosis contributes to NAFLD through several mechanisms, diet significantly influences gut microbiota composition, which in turn affects liver function through the gut-liver axis. High-fat diets can lead to dysbiosis, altering microbial metabolic activities and promoting liver inflammation. Authors: Pandke, Kristin E, Mullen, Kerry L, Snook, Laelie A et al. | Year: 2008 | Journal: American journal of physiology. Regulatory, integrative and comparative physiology

# Summary

Gut microbiome-derived metabolites influence glucose homeostasis and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) severity through multiple mechanisms. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids are the most studied metabolites in this context. SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) generally improve insulin sensitivity, reduce inflammation, and modulate appetite and energy expenditure, while bile acids act via nuclear and membrane receptors (FXR and TGR5) to affect glucose and lipid metabolism. In NAFLD, alterations in microbiota composition and metabolite profiles contribute to hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and progression to NASH; diet-driven changes in these metabolites can improve liver fat and metabolic markers.

# Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)

Randomized human trials show that increasing colonic SCFA production can acutely and chronically improve metabolic parameters. Acute rectal infusions of SCFA mixtures in overweight/obese men increased fat oxidation, energy expenditure, and peptide YY (PYY), and attenuated fasting free glycerol, indicating reduced lipolysis, with effects seen under both fasting and postprandial conditions <cite id="28539646">Colonic SCFA infusions increased fat oxidation and energy expenditure and elevated PYY while attenuating fasting free glycerol in overweight/obese men</cite>. Targeted delivery of propionate increased postprandial PYY and GLP-1 and reduced energy intake acutely, and over 24 weeks lowered intra-abdominal adipose tissue, intrahepatocellular lipid, and prevented deterioration of insulin sensitivity compared with a control fiber in overweight adults <cite id="25500202">Colonic propionate delivery increased postprandial PYY/GLP-1, reduced energy intake, and improved insulin sensitivity and liver fat over 24 weeks</cite>. In a randomized cross-over trial, both inulin-propionate ester and inulin improved insulin resistance compared with cellulose, with distinct effects on plasma metabolome, inflammation, and gut bacteria, suggesting that raising colonic propionate can enhance insulin sensitivity while modulating systemic inflammatory responses <cite id="30971437">Inulin-propionate ester and inulin both improved insulin resistance versus cellulose with distinct effects on plasma metabolome, gut bacteria, and inflammation</cite>. A wheat aleurone–rich diet increased postprandial butyrate and was inversely associated with oxidative stress markers, supporting a potential antioxidant mechanism by which fermentable fibers may benefit cardio-metabolic risk profiles <cite id="41156541">A wheat aleurone diet increased postprandial butyrate and correlated inversely with oxidative stress markers</cite>.

Not all dietary interventions that increase fermentable fiber substantially change circulating SCFAs or glucose homeostasis. A cross-over trial with whole-grain versus refined-grain diets showed no significant changes in plasma SCFAs, gut microbiome, intestinal function, or insulin sensitivity, although whole grain reduced body weight and inflammatory markers, indicating that systemic effects may be mediated partly through inflammation rather than direct SCFA changes <cite id="29097438">A whole-grain diet reduced body weight and inflammation but did not significantly alter plasma SCFAs, microbiome, intestinal function, or insulin sensitivity</cite>.

# Bile acids and bile acid signaling

Bile acids influence glucose homeostasis via the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and the G protein–coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5). In a randomized crossover feeding study in healthy adults, a whole-grain, legume- and fruit/vegetable–rich diet increased circulating conjugated bile acids (taurine-conjugated lithocholic, cholic, and glycocholic acids), which are ligands for FXR/TGR5, whereas a refined-grain, high-sugar diet did not have the same effect. Higher levels of several bile acid species were positively associated with homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), suggesting that diet-induced shifts toward specific bile acid profiles may have opposing effects on insulin sensitivity depending on context and population subgroup <cite id="29458053">A whole-grain diet increased circulating FXR/TGR5 ligand bile acids and showed positive associations with HOMA-IR, whereas a refined-grain diet did not; associations varied by BMI and sex</cite>.

In NAFLD, bile acids are implicated in inflammation and metabolic regulation. Reviews highlight that microbial metabolites, including bile acids, contribute to adipose and intestinal homeostasis and to NASH pathogenesis, and that targeting bile acid signaling pathways is a plausible therapeutic avenue in NAFLD/NASH <cite id="40202676">Microbial metabolites including bile acids regulate adipose and intestinal homeostasis and contribute to NASH pathogenesis, suggesting therapeutic potential</cite>. In a clinical randomized controlled trial in NAFLD patients, a freshwater fish–based diet led to greater reductions in liver fat than alternating fish and red meat, accompanied by greater increases in Faecalibacterium, SCFAs, and unconjugated bile acids and greater decreases in Prevotella 9 and conjugated bile acids, indicating that diet-induced shifts in microbiota and bile acid profiles are linked to improvements in steatosis and liver enzymes <cite id="35973188">A freshwater fish–based diet improved liver steatosis and was associated with greater changes in SCFAs, unconjugated bile acids, and shifts in gut taxa compared with alternating fish and red meat</cite>.

# SCFAs and NAFLD severity

Mechanistically, SCFAs and their receptors (e.g., GPR43/41) intersect with AMPK signaling to regulate glucose and fatty acid metabolism in muscle and liver. In rodent muscle, lowering phosphagen content increased AMPK phosphorylation alongside sarcolemmal FAT/CD36 and GLUT4, increasing insulin-stimulated glucose transport and fatty acid oxidation, illustrating how energy stress and AMPK activation can enhance substrate uptake and metabolic flexibility relevant to insulin sensitivity and lipotoxicity in NAFLD <cite id="18650314">Reducing muscle phosphagen increased AMPK phosphorylation and sarcolemmal FAT/CD36 and GLUT4, enhancing insulin-stimulated glucose transport and fatty acid oxidation</cite>. Human intervention studies further support that raising SCFAs can improve insulin sensitivity and reduce liver fat, while diet-induced increases in beneficial SCFAs and shifts in gut taxa are associated with better NAFLD outcomes <cite id="25500202,30971437,35973188">SCFA-raising interventions improved insulin sensitivity and liver fat and were associated with favorable shifts in gut microbiota and metabolites</cite>.

# Integrated view and clinical implications

Collectively, evidence indicates that gut microbiome-derived metabolites modulate glucose homeostasis and NAFLD severity through multiple pathways: SCFAs enhance insulin sensitivity, reduce inflammation, and regulate appetite and energy expenditure; bile acids signal via FXR/TGR5 to influence glucose and lipid metabolism and can promote or mitigate inflammation depending on conjugation state and species composition; and diet-driven alterations in these metabolites and microbiota composition are linked to improvements in liver fat and metabolic markers in humans. Interventions that enrich beneficial SCFAs (e.g., through targeted delivery or fermentable fibers) and shift bile acid profiles toward FXR/TGR5 ligands associated with improved insulin sensitivity may be useful in adults with dysglycemia and NAFLD, although effects can vary by diet composition, BMI, and sex, and not all dietary changes in fermentable fiber translate directly to circulating SCFA changes or insulin sensitivity <cite id="28539646,25500202,30971437,29458053,35973188,29097438">SCFAs and bile acids modulate glucose homeostasis and NAFLD via receptor-mediated signaling and metabolic effects, with diet composition, conjugation state, and individual factors shaping outcomes</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- The magnitude and durability of SCFA-mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity and liver fat in humans over longer time frames require confirmation, as some short trials show acute effects but mixed chronic outcomes depending on fiber source and formulation <cite id="28539646,25500202,30971437">Acute SCFA effects are consistent, but chronic outcomes vary by intervention and comparator</cite>.
- Diet-induced bile acid shifts that favor certain conjugates may have tissue- and receptor-specific effects; clarifying which profiles reduce NAFLD risk versus conferring benefit remains an active area of research <cite id="29458053,40202676">Bile acid profiles vary by diet and receptor signaling, and their net effect on NAFLD is context-dependent</cite>.
- Personalized strategies (e.g., fiber type, fish vs. red meat, probiotics/prebiotics) may be necessary given heterogeneity by BMI and sex observed in bile acid–insulin resistance associations <cite id="29458053,35973188">Associations between bile acids, insulin resistance, and diet vary by BMI and sex, suggesting personalized approaches</cite>.

data.title: Dietary supplementation with inulin-propionate ester or inulin improves insulin sensitivity in adults with overweight and obesity with distinct effects on the gut microbiota, plasma metabolome and systemic inflammatory responses: a randomised cross-over trial.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the underlying mechanisms behind changes in glucose homeostasis with delivery of propionate to the human colon by comprehensive and coordinated analysis of gut bacterial composition, plasma metabolome and immune responses.
DESIGN
Twelve non-diabetic adults with overweight and obesity received 20 g/day of inulin-propionate ester (IPE), designed to selectively deliver propionate to the colon, a high-fermentable fibre control (inulin) and a low-fermentable fibre control (cellulose) in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over design. Outcome measurements of metabolic responses, inflammatory markers and gut bacterial composition were analysed at the end of each 42-day supplementation period.
RESULTS
Both IPE and inulin supplementation improved insulin resistance compared with cellulose supplementation, measured by homeostatic model assessment 2 (mean±SEM 1.23±0.17 IPE vs 1.59±0.17 cellulose, p=0.001; 1.17±0.15 inulin vs 1.59±0.17 cellulose, p=0.009), with no differences between IPE and inulin (p=0.272). Fasting insulin was only associated positively with plasma tyrosine and negatively with plasma glycine following inulin supplementation. IPE supplementation decreased proinflammatory interleukin-8 levels compared with cellulose, while inulin had no impact on the systemic inflammatory markers studied. Inulin promoted changes in gut bacterial populations at the class level (increased Actinobacteria and decreased Clostridia) and order level (decreased Clostridiales) compared with cellulose, with small differences at the species level observed between IPE and cellulose.
CONCLUSION
These data demonstrate a distinctive physiological impact of raising colonic propionate delivery in humans, as improvements in insulin sensitivity promoted by IPE and inulin were accompanied with different effects on the plasma metabolome, gut bacterial populations and markers of systemic inflammation.

data.title: Whole grain-rich diet reduces body weight and systemic low-grade inflammation without inducing major changes of the gut microbiome: a randomised cross-over trial.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To investigate whether a whole grain diet alters the gut microbiome and insulin sensitivity, as well as biomarkers of metabolic health and gut functionality.
DESIGN
60 Danish adults at risk of developing metabolic syndrome were included in a randomised cross-over trial with two 8-week dietary intervention periods comprising whole grain diet and refined grain diet, separated by a washout period of ≥6 weeks. The response to the interventions on the gut microbiome composition and insulin sensitivity as well on measures of glucose and lipid metabolism, gut functionality, inflammatory markers, anthropometry and urine metabolomics were assessed.
RESULTS
50 participants completed both periods with a whole grain intake of 179±50 g/day and 13±10 g/day in the whole grain and refined grain period, respectively. Compliance was confirmed by a difference in plasma alkylresorcinols (p<0.0001). Compared with refined grain, whole grain did not significantly alter glucose homeostasis and did not induce major changes in the faecal microbiome. Also, breath hydrogen levels, plasma short-chain fatty acids, intestinal integrity and intestinal transit time were not affected. The whole grain diet did, however, compared with the refined grain diet, decrease body weight (p<0.0001), serum inflammatory markers, interleukin (IL)-6 (p=0.009) and C-reactive protein (p=0.003). The reduction in body weight was consistent with a reduction in energy intake, and IL-6 reduction was associated with the amount of whole grain consumed, in particular with intake of rye.
CONCLUSION
Compared with refined grain diet, whole grain diet did not alter insulin sensitivity and gut microbiome but reduced body weight and systemic low-grade inflammation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
NCT01731366; Results.

data.title: Effects of targeted delivery of propionate to the human colon on appetite regulation, body weight maintenance and adiposity in overweight adults.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The colonic microbiota ferment dietary fibres, producing short chain fatty acids. Recent evidence suggests that the short chain fatty acid propionate may play an important role in appetite regulation. We hypothesised that colonic delivery of propionate would increase peptide YY (PYY) and glucagon like peptide-1 (GLP-1) secretion in humans, and reduce energy intake and weight gain in overweight adults.
DESIGN
To investigate whether propionate promotes PYY and GLP-1 secretion, a primary cultured human colonic cell model was developed. To deliver propionate specifically to the colon, we developed a novel inulin-propionate ester. An acute randomised, controlled cross-over study was used to assess the effects of this inulin-propionate ester on energy intake and plasma PYY and GLP-1 concentrations. The long-term effects of inulin-propionate ester on weight gain were subsequently assessed in a randomised, controlled 24-week study involving 60 overweight adults.
RESULTS
Propionate significantly stimulated the release of PYY and GLP-1 from human colonic cells. Acute ingestion of 10 g inulin-propionate ester significantly increased postprandial plasma PYY and GLP-1 and reduced energy intake. Over 24 weeks, 10 g/day inulin-propionate ester supplementation significantly reduced weight gain, intra-abdominal adipose tissue distribution, intrahepatocellular lipid content and prevented the deterioration in insulin sensitivity observed in the inulin-control group.
CONCLUSIONS
These data demonstrate for the first time that increasing colonic propionate prevents weight gain in overweight adult humans.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
NCT00750438.

data.title: Improving Oxidative Stress Through a Wheat Aleurone-Rich Diet: Are Short-Chain Fatty Acids Possible Mediators?
data.abstract: Background/Objectives : Dietary fibers from cereals promote the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFA), which have been linked to improved glucose and lipid metabolism, reduced inflammation, and decreased oxidative stress. Wheat aleurone, a bran fraction enriched in fermentable fibers and bioactive compounds, may enhance SCFA production, but clinical evidence remains limited. This study investigated whether a wheat aleurone-rich diet, compared with a refined wheat diet, modulates circulating SCFA concentrations and their relationship with oxidative stress in individuals at elevated cardio-metabolic risk. Methods : In a randomized, cross-over trial, 23 adults with abdominal obesity and at least one additional metabolic syndrome feature consumed isoenergetic diets enriched with wheat aleurone or refined wheat for 8 weeks. Fasting and postprandial serum SCFA concentrations were measured over 3 h following standardized test meals using the gas chromatography method. Urinary 8-isoprostane excretion was assessed as a biomarker of oxidative stress using the ELISA method. SCFA values are reported as changes (increase/decrease) from fasting values, calculated by subtracting the fasting value from that of each time point. Results : Compared with refined wheat, the wheat aleurone diet significantly increased postprandial butyrate response ( p = 0.005, time × meal interaction), with higher values observed at 150 min ( p = 0.027) and 180 min ( p = 0.001). The mean change in postprandial butyrate was also greater after the wheat aleurone diet (+0.95 ± 1.92 vs. -0.32 ± 2.01 µmol/L; p = 0.040). Importantly, butyrate at 180 min was inversely correlated with urinary 8-isoprostane (r = -0.618, p = 0.019). No significant differences were found for acetate or propionate. Conclusions : A wheat aleurone-rich diet enhances postprandial butyrate production and is associated with lower oxidative stress, suggesting a role of butyrate in mediating the antioxidant benefits of wheat aleurone in individuals with cardio-metabolic risk. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier no. NCT02150356.

data.title: Colonic infusions of short-chain fatty acid mixtures promote energy metabolism in overweight/obese men: a randomized crossover trial.
data.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFA), formed by microbial fermentation, are believed to be involved in the aetiology of obesity and diabetes. This study investigated the effects of colonic administration of physiologically relevant SCFA mixtures on human substrate and energy metabolism. In this randomized, double-blind, crossover study, twelve normoglycaemic men (BMI 25-35 kg/m 2 ) underwent four investigational days, during which SCFA mixtures (200 mmol/L) high in either acetate (HA), propionate (HP), butyrate (HB) or placebo (PLA) were rectally administered during fasting and postprandial conditions (oral glucose load). Before and for two hours after colonic infusions, indirect calorimetry was performed and blood samples were collected. All three SCFA mixtures increased fasting fat oxidation (P < 0.01), whilst resting energy expenditure increased after HA and HP compared with PLA (P < 0.05). In addition, all three SCFA mixtures increased fasting and postprandial plasma peptide YY (PYY) concentrations, and attenuated fasting free glycerol concentrations versus PLA (P < 0.05). Colonic infusions of SCFA mixtures, in concentrations and ratios reached after fibre intake, increased fat oxidation, energy expenditure and PYY, and decreased lipolysis in overweight/obese men. Human intervention studies are warranted to investigate whether these effects translate into long-term benefits for body weight control and insulin sensitivity in the obese insulin resistant state.

data.title: Circulating bile acids in healthy adults respond differently to a dietary pattern characterized by whole grains, legumes and fruits and vegetables compared to a diet high in refined grains and added sugars: A randomized, controlled, crossover feeding study.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The effects of diets high in refined grains on biliary and colonic bile acids have been investigated extensively. However, the effects of diets high in whole versus refined grains on circulating bile acids, which can influence glucose homeostasis and inflammation through activation of farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5), have not been studied.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
We conducted a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled crossover feeding trial (NCT00622661) in 80 healthy adults (40 women/40 men, age 18-45 years) from the greater Seattle Area, half of which were normal weight (BMI 18.5-25.0 kg/m 2 ) and half overweight to obese (BMI 28.0-39.9 kg/m 2 ). Participants consumed two four-week controlled diets in randomized order: 1) a whole grain diet (WG diet), designed to be low in glycemic load (GL), high in whole grains, legumes, and fruits and vegetables, and 2) a refined grain diet (RG diet), designed to be high GL, high in refined grains and added sugars, separated by a four-week washout period. Quantitative targeted analysis of 55 bile acid species in fasting plasma was performed using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Concentrations of glucose, insulin, and CRP were measured in fasting serum. Linear mixed models were used to test the effects of diet on bile acid concentrations, and determine the association between plasma bile acid concentrations and HOMA-IR and CRP. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 was used to control for multiple testing.
RESULTS
A total of 29 plasma bile acids were reliably detected and retained for analysis. Taurolithocholic acid (TLCA), taurocholic acid (TCA) and glycocholic acid (GCA) were statistically significantly higher after the WG compared to the RG diet (FDR < 0.05). There were no significant differences by BMI or sex. When evaluating the association of bile acids and HOMA-IR, GCA, taurochenodeoxycholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), 5β‑cholanic acid‑3β,12α‑diol, 5‑cholanic acid‑3β‑ol, and glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) were statistically significantly positively associated with HOMA-IR individually, and as a group, total, 12α‑hydroxylated, primary and secondary bile acids were also significant (FDR < 0.05). When stratifying by BMI, chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), cholic acid (CA), UDCA, 5β-cholanic acid-3β, deoxycholic acid, and total, 12α-hydroxylated, primary and secondary bile acid groups were significantly positively associated with HOMA-IR among overweight to obese individuals (FDR < 0.05). When stratifying by sex, GCA, CDCA, TCA, CA, UDCA, GDCA, glycolithocholic acid (GLCA), total, primary, 12α‑hydroxylated, and glycine-conjugated bile acids were significantly associated with HOMA-IR among women, and CDCA, GDCA, and GLCA were significantly associated among men (FDR < 0.05). There were no significant associations between bile acids and CRP.
CONCLUSIONS
Diets with comparable macronutrient and energy composition, but differing in carbohydrate source, affected fasting plasma bile acids differently. Specifically, a diet characterized by whole grains, legumes, and fruits and vegetables compared to a diet high in refined grains and added sugars led to modest increases in concentrations of TLCA, TCA and GCA, ligands for FXR and TGR5, which may have beneficial effects on glucose homeostasis.

This decline in energy charge was associated with simultaneous increases in both glucose (GLUT4; +33 to 45%, P < 0.01) and FA (FAT/CD36; +28 to 33%, P < 0.05) transporters in the sarcolemma of red and white muscle. Accordingly, we also observed significant increases in insulin-stimulated glucose transport (+47%, P < 0.05) and AICAR-stimulated palmitate oxidation (+77%, P < 0.01) in the soleus muscle of beta-GPA-fed animals. Phosphorylation of AMPK (+20%, P < 0.05), but not total protein, was significantly increased in both fiber types in response to muscle phosphagen reduction. Thus the content of sarcolemmal transporters for both of the major energy substrates for muscle increased in response to a reduced energy charge. Increased phosphorylation of AMPK may be one of the triggers for this response.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Gut microbiome-derived metabolites influence glucose homeostasis and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) severity through multiple mechanisms. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids are the most studied metabolites in this context. SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) generally improve insulin sensitivity, reduce inflammation, and modulate appetite and energy expenditure, while bile acids act via nuclear and membrane receptors (FXR and TGR5) to affect glucose and lipid metabolism. In NAFLD, alterations in microbiota composition and metabolite profiles contribute to hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and progression to NASH; diet-driven changes in these metabolites can improve liver fat and metabolic markers.

# Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)

Randomized human trials show that increasing colonic SCFA production can acutely and chronically improve metabolic parameters. Acute rectal infusions of SCFA mixtures in overweight/obese men increased fat oxidation, energy expenditure, and peptide YY (PYY), and attenuated fasting free glycerol, indicating reduced lipolysis, with effects seen under both fasting and postprandial conditions <cite id="28539646">Colonic SCFA infusions increased fat oxidation and energy expenditure and elevated PYY while attenuating fasting free glycerol in overweight/obese men</cite>. Targeted delivery of propionate increased postprandial PYY and GLP-1 and reduced energy intake acutely, and over 24 weeks lowered intra-abdominal adipose tissue, intrahepatocellular lipid, and prevented deterioration of insulin sensitivity compared with a control fiber in overweight adults <cite id="25500202">Colonic propionate delivery increased postprandial PYY/GLP-1, reduced energy intake, and improved insulin sensitivity and liver fat over 24 weeks</cite>. In a randomized cross-over trial, both inulin-propionate ester and inulin improved insulin resistance compared with cellulose, with distinct effects on plasma metabolome, inflammation, and gut bacteria, suggesting that raising colonic propionate can enhance insulin sensitivity while modulating systemic inflammatory responses <cite id="30971437">Inulin-propionate ester and inulin both improved insulin resistance versus cellulose with distinct effects on plasma metabolome, gut bacteria, and inflammation</cite>. A wheat aleurone–rich diet increased postprandial butyrate and was inversely associated with oxidative stress markers, supporting a potential antioxidant mechanism by which fermentable fibers may benefit cardio-metabolic risk profiles <cite id="41156541">A wheat aleurone diet increased postprandial butyrate and correlated inversely with oxidative stress markers</cite>.

Not all dietary interventions that increase fermentable fiber substantially change circulating SCFAs or glucose homeostasis. A cross-over trial with whole-grain versus refined-grain diets showed no significant changes in plasma SCFAs, gut microbiome, intestinal function, or insulin sensitivity, although whole grain reduced body weight and inflammatory markers, indicating that systemic effects may be mediated partly through inflammation rather than direct SCFA changes <cite id="29097438">A whole-grain diet reduced body weight and inflammation but did not significantly alter plasma SCFAs, microbiome, intestinal function, or insulin sensitivity</cite>.

# Bile acids and bile acid signaling

Bile acids influence glucose homeostasis via the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and the G protein–coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5). In a randomized crossover feeding study in healthy adults, a whole-grain, legume- and fruit/vegetable–rich diet increased circulating conjugated bile acids (taurine-conjugated lithocholic, cholic, and glycocholic acids), which are ligands for FXR/TGR5, whereas a refined-grain, high-sugar diet did not have the same effect. Higher levels of several bile acid species were positively associated with homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), suggesting that diet-induced shifts toward specific bile acid profiles may have opposing effects on insulin sensitivity depending on context and population subgroup <cite id="29458053">A whole-grain diet increased circulating FXR/TGR5 ligand bile acids and showed positive associations with HOMA-IR, whereas a refined-grain diet did not; associations varied by BMI and sex</cite>.

In NAFLD, bile acids are implicated in inflammation and metabolic regulation. Reviews highlight that microbial metabolites, including bile acids, contribute to adipose and intestinal homeostasis and to NASH pathogenesis, and that targeting bile acid signaling pathways is a plausible therapeutic avenue in NAFLD/NASH <cite id="40202676">Microbial metabolites including bile acids regulate adipose and intestinal homeostasis and contribute to NASH pathogenesis, suggesting therapeutic potential</cite>. In a clinical randomized controlled trial in NAFLD patients, a freshwater fish–based diet led to greater reductions in liver fat than alternating fish and red meat, accompanied by greater increases in Faecalibacterium, SCFAs, and unconjugated bile acids and greater decreases in Prevotella 9 and conjugated bile acids, indicating that diet-induced shifts in microbiota and bile acid profiles are linked to improvements in steatosis and liver enzymes <cite id="35973188">A freshwater fish–based diet improved liver steatosis and was associated with greater changes in SCFAs, unconjugated bile acids, and shifts in gut taxa compared with alternating fish and red meat</cite>.

# SCFAs and NAFLD severity

Mechanistically, SCFAs and their receptors (e.g., GPR43/41) intersect with AMPK signaling to regulate glucose and fatty acid metabolism in muscle and liver. In rodent muscle, lowering phosphagen content increased AMPK phosphorylation alongside sarcolemmal FAT/CD36 and GLUT4, increasing insulin-stimulated glucose transport and fatty acid oxidation, illustrating how energy stress and AMPK activation can enhance substrate uptake and metabolic flexibility relevant to insulin sensitivity and lipotoxicity in NAFLD <cite id="18650314">Reducing muscle phosphagen increased AMPK phosphorylation and sarcolemmal FAT/CD36 and GLUT4, enhancing insulin-stimulated glucose transport and fatty acid oxidation</cite>. Human intervention studies further support that raising SCFAs can improve insulin sensitivity and reduce liver fat, while diet-induced increases in beneficial SCFAs and shifts in gut taxa are associated with better NAFLD outcomes <cite id="25500202,30971437,35973188">SCFA-raising interventions improved insulin sensitivity and liver fat and were associated with favorable shifts in gut microbiota and metabolites</cite>.

# Integrated view and clinical implications

Collectively, evidence indicates that gut microbiome-derived metabolites modulate glucose homeostasis and NAFLD severity through multiple pathways: SCFAs enhance insulin sensitivity, reduce inflammation, and regulate appetite and energy expenditure; bile acids signal via FXR/TGR5 to influence glucose and lipid metabolism and can promote or mitigate inflammation depending on conjugation state and species composition; and diet-driven alterations in these metabolites and microbiota composition are linked to improvements in liver fat and metabolic markers in humans. Interventions that enrich beneficial SCFAs (e.g., through targeted delivery or fermentable fibers) and shift bile acid profiles toward FXR/TGR5 ligands associated with improved insulin sensitivity may be useful in adults with dysglycemia and NAFLD, although effects can vary by diet composition, BMI, and sex, and not all dietary changes in fermentable fiber translate directly to circulating SCFA changes or insulin sensitivity <cite id="28539646,25500202,30971437,29458053,35973188,29097438">SCFAs and bile acids modulate glucose homeostasis and NAFLD via receptor-mediated signaling and metabolic effects, with diet composition, conjugation state, and individual factors shaping outcomes</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- The magnitude and durability of SCFA-mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity and liver fat in humans over longer time frames require confirmation, as some short trials show acute effects but mixed chronic outcomes depending on fiber source and formulation <cite id="28539646,25500202,30971437">Acute SCFA effects are consistent, but chronic outcomes vary by intervention and comparator</cite>.
- Diet-induced bile acid shifts that favor certain conjugates may have tissue- and receptor-specific effects; clarifying which profiles reduce NAFLD risk versus conferring benefit remains an active area of research <cite id="29458053,40202676">Bile acid profiles vary by diet and receptor signaling, and their net effect on NAFLD is context-dependent</cite>.
- Personalized strategies (e.g., fiber type, fish vs. red meat, probiotics/prebiotics) may be necessary given heterogeneity by BMI and sex observed in bile acid–insulin resistance associations <cite id="29458053,35973188">Associations between bile acids, insulin resistance, and diet vary by BMI and sex, suggesting personalized approaches</cite>.
